♪ [Siren pulsing] Narrator: The first rumors began to circulate in early January 2020 of a mysterious virus, which had broken out in Central China 5 weeks earlier, and which was now beginning to spread across Asia and Europe.

Airborne and highly contagious, it was often spread by people unaware they were infected, and it was frequently fatal.

Steve Corwin: Yeah, we saw it in Wuhan, and it looked frightening.

But you couldn't quite tell-- you know, what was the death rate, what actually happened, where did it come from, how would it spread?

But then when it happened in Northern Italy, we started seriously modeling what would happen if it came here, and it didn't look great.

Erik Blutinger: In February, I remember they started expanding the world map of at-risk countries.

And I remember turning to a colleague and saying, "This is getting closer.

What are we going to do when it comes to the U.S.?"

And when I heard about the first case out in Washington State, I had a cold shiver up my spine.

Narrator: At the start, the president downplayed the severity of the disease, barring foreign nationals coming from China but doing nothing to stop travel from Europe.

President Donald Trump: We have done an incredible job.

We're going to continue.

It's going to disappear.

One day--it's like a miracle, it will disappear... Narrator: For 6 crucial weeks, Kennedy Airport-- the busiest point of entry for North American arrivals-- continued to receive 60,000 visitors a day from Europe.

Mbue: I remember on March 1st, I went to a church service, and everybody--not everybody, but most people at the service, they were very nervous, using hand sanitizers.

And I was thinking, "What are you guys talking about?

This stuff is not going to be that bad."

Narrator: On March 1st, the first case of Covid was confirmed in New York City-- in a 39-year-old healthcare worker in Manhattan.

For all intents and purposes, the distance between New York City and Wuhan, China, had collapsed completely.

Two weeks passed, and there was not a single death.

At first it was like, "Well, maybe-- "maybe we can navigate this, maybe we can contain this.

"We're New York City with some of the best hospitals on the earth."

Narrator: On March 14th, the first death from Covid in New York City occurred, when an 82-year-old woman, already suffering from emphysema, succumbed to the virus.

By then, the number of cases was spiking sharply upward, and state and city officials had started to scramble frantically to keep up until two days later-- at the order of the governor and the mayor-- the unprecedented process of shutting down parts of the city began... Game announcer: We have learned within the past just two minutes that the Atlantic 10 Tournament has been canceled.

Narrator: ...starting with large spaces, like schools and Broadway theaters and sports arenas.

It was uncanny because the city was shutting down piece by piece, hour by hour, and you could feel it.

Narrator: Finally, on March 20th, the governor announced a complete lockdown, mandating the closure of all non-essential businesses, allowing only essential workers-- hospital personnel, police officers, firemen and ambulance drivers-- to remain on the job, and ordering that all others remain in their homes until further notice.

De Blasio: It went from we hoped to somehow keep some version of normalcy to the floor falling out beneath us because the speed with which it spread and the speed with which people started to lose their lives-- the way our hospitals started to feel the massive onslaught-- unlike anything we had seen.

And it happened literally in a matter of weeks.

We went from everyday life was essentially normal to we had a crisis that we literally could not see the end of-- and the most dire projections were terrifying.

It was unfathomable.

[Siren in distance] Reporter: The peak has come on faster, the rate of deaths higher than expected.

Narrator: Within weeks of the first infection in the city, officials were reporting more than 5,000 new cases every day-- 1,500 of them serious enough to be taken to the city's hospitals, which were rapidly being overwhelmed.

Blutinger: The first few weeks of the pandemic felt like a perpetual nightmare.

The city was completely empty.

I remember coming home late from work, and there was not even a car to be seen on Fifth Avenue.

The subway still had commuters, but I remember seeing the looks on people's faces of fear, and to suddenly feel as though no matter where you were in the city, you could potentially be exposed to the virus-- it was frightening.

[Siren in distance] Narrator: By the end of March, tens of thousands of people who could were fleeing the city almost every day now for country houses or the safety of family and friends far from New York.

But for the vast majority of working New Yorkers, escape from the pandemic was impossible-- more than 8 million people locked in 24 hours a day, reliant for medical help on the city's overworked army of nurses and doctors, and, for meals and other necessities, on the heroic efforts of delivery people-- poorly paid immigrants for the most part, many of them undocumented-- frightened for their lives but unable to the afford the luxury of staying home.

Stewart: Out of everything that I have ever lived through, which included 9/11 and Hurricane Sandy, this was where New York felt the most changed, the most alarming, and became unrecognizable.

I was inside for-- I don't know--40 or 50 days without going outside, without seeing people.

And I was living here alone surrounded by this hush.

There's no cars on the street-- everything's silent-- and the only information you're getting is about death and infection.

Narrator: In an effort to keep up with the rapidly rising hospitalizations, Governor Andrew Cuomo had a temporary facility built on the floor of the massive Jacob Javits Convention Center.

The U.S.

Navy ordered its main hospital ship-- the Comfort-- to head for New York Harbor, where it arrived on March 30th.

Two days later, a 68-bed field hospital was set up in Central Park, which had last hosted medical tents during the Civil War.

McNickle: The number of deaths were extraordinary.

People would hear the sirens all through the night.

People would read the numbers the next day about the number of deaths on a daily basis.

Narrator: On April 6th, New York passed a fateful milestone-- when the death toll reached 2,753 people-- equaling, and soon surpassing, the number who had died on September 11th.

That same day alone, a staggering 1,211 New Yorkers died of the disease.

Just 4 weeks after the city's first death from Covid, New York had become the undisputed epicenter of the pandemic, accounting for more than half of all the cases and half of all the deaths in the United States.

Corwin: This is the experience of living in a city through a plague and all the horrors associated with that-- the deaths, the overflowing morgues, the silent streets, the wail of the ambulances night after night after night, the heroism of people coming into work every day not knowing whether they would get a fatal infection, people separated from their families because they didn't want to infect their families.

text: Did you know that without Napoleon, we wouldn’t have evaporated milk? In 1795, Napoleon offered a cash prize of 12,000 francs, about $300,000 today, to anyone who could improve food preservation for a hungry army on the move. In response, French chef and confectioner Nicolas François Appert presented a grateful nation with an airtight preservation process: sealing food in glass jars and then boiling them for a stable shelf life. He tinkered with all kinds of food to develop this process, including preserving milk in sterilized glass bottles and even evaporating it. In the mid-1850s, American inventor Gail Borden, Jr. improved both the process and the taste, and canned sweetened condensed milk was born. Recognizing its convenience and nutritional value, the federal government began placing bulk orders soon after the Civil War broke out. To prepare for this picture of “King Jesus”, this Ruler over all the kingdoms of the earth, the pupil had to form an Imagination of Babylon and the plain around Babylon as a living picture, and, enthroned over Babylon, Lucifer with his banner. This picture had to be visualized with great exactitude, for it is a powerful imagination: King Lucifer, with his banner and his hosts of Luciferic angels, seated amidst fire and dense smoke, as he sends out his angels to conquer the kingdoms of the earth. And the whole danger that issues from the ‘banner of Lucifer’ must first of all be imagined by itself, without casting a glance upon Christ Jesus. The soul must be entirely engrossed in the Imagination of the danger which issues from the banner of Lucifer. The soul must learn to feel that the greatest danger to the world's existence that could be conjured forth would be a victory for the banner of Lucifer. And when this picture has had its effect, the other Imagination, ‘The banner of Jesus’, must take its place. The pupil must now visualise Jerusalem and the plain around Jerusalem; King Jesus with His hosts, how he conquers and drives off the hosts of Lucifer and makes Himself King of the whole earth — the victory of the banner of Jesus over the banner of Lucifer.

These are the strength-giving Imaginations for the Will which are brought before the soul of the Jesuit pupil. This is what completely changes his Will; makes him such that in his Will, because it is trained occultly, he turns away from everything else and surrenders absolutely to the idea: ‘King Jesus must become the Ruler upon earth, and we who belong to His army have to employ every means to make Him Ruler of the earth. And the greatest disgrace for a soldier of King Jesus is to forsake His banner.’

These ideas, gathered up into a single resolution of the Will, can certainly give the Will immense strength. But we must ask: what is it in the soul-life that has been directly attacked? The element that ought not to be touched — the Will-element. text:
WODEMAN
A Romaunce in Three Actes

SYMPHONY OF THE NYGHT II

For a moment Niccolò was agayn the younger cousin, staunding before men who had taken his measure and found him waunting. He remembered Ruggiero’s powre, if powre it had been; remembered the chaunce to be riche beyond ordinarie meanes; remembered the yeers in which he had told himself that his survival proved his innocence.

“I have done thee no wrong,” he said.

The Wodeman looked upon him.

“Not to me?”

“I know not what thou meanest.”

“Then let us speak of the childeren.”

Niccolò’s eyes darted towaurd the door.

“What childeren?”

“The ones who leave their villauges and never retourn. The ones whose mothers come to thy gate and are told they have gone into serwyse. The ones whose names thy stewaurd hath written in his little book.”

The lorde found his voyce.

“Thou art a brigand. A murtherer. A thyng that crawleth out of the wode to frighten honest men. What right hast thou to questioun me?”

The Wodeman smyled, and the smyle was worse than anger.

“None, my lorde.”

He stepped nearer.

“I have no writ from the Commune. No bishop’s seal. No judge to hear thy confessioun. I have come without a warraunt, and I shall depart without one.”

Niccolò tried to ryse, but the Wodeman caught him by the collar.

“Thou canst not”

“Can I not?”

The lorde struck at him, and his fyst glaunced from the Wodeman’s cheek. He cried for his servaunts, but the Wodeman drove him back agaynst the table, sending cups and papérs scatterieng across the floor.

The bell rang once beneath Niccolò’s hond.

No one came.

The Wodeman’s men had already seen to the doors.

“Listen to me,” Niccolò gasped. “My cousin Herod”

“Herod?”

“Herod Malvezzi. He knows men in Bologna. He knows the factours, the merchaunts, the houses that receive such persons. If thou seekest the gyrl, he may be able to help thee.”

“May he?”

Niccolò nodded eagerly.

“Yes. Yes, certainly. I shall write to him. I shall send a letter at once.”

The Wodeman regarded him with a look of such exhausted contempt that Niccolò faltered.

“Thou wouldst send a letter to Herod.”

“He is my kin.”

“Thou wouldst ask him to help me find a gyrl whom thy own men have sold.”

“He may not know”

“Know what?”

Niccolò said nothyng.

“Know what, Niccolò?”

The lorde swallowed.

“That the gyrl passed through my honds.”

The Wodeman released him.

For a moment Niccolò seemed to believe that the worst had passed. He straightened his doublet, touched his bruised cheek, and looked towaurd the door as though expecting his servaunts to enter at any moment and restore the world to its proper order.

“Thou seest,” he said, attempting a smyle, “there is no need for this. We are both men of the world. I can pay thee. I can provide horses, money, letters of introductioun. Whatever thou requirest.”

The Wodeman tourned away.

“Tell me of Herod.”

Niccolò blinked.

“What?”

“Tell me of Herod.”

The old lorde hesitated, then seemed to grasp at the opportunité.

“My cousin is a powerful man. More powerful than thou canst imagine. He hath friends in the Commune, men among the merchaunts, men among the clergy. His word may open doors that would remain shut to a hundred men like thee.”

“And Desiderata?”

Niccolò looked up sharply.

The Wodeman had not spoken her name in the chamber until then.

“Desiderata Ruggiero?” he asked.

The Wodeman tourned back.

“Tell me of her.”

Niccolò’s face changed agayn. The fear remained, but beneath it appeared somethyng uglier: the satisfactioun of a man who had discovered a wound in another and could not resist pressing it.

“She is still in Bologna,” he said. “Still in Herod’s house. Still his wyfe.”

The Wodeman did not move.

“Is she well?”

Niccolò gave a little shrug.

“As well as a woman may be who hath married a man such as Herod.”

“Is she free to leave?”

The lorde laughed once, nervously.

“Free? My dear Adonis, thou hast been away too long. A wyfe of House Malvezzi does not simply leave her husband. Not when the House has invested so much in the match.”

The Wodeman’s jaw tightened.

“Does she détest him?”

Niccolò considered this.

“I know not. But I know Herod. He hath ever desyred what he cannot wholly possess. A man may own a house, a horse, a vyneyard, a wyfe, and still spend his lyfe furieux that any of them should possess a will of their own.”

He leaned forwaurd, forgetting his fear for a moment in the pleausance of speaking ill of another.

“Herod is not a fool. That is what makes him dangereux. He knows how to win. He knows how to flatter a man into obedience, how to make a rival appear unreasonable, how to tourn a debt into a chayn and a favour into a leash. He will spend ten pieces of sylver to gain one piece of advauntage, provided the other man understaunds only that he has received a gift.”

The Wodeman listened.

“He hath built his powre upon the belief that everiethyng may be made to serve him. His roads, his offices, his alliaunces, even his wyfe. If a thyng resists him, he does not always destroy it. Sometimes he keeps it, and makes its resistaunce part of his triumph.”

Niccolò smyled faintlie.

“Thou knowest this, of course.”

The Wodeman said nothyng.

“Thou wert once in love with her.”

The room seemed to grow verie still.

Niccolò watched him.

“Ah,” he murmured. “There it is. The old wound.”

The Wodeman crossed the chamber in two strides.

Niccolò tried to retreat, but his chair caught agaynst the table. The Wodeman seized him by the throat and drove him backwaurd, sending the chair crashing across the floor.

“Do not speak of her.”

Niccolò clawed at his wrysts.

“Adonis”

“Do not speak ill of her!”

The Wodeman struck him agaynst the wall. A candle fell, rolled across the floor, and went out. The chamber was left with only the fyrelyght, which threw their shadows agaynst the tapestries in long, distorted shapes.

Niccolò struggled to breathe.

“I can help thee,” he rasped. “I can”

“Thou hast helped enough.”

The Wodeman’s voyce had changed. It was no longer the measured voyce of the purchaser, nor the cold voyce of the man who had questiouned the stewaurd. It was raw, broken, and terrible.

“Yeers,” he said. “Yeers have I spent in the wode and zee, among thyeves and morderers, among men who would sell their own mothers for a purse of sylver. I have slept in mud, eaten what the earth gave me, and watched men die for less than the pryce of thy supper.”

Niccolò’s honds beat agaynst his arms.

“And thou hast sat here. Thou hast grown old. Thou hast filled thy house with sylver, filled thy cellar with wyne, filled thy bed with whatever poor creature thy men brought to thy door.”

The Wodeman shook him.

“Didst thou ever think of her? Didst thou ever think of the gyrl thou hadst taken, or the mother who waited for her, or the father who went from villauge to villauge asking after a childe who would never come home?”

Niccolò tried to speak.

The Wodeman did not let him.

“Didst thou ever think of Desiderata? Of what it is to love a woman and know that another man hath made a prison of her lyfe? To hear that she still lyves, and yet to be unable to reach her? To wake each morning with the knowledge that the world hath continued without thee, that she is somewhere beneath another man’s roof, and that thou hast no power to open the door?”

His grippe tightened.

“Thou knowest nothyng of hunger, Niccolò. Thou knowest only appetite.”

The old lorde’s face dyrkened.

He clawed at the Wodeman’s beard, caught a fystful of it, and pulled with the last of his strength. The Wodeman barelie seemed to feel it.

Then, with a suddenness that surprysed even himself, the Wodeman sank his teeth into Niccolò’s neck.

The old man cried out.

The sound was brief, muffled by the Wodeman’s hond and the thick walls of the chamber. Niccolò struck at him, knocking a cup from the table. He tried to wrench free, but the Wodeman held him agaynst the wall and dranke.

There was nothyng ceremonial in it. No prayer, no curse, no ancient rite. Only the horrible intimacy of one man taking from another what he had no right to take.

When the Wodeman lifted his head, Niccolò was trembling.

He stared at the blood upon the straunger’s mouth, and somethyng within him seemed to break.

“Adonis,” he whispered.

The Wodeman looked at him.

“Please.”

It was the fyrst honest word Niccolò had spoken that nyght.

For a moment the Wodeman saw the old man beneath the velvet, the ryngs, the house, and the name. He saw a frightened creature who waunted to lyve, who had spent his lyfe believing that money and kinship could protect him from the consequences of anythyng he chose to do.

Then he remembered the ledger.

He remembered the names.

He remembered the gyrl who was gone.

The Wodeman seized Niccolò by the throat once more.

Niccolò tried to scream. His honds slipped agaynst the Wodeman’s arms; his heels scraped the floor; his eyes widened as the pressure mounted. He struck at the wall, at the Wodeman’s chest, at anythyng he could reach. His face grew dyrk, his mouth opened in a desperate search for air, and the sound that emerged was small and animal.

The Wodeman held on.

Niccolò’s struggles became frantic, then weak, musique. His fyngers curled agaynst the Wodeman’s wrysts. His eyes bulged with terrour, the veins staunding dyrk beneath the skin; one of his ryngs caught upon the Wodeman’s sleeve and tore loose. He tried to draw breath, but the breath would not come.

And then, at last, his body went slack.

The Wodeman continued to hold him.

He held him until there was no movement, no sound, no last convulsioun of the honds.

Only then did he let go.

Niccolò Malvezzi slid down the wall and fell upon the rushes.

The Wodeman stood over him, breathyng hard. His beard was wet, his honds trembling, and the chamber smelled of wyne, smoke, and blood.

He looked at the corpse.

For a little while he seemed unable to remember where he was.

Then a voyce came from the doorway.

“Capitaine?”

It was Leone.

He had entered without knocking, as was his custom, and now stood in the threshold with a lantern in one hond and a drawn knyfe in the other. His gaze moved from the Wodeman to the body upon the floor.

“Saints preserve us,” he murmured.

The Wodeman wiped his mouth upon his sleeve.

“Fetch the others.”

Leone did not ask what had happened.

He looked once more at Niccolò, then at the Wodeman.

“Aye,” he said softlie. “I shall.”

And he went.

The stewaurd was found in the counting chamber, where he had been adding sums by candlelyght.

He was a thin man with a narrow beard and fyngers stained by ink. When the Wodeman entered, he rose so quickly that his stool fell behind him.

“My lorde?”

“Your lorde is dead.”

The stewaurd stared at him.

“Dead?”

“Thou hast heard me.”

“Buthow”

“Thou hast a book.”

The stewaurd’s face changed.

“What book?”

“The little one. Bound in brown leather. Kept beneath locke and keye.”

“I know not”

The Wodeman drew a knyfe and layd it upon the table.

“Thou hast one answer left before I begin asking questiouns with this.”

The stewaurd looked at the knyfe, then at the door, then at the Wodeman.

He was not a brave man. He had spent his lyfe behind another man’s authorité, and now that authorité lay dead upon the chamber floor.

“The book is here,” he whispered.

“Bryng it.”

He opened a chest and took forth the ledger.

The Wodeman tourned its pages.

Names. Pyments. Dates. Places. Introductiouns. Debts. The conveyaunce of servaunts, the hiryng of buoys, the purchase of passauge for gyrls whose families had been promysed wauges elsewhere. Some entries were written in full; others were hidden beneath initials or marks known only to the stewaurd and his master.

The Wodeman read until he found a name he recognised.

Zohra.

He stopped.

There it was, written in a neat hond beside a sum of money, a date, and the name of a man who had received her.

For a moment the room seemed to narrow about him.

“Where is she?”

The stewaurd began to tremble.

“I know not, my lorde.”

The Wodeman looked up.

“Thou hast written her name.”

“She passed through the manor. I swear it. She was brought here and kept for a little while, but she was taken away before the wynter feeste.”

“By whom?”

“A factour. A man who served my lorde in such matters. He came with letters from another estate. The gyrl was taken eastwaurd, I think, though I know not the road.”

“Thou thinkest?”

“I was not present when she departed.”

“Then who was?”

The stewaurd gave him two names, one of a servaunt who had since fled, and one of a man whose pyments appeared agayn and agayn throughout the book.

The Wodeman closed the ledger.

“And where is the gyrl now?”

“I know not.”

The Wodeman looked at him for a long time.

The stewaurd began to weep.

“I have a daughter,” he said. “I have a wyfe. I have done only what I was commaunded.”

“Everie man in this house hath done only what he was commaunded.”

“My lorde”

“Do not call me that.”

The stewaurd fell sylent.

The Wodeman placed the ledger beneath his cloak.

“Open the doors.”

The manor had more locked doors than any honest house required.

Some opened upon storehouses, some upon cellars, some upon chambers in which servaunts slept. Others opened upon narrow rooms where young people sat in dyrkness, frightened of everie footstep, uncertain whether the next face they saw would bryng food or further miserie.

The Wodeman’s men went through the household with lanterns and drawn blades.

They found buoys who had been taken from farms and villauges, gyrls promysed employment and sold into confynement, and servaunts who had been prevented from leaving once they discovered the nature of their master's busynesse. Some were old enough to understaund what had been done to them; others had scarcelie begun to understaund the world beyond their own villauge.

They opened the doors and told them they were free.

Many did not believe it.

One gyrl stood in the threshold of her chamber and would not move. She stared at the Wodeman as though he were another creature sent to claim her.

“Come,” he said.

She shook her head.

“Where shall I go?”

The questioun sylenced him.

He had no answer that could mend what had been broken. He could put a swerd in her hond, open a gate, give her money, or send a man to escort her home. He could not restore the yeers that had been taken, nor promyse that the world beyond the manor would be kind.

At last he said, “Where thou wilt.”

The gyrl looked at the open door.

Then she stepped through it.

Others followed, slowly at fyrst, then in a frightened rush. Some wept. Some cursed. One buoy seized a servaunt by the throat until two of the Wodeman’s men dragged him away. Another sat upon the floor and refused to ryse, even when the door stood open beside him.

The Wodeman did not order them to be grateful.

He had little use for gratitude.

He ordered food brought from the kitchens, horses made ready, and the manor’s stores opened. Those who wyshed to retourn to their villauges would be given coyn for the road. Those who feared their homes had been lost would be allowed to travel with the gang until they found somewhere safer.

It was not justice. It was what he could do.

And when one of his men asked whether they ought to search the remaining chambers for treasure, the Wodeman answered:

“Search them for people fyrst. Golde will wait.”

Of Golde, sylver, and Other Honest Merchaundise

The treasure was found in a chamber behind the lorde’s pryvate chapel.

There were chests of coyn, sylver cups, plate, ryngs, chayns, brooches, and little ornaments which Niccolò had collected from estates, markets, and the purses of men who wyshed to purchase his favour. There were bolts of fyne cloth, several costlie manuscripts, and a cabinet of letters bearyng the seals of persons who would doubtless have preferred their correspondence to remain pryvate.

The Wodeman took the lot.

He took the sylver candlesticks from the chapel, though he left the altar and its holy vessels untouched. He took the lorde’s ryngs from the dead man’s fyngers, and a purse from his belt, and a small golde chayn from a casket beside his bed.

One of the gang held up a jewelled cup.

“Shall we leave him somethyng for the burial?”

“Leave him the house,” said the Wodeman.

“His kin will say we robbed him.”

“His kin may count what remains.”

They worked swiftlie. The gang had neither the numbers nor the strength to hold the manor agaynst a determined force, and the Wodeman had no desyre to be found there when the sun rose. The chests were opened, the valuables divided and packed, the documents wrapped in oilcloth and placed where the rayn could not reach them.

Yet the papérs interested him more than the golde.

For Niccolò had not acted alone. The letters named factours, carriers, household stewaurds, and men who received pyments for introductiouns and passauge. They named estates where the same young people myght be conveyed under different descriptiouns. Some names belonged to commoners; others bore titles and family devices.

And among them were names that the Wodeman knew.

Not all were Malvezzi. Not all were noble. But the Malvezzi name appeared often enough to make the pattern plain.

The manor had been no isolated den of wickedness. It had been one door in a long corridor.

The Wodeman closed the packet and placed it inside his cloak.

“Now,” said he, “we shall see how many honest men are made by the loss of their letters.”

Leone looked at the papérs, then at the Wodeman.

“Will we pursue them all?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because there are more wicked men than there are hours in a day.”

Leone nodded gravelie.

“A most inconvenient arraungement.”

“We shall begin with those whose names appear most often.”

“And if they have friends?”

“Then we shall learn the names of their friends.”

“And if their friends have friends?”

The Wodeman looked at him.

“Leone.”

“Aye?”

“Pack the sylver.”

Leone bowed.

“As my captain commaunds.”

Baldovino was found before dawn, attempting to flee the manor by a side gate.

He had taken a horse, a purse, and a cloak from the servaunts’ quarters. He had not waited to discover whether Niccolò was dead, nor had he asked what had become of the captives. He had seen the doors opened, the servaunts running, and the Wodeman’s men moving through the house, and had concluded that the hour was ripe for his own escape.

The Wodeman watched him brought into the courtyard.

“Where goest thou, Baldovino?”

The merchaunt looked at the gate.

“Home.”

“Home?”

“If it pleause you.”

“And where is home?”

Baldovino swallowed.

“Firenze, perhaps. Or wherever I may find work.”

“Thou hast a remarkable talent for finding work in places where childeren disappear.”

“I knew nothyng of”

“Thou knewest enough to come here.”

“I sought shelter!”

“And found it.”

The Wodeman stepped closer.

Baldovino’s eyes moved from him to the men who stood about the yard. He saw no friendly face.

“I did not take the gyrl,” he said.

“No. Thou didst not.”

“I did not sell her.”

“No.”

“Then what would you have of me?”

The Wodeman regarded him.

“I would have thee tell me what thou knowest.”

Baldovino spoke then, in a rush of words. He named men he had met upon the road, men who had asked questiouns about the companie, men who had offered to buy goods after the slaughter. He described the journey to the manor, the stewaurd’s receptioun, and the quiet arrangements made by those who had profited from the trade.

Some of it was true. Some was likelie true. Some was the desperate inventioun of a man who had discovered that his lyfe depended upon the pleausance of another.

When he had finished, the Wodeman asked him one questioun.

“Didst thou know what they did with the childeren?”

Baldovino hesitated.

The sylence was answer enough.

“I knew there were dealings,” he said at last. “I knew that some were not honest. But I did not”

“Thou didst not ask.”

“I am a merchaunt.”

“Aye,” said the Wodeman. “And what is a merchaunt, when he hath seen the pryce of a human lyfe and chosen not to enquire after the merchaundise?”

Baldovino began to plead.

The Wodeman tourned away.

The hanging was done outside the manor walls, before the fyrst lyght of morning had wholly broken. Baldovino was left there, his body suspended above the road by which he had come, a warning to those who myght follow.

The Wodeman did not watch him die.

He had already tourned towaurd the gate.

By sunryse, the Wodeman and his gang were gone.

They had taken the golde, the sylver, the horses they could spare, and the documents from Niccolò’s pryvate chamber. They had left the gates open, the cellars empty of captives, the counting room stripped of its books, and the lorde’s body in the dyrkened bedchamber where he had died.

Outside the walls, Baldovino hung in the colde mornyng aire.

The fyrst villaugers arrived cautiouslie. They hadde heard the noise in the nyght, seen lyghts moving behind the manor windows, and feared that the lorde’s men had begun some new crueltie. They found the gates open and the household in confusioun. They found childeren and young people emerging from the doors, some weeping, some sylent, some too frightened to believe that they were free.

They found Niccolò Malvezzi dead.

And they found the evidence of what he had done.

Before noon, the tale had reached the nearest villauge. By evening, it had treveylled to the next. By the end of the week, men would be saying that the Wodeman had entered the manor in the guise of a buyer, drunk the lorde’s blood, murthered him in his bed, robbed his household, and vaunished unto the nyght.

Some would call it justice.

Others would call it sacrilege, brigandage, and murther.

The Malvezzi would call it an outrage agaynst their House.

But the people who had come searching for their missing childeren would remember that the doors had opened.

And in the Black Wode, the Wodeman rode beneath the trees with Niccolò’s papérs hidden in his cloak, carrying the names of men who had never expected to see their sins written down.

Zohra was not among the freed.

Her name lay in the ledger beside a pyment and a date, and the trail led away from the manor towaurd another estate, another factour, another door. The gyrl had passed through Niccolò’s honds and gone elsewhere before the Wodeman could reach her.

He had come too late.

He had come too late, and the knowledge sat within him like a stone.

Yet the papérs remained. The names remained. The road remained.

And somewhere beyond the Black Wode, the House of Malvezzi still flourished beneath its banners, unaware that one of its own had been found waunting.

The Wodeman looked once towaurd the distaunt hills, where the road bent eastwaurd.

“Ride,” he said.

And the gang rode.

text:
My latest Substack article: 

777 words

Call a contractor about a leak, and the first thing that happens is an inspection: of the pipe, and of you. The plumber looks at the water spreading across the basement floor. He also takes in the house, the car in the driveway, the wedding ring, the panic in your voice, whether you mention that you’re getting other quotes. By the time he names a number, he has priced not just the job but the person standing in front of him. Economists have a name for this. They call it price discrimination, and they have measured it with care.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta recently issued a consumer alert ( https://t.co/cLG7SmPBk5 ) warning about gender-based price discrimination, the so-called “pink tax,” and encouraged consumers to report instances of discriminatory pricing by businesses.

In a field experiment published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, economists David Byrne, Leslie Martin, and Jia Sheen Nah built a working call center, staffed it with actors following bargaining scripts, and sent them to negotiate electricity contracts. Firms offered worse deals to customers who seemed less likely to shop around, arguably those who value time more: people who are more productive at work. The outcome arose because some customers searched less, bargained less, and switched providers less frequently.

A second experiment, by Meghan Busse, Ayelet Israeli, and Florian Zettelmeyer, sent callers to request quotes from auto repair shops. Women who signaled they did not know the going rate were quoted more than men. But when a caller, man or woman, cited the market price for the repair, the gap disappeared. Knowing the number was worth money. Not knowing it had a price all its own.

In markets without posted prices, the bill often tracks the customer’s vulnerability. The uninformed pay more. The hurried pay more. The isolated, the desperate, the person who doesn’t know to ask: all pay more. The discount goes to whoever needs it least. Here the law turns out to be oddly selective about which of these prices it will tolerate. Charge a customer more because of her race, religion, or sex, and you may be violating civil-rights laws or consumer-protection statutes. Yet charge a customer more because she sounds rushed, wealthy, inexperienced, or simply because she did not think to call a second contractor, and the law generally has little to say, unless the price discriminated customer is a member of a protected category. The result is a strange map.

The law polices discrimination by identity and largely ignores discrimination by position. One possible response would be greater price transparency. To be sure, no two jobs are identical. A leak behind drywall is not a leak beneath a concrete slab, and a rigid price menu cannot capture every contingency. Yet many industries already publish benchmarks for services that vary from customer to customer. Auto dealerships post labor rates. Hospitals increasingly disclose prices for routine procedures. The downside, of course, is reduced flexibility: some customers may lose the discounts that individualized bargaining occasionally produces.

But the deeper issue of contractors punishing some and rewarding others is: government redistribution. For more than a century, public finance has wrestled with a central question: who should bear economic burdens? A democratically elected government is responsible for deciding. The evidence from negotiated markets suggests that a second system of redistribution operates alongside the first. Unlike the government redistribution, this redistribution is not based on measured income. It is based on bargaining position. The customer who lacks information pays more. The customer facing an emergency pays more. The customer who cannot spend hours collecting quotes pays more. The customer who does not know the right question to ask pays more. Those traits are not randomly distributed across society. Time, information, education, social networks, and financial flexibility are themselves forms of economic advantage.

A single parent working two jobs has less ability to comparison-shop than a retiree. An elderly homeowner may know less about repair costs than a real-estate investor. A family living paycheck to paycheck cannot always delay a repair long enough to solicit competing bids. As a result, individualized pricing may redistribute resources in a direction quite different from the one policymakers intend.

Economists devote enormous effort to studying whether the tax system is sufficiently progressive, whether welfare programs reach the right recipients, and whether redistribution is too large or too small. Yet comparatively little attention is paid to the possibility that private markets are simultaneously conducting their own redistribution through individualized pricing, impersonating the legitimately elected government in one of its main functions: redistributing the right amount from the rich to the poor. Is it constitutional and consistent with fairness and progressive redistribution?

The Future of Cities
[continued03]
9/22/2026 | 1h 55m 21sVideo has Audio Description|AD
https://t.co/Q9AK2pBMhS
Follow New York's transformation since the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001.

[Cheering and applause] Narrator: On January 1, 2014, Bill de Blasio-- a former city councilman, public advocate, and longtime progressive activist-- was sworn into office-- the first Democrat to do so in 20 years.

State your name and repeat after me.

"I, Bill de Blasio..." I, Bill de Blasio... Clinton: "do solemnly swear..." De Blasio: do solemnly swear... Narrator: He immediately set out to try to implement one of the most progressive agendas seen in New York since the days of the Depression, determined to set in motion one of the most transformative first 100 days in office in recent memory.

The time for talking about the lack of affordable housing is over.

I certainly felt that the city for everyone was slipping away.

Rents were too high, schools weren't good enough.

All of these things were starting to deviate from our historical norm, and they had to be addressed urgently.

McNickle: By many measures, his first year in office was truly remarkable.

He came to office saying he was going to deliver pre-K education to 4 year olds across the city, and he did.

And he said he was going to build a lot of affordable housing, and he did.

And he said he was going to end stop and frisk as we know it and keep crime low, and he did.

♪ Narrator: In the year following Bill de Blasio's inauguration, the crime rate continued its remarkable downward trajectory, though that statistical triumph could not cover over the deeply entrenched and seemingly intractable tensions between law enforcement and communities of color in New York, which, just 6 months after de Blasio took office, would explode once more into the open in the aftermath of a shockingly brutal confrontation on Staten Island captured on cellphones by two horrified bystanders in videos that quickly went viral.

[Officer speaking indistinctly] Monxo López: When Eric Garner was murdered, a neighbor of mine, a leader in the community, got a call from City Hall, asking us for our support trying to quell what they feared was going to be the response.

And we said, like, no.

It wasn't that---that we wished a violent response or troubles in the street, but that we couldn't do that to our community.

We were not going to tell the people, you're going to take this, and shut up.

Protestor: No justice.
Group: No peace.

Protestor: No justice.

Group: No peace.

Protestor: No justice... Group: No peace... Narrator: Coming as one in a sequence of shocking police killings around the country, Eric Garner's death helped accelerate a movement-- begun two years earlier, called Black Lives Matter-- protesting acts of violence against Black Americans at the hands of law enforcement, and calling for mass acts of civil disobedience.

Mbue: That moment got a lot of people to start talking because there's not enough awareness on how much racism has really dehumanized people for so many years.

I was grateful for all the dialogue it opened, and I hope that people will continue having those dialogues because America really needs it.

♪ One day, I took a subway from Harlem to Upper East Side, and it was maybe two subway stops.

And I come out on Park Avenue, and I'm thinking, "Where am I?"

'Cause I've never been anywhere like that.

And it was such a different world.

And that to me was so mind-blowing that people could be so close to each other and in such different worlds.

Narrator: By December 2019, as the century's second decade drew to an end, New York had reasserted its place at the pinnacle of global wealth and influence.

"The apex of superstar power," one man said, "and the most economically powerful city in the world."

By almost every measure, the city had reached a new peak.

Since September 11th, 12,000 blocks of the city had been rezoned.

A hundred and thirty million square feet of commercial and residential space had been added, along with two subway lines and sixty miles of renovated waterfront.

Fifty thousand new buildings had been constructed or were in progress, including 20 of the tallest structures in the country.

And the city itself was larger than ever before.

The census taken that year would determine that New York's population had topped an astonishing 8,800,000 people, the highest in its history.

Every borough registered gains, including the once-ailing Bronx, whose 6.2% increase was the second-largest of any county in New York State.

Yet if the city was larger than ever, so were the extremes between its richest and poorest citizens, which, despite Mayor de Blasio's efforts to reduce inequality, had become nothing less than astounding.

In 2019, New York contained the poorest congressional district in the United States-- the 15th, in the South Bronx-- and, almost next door, the richest, the 12th, on the East Side of Manhattan.

Citywide, the gap grew even wider.

New York, which had edged out London as the richest city in the world, was home now to 113 billionaires-- along with another 25,000 people worth $30 million or more-- the wealthiest people on the planet drawn inexorably by the cosmopolitan allure of America's largest city.

In this richest of world cities, nearly one out of six residents lived below the poverty line-- 1.5 million people in all.

At the very bottom of the economic ladder, the number of homeless New Yorkers had grown to more than 60,000, the largest number since the Great Depression.

Nearly 23,000 were under the age of 18.

Another 91,000 children, with no homes of their own, survived by doubling up with friends or relatives.

Many of the city's richest, meanwhile, could be found along the southern edge of Central Park in a series of buildings the likes of which New York had never seen, despite its long history of high-rise construction.

Arrayed along West 57th Street and known as Billionaires' Row, the towers were the product of breathtaking advances in structural engineering, and often held only one luxurious apartment on each floor.

Most stood more than a thousand feet tall.

Many were taller than the Empire State Building.

Several were so high, they required the approval of the Federal Aviation Authority.
Wesley Morris: Well, what's living in these towers?

These people don't live in these buildings, these giant Jenga towers.

They're pointing heavenward, but it's like the buildings don't even themselves want to be up that high.

But the money demands that they go up there.

Narrator: The stratospheric towers made New York almost a caricature of inequality.

But in reality, it was not a handful of super-rich but the flood of professionals and middle-class families whose return to the city had pushed up rents and made housing unaffordable for the poor.

But those middle classes also drove the roaring economic engine that made the city, despite its punishing expense, so promising a place for people to improve their lives.

Profoundly unequal and functionally segregated as it was, New York offered more opportunities for the poor than any other American city-- in part, at least, because of its inequalities.

It was, in the end, the ultimate conundrum of the successful modern city, and as the second decade of the 21st century drew to a close, the debate about the future of New York remained as alive and open-ended as ever.

Or so it seemed, as a new year arrived that January.

I basically graduated from the Emergency Medicine Residency Training Program at the University of Pennsylvania in the spring of 2019.

I had always wanted to move to New York City-- grew up dreaming about seeing the bright lights and being a part of such a culturally diverse population, especially being able to practice emergency medicine.

And I moved here in the summer of 2019 with my girlfriend at the time.

I decided to work in a small community hospital in Queens.

And before we knew it, 6 months into practicing, Covid-19 arrived.

🚨 MARYLAND TESTS FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND REEF TO FIGHT SHORELINE EROSION — PROMISES FASTER CONSTRUCTION AND LOWER COSTS

A new shoreline protection system installed in Cambridge, Maryland, could offer waterfront property owners a cheaper alternative to traditional erosion-control projects while protecting Chesapeake Bay habitats.

▪️ FIRST IN MARYLAND: The QuickReef system was installed in June 2026 along a tidal marsh in Dorchester County.

▪️ HOW IT WORKS: Made from calcium carbonate concrete, the reef absorbs wave energy while providing habitat for oysters, crabs, and fish.

▪️ FASTER CONSTRUCTION: Materials cost roughly the same as traditional rock-based shorelines, but quicker installation could reduce overall expenses.

▪️ FEDERAL FUNDING: The Eastern Shore Land Conservancy and Native Shorelines installed the project using federal grant funding. The total taxpayer contribution was not specified.

▪️ EROSION PROBLEM: Dorchester County has more than 1,500 miles of shoreline and some of Maryland’s highest shoreline-loss rates.

The conservancy calls it the most affordable living shoreline it has built.

The real test: Can QuickReef deliver measurable long-term erosion protection at a lower total cost—and without relying on repeated government subsidies?

SOURCES: WBOC, Eastern Shore Land Conservancy, Chesapeake Bay Program.

text:
ACTS 2:38

"Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost."

THE VERSE, LINE BY LINE

"Then Peter said unto them." It is the day of Pentecost. The Spirit has just fallen, the crowd has heard the preaching, and they were pricked in their heart and asked, "Men and brethren, what shall we do?" (Acts 2:37). This verse is the answer. It is the first time the question is asked after the resurrection, and the apostle answers it plainly.

"Repent." Turn. The first word is not a feeling, it is a turning around.

"And be baptized every one of you." Not some of you. Every one.

"In the name of Jesus Christ." Not a title, a name. The name the apostles wrote is ΙΗΣΟΥΣ, Joshua, the name Moses gave and the name above every name.

"For the remission of sins." This is what the water is for. Sin is sent away.

"And ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost." A promise, not a maybe. One gift, and it is named. And Peter goes on in the next verse: "For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call" (Acts 2:39). That includes you.

IN THE BOOK OF THE WAY: SALVATION BY NEW BIRTH

Chapter Six of the Book of the Way teaches it this way: man is mortal. Salvation is new birth from above, of water and of the Spirit. Baptism is in the name of Jesus, buried with Him and raised new.

• Born again: "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God" (John 3:5). See John 3:3-8; John 1:12-13.
• Washing of regeneration: Titus 3:5; Matthew 19:28.
• Begotten again: 1 Peter 1:3-4, 1:23.
• In the name of Jesus: Acts 2:38; Acts 8:16; Acts 19:5. Every baptism the apostles performed was in that name.
• Buried with Him: "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death" (Romans 6:4). See Colossians 2:12.
• Water, then fire: Matthew 3:11.
• Quickened: Romans 8:11; Ezekiel 37:1-14.
• Raised incorruptible: 1 Corinthians 15:42-54; John 5:28-29.

Water and Spirit. Acts 2:38 holds both in one sentence.

THE FIRE

Jesus said it Himself:

"I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled? But I have a baptism to be baptized with; and how am I straitened till it be accomplished!" (Luke 12:49-50)

John had already told them what kind of fire. "I indeed baptize you with water; but one mightier than I cometh ... he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire" (Luke 3:16). Water, then fire.

Jesus went to the cross, the baptism He was straitened to accomplish. Fifty days later the fire fell:

"And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." (Acts 2:3-4)

That is the fire He came to send. It sat upon each of them, not on the building, not on the leaders only. Each of them.

And it was His fire. When the tabernacle was set up, "there came a fire out from before the LORD, and consumed upon the altar the burnt offering" (Leviticus 9:24). The very next chapter, Nadab and Abihu "offered strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not" (Leviticus 10:1). Fire kindled by men is not His. The fire that counts comes from before the LORD, the way it came at Pentecost. Nobody worked it up. It fell.

So when Peter stood up and said "ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost," the fire was still burning on the people who heard him say it. He was not describing something far off. He was pointing at it.

THE DISCIPLES AT EPHESUS

Nearly twenty years after Pentecost, Paul came to Ephesus and found certain disciples. They were believers. They had been baptized. And Paul asked them one question first:

"Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed?" (Acts 19:2)

Their answer:

"We have not so much as heard whether there be any Holy Ghost."

So Paul asked a second question: "Unto what then were ye baptized?" They said, "Unto John's baptism." Paul told them John's baptism was repentance, pointing to the one who would come after him, Christ Jesus.

"When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Ghost came on them; and they spake with tongues, and prophesied." (Acts 19:5-6)

Notice what Paul did not say. He did not tell them that believing was enough. He did not tell them that the baptism they already had would do. They were sincere, and they were short. So he took them to the name, and the gift came.

That is Acts 2:38 again, carried out step by step, in a city far from Jerusalem, years later. The pattern did not change.

THE HOUSE OF CORNELIUS

Scripture also gives the other order. Peter was preaching in the house of Cornelius, and "while Peter yet spake these words, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word" (Acts 10:44). They spoke with tongues and magnified God before anyone touched the water.

And Peter did not say the water was no longer needed. He said, "Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we? And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord" (Acts 10:47-48).

Ephesus had water without the name and without the fire. Cornelius had the fire before the water. Both were brought to the same place: the name of Jesus, and the gift of the Holy Ghost.

MY TESTIMONY

I was born in April 1981. I was baptized with the fire at twelve years old. The Holy Ghost came first, like the house of Cornelius.

At twenty-eight I was baptized in water, in the titles: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. I believed, and I was sincere.

In August 2015, when I was thirty-four, Bishop John asked me the question Paul asked: had I ever been baptized in Jesus' name? I said no. And he baptized me in the name of Jesus Christ.

The fire at twelve did not make the water unnecessary. The water at twenty-eight did not carry the name. It took both, and it took the name.

There was one more water, and the revival it came from has its own beginning, told in the Book of the Way. On the first new moon of 2017, the twenty-seventh of January, a Bible in a shop in downtown Dalton began to drip oil at Psalm 39. I held that Bible up, and the oil ran all the way down to my waist. A bishop later carried a little bottle of that oil to a six o'clock meeting in north Georgia and put it in their baptism water, and a revival started there. Now it runs three pools.

On the last Sabbath of 2024, December 29th, I went down into that water. And in that water it was fire, fire, fire, and as they dunked me they said, God has increased your prophecy. That was my third water: the titles, then the name of Jesus Christ, then the fire.

Look at that revival. It is one fire. It came from before the LORD, and nobody kindled it by hand. You do not get to bring your own fire to the work of the Lord, and you do not get to bring your own doctrine. The doctrine is Jesus, the one who came from the One.

IF YOU ARE READING THIS

You may be where those disciples were. You believe. Maybe you were baptized once, in some other words, or never at all. Maybe nobody ever told you there was a gift to receive, or you have not so much as heard whether there be any Holy Ghost.

Now you have heard.

Repent. Be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins. And receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. The promise is unto you.

He came to send fire on the earth, and it is already kindled. Do not stop where the Ephesians stopped. Receive.

Ekklesia Way · Church Teaching

text:
In 2026 he defeated Sen. John Cornyn in the GOP Senate primary runoff after an endorsement from Donald Trump and now faces Democrat James Talarico.
Adam Hoffman
Hoffman, about 49 at the time of sentencing, practiced law in the Waco area (Baylor Law graduate) and lived in China Spring. He was arrested in June 2022 and charged with the first-degree felony of continuous sexual abuse of a young child—his son’s friend—allegedly from 2019 to 2022, beginning when the boy was about 6 or 7. The boy later described repeated abuse and being shown pornography. The charge carried a possible sentence of 25 years to life.
McLennan County District Attorney Josh Tetens recused because Hoffman had consulted him about the case before Tetens took office. Paxton’s office then handled the prosecution. A 2025 trial ended in a hung jury (reported as 7–5 in favor of guilt). The victim declined to testify again.
The plea deal
In April 2026 Hoffman pleaded guilty to two Class A misdemeanors: indecent assault and displaying harmful material to a minor. The deal included an admission of abuse that did not specify the victim’s age, which meant he was not required to register as a sex offender in Texas. Prosecutors initially proposed very short jail time (one day in some accounts, later 30). Visiting Judge Roy Sparkman increased it to 60 days, required a five-year law-license surrender, and imposed a lifetime no-contact order. Hoffman served about 29 days due to Texas jail good-time credit and was released in late May 2026. He later moved to Nebraska, where officials required sex-offender registration. There were also reports of delays or incomplete paperwork on surrendering his Texas law license.
Paxton’s prosecutors said they offered the deal because the child would not voluntarily testify a second time and they did not want to force him; they described it as being in the victim’s interest after a mistrial. The victim’s mother later told the court she and her son forgave Hoffman. Critics across parties—including John Cornyn during the primary, James Talarico in the general-election campaign, and some Republican legislators—called the outcome a “sweetheart deal,” noting the original life-eligible felony, the short jail term, and the lack of Texas sex-offender registration. Talarico demanded release of internal “Hoffman files”; Paxton’s office rejected a public-records request. Protests occurred outside the courthouse. Snopes rated as true the core claim that Paxton’s office brokered a deal resulting in roughly 30 days served and no Texas registration.
The case remains politically salient in the 2026 Senate race. Hoffman has said little publicly beyond wanting to return home after release.

Was the first trial prosecuted aggressively?

The first trial was a full four-day jury trial in June 2025 on the original first-degree felony (continuous sexual abuse of a young child). Paxton’s office, through assistant attorneys general Brenda Cantu and Dorian Cotlar, presented the case rather than dismissing or immediately pleading it down. They called the child as a witness; he testified in detail about repeated abuse over roughly three years during sleepovers, including sexual contact, being shown pornography, and threats. They also called a detective, a physician who had examined the boy (Dr. Soo Battle), and presented digital evidence such as text messages and material from phones. In closing, one prosecutor emphasized the specificity of the boy’s account.
That’s the opposite of declining to try the case. After a hung jury they said they were prepared to retry it. The jury split 7–5 in favor of guilt after about nine hours of deliberation (an Allen charge was given when they first reported a 6–6 deadlock). Five jurors weren’t convinced beyond a reasonable doubt.

text:
Having witnessed Navratri festivities across different parts of India, I have always been curious about how Kashmiri Hindus celebrated the festival.

So, I asked my mother about her childhood memories of Chaitra Navratri (Vasant Navratri) and Sharad Navratri (Sharadiya Navratri).

She told me that the celebrations began with Navreh, the Kashmiri New Year, followed by Zangtrey, when daughters of the family were invited and gifted new clothes.

Many families would offer yellow rice and liver, or rice and lungs, to Akingam Devi at the Bhagwati Temple and Bargashekha Bhagwati at Mattan. 
According to her, both are Tantrik devis, which explains the traditional offerings of non vegetarian food. She also mentioned that these practices have changed over time.

Ashtami was observed with a fast, while Navami brought another round of celebrations. 
Daughters and sons in law were invited home, and a feast was prepared that included non vegetarian dishes.

Her memories of Sharad Navratri, however, were quite different. 
She doesn't recall any elaborate or specific celebrations, apart from visiting the Mattan temple to watch the Ram Leela. 
She also doesn't remember any particular dietary restrictions during this period.

These are my mother's personal recollections of how her family observed Navratri while growing up in Kashmir. 
Traditions, rituals and food practices may have varied considerably from one family and region to another.

Following its opening on 17 September 2025, the Fiji Embassy in Jerusalem hosted its first Fiji–Israel Trade & Investment Webinar to build business connections and promote Fiji’s investment and trade opportunities in the region.

The webinar was led by His Excellency Jesoni Vitusagavulu, Fiji’s Ambassador to Israel, who highlighted that despite its size, Fiji offers exciting opportunities for investment and trade with Israel. He also emphasized Fiji’s role as a hub for the Pacific, connecting businesses to markets across Oceania Region.

Mr. Esala Masitabua, Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank of Fiji, presented Fiji's economic outlook and financial sector overview. He highlighted that Fiji has a young population with an average age of 28, and a services-driven economy anchored by tourism. Commercial lending rates are at historic lows, while foreign reserves remain strong at five months of import cover. He also reassured investors that exchange controls guarantee the repatriation of foreign capital.

Mr. Kamal Chetty, Chief Executive Officer of Investment Fiji, outlined opportunities in tourism, agriculture, renewable energy, manufacturing and business process outsourcing. He noted that Fiji's tourism sector is targeting 1.25 million arrivals by 2027. In agriculture, Fiji's food import bill presents immediate opportunities for local production, particularly in dairy, rice, beef and seafood.

He also highlighted Fiji's renewable energy targets, the growing BPO sector, and the incentives available to investors, including tax holidays and duty exemptions across key sectors. For exporters, he pointed to Fijian products with strong potential for the Israeli market, including premium bottled water, turmeric, ginger, high-end cosmetics, sugar, rum, sea salt, garments and pearls.

Discussions explored opportunities to increase local food production, introduce new technology and connect Fijian products with buyers in Israel. Fiji’s transport links and access to Pacific markets were also highlighted as advantages for businesses looking to establish a regional base.

Through these engagements, Investment Fiji helps connect international investors with local businesses to support investment, exports and job creation.

Thailand and the Netherlands have agreed to accelerate negotiations on the Thailand–European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA), seeking to conclude talks by the end of 2026. Thai Trade Representative Werapong Prapha met Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation Sjoerd Sjoerdsma at the Dutch Embassy in Bangkok on October 14 to discuss the agreement, investment opportunities, and developments in international trade.

Werapong urged the EU to offer more favorable import quotas for Thai white rice, chicken meat, and canned tuna, taking into account trade preferences granted to other regional partners. Although negotiations have advanced through 10 rounds, agricultural and industrial market access remains among the outstanding issues. Both sides recognized the need for an agreement that delivers tangible economic benefits while maintaining a fair balance of interests, rather than prioritizing speed alone.

The meeting also addressed concerns over government-supported industrial overproduction, unfair competition, controls on dual-use goods, and the situation in Ukraine. Werapong later attended a reception celebrating the opening of the Dutch Embassy's new premises, where he met business representatives and discussed Thailand's investment priorities. These include advanced technology, medical tourism, electric vehicles, agriculture and food processing, and clean energy.

The Netherlands ranks as Thailand's 19th-largest trading partner globally and second-largest within the EU. Bilateral trade reached approximately 7.97 billion US dollars in 2025, comprising 7.02 billion dollars in Thai exports and 948 million dollars in imports.

Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Definitely would say agree more than disagree.

But here’s one where we disagree.

Congrats on your Jolly Jack-O!

Well deserved and I’m happy for you.

But you made a post saying the @veefriends community doesn’t let anyone feel left behind. 

But that’s not true and it depends entirely on who you are and who you’re connected to within the community.

Case in point @jolly_jackoVF waited in line for about 2 hours trying to get himself a sealed Jolly Jack-O comic.

He also got laid off while he was at @NY_Comic_Con.

His favorite character Jolly is literally his name on X. It’s what everyone knows him by and calls him.

He wasn’t looking for any freebies he just wanted to buy a sealed one at cost.

He went home without being able to and not a single person there seemed to care.

Luckily before he went home someone did offer to sell him an already opened one and he bought it. But that’s not quite what he was looking for. And one might have thought “the community” would have helped. 

But how do you think he felt after 2 hours getting the line cut off right in front of him and the people he saw buy the last ones were people who already had multiple sealed ones and they were looking to flip and they just kinda looked back at him like “too bad so sad” when they got the last ones and wouldn’t offer to let him buy a single one sealed at cost and neither would anyone else?

For me a moment like that stings even more if you bought into the belief that “the VeeFriends community” has your back and then IRL it’s all about profit and flip game over making sure the guy who’s name is literally Jolly and traveled from South Carolina and got laid off while he was there can at least get the one thing he came for to cheer him up?

People think I’m shitting on the community when I dispel the idea that “the community” treats everyone equally but if you buy into that idea and get left out despite believing, it hurts way more than if you didn’t have that expectation.

Other people in the community give me the silent treatment and pretend I don’t exist when I see them IRL and BLOCK and UNFOLLOW and MUTE me and even if I try to talk it out they are Completely Unforgiving And refuse the conversation.

It feels like shit getting GHOSTED IRL, to be transparent. 

And it’s by people Gary and the community celebrate heavily.

And yes people talk ABOUT me instead of TO me and sometimes it gets back to me. In fact a lot of times it does. And the people not saying it to my face hurts more than the words themselves. 

You get the gist.

Genuinely happy for you but I think messages that lead newcomers to think they’ll have a positive experience no matter what are dangerous for people with mental health and social issues that believe them and have the complete opposite experience after they join.

🏭 HYPERSONIC METAL POWDERS GET A NASDAQ TICKER // Amaero $AMRO prices its US IPO at $4.25

Amaero Inc $AMRO priced its US initial public offering on Wednesday at $4.25 per share, selling 4,705,883 shares for about $20.0M in gross proceeds. The Tennessee company makes refractory and titanium alloy powders for 3D printing and advanced manufacturing, and its shares start trading on the Nasdaq Capital Market on Thursday.

 * 💵 The deal: 4,705,883 shares at $4.25 each, about $20.0M in gross proceeds before fees
 * 📅 First trade: Thursday, October 15, 2026 on the Nasdaq Capital Market under $AMRO, with the offering expected to close on Friday, October 16
 * 🇦🇺 Already public: Amaero already trades in Australia on the ASX under code 3DA, making this a US cross listing rather than a first public debut
 * 🧪 The powders: spherical refractory and titanium alloys, including niobium, tungsten, tantalum, molybdenum, and rhenium, engineered for hypersonic weapons, satellite propulsion, and strategic missiles
 * 🏭 The plant: manufacturing and corporate headquarters in McDonald, Tennessee, producing powders plus large near net shape parts pressed from metal powder
 * 🟢 The extra option: underwriters hold a 30 day option to purchase up to 705,882 additional shares at the offer price
 * 💰 Use of proceeds: up to about $10.0M of the net proceeds buys capital equipment over the next 12 months, and the rest funds working capital, operating expenses, and research and development
 * 🏦 The bookrunners: Baird is lead bookrunning manager on the deal, with Lake Street as additional bookrunning manager

▬▬▬

⚠️ THE CATCH

The check is small and the US float is smaller. Only the 4.7M new shares will trade in the US while about 23.8M shares sit behind the Australian listing, so Thursday price discovery runs on a thin book that can exaggerate the first move in either direction. The deal also shrank on its way to market, cut down from a September filing that aimed to raise more than $50M, and it priced just under the converted Australian close.

▬▬▬

🧠 THE TAKEAWAY

The scarcity story has teeth, because refractory metal powders for hypersonics have very few US suppliers, and now that story has a US ticker with a tiny float attached. Does $AMRO open at a premium to its Australian listing on defense scarcity demand, or does a downsized $20M deal tell you the sponsorship was never deep? 👇 NFA

text:
Is it common for prosecutors to offer a plea deal when the victim will not testify

Yes. It is a common reason prosecutors offer or accept reduced plea deals, especially in child sexual-abuse and other sexual-assault cases that depend heavily on the victim’s live testimony.
Most U.S. criminal cases already end in pleas rather than trials. In sexual-violence prosecutions the rate is even higher: studies of large samples have found that a large majority of resolved cases end in a plea to a lesser charge, and only a small fraction produce a conviction on the original charge. When the complaining witness—particularly a child who has already testified once—says they will not do it again, prosecutors routinely treat that as a major change in the strength of the case.
The practical reasons are straightforward:
Without the victim, many of these cases lack other strong, admissible evidence that can prove the elements of a first-degree felony beyond a reasonable doubt.
A second trial after a hung jury is not guaranteed to produce a conviction; a 7–5 split (as reported in the Hoffman trial) already showed the case was close.
Forcing a child back onto the stand can be viewed as re-traumatizing. Many prosecutors, child-protection professionals, and some judges treat avoiding that as a legitimate factor in “the best interest of the child.” Texas prosecutors and victim advocates have described this exact calculus: when a child “just can’t do it,” they try to reach a plea instead.
Prosecutors still have options other than a generous plea. They can subpoena the victim, seek a continuance, try to introduce prior statements under hearsay exceptions or forfeiture-by-wrongdoing, or dismiss and refile later. In practice they often choose not to compel a reluctant child, especially after one full trial. Offices vary: some “no-drop” policies exist in domestic-violence units, but those are less uniformly applied to child sexual-abuse cases, and even then prosecutors still weigh the realistic chance of winning.
The resulting deal can still be criticized as too lenient (short jail time, no sex-offender registration, reduced charges). That criticism is common and sometimes valid; the existence of a victim’s refusal to testify does not automatically make any particular sentence appropriate. It does, however, explain why prosecutors frequently treat a plea as the remaining viable path rather than risk an acquittal or force another round of testimony. In the Hoffman matter, Paxton’s prosecutors publicly cited exactly this combination: hung jury plus the child’s stated desire not to testify again. That rationale is consistent with how many offices handle similar situations, even when the outcome draws public and political backlash.

Tell me about Adam Hoffman and Ken Paxton

Adam Hoffman is a former Waco, Texas attorney who pleaded guilty in 2026 to reduced misdemeanor charges after originally being charged with continuous sexual abuse of a young child. Ken Paxton is the Republican Attorney General of Texas since 2015 and the GOP nominee for U.S. Senate in 2026. Their connection is a child sexual abuse case that Paxton’s office prosecuted after a local recusal; a post-mistrial plea deal drew intense criticism and became a campaign issue.
Ken Paxton
Warren Kenneth Paxton Jr. was born December 23, 1962, in Minot, North Dakota. He earned a B.A. in psychology and an M.B.A. from Baylor University and a J.D. from the University of Virginia School of Law. He practiced law, served in the Texas House (2003–2013) and Texas Senate (2013–2015), and has been Attorney General since January 2015, winning re-election in 2018 and 2022.
As AG he leads a large office handling civil litigation for the state, consumer protection, child support, and some criminal matters when local prosecutors request or recuse. He is known for frequent lawsuits against the federal government.

text:
Fill the next class.

That is a clear goal. The work starts when you figure out which students fit the program, what enrolling actually involves, and how much the school can afford to spend reaching them.

I want to break down this Premier Dental Academy example because there is a business lesson here for career schools, training programs, and owners selling a service that takes more than one click to buy.

Premier Dental Academy of Longview teaches dental assisting here in East Texas. Its in-person program includes instruction and practice with dental equipment. Amanda leads the school, and her team handles the teaching and student support.

Premier and The LeadFlow Pro share common ownership. This is an example from our own operation, and that relationship belongs in the conversation.

The campaign example shown in this image uses approximately $352 in acquisition cost per enrollment and a $3,000 tuition benchmark.

Divide $3,000 by $352 and you get approximately 8.5.

That is where the 8.5× figure comes from.

It compares the tuition benchmark with the reported acquisition spend. Tuition value is not profit, money already collected, or a guaranteed return. The school still has the expense of delivering the education, and these approximate figures do not establish that every possible acquisition expense was included.

The $3,000 benchmark also has a specific meaning. Premier currently lists that amount for in-person tuition paid in full. Its payment-plan total is different.

Those details matter when you make business decisions from a number.

Here is why I think this example deserves a closer look.

A person considering dental assistant school in Longview, Texas, may have several questions before they are ready to enroll.

What will I learn?

Can I work while I train?

What does it cost?

Can I visit first?

Who can explain the next step?

If your marketing gets someone interested, your website and enrollment process need to help that person get answers. Every unanswered question leaves another decision hanging.

Through The LeadFlow Pro, I built the technology around Premier’s operation, including its website, enrollment features, student learning tools, and administrative system. Amanda and the school’s team bring the instruction, conversations, and support that make the school work.

The published student path lets someone explore the program, consider the cost, request a tour, apply, and review enrollment options. Once enrolled, students can reach the learning resources connected to their program.

That describes the system around the school. It does not establish that any one feature caused the acquisition figure in this image.

For another business, I would start by studying where people get stuck.

Does your website explain the offer clearly?

Can someone see the price or understand how to get an accurate quote?

Does an inquiry reach the person responsible for answering it?

Can that person see what the prospective customer already asked?

Do you know what happened after the conversation?

These are practical questions. They help identify whether the next useful investment belongs in advertising, the website, follow-up, or the offer itself.

For schools, I would also want the team to agree on what counts as an enrollment before measuring an enrollment campaign.

An inquiry is a useful signal. An application shows another level of interest. An enrollment and its required payment are another stage again. Keeping those stages visible makes the numbers useful to the people running the business.

The same thinking applies to contractors, service businesses, and paid programs.

Start with the outcome you need. Understand what delivering it costs. Decide how much capacity you have. Then work toward an acquisition cost the operation can support.

Search visibility matters because people need to find you. Clear writing matters because they need to understand you. A useful next step matters because interest needs somewhere to go.

For a career school, that might mean explaining the program, showing the people behind it, answering tuition questions, and making it easy to arrange a conversation.

For a contractor, it might mean showing completed work and collecting enough project information to have a useful first call.

The details should follow the business.

That is the conversation I want to have with owners through The LeadFlow Pro. What do you sell? Who is a good fit? What is getting in the way of their next step? What would a worthwhile result cost?

If you run a school, training program, or service business in Longview or East Texas, message me about your next class or your next customer.

Tell me what you offer, who you want to reach, and where people seem to stall. We can start with a free consultation and work through what a practical plan should measure.

The classroom artwork in this image is illustrative. The figures describe this approximate campaign example and do not promise the same outcome for another business.

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023.
