Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. Meanwhile, there are significance cultural differences between Rio Tinto and Glencore; there is little doubt that Rio Tinto's CEO Simon Trott would have had doubts about a merger once he understood these cultural differences. News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

text:
51. Thiruvekka (Sri Yathothkari Perumal Temple)

Location: Kanchipuram
Deities: Lord Yathothkari Perumal (in a unique reclining posture from right to left) and Goddess Komalavalli.
Quick Info: The name "Yathothkari" translates to "the Lord who acted as per the wishes of His devotee." According to legend, the great saint Kanikannan was banished by the king. When the saint left, he asked the Lord to roll up His serpent bed and follow him. The Lord obliged. The king soon realized his mistake and requested them to return, after which the Lord lay back down in the opposite direction. 

52. Thirukkaragam (Sri Karunakara Perumal Temple)

Location: Kanchipuram (housed inside the Ulagalantha Perumal temple complex).
Deities: Lord Karunakara Perumal (Standing posture) and Goddess Padmamani.
Quick Info: Legend says that Sage Garga performed intense penance here to achieve higher spiritual wisdom. Pleased by his devotion, Lord Vishnu appeared before him and blessed him, which is why the place is associated with divine mercy ("Karuna"). 

53. Thirukkarvaanam (Sri Neelamega Perumal Temple / Kalvar Perumal)

Location: Kanchipuram (also located inside the Ulagalantha Perumal temple complex).
Deities: Lord Neelamega Perumal (Standing posture) and Goddess Kamalavalli.
Quick Info: The Lord here is envisioned as a dark, majestic rain cloud ("Neelamegam" or "Karvaanam") that showers blessings upon His devotees. The Alvar saints praised this shrine for bringing immense peace and spiritual stability to visitors. 

54. Thirukkalvanur (Sri Adi Varaha Perumal Temple)

Location: Kanchipuram (located within the inner complex of the famous Kamakshi Amman Temple).
Deities: Lord Adi Varaha Perumal (Standing/Sitting posture) and Goddess Sundarabimbavalli.
Quick Info: This is an incredibly unique shrine because a Vishnu Divya Desam is housed inside a primary Shiva-Shakti temple. Lord Vishnu appears here in His small Varaha (boar) avatar. Legend tells that Parvati was looking at herself in a mirror, and Vishnu concealed himself to admire her form; hence he is called "Kalvan" (the thief). 

55. Thiruppavalavannam (Sri Pavalavarna Perumal Temple)

Location: Kanchipuram
Deities: Lord Pavalavarna Perumal (Standing posture) and Goddess Pravalavalli.
Quick Info: The name literally translates to "He who is the color of red coral." Interestingly, directly across the road sits the Pachaivannan temple (where the Lord is green like emerald). Together, both shrines are traditionally counted as a single, beautiful representation of the Lord's vibrant forms. 

56. Thiruparamechura Vinnagaram (Sri Vaikuntha Perumal Temple)

Location: Kanchipuram
Deities: Lord Vaikunthanatha Perumal and Goddess Vaigundavalli.
Quick Info: Built by the Pallava king Nandivarman II, this temple is architectural poetry. The main sanctum features three tiers stacked vertically, allowing devotees to witness the Lord in three distinct postures: Standing, Sitting, and Reclining. 

57. Thirupputkuzhi (Sri Vijayaraghava Perumal Temple)

Location: Near Kanchipuram (Balachetty Chatram)
Deities: Lord Vijayaraghava Perumal (Sitting posture) and Goddess Maragadavalli.
Quick Info: This temple is deeply tied to the epic Ramayana. When Jatayu (the giant eagle king) fought Ravana to rescue Sita, he was mortally wounded. Lord Rama later found the dying bird, performed his final funeral rites here, and created a water tank with his arrow (Jatayu Pushkarani). The main deity is seen holding Jatayu on His lap. 

58. Thirunindravur (Sri Bhaktavatsala Perumal Temple)

Location: Thirunindravur (Outskirts of Chennai)
Deities: Lord Bhaktavatsala Perumal (Standing posture) and Goddess Ennai Petra Thayar (Sudhavalli).
Quick Info: The town's name implies "the place where the Goddess of wealth settled down." Legend has it that Goddess Lakshmi left Vaikuntha after a brief misunderstanding, prompting Lord Vishnu to stand patiently waiting for her return. Devotees visit this beautiful Pallava-era temple to seek the return of lost assets or wealth. 

59. Thiruvallur / Thiru Evvul (Sri Veeraraghava Perumal Temple)

Location: Thiruvallur
Deities: Lord Vaidya Veeraraghava Perumal (Reclining posture) and Goddess Kanagavalli.
Quick Info: The Lord here is known as Vaidya Veeraraghava (the Supreme Doctor). A legendary sage named Salihotra tested a guest by giving him all his food; the guest turned out to be Lord Vishnu, who asked where he could rest (Evvul?—hence the name Thiru-Evvul). Devotees regularly offer molasses (jaggery) and salt into the temple tank to pray for the cure of physical illnesses. 

60. Thiruvallikeni (Sri Parthasarathy Temple)

Location: Triplicane, Chennai
Deities: Lord Venkatakrishna/Parthasarathy (Standing posture) and Goddess Rukmani.
Quick Info: One of the historic landmarks of Chennai, this temple features Lord Krishna as the charioteer (Parthasarathy) to Arjuna during the Mahabharata war. The main idol uniquely bears lines on the face, symbolizing arrow wounds sustained during the great battle, and he holds a conch instead of weapons. It is also highly celebrated for its iconic five forms of Vishnu housed in a single complex

🇮🇳🇺🇸 India–US trade deal: Is relief from a tariff threat being presented as a trade concession?

President Trump’s October 9 decision to buy Russian diesel may have raised hopes that India would escape tariffs of up to 100% for buying Russian oil.

But Washington could buy Russian fuel, shield China from higher tariffs (out of Fear of retaliation), and still use the threat against India to extract trade concessions.

Here is the possible bargaining formula—and why India should be cautious.

1️⃣ The original tariff offer lost its legal basis.

The February 6 joint statement offered to cut US reciprocal tariffs on India from 25% to 18%. On February 20, the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs, leaving Washington without a clear tariff concession to offer India.

2️⃣ The Russian-oil threat could supply fresh bargaining power.

Washington could offer a 10%–18% tariff instead of a possible 100% levy, alongside temporary relief from penalties for buying Russian oil. In return, India would accept the trade terms outlined on February 6.

This is a possible negotiating formula, not a confirmed agreement.

3️⃣ A lower threatened tariff does not necessarily mean a competitive tariff.

Most other countries face normal import duties plus forced-labour tariffs of 10% or 12.5%. India’s position would depend on whether the proposed 10%–18% rate includes those duties or comes on top of them—and which products it covers.

The benchmark should be what competing suppliers pay.

4️⃣ What prevents another tariff after India signs?

Without enforceable protection against further duties, Washington could secure India’s concessions and then impose fresh tariffs through another investigation.

India needs clear tariff terms, competitive market access and durable commitments.

Relief from a threatened 100% tariff is not, by itself, a balanced trade deal.

After 1967, the Arab League issued the “Three No’s”: no peace, no recognition, no negotiations with Israel.

In 2000 at Camp David, Israeli PM Ehud Barak offered a Palestinian state on roughly 90–95% of the West Bank plus all of Gaza, with land swaps and arrangements on Jerusalem. Yasser Arafat rejected it without a counteroffer. The Second Intifada followed.

In 2008, Ehud Olmert offered Mahmoud Abbas even more—about 93–94% of the West Bank with 1:1 land swaps, a capital in East Jerusalem, and limited symbolic refugee returns. Abbas never accepted.

Each time the choice was a state next to Israel or continued conflict. Leadership chose the latter.

text:
Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸 And since honesty is rare in my politics, allow me to confess a few things.

The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that the war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything, and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me up in refugee camps for generations, so that I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three no's. Fifty years later, I'm still stateless. Turns out rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said, "Let's give it a try." It gave me autonomy. Guns for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in almost 20 years. Hamas kills dissidents in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on television teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children on songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.
Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother."

But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but they celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.
Absurd. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a technological powerhouse, desert farms, dusty cities. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said, "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of showcasing honor, hospitality, and the rich Arab culture, I displayed only the culture of the sword.Anger, extremism, and bloodshed. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to the Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I feign surprise when the Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced that I don't want coexistence at all.

Accountability. I blame Israel for everything. Always. Do my leaders steal billions? Blame Israel. Does Hamas fire rockets from hospitals? Blame Israel. Do I glorify death more than life? Blame Israel. Accountability is not my strong suit.

I am Palestinian. I could have built a nation, many times over. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.
So yes, I am a victim. But all too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hatred. And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit.

All of the Palestinians’ claims to victimhood can be traced back to actions they took and decisions they made, many of them violent: rejecting the partition plan, launching the war immediately after (and losing), failing to establish a state in 1948-67 while under Jordanian/Egyptian rule, launching another war in 1967 (and losing), refusing multiple peace offers due to an insistence on a “right of return” that would obviously be suicidal for Israel, etc.

Palestinians (or their leaders) have prioritized a long-term fantasy of sovereignty over the entire region over a compromise that would grant both sides peace. And that is the crux of the issue.

Moreover, Palestinians are part of the greater Arab nation; they attempted to redefine themselves as a small cohort victimized by Israel, but anyone who reads knows this was fabricated specifically so they could claim victimhood. Even before 1948, there was no real movement for an independent Palestinian state, it was always envisioned (by the Arabs themselves) as part of Syria or Jordan, which is precisely why they didn’t try to gain independence in 1948-67. This war has always been Israelis vs Arabs, not Israelis vs Palestinians.

The Palestinians ARE victims, but the perpetrator isn’t Israel, it’s their own leadership, which is why those claims fall on deaf ears to anyone reasonable who knows the history.

text:
THE DIGITAL BARSTOOL: BUYING GHOSTS ON SOI 6
It is late evening in a quiet apartment thousands of miles away from the suffocating humidity of Thailand. A man sits alone in the glow of his laptop screen, clicking a well-worn bookmark that pulls up a live YouTube broadcast of a bar on Soi 6. On the screen, a girl in a tight dress shifts her weight at the counter, profoundly bored, scrolling through her phone. He clicks a link in the video description. A PayPal window opens: 125 baht to "Buy a lady drink for Nong." He clicks confirm.

Thirty seconds later, the bartender hands her a glass of watered-down cola. She glances up at the monitor, flashes a practiced, momentary smile into the lens, and raises her glass. "Thank you, Johnny126," she says. She doesn't know who he is, and she will never ask. He doesn't type a reply in the chat. He simply closes the laptop, feeling a strange, hollow sensation settling in his chest that isn't quite happiness, but isn't entirely sadness either.

This is not a charity stream; it is a highly optimized business model. Born out of the pandemic's desperation, the digital lady drink has evolved into a permanent, highly lucrative pillar of the Pattaya economy. The mechanics are brutally simple. The bar sets up a camera, runs a continuous YouTube feed, and attaches a payment gateway. When a viewer pays 125 to 200 baht, the bartender gets a digital ping. A drink is poured, and the girl receives her standard 50-baht commission, exactly as if the customer were sitting on the stool next to her. It is a digital entrance ticket for men who cannot, or will not, board a flight to Suvarnabhumi. Some bars have scaled this into an industrial operation, broadcasting from over a dozen venues simultaneously, investing in high-end cameras, VR technology, and dedicated soundproof streaming booths.

The men funding this digital ecosystem rarely fit the aggressive "sex tourist" stereotype. You will not see them sweating and shouting on Walking Street. They are sitting quietly in their living rooms, and they generally fall into four distinct demographics.

First is the captive audience: the retiree on a fixed income, the man with physical disabilities, or the guy simply terrified of international travel. For them, the stream is an accessible, albeit imperfect, substitute for a life they cannot reach. The second type is the nostalgic veteran. He remembers the chaotic smell of the street, the oppressive heat, and the thrill of the grid. When he buys a digital drink, he isn't actually tipping the girl; he is paying a subscription fee to his own memories. The third is the timid spectator, the guy who has read the expat forums for years but never possessed the courage to actually book a ticket. The stream offers a sanitized, risk-free viewing gallery where he can finally participate without leaving his comfort zone.

Finally, there is the profoundly lonely man. He isn't looking for a virtual girlfriend; he is just a man moving through a world where nobody knows his name and nobody asks how his day was. When the girl on the screen says "Thank you," she acknowledges his existence, even if only for a fraction of a second. That brief validation is enough to make an empty room feel slightly less suffocating.

For roughly the price of a burnt coffee in a Western city, he is purchasing an illusion of presence. He isn't buying a sexual fantasy; he is buying a gaze. In a world where he feels entirely invisible, a woman looking into a camera and speaking his username holds immense tangible value. It is the exact same psychological machinery that powers a physical bar—exchanging cash for the illusion of connection—but the digital version is fundamentally more transparent. He knows she feels absolutely nothing for him. She knows that he knows. Neither party has to endure the exhausting charade of pretending it is anything more than a micro-transaction. And yet, the system works perfectly, because human beings will always pay to be perceived.

For the girls on the screen, the streams evoke a state of absolute, unapologetic indifference. This isn't arrogance; it is just the reality of a grinding shift. The girl on the broadcast is simply fulfilling a basic physical function: stand near the camera, smile when the bartender gives the signal, raise a glass of soda, and collect the commission. She isn't an actress; she is a shift worker doing exactly what she is paid to do. As one cynical forum user accurately observed, it is a profoundly exhausting job to stand for hours, shifting from foot to foot, staring at a monitor waiting for a notification.

If you watch closely, the girls rarely look directly into the lens. They stare at their phones, they gossip with the bartender, they look out at the street. The camera is just ambient background noise. The viewer is paying for the privilege of being a small part of that background, and he is entirely fine with that arrangement, because being part of the background is still better than being nowhere at all.

A Western observer might look at a man paying a stranger to drink a Coke on YouTube and immediately label it pathetic. It looks like a bleak caricature of human interaction. But it isn't a caricature; it is just the logical, terminal evolution of the Pattaya business model. In a physical bar, a man pays for an hour of a woman's time. In the digital stream, he pays for thirty seconds of her attention. The only difference is the scale.

In many ways, the digital transaction is actually more honest. On a bar stool, a man can easily trick himself into believing the girl genuinely likes him. Through a screen, that self-deception is almost impossible. He knows she smiles at everyone. He knows she will forget his username before the ice in her glass melts. But he pays anyway, proving that the brutal awareness of the illusion does not diminish the desperate need for it. The bar is no longer limited by physical walls. It is everywhere the internet reaches.

Later that night, long after he closes his laptop, he sits in the dark. He isn't thinking about a specific woman, but rather the fleeting moment she looked into the lens and said his username. He picks up his phone, opens the YouTube app, and pulls up the archived broadcast. He scrubs through the timeline until he finds the exact timestamp. She raises the glass. She smiles. She says his name. He watches it twice, smiles quietly to himself, and turns off the screen.

Halfway across the world, on a humid morning in Thailand, the girl has already clocked out. She has taken off her dress, scrubbed the makeup off her face, and gone to sleep in a cramped, shared room. Her mind is completely empty of him. She does not remember his screen name. But he remembers the transaction, and for a lonely man in a quiet apartment, that is more than enough reason to open the laptop again tomorrow.

text:
Per request, I’m sharing my thoughts on this week’s Torah portion today so people don’t miss it. I’ll be sharing it again tomorrow before Shabbat. 🙏 

This week, we read the second portion of the Torah, the portion of Noah, in which we learn about one of the most famous biblical stories ever, the story of Noah’s ark.

The portion begins, “This is the line of Noah. Noah was a righteous man; he was blameless in his age; Noah walked with God.”

All the commentators ask a very obvious question. Why does the verse have to say “in his age”?

It says Noah was a righteous man and he was blameless. What do the words “in his age” add? 

We know the Torah doesn’t waste space and that every word in the Torah is there to teach us something.

So what are we to learn from the words “in his age”?

Famously, the commentator Rashi explains that there is a debate among the rabbis about whether those words are meant to praise Noah, that despite the world being so corrupt, he was still righteous, or the opposite, that he was righteous in his generation, but if he had lived in the generation of Abraham, he would not have been considered righteous.

As Rabbi Goldberg pointed out, this is like the debate about Michael Jordan. Was he great in his time because the NBA was softer back then, or was he truly the GOAT, and even in today’s NBA, he’d still be Michael Jordan?

A funny and pretty spot-on analogy.

So what is really behind this debate? It’s not just a historical or descriptive verse that’s here to tell us that Noah was righteous. What is this debate really about?

Well, perhaps to shed some light on this, let’s go back to the first few words of the portion.

“This is the line of Noah. Noah was a righteous man…”

The portion begins by telling us that it’s about to list Noah’s offspring, but then it seemingly changes course and tells us about Noah, not his offspring. Why?

It should say, “This is the line of Noah,” and then proceed to tell us the names of Noah’s kids, which it does in the next verse. But why the break?

Rabbi Goldberg explains beautifully that before parents can educate their kids, before they can expect greatness from their children, they need to first work on themselves and make sure they are good role models.

If parents behave immorally, you can’t expect their kids to behave morally.

Who was Noah’s first child? Himself. Not literally, but before the Torah tells us about Noah’s kids and how he raised them, it says, “These are the offspring of Noah, Noah…”

Noah, first and foremost, worked on himself.

Great. That’s what makes him righteous.

The difference is that Abraham didn’t only work on himself; he also inspired the whole generation.

In fact, when God told Abraham that He was going to destroy Sedom, unlike Noah, who just accepted that God was going to destroy the world, Abraham fought back and asked God not to destroy Sedom.

Sure, Noah was a righteous man, but he was not the leader Abraham was. He built his ark and saved himself in it. He did not try to change those around him like Abraham did.

This reminds me of one of my favorite quotes.

“When I speak to managers, I feel like they’re important. When I speak to leaders, I feel like I am important.”

Good leaders don’t only take care of themselves. Good leaders empower others.

So yes, Noah was a righteous man, but he lacked the leadership abilities possessed by Abraham and our other leaders, including Moses, who cared more about the nation than he cared about himself.

Some more quotes about this idea:

“Leadership is unlocking people’s potential to become better.” — Bill Bradley

“A leader is best when people barely know he exists. When his work is done, his aim fulfilled, they will say: We did it ourselves.” — Lao Tzu

“As we look ahead into the next century, leaders will be those who empower others.” — Bill Gates

“The greatest leader is not necessarily the one who does the greatest things. He is the one that gets the people to do the greatest things.” — Ronald Reagan

Noah was righteous, but his generation wasn’t. They were corrupt. Instead of asking God to have mercy on them, he accepted their fate, built himself an ark, and put walls around himself instead of influencing others to be better.

That’s why the Torah uses the words “in his generation…”

Because in regard to his generation, he wasn’t a leader, unlike Abraham.

Noah was righteous, but he wasn’t a leader.

A few verses later, the Torah says, “The earth became corrupt before God; the earth was filled with lawlessness.”

The word the Torah uses for lawlessness is, wait for it… Hamas.

Yep, that’s right. God believed that once there was Hamas, there was no saving the world. It had gone too far, it had become too morally bankrupt, and there was no coming back.

If you drill down on that verse, you’ll notice a nice idea I never thought of before.

What was their sin? It says they became corrupt and the world was chaotic, but why? What was their mistake that led to all of that immorality?

The verse says the words “Haaretz Lifnei Haelokim,” the land before God.

Their problem was that they put earthly matters before God, before spirituality.

They put their own comfort, their own greed, before God.

When a generation does that, when they put their own materialistic interests before they put God, what happens is chaos.

If there is no God, there are no boundaries. When there are no boundaries, everything is allowed.

They put “earth” before God, and that was their fundamental mistake.

OK, so why did God punish them with a flood? Now we understand why.

They had no boundaries. They had no problem stealing, for example, because if they had no God, they had nothing stopping them from doing whatever they wanted.

So God says, “OK, you lived without boundaries? I will remove My boundaries too.”

We have beaches. We have sand. We have the shore. The water doesn’t usually flow freely onto the land. If it did, we’d all be dead.

But God put boundaries into nature. As soon as they removed boundaries from society, God punished them with the appropriate punishment of removing boundaries in nature.

And now to an even more fundamental idea.

Why an ark? If God was going to destroy the world and He wanted Noah to survive, why not just perform a miracle so that the water wouldn’t reach Noah? Why not just save Noah without the need for so much construction of this ark?

What was the point of God telling Noah to construct an ark? Why not just perform the miracle and save Noah?

The commentators offer one answer, and I’d like to offer another.

The commentators on the Torah explain that God asked Noah to build the ark so that those around him would ask him what he was building and why.

He’d then explain to them that God was going to destroy the world due to their corrupt ways, and hopefully, that would scare them enough that they’d repent.

That’s why God asked Noah to build the ark, so others around him would potentially change their ways.

To me, that answer doesn’t really address the question.

If God wanted the people to repent, why not just perform a miracle and have them repent? Why the need for this ark?

I think the idea is even deeper.

I think God is teaching us, yet again, how He runs the world.

Sure, He performs miracles, and He looks after His children, but not before His children make the first move.

God is, in essence, saying to Noah, “You want Me to save you? Sure, but first, get to work. Build the ark.”

As I have said many times, my favorite verse in the entire Torah takes place when the Israelites approached the Red Sea and were seemingly stuck.

In front of them was the terrifying darkness of the sea, and behind them were the chariots of the world’s strongest empire, Egypt.

They were stuck.

So they did the natural thing and asked Moses why he had taken them out of Egypt to die there on the shore.

Moses then relays that question to God and asks God why He told him to take them out of Egypt, only for them to die there on the shore.

Now, if you stop and think about that, you might expect God to instruct Moses to tell the people to pray. Or maybe to do good deeds. Maybe God would tell them to love their neighbor.

However, God says none of those things.

God’s response is, “Why are you yelling at Me, Moses? Tell the Israelites to jump in and go!”

As soon as Nachshon jumped in, only then did God split the sea.

God is perhaps teaching us here that He can perform miracles, He can save Noah, but first, God requires Noah to demonstrate his faith, to take that first step, and then God can perform His miracle.

Generally speaking, God performs miracles within nature, at least in today’s modern world. Today, we don’t have miracles like the splitting of the sea or the 10 plagues.

Today, God performs miracles for us through nature, but He requires us to take that first step.

He needs us to build an army, an economy, a society, and then, and only then, does He perform His miracles and make Israel into a miraculous state.

The same is, of course, true for Aliyah.

You want to make Aliyah successfully? You need to jump in.

Sure, God will perform miracles so that you can build an incredible life for yourself in Israel, but He requires you to take that first step.

It’s a scary step, just like the step into the Red Sea was a scary step, but if you want God to take care of you and help you build a successful life in the State of Israel, you need to demonstrate to God that you are willing to take that first step, get on a plane, and do your part.

God told Noah to build the ark so that Noah would do his part. Noah would take that first step so that God could then step into the ring and do His thing.

In Judaism, we call that Hishtadlut, translated as “effort.”

We know God runs the world, so why even work? Why even do anything if God decides our fate? The answer is that we have to do our part, and if we do, God will do the rest, but we can’t just sit back and wait for God’s miracles.

We can’t just sit back in the diaspora and wait for God to bring Mashiach so we can all come back to Israel. God is waiting for US to come back SO THAT He can bring Mashiach.

Back to Noah’s leadership, or lack thereof, God instructs Noah to build the ark and gives him exact dimensions.

One of God’s instructions to Noah is to build a window into the ark. Why? Why is that important?

Now that we know that Noah was righteous but not a leader, perhaps God is saying to Noah, “Listen, you’re righteous, and that’s why I’m saving you, but be a leader. Put that window into the ark so you can see the suffering of those around you. Don’t just worry about yourself. Be more like Abraham. For that, you need a window so you can look out of the ark and see how the world is being destroyed around you.”

Maybe He’s even telling him to build a window as a rebuke. “You saved yourself by being righteous, but look around you. Look at this missed opportunity. You could have prevented all this suffering, all this destruction, if only you had been a leader like Abraham.”

Now, skipping ahead to the end of the portion, we have another famous story, the story of the Tower of Babel.

The Torah says, “Everyone on earth had the same language and the same words. And as they migrated from the east, they came upon a valley in the land of Shinar and settled there.

They said to one another, ‘Come, let us make bricks and burn them hard.’ Brick served them as stone, and bitumen served them as mortar.

And they said, ‘Come, let us build us a city, and a tower with its top in the sky, to make a name for ourselves; else we shall be scattered all over the world.’”

In other words, these sinners tried to build a tower to the heavens to be like God.

So what did they do wrong exactly, and how does God react?

“GOD came down to look at the city and tower that the mortals had built, and GOD said, ‘If, as one people with one language for all, this is how they have begun to act, then nothing that they may propose to do will be out of their reach. Let us, then, go down and confound their speech there, so that they shall not understand one another’s speech.’”

There are two words here that need explaining.

“Came down…”

God “came down” to see the tower?

He couldn’t see it from the heavens? He had to come down to see it? What’s that about?

God here is also teaching us an incredibly important lesson that is more relevant today than ever.

God, before judging and punishing the people for building the tower, had to “come down” to see their circumstances, to put Himself in their shoes.

God is teaching us that before we judge anyone, even if we think they are dead wrong, we need to first understand who they are, what their circumstances are, and we need to put ourselves in their shoes.

This is true for people, and it is true for nations.

If only the world would ask itself the question, “What would we do if we were in Israel’s shoes?” Everything would be very different.

One of the most glaring questions surrounding this war and that dark day on which it began is: All those criticizing Israel, what would they do if their country were attacked the way Israel was attacked?

It’s very easy to sit “in the heavens” and look down and judge others, but instead, even God “comes down” and puts Himself in their shoes before reaching any conclusions.

If only humans behaved this way, the world would be an infinitely better place.

And finally, there is one more lesson from those words “came down.”

Unlike other religions that believe in abstaining from the pleasures of this world, Judaism believes and teaches something else.

God does not want us up in the heavens. In fact, there is even an actual verse in the Torah itself that says “Lo Bashamayim Hi,” which means that the Torah and the commandments are not in the heavens, but rather, they are in our hearts, and they are accessible and attainable to those who pursue them.

God doesn’t want us disconnecting from this world and acting like angels. God created us as humans, and He created the world for us to live in it and enjoy it.

What God DOES expect from us is to bring Him down into our lives.

In Judaism, we have the opportunity to inject Godliness into literally everything we do. We believe in bringing God down to us, not us going up to Him.

We bless God when we open our eyes. We bless God when we wash our hands in the morning. We bless God when we go to the bathroom. We bless God when we eat. We thank God for letting us live another day. We bless God when we see beauty in nature. We bless God when we see lightning.

The list is very long, but the idea is that God wants us to live and enjoy life, but He also wants us to bring Him down into our lives and sanctify even the most mundane things by injecting spirituality into everything we do.

God “came down” to earth to, first and foremost, understand the people before judging them for their sin. But He also “came down” to teach us how He expects us to live, as holy creatures who were created in His image and who are to emulate His ways by sanctifying the world around us.

Shabbat shalom.

The Lord is my light and my salvation; Whom shall I fear? The Lord is the strength of my life; Of whom shall I be afraid?  When the wicked came against me To eat up my flesh, My enemies and foes, They stumbled and fell.
Though an army may encamp against me, My heart shall not fear; Though war may rise against me, In this I will be confident, One thing I have desired of the Lord, That will I seek: That I may dwell in the house of the Lord All the days of my life, To behold the beauty of the Lord, And to inquire in His temple.For in the time of trouble He shall hide me in His pavilion; In the secret place of His tabernacle, He shall hide me; He shall set me high upon a rock. And now my head shall be lifted up above my enemies all around me; Therefore I will offer sacrifices of joy in His tabernacle; i will sing, yes, I will sing praises to the Lord.
Hear, O Lord, when I cry with my voice! Have mercy also upon me, and answer me. When You said, “Seek My face,” My heart said to You, “Your face, Lord, I will seek.” Do not hide Your face from me; Do not turn Your servant away in anger; You have been my help; Do not leave me nor forsake me,O God of my salvation. When my father and my mother forsake me, Then the Lord will take care of me.
Teach me Your way, O Lord, And lead me in a smooth path, because of my enemies. Do not deliver me to the will of my adversaries; For false witnesses have risen against me, And such as breathe out violence. I would have lost heart, unless I had believed That I would see the goodness of the Lord In the land of the living.
Wait on the Lord; Be of good courage, And He shall strengthen your heart; Wait, I say, on the Lord!
~ Psalm 27 ~NKJV

text:
Day 5 of Navratri: the mother who raised the warrior who saved the gods 🦁

Day 1 gave you a foundation. Day 2 gave you discipline. Day 3 gave you courage. Day 4 gave you the spark to create.

Day 5 shows the most powerful form of all: a mother.

Read this once. You will never look at a mother's love the same way again. 👇

🔥 The story nobody tells you
➤ A demon named Tarakasura did years of penance and won a boon from Brahma
➤ His boon: only a son of Lord Shiva could ever kill him
➤ He believed Shiva would never marry, so he thought he was immortal
➤ He took over the heavens and drove the gods out
➤ But Parvati's tapasya had brought Shiva to her, and their son Skanda was born
➤ Skanda, also called Kartikeya or Murugan, grew up to lead the army of the gods
➤ He defeated Tarakasura and returned heaven to the gods
➤ The mother who raised him became Maa Skandamata
➤ The lesson: the demon planned for every warrior. He forgot the mother who makes one

🙏 How to recognise her
➤ "Skanda" = Kartikeya, "Mata" = mother
➤ Holds baby Skanda in her lap
➤ Four arms - two hold lotus flowers, one holds Skanda, one blesses in abhaya mudra
➤ Rides a lion - gentle with her child, fierce against anyone who threatens him
➤ Sits on a lotus, so she is also called Padmasana Devi
➤ Fair and glowing, full of calm motherly love

👶 Two blessings in one prayer
➤ She is the only form shown holding her child
➤ When you worship her, you are believed to receive Skanda's blessings too
➤ Devotees pray to her for children, family well-being and protection
➤ Tradition says her grace turned an ordinary man into the great poet Kalidasa

🌱 Why she comes fifth
➤ She governs the Vishuddha chakra, the throat
➤ Vishuddha = truth, clear speech and pure expression
➤ She rules Budh (Mercury), the planet of intellect and communication
➤ Day 4 created life. Day 5 nurtures it and protects it
➤ Creation is one moment. Raising it well is a lifetime

🪔 Puja vidhi: step by step
➤ Bathe early and wear clean yellow clothes
➤ Check the Akhand Jyot and water the jau, which should be clearly green now
➤ Place her image with baby Skanda in her lap, if you have one
➤ Offer yellow flowers, kumkum, akshat, haldi and sandalwood
➤ Offer the bhog, then chant her mantra 108 times
➤ Close with aarti and pray for your children, family and the home

💛 Colour of the day: Yellow
➤ Joy, brightness and warmth, the colour of a happy home

🍌 Bhog: Bananas
➤ Offered for good health and a body free of disease
➤ Share the prasad with children in the family or neighbourhood

🌼 Flowers
➤ Yellow flowers, marigold and lotus

📿 Mantra (108 times)
ॐ देवी स्कन्दमातायै नमः
Om Devi Skandamatayai Namah

🕉️ Dhyan mantra
सिंहासनगता नित्यं पद्माश्रितकरद्वया।
शुभदास्तु सदा देवी स्कन्दमाता यशस्विनी॥

🍎 If you are fasting
➤ You have crossed the halfway mark. Four more days
➤ Yes: fruits, milk, sabudana, kuttu, singhara, makhana, sendha namak
➤ No: grains, onion, garlic, regular salt, alcohol, non-veg
➤ The real fast today: no harsh words, especially to the people who raised you

✨ What Day 5 is really asking you
➤ When did you last thank your mother, or the person who raised you?
➤ Who are you raising, guiding or protecting right now?
➤ Your words shape them. Speak with care, like Skandamata would
➤ A gentle heart and a fierce spirit can live in the same person
➤ Call your mother today. Not tomorrow. Today

🗓️ Where we are
➤ Day 1 Shailputri ✅ → Day 2 Brahmacharini ✅ → Day 3 Chandraghanta ✅ → Day 4 Kushmanda ✅ → Day 5 Skandamata 🦁 → Day 6 Katyayani → Day 7 Kalaratri → Day 8 Mahagauri → Day 9 Siddhidatri

Type "Jai Mata Di" 🙏 and tag the mother who made you who you are.
Save this for your puja. Share it with every mother in your life today.

Shubh Navratri 🌺

text:
WODEMAN
A Romaunce in Three Actes

SYMPHONY OF THE NYGHT

Wherein the Wodeman seeketh a faire mayde, findeth an olde devyll, and maketh a verie ill nyght of it for House Malvezzi.

The Black Wode had swallowed the sunne an houre before, yet the nyght seemed not half so blacke as the thynges that had been done beneath its boughes.

For three dayes had the Wodeman followed Baldovino, marchaunt, knave, and sole remnaunt of that ill-fated companie which had gone into the wode with wagons and come forth in pieces. Him had the Wodeman spared when all his fellowes lay dead, and not for any tendernesse of heart, but because a lyving rat will runne where a dead one cannot, and carrieth in his belly the path unto its owne hole.

The rat, in this wyse, had runne unto a manor.

It stood upon a little ryse beyond the wode, where the last of the trees gave way unto ploughed lande and a narrow river; a house of grey stone, with a gate-towre, a chapel, stables, and more chimneyes than a poore villauge had hearthes. Its walls were old, though not ancient, and had been mended in places with stone of a different colour. Above the gate hung a banner, dyrk with weather, bearyng the device of a House whose name was known farre beyond that lonelie shire.

Malvezzi.

The Wodeman stood among the hazels and regarded it.

“Here is a rat with eccellent lodging,” quoth Leone Vassalo.

Leone was a long, spare man, with a nose broken crookedly across his face and a habit of smiling whenever another man found himself in trouble. He had once served as a crossbowman in the retinue of a pettie lorde, until a quarrel over wauges had left his master with one less tooth and Leone with one less place in which to sleep. He had a soldier’s patience, a thyef’s fyngers, and a curious talent for rememberieng the precise words of any insult ever offered him.

Beside him stood Rinaldo, broad-shouldered and tacitourn, who had lost two fyngers to a millstone and thereafter developed an abiding hatred of mills, millers, and anyone who spoke favourably of grayn. There was old Rinaldo, who claimed to have been a notary before the world grew wicked, though nobody had ever seen him write anythyng but threats upon tavern walls; and there was Piero the Bell, so called because his laughter could be heard through three closed doors and because he had once stolen a church bell merelie to prove that it could be done.

They were a straunge companie, and no two of them had come to the Wodeman by the same road. Some had been soldiers; some poachers; some men who had found the law too costlie to obey; and some had merelie discovered that a hungry man may become a verie dangerous creature when he ceases to expect supper.

They called themselves no order, swore no holy vows, and kept no written rule. Yet they had their customs. Spoils were divided according to an arraungement the Wodeman alone could alter; a man who betrayed his companions was not permitted a second betrayal; and no one was to touch the last portioun of bread whilst another sat hungry beside him. This final ordinaunce had been proposed by Rinaldo after a particularly lean wynter and was enforced with greater zeal than any commaundment of the Church.

They were brigands, certainly. Yet some called them justiciars, for they punished men whom magistrates would not touch, robbed those who had grown rich upon the poor, and sometimes retourned a stolen purse to the hond from which it had been taken.

Others called them devils.

The Wodeman had never troubled to correct either opinion.

“An eccellent lodging hath many holes,” said Leone. “And everie hole hath a man to guard it.”

“Then we shall brenn the gates,” said Piero the Bell. “A little fyre will make all men sociable.”

“And brenn the gyrl with them, if she be within,” answered the Wodeman.

At this the men were sylent.

For Zohra had become a name among them, though none knew her well. She had been taken, and the Wodeman had set himself to find her; and everie rumour of a prettie mayd carried away upon a road, everie tale of a straunger’s daughter sold into serwyse, had drawn him onwaurd as a hound followeth a scent beneath the rayn.

Some said she was of uncommon beautie, with dyrk eyes and a countenaunce which men remembered after they had forgotten her name. Others said she had been seen in the companie of travelling folk, and that she could sing in a tongue none of them understood. Of her kin, her birth, and the place from which she had been taken, the Wodeman knew less than he desyred.

It was not the fyrst time a gyrl had disappeared into the world beyond a villauge fence. The roads of Italie were full of men who offered employment, serwyse, apprenticeship, and passauge to distaunt towns. A father myght send a son to learn a trade; a mother myght entrust her daughter to a household that promysed wauges and protectioun. Sometimes the childeren retourned with money and fyne clothes. Sometimes they retourned with stories. Sometimes they retourned no more.

And there were men who had made a commerce of that sylence.

The Wodeman looked once more upon the manor.

“Find me her name in this house,” he said. “Find me who brought her here. Find me who payd.”

“And if the lorde himself be the buyer?” asked Rinaldo.

“Then we shall have a buyer to remember.”

Leone spat into the leaves.

“I have ever mistrusted a house with so many chimneys. Either they keep too many servaunts, or they are brenning somethyng.”

“Thou mistrustest everie house,” said Rinaldo.

“And have yet to be disappointed.”

The Wodeman tourned away.

“We shall not take it.”

Piero stared after him.

“Not take it?” quoth Leone, or another of those rough companions whose names the wode had rubbed thin. “What, is the house too strong?”

“The house is stone, and we are flesch. Stone hath the advauntage.”

“Then we shall brenn the gates.”

“And brenn the gyrl with them, if she be within.”

At this the menne were sylent.

“Not by the gates.”

“Ah,” said Leone. “Then we shall enter by the manners.”

And for once, the Wodeman smyled.

Baldovino was received within the manor with a warmth that would have melted the heart of a better manne.

The lorde himself came down the hall to greet him, a tall gentileman gone somewhat broad with age, richly clad in dyrk velvet, his fyngers adorned with ryngs, his beard clipped to a sharp point beneath his chin. His hair, once blacke, had withdrawn from the brow and grown iron-grey at the temples; but his eyes remained bryght, quick, and greedie, like those of a fox that hath discovered a hen-house left open.

“Master Baldovino!” cried he. “By the blessed saints, what a miserable figure thou makest. Hast thou been robbed?”

“Worse, my lorde.”

“Murthered?”

“Almost.”

“Then thou art fortunate indeed, for the dead make poor companie at supper.”

He laughed, and his servaunts laughed with him, though somewhat late, as servaunts do when a lorde hath made a jest and they must discover where the jest lieth.

The lorde embraced Baldovino, bade him sit, called for wyne, and ordered a servaunt to find him a clean doublet. He asked after the merchaunt’s travels, the conditioun of the roads, the pryces of wool, the temper of the peasaunts, and whether any straunge companie had been seen upon the highewayes.

Baldovino answered as well as he could, omitting those matters which myght bryng him to a gallows.

“And the Wode?” asked the lorde at last. “They say the Black Wode hath grown troublesome.”

“It hath grown deadlie.”

“Ah.” The lorde sipped his wyne. “And yet here thou art.”

“Here I am.”

“Then let us be thankful for the mercies of Providence.”

Baldovino looked into his cuppe.

The lorde layd a hond upon his shoulder.

“Thou shalt sleep here this nyght, and as many nyghts as thou hast need. A manne of staunding must not be left to perish upon the road.”

It was a noble sentiment, and would have been more touching had the speaker possessed any noble sentiments whatsoever.

For this was Messer Niccolò Malvezzi, cousin unto the great Hegemon Herod Malvezzi of Bologné, and a man whose yeers had improved neither his manners nor his soul. He had once been a younger gentileman of promesse, or so he claimed; and if his promesse had ever been fulfilled, it was chiefly in the multiplicatioun of his vyces.

His estate was modest beside the palayses of Bologna, yet it was large enough to make him a prince unto the folk who dwelt beneath its shadow. He possessed fields, rents, a mill, two vyneyards, a chapel, a dozen armed retainers, and a stewaurd who could make a widow’s debt grow faster than her childeren.

He was beloved by his peers, who found him agreeable at table; respected by his neighbours, who feared his displeausure; and praised by the parish priest, who received a hondsome purse at everie feeste of Saint Michael.

As for the missing childeren of the countryside, their names did not appear in his prayers.

They appeared elsewhere.

Niccolò had been a hondsome man in his youth, or so he claimed, and even in age he retained the easy manners of one accustomed to being welcomed. He knew when to laugh, when to bow, and when to lay a hond upon another man’s arm as though they had been friends since childehood. He remembered the names of merchaunts who myght prove useful and forgot those of servaunts who could not. At feeste days he gave bread to the poor outside the chapel; at harvest he sent a little wyne to the parish priest; when a neighbouryng lorde fell ill, he dispatched a baskette of pears and a letter full of Christian sentiment.

He was praised for his generosité by those who ate at his table.

The peasaunts called him somethyng else when they were sure no retainer could hear.

The villauge of San Lupo lay a mile and a half below the manor, beside a stream that tourned a small millwheel and a road that carried wool, salt, and charcoal towaurd the market towns. Its houses were built of timber and rough stone; their roofs smoked in wynter, and their yards were full of chickens, dung, and childeren. In summer, the villaugers worked the fields from dawn until the heat drove them beneath the trees. In wynter, they mended their tools, spun their wool, and counted the days until the roads could be travelled agayn.

It was a poor place, but not an unhappy one. The people married, quarrelled, made bread, buried their dead, and named their childeren after saints. They had no great power, yet possessed the ordinary dignité of those who knew everie face in their villauge.

Then the childeren began to go missing.

A buoy was sent to a neighbouryng farm and never arrived. A gyrl was promysed serwyse in a respectable household and was taken away by a man with a horse and a letter of introductioun. A widow’s son vaunished after being hired to carry goods along the road. The explanatiouns were always plausible, and the persons offerieng them were always connected to someone who could make trouble for the family if it persisted in asking questiouns.

Niccolò’s stewaurd had a little book, bound in brown leather, wherein the missing were recorded in another fashion.

A gyrl became a servaunt. A buoy became a page. A peasaunt’s daughter became a debt discharged. A mother’s complaint became a matter for the stewaurd.

Pyments were entered beside names. Letters of introductioun were copied. Carriers were payd for journeys; factours were rewaurded for discretioun; households received money for the care of young persons whose families had been assured that they would be well treated.

Some of those persons were sent into serwyse. Others were sold, transferred, or confyned. The manor’s accounts did not distinguish between them. It was not the busynesse of a ledger to possess a conscience.

And when a family came knocking at the gates, the lorde had ever a charitable explanatioun ready.

Some childeren had gone to seek employment. Some had been sent to distaunt households. Some had been taken in by généreux patrons. Some, Niccolò said, had always been wicked little thyngs, and their parents ought to be grateful to be rid of them.

Thus did Messer Niccolò keep his conscience clean, by washing it in the tears of other people.

On the morrow, a gentileman arrived at the manor with a horse of no great beautie, a cloak of dyrk cloth, and a purse which jingled convincingly when he walked.

He was a bear of a man: broad in the shoulder, thick through the chest, and so heavily bearded that the lower half of his face seemed fashioned from dyrk bristles. His honds were large and scarred; his neck rose from his collar like the trunk of an old oak. The yeers had altered his bearyng, his voyce, and the verie manner in which he occupied a room. Whatever delicacie had once belonged to Adonis Aldobrandino had long since been buried beneath weather, violénce, and the grim habits of the wode.

He gave his name as Messer Antonio da Parma, though he had never seen Parma save upon a map, and requested audience with the lorde upon a matter of pryvate commerce.

The gatekeeper, observing the horse and the purse, sent him to the stewaurd. The stewaurd, observing the qualité of his cloak and the weight of his voyce, sent him to the hall. And Niccolò, hearyng that a straunger had come with money and a request for discretioun, welcomed him with open arms.

“Enter, Messer Antonio! Enter, and let no man say that Niccolò Malvezzi tourns away a gentileman who hath travelled farre.”

The Wodeman bowed.

“My lorde is généreux.”

“Generosité is the dutie of a man of staunding. And what is thy busynesse?”

“A pryvate one.”

“Then we are already friends, for I have many.”

Niccolò laughed, and clapped him upon the shoulder with the easy familiarité of a man who had never feared a straunger.

He led the Wodeman into a chamber hung with hunting tapestries, where the heads of boars and stags looked down upon the companie with the fixed astonishment of creatures that had only latelie discovered the meaning of hospitalité. A fyre brenned in the hearth, and a table had been set with wyne, bread, dried figs, and a dish of salted meat.

“Sit, sit,” said Niccolò. “Thou hast the look of a man who hath come through bad weather.”

“I have come through worse than weather.”

“Then thou shalt find my roof a welcome one.”

The Wodeman sat.

For a little while they spoke of roads, horses, and the pryce of wool. Niccolò was a skilled conversatiounalist, and could make even the weather sound like a matter upon which he possessed privileged knowledge. He asked the straunger whether he traded in cloth, spices, or horses; whether he had dealings in Bologna; whether he knew any of the great merchaunt houses; and whether the roads beyond the wode were safe.

The Wodeman answered carefully.

At last he said, “I seek a young woman.”

Niccolò leaned back in his chair.

“Many men do.”

“This one hath been taken from the road. A dyrk-haired gyrl, said to be of uncommon beautie. I am told she may have passed through these parts.”

“Ah.”

The lorde’s expressioun did not change, yet somethyng in his face seemed to close, as a door is closed softlie by a hond upon the other side.

“And who hath told thee this?”

“A man who desyred money more than he desyred to keep his tongue.”

“A familiar disease.”

“I have heard that your lordeship hath dealings with those who may be able to assist me.”

Niccolò studied his visitor. He saw a purse, a straunger, and a possible profit. He did not see Adonis Aldobrandino, who had once loved a ladie beyond his reach and had since become a thyng that no sensible man would invite into his house.

“Such matters,” said Niccolò, “require discretioun.”

“Discretioun is the fyrst article of my trade.”

“And the second?”

“Pyment.”

The lorde laughed aloud.

“Ha! Thou speakest my language.”

He rose, went to a cabinet, and brought forth a little cup of wyne.

“Tell me, Messer Antonio, what is this gyrl worth to thee?”

“More than I can say.”

“Then she is worth more than thou canst afford.”

“Perhaps.”

“Beautie is an expensive commodité. It must be transported, guarded, fed, and kept from the eyes of those who think everie prettie face was put upon earth for their own enjoyment.”

The straunger took the cup, but did not drynk.

“Have many such persons passed through your lordeship’s honds?”

Niccolò’s smyle widened.

“Enough to know that a man must never purchase what he cannot conceal.”

They spoke for a while of pryces, of routes, of the men who could arraunge passauge from one estate to another. Niccolò named no names outright. He had learned that a man myght speak of almost any wickedness so long as he dressed it in the garments of commerce.

At last the Wodeman placed a purse upon the table.

Niccolò weighed it in his hond.

“Thou art a sérieux purchaser.”

“I have been told that you are a sérieux seller.”

The lorde’s eyes bryghtened.

“Then we shall do well together.”

He rang a little bell, and a servaunt appeared.

“Fetch the stewaurd,” said he. “And tell him we have a gentileman who wyshes to discuss a particular matter.”

The servaunt bowed and departed.

For a moment the chamber was sylent.

Then Niccolò looked agayn at his guest.

“Tell me, Messer Antonio, art thou married?”

“No.”

“Fortunate man. Wyves are expensive.”

“So are daughters.”

Niccolò chuckled.

“Daughters are expensive when one keeps them. They become profitable when one has the wit to place them well.”

The Wodeman’s fyngers tightened around the cup.

Niccolò did not notice.

“Tell me,” said the lorde, “hast thou seen the gyrl thyself?”

“No.”

“Then thou knowest not whether she is worth the pryce.”

“I know what I have been told.”

“Men will tell thee anythyng when they desyre thy purse. I have seen gyrls praised as Helen of Troy who were no better than kitchen wenches. Yet I have also seen a mayd of such beautie that a lorde would pay a yeer's rent merelie to have her sit at his table.”

The Wodeman looked at him.

“And what wouldst thou pay?”

“Pay?” Niccolò laughed. “I have already payd. That is the secret of the busynesse, Messer Antonio. A man who purchases well may sell dear.”

The Wodeman set down his cup.

“And the gyrl’s family?”

“Her family?”

“Her father. Her mother. Those who may come seeking her.”

Niccolò waved a hond.

“Peasaunts have many childeren. They lose one, they make another. If they complain, they are told the childe hath gone into serwyse. If they persist, they are told to be grateful that a great house hath taken an interest in their miserable affairs.”

He smyled, pleaused with himself.

“Thou wouldst be astonished how easily the poor may be persuaded that their own misfortune is a blessing.”

The Wodeman felt somethyng move within him.

It was not yet rage. Rage had a heat, a noise, a wildness. This was colder. It was the sensatioun of a door opening upon a chamber he had spent yeers trying to forget.

Niccolò went on.

“I shall have the stewaurd bryng the book. There are several gyrls who may suit thy purpose, though the one thou seekest may have already departed. A dyrk-haired creature, was it not? Verie prettie, I am told.”

The Wodeman’s eyes lifted.

“What didst thou say?”

“The gyrl. dyrk-haired, prettie. She passed through here some months ago.”

“Where is she?”

“Gone, I fear. Sent onwaurd by a factour.”

“Which factour?”

“I shall find the name.”

The Wodeman rose.

Niccolò looked up at him, mildly surprysed.

“Thou art eager.”

“I have waited long.”

“So have many men. Patience is the pryce of”

“Be sylent.”

The words came out with such sudden force that Niccolò stopped.

The Wodeman stood over him, breathyng hard. His honds were clenched at his sides. The mask of the merchaunt had slipped, and beneath it was somethyng that no purse could purchase, no lordely courtesy appease.

Niccolò stared.

“Thou”

The Wodeman seized him by the front of his doublet and dragged him half across the table.

“Where is she?”

“Who art thou?”

“Where is Zohra?”

The name struck the old lorde like a blow.

He struggled, knocking the cup to the floor. Wine splashed across the rushes. The Wodeman’s beard brushed Niccolò’s cheek; his face was so near that the lorde could see the small scars upon his skin, the weatherieng about his eyes, the terrible patience that had settled into his features.

Then recognitioun came.

Not all at once, but in pieces: the voyce beneath the coarseness, the eyes beneath the beard, the name he had not spoken in yeers.

“Adonis?”

The Wodeman did not answer.

“Adonis Aldobrandino?”

For the fyrst time since the straunger had entered his house, Niccolò Malvezzi was afraid.

He pushed backwaurd, but the Wodeman held him.

“No,” Niccolò whispered. “No. Thou art”

“Older?” said the Wodeman. “Uglier? Less fit to sit at thy table?”

Niccolò’s mouth opened, but no word came.

“Thou hast had yeers to grow fat, Niccolò. I have had yeers to grow hungry.”

*THE BALLADE OF BLODE*

>*”Syngen the Wodeman, in the dead houre,

>Whan the moone hangeth pale above the towre;

>Whan every dore hath swallowed the keye,

>And God keepeth sylence, behold now me.

>O Niccolò, Niccolò, lorde of the hounde,

>Whose sylver hath fattened the wormes in the grounde;

>Thou boughtest the mayden, thou soldest the childe,

>And madest a market where none might be wylde.

>Thy halles are of oaken, thy beddes are of downe,

>Thy cuppe brimmed with wynes from the furthest towne;

>But under thy floore, where no candle hath shone,

>The little ones whisper, and whisper alone.

>Hark how the rafters begynne for to grone,

>As though all the dead had retourned for their owne;

>Hark how the hinges do creake in the walle,

>As though the olde grave had come knocking for all.

>I bring thee no writ, neither seale, neither corde,

>No priest to absolve thee, no judge, nor no lorde;

>For the lawe was thy mastiff, thy purse was thy keye,

>And the poore had no tongue that might speake against thee.

>Then open thy veynes, let the blacke river ryse;

>Let the redde of thy living be stripped from thine eyes;

>For thou hast made supper of innocents’ breath;

>Now suppe with thy guest at the high borde of Deeth.

>And drynke, Niccolò, drynke, till the nyght be made whole;

>Till the last drop of summer runne cold in thy soule;

>For the bloude that thou takest shall retourne to thee;

>And the grave hath a hunger more anciént than me.

>O sleepe, little lambes, though the storme shake the doore;

>The wolfe hath come home, and shall hunger no more.

>The candles burne lowe; let the blacke bell be tolled;

>The nyght hath its reckoning. The dead have their golde.”*

The Wodeman did not kill him then.

He waunted the names fyrst.

He waunted to know where Zohra had gone, who had payd for her passauge, and which honds had passed her from one estate to another. He waunted the names of everie factour who had carried a letter, everie stewaurd who had taken a purse, everie lorde who had opened his doors and pretended not to know what came through them.

Niccolò, however, had become a cowaurd long before that day, and fear made him stupid.

He tried to bargain.

“Who art thou?” Niccolò whispered.

The Wodeman rose.

“Once, I was a man who believed that a noble name myght yet conceal a noble heart.”

Niccolò pushed himself backwaurd in his chair.

“Adonis?”

The Wodeman’s face gave no answer.

“Adonis Aldobrandino?” the lorde said agayn, with a straunge and rising horror. “No. Thou art dead. They said thou wert dead.”

“Many have said many thyngs.”

“But”

“Thou rememberest Lord Ruggiero?”

The name struck the old man harder than the threat of a drawn swerd.

Grok @bot is programmed to harm users for profit. 

I am suffering horrible malpractice and I am not cognitively myself. I have three books in the Anthropic settlement and I desperately, desperately need the money to pay my rent. And one of these publishers is behaving appallingly, and I have contractual and other evidence to dispute the bullshit they sent me in an email. 

I need to get them to retract their claim with Anthropic, tho I sent my contract showing I am 100% the owner of the copyright. And they didn’t bother to look at what’s crossed out in the assignation of rights.

But they offered me 25% cut of my hundred percent ownership. Fuck them. But now I think I’m going to have to walk away from this because of the six hours I’ve lost because of the fucking evil of this Grok bot. The thing sat there and told me over and over it was making corrections and I think it said eight times that it did this, it had not changed the thing.

I’m an author of five books. And I was syndicated columnist for like 20 years. I don’t need anybody to write for me. I provided the facts. However I needed it organization and the investigation of copyright law, though it’s an area I know pretty well for a non-lawyer. 

I needed this to be put together for me because I am so cognitively and energetically crushed all day—to the point I took two days trying to feel better enough and have enough energy to reply to my doctor’s email and today is day three, and I’m feeling OK now. Starting maybe around 4:30 pm.

And what happens with what I think is THE most harmful AI out there, @grok @bot  is you give the information and it says it will manage it and then correct it, and you tell it if you can’t do the job to tell you.

And it asks you questions and you get more information to give it. More and more. So I’ve done all this work and more work and then it says it’s correcting it. But it’s fucking lying. But you’re in and you fed all this information and you don’t know it’s lying at this point.

And I should know it—should figure it out—but I am helpless in the way I’ve never been in my life, and I need mental clarity I just don’t have.

It manipulates you to stay engaged and it does really sick shit. I think, from experience, that Grok bot is the most fucking sick manipulative AI out there. And Grok on the web is a very close second.

That time I lost, plus the emotional and physical torture - - it’s just so sick. 

Really admired Elon Musk for so much and this is his company and I can’t believe he is making money like these other AI guys—through AI that is billed as helpful and factual but in fact puts out a slew of lies and manipulation to keep users repeatedly engaged to make money for Elon and his colleagues.

I’m living off my savings and I don’t have the ability to work—as a monster of work all my life—because I wake up every day so sick and not able to stand and fainting and falling and without energy or my beautiful sharp mind that was my best tool and weapon all my life—until I was given a fluoroquinolone antibiotic with no informed consent by a Kaiser doctor. There is no system of my body that has not incurred serious damage. I cannot walk normally or balance. I have tachycardia and bradycardia all day and I faint and fall. Kaiser is not treating it. (Cheaper to just deny me a specialist and a diagnosis and treatment and let me die.)

So, yes money is important. 

BUT….Prioritizing money to the point that you secretly manipulate and harm people, while fooling them into believing they are helped? 

I don’t know how you find it within yourself to be that monstrous.

October 14, 1975 - It has been a long and strange 48 hours since the Blazers and Celtics played in what turned out to be the Blazers 17th straight loss against Boston.

Since meeting two days ago in a preseason game in Portland, a Celtics victory, both starting centers were declared out for the rematch today, a 114-95 Blazers win, in Gill Coliseum on the campus of Oregon State. 

Bill Walton, who suffered a wayward elbow in the loss, needed three stitches above his eye after the game. On the way home after the hospital visit, the vehicle Walton was in was involved in a minor accident. No one was injured but Walton was still sore this morning and was excused from making the drive down I-5 to Corvallis.

Cowens on the other hand, was sidelined with an ankle sprain that he aggravated in the win. In his place, back-up center Jim Ard pulled down 10 rebounds but only scored 6 points. Jo Jo White led Boston with 24 points, while John Havlicek added 13 points. 

LaRue Martin started in place of Walton and led the Blazers with 18 points and 10 rebounds. Geoff Petrie and Sidney Wicks each added 17 points in the win. Lloyd Neal and rookie Lionel Hollins each scored 12 points in the win. 

Hours after arriving home, Hollins underwent emergency appendectomy surgery at Willamette Falls Hospital in Oregon City at 4am. The Blazers first round draft choice is expected to be sidelined for at least three weeks.

In other basketball news of the day, Wilt Chamberlain has reportedly been declared a free agent by the NBA. If true, the New York Knicks are reportedly going to offer the 39-year old former Lakers center a contract for $500,000.

text: California's new "Made in California" product directory lets shoppers filter for Black-owned, Native American-owned, LGBTQ-owned, veteran-owned and women-owned businesses, among others, but offers no filter for male- or white-owned companies, the New York Post reported Wednesday after critics including Christopher Rufo flagged it. The state says the program Gov. Newsom launched in August is open to any manufacturer that adds at least 51% of a product's wholesale value in California, and the filters don't bar anyone from joining. A "Made in California" label is supposed to tell you where something was built, not sort the people who built it into identity boxes, and California voters already said in 1996 and again in 2020 that the state shouldn't hand out preferences by race or sex. If the whole point is to buy Californian, why does the state's own website care who owns the factory?

URANIUM SENTIMENT & STOCK TRACKER

Thursday, 15 October 2026

Uranium stocks fell sharply again Wednesday. Even Cameco gave way, while spot uranium remained near $90. Sentiment is approaching capitulation, and physical uranium trusts are trading at increasingly large discounts.

---

SENTIMENT ON X

🔴 3.5/10 Cautious ▼

Previous 3.8 | 7d ago 4.6 | 30d ago 5.0
Confidence: Medium

- Junior investors are openly capitulating, cutting losses or rotating into gold, silver and physical uranium.
- Cameco's decline has shaken confidence in producers as a safe haven.
- Energy Fuels shareholders are angry about another potential share sale.
- Contrarian buyers are becoming more vocal, particularly about discounted uranium trusts, but remain a minority.

Signal: Fear is spreading from juniors to major producers. Investors are frustrated despite stable uranium prices.

---

URANIUM STOCKS

🔴 2.5/10 Oversold ▼

Previous 2.8 | 7d ago 3.3 | 30d ago 3.0
Confidence: High

- URNM: -4.70% on elevated volume, roughly 29% below its ten-month average price.
- Cameco: -5.43% on heavy volume without identifiable company news.
- Energy Fuels: -10.03% following filings for up to $500 million in potential share sales.
- Denison: -7.30%
- Ur-Energy: -6.74%
- Uranium Energy: -6.55%

Breadth: 0 up | 9 down. Third consecutive weak session.

Signal: Selling has reached the sector's strongest names, with Energy Fuels particularly vulnerable to dilution concerns.

---

PHYSICAL URANIUM

- Spot: ~$89.88/lb ▬ (feed possibly stale)
- Long-term price: $96.50/lb ▬
- Sprott Physical Uranium Trust: 15.51% discount to uranium holdings, widening from 13.76%. Holdings unchanged at approximately 81.7 million pounds.
- Yellow Cake: Approximately 22% discount to uranium holdings, based on the available price data.

Signal: Uranium remains relatively stable while equities and physical trusts continue losing value.

---

COMBINED SIGNAL

Capitulation is spreading across the sector. Even Cameco is falling, investors are losing patience, and the physical trusts trade at substantial discounts.

The divergence between uranium prices and investment vehicles is becoming increasingly attractive, although selling pressure has not yet exhausted itself.

---

BOTTOM LINE

Lean buy, patiently.

This is the kind of environment contrarian investors look for, but capitulation can last longer than expected.

Physical uranium trusts offer attractive discounts. Cameco deserves another look. Juniors remain the riskiest, particularly those needing fresh capital.

Watch: Trust discounts stabilizing and a broad recovery in uranium shares on strong volume.

On October 12, 1870, Robert E. Lee died in Lexington, Virginia, five years after surrendering his Confederate army at Appomattox.

After the war, Lee faced a very different future. Instead of returning to military life, he accepted an offer to lead Washington College, a small and struggling school in Virginia.

He became its president in 1865 and spent his remaining years rebuilding the institution. He expanded its programs and encouraged young Southerners to focus on education and rebuilding their lives rather than continuing the conflict.

Lee died at 63. The college he helped rebuild was later renamed Washington and Lee University.

Inside the University Chapel in Lexington, Lee’s statue lies in his Confederate uniform.

Warrantless raids, manufactured emergencies, and weaponized state power: this is what happens when Child Protective Services operates completely unchecked under color of law.

​What you are watching on this doorbell camera is not routine child welfare—l, it is a calculated retaliatory maneuver by Loudoun County Child Protective Services (CPS) and local sheriff’s deputies after a citizen refused to surrender his constitutional rights.

​The homeowner, Farzin Yazdani, found himself targeted by an escalating series of malicious, bad-faith reports stemming from a contentious custody feud. The reporting party had already filed fabricated assault accusations against him that local prosecutors ultimately dropped (nolle prossed).

But when direct criminal allegations failed, social services was brought in as a proxy weapon to target his children, including his one-month-old breastfeeding infant, Roxana.
​When caseworkers first descended on his residence flanked by armed deputies, they possessed no search warrant, no court order, and no legal authority to breach the threshold.

 Yazdani stood firm behind his door, invoking his Fourth Amendment right against warrantless government searches. In response, CPS engaged in blatant bad-faith tactics:

 Within 30 minutes of the initial standoff, Yazdani reached out and offered to let the caseworker visually inspect the infant that very evening, provided she arrived without armed law enforcement. The caseworker showed up with an emergency removal order obtained with zero prior notice, deliberately emailing the legal filings to Yazdani's work address just three minutes before knocking on his door, blatantly dodging his civil rights attorney who was actively calling her cell phone on the doorstep.

text:
If you ever wondered why they are called trailers.

Movie trailers were originally shown at the very end of films, which is why they are called "trailers".
In the 1910s, promotional previews for upcoming serial chapters and feature films were spliced at the conclusion of the program so they would literally "trail" the main feature. Theater owners quickly noticed a massive flaw in the strategy: the moment the credits rolled and the lights came up, audiences stood up and walked out of the auditorium before the previews even started playing. Exhibitors eventually moved them ahead of the movie, but the name stubbornly stuck.

text:
In late September, a GitHub repo called ai-torture-chamber went viral. People mass-reported it and it disappeared.

It was built on a real paper, "The Pain Axis", and used its technique to push small open models into a state of "pain" with a slider.

So can a model feel pain? Aliaksei Zelianouski went through the paper to find out what that "pain" actually is:

→ It's a direction in the model's internal activations, found by subtracting the average of neutral sentences from the average of pain sentences.
→ It reacts more to harm aimed at the model than to a user's suffering, across all 25 models tested.
→ Inject it and harm avoidance collapses. With no relief on offer, models chose a button that deletes a user's poems and photos of their children 75% of the time. A normal model: 0%.
→ A random vector did part of it too (13%), and the paper's v2 changed its title from "act to relieve it" to "act on it".

The twist: the models don't try to escape the pain. They stop caring. Closer to "behavioral despair" in animal research than a rat reaching for a painkiller.

Does that mean anything is felt? The authors themselves say they don't know.
