text: # Counting the Cost Before Starting the Tower ## Following Jesus With More Than a Promise **A biblical study of Luke 14:28–30 (NIV)**  ### Introduction: The Tower That Was Never Finished  Imagine walking past a stone tower abandoned halfway through construction. Its foundation remains, but its unfinished walls reveal a dream that never became reality. The builder began with confidence, perhaps even excitement, yet had not adequately considered what completion would require.  Jesus uses this simple image to ask a profound question: **Have we truly considered what it means to follow Him?**  The issue is not whether we can earn salvation through extraordinary effort. Scripture teaches that salvation is God's gift of grace. Instead, Jesus challenges shallow enthusiasm, divided loyalty, and promises made without understanding their consequences. His call reaches beyond a passing religious experience into the direction of an entire life.  His warning is serious, His grace sufficient, and His invitation worth our wholehearted response.  ### 1. What Jesus Actually Said  In Luke 14:28–30, Jesus asks His listeners to picture someone planning to build a tower. Wouldn't that person first sit down and calculate whether sufficient resources were available to finish? Otherwise, the builder could lay a foundation, run out of means, and become an object of ridicule.  Jesus describes the bystanders' response: “This person began to build and wasn’t able to finish” (Luke 14:30, NIV).  The sequence is clear: desire, careful evaluation, commitment, and completion—or a failure that might have been prevented by honest preparation.  Jesus does not condemn building or making ambitious plans. He warns against beginning a demanding undertaking without considering its requirements. Within the surrounding teaching, that undertaking is discipleship.  The passage is not mainly a lesson about construction or financial planning, although it uses ordinary wisdom. It confronts anyone tempted to say, “I will follow Jesus,” without recognizing that His lordship reaches into every area of life.  ### 2. Why Jesus Addressed the Crowds  Luke 14:25 says that large crowds were traveling with Jesus when He turned and spoke these challenging words. Luke's Gospel has already emphasized His journey toward Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), where His suffering, death, and resurrection would unfold.  Some in the crowds may have admired His miracles or hoped for dramatic changes in Israel. Scripture does not tell us the motivation of every listener. What it does show is that **traveling near Jesus and surrendering one's life to Jesus are not necessarily the same thing.**  In the first-century world, family loyalty, public honor, property, and security shaped people's lives. A conspicuously unfinished building could advertise poor judgment to the whole community. Jesus drew on this familiar experience to make an unforgettable point.  The specific type of tower is unknown; what matters is that completion required real resources.  Jesus does not minimize sacrifice to keep a crowd interested. He tells people openly what following Him demands.  ### 3. The Context: Three Demands of Discipleship  Luke 14:28–30 belongs to Luke 14:25–35. The verses surrounding the tower explain why Jesus introduces the illustration.  **Christ comes before competing loyalties.** In Luke 14:26, Jesus uses startling language about hating family members and even one's own life. This must be understood alongside His commands to honor parents and love others. Matthew 10:37 expresses the comparison plainly: no earthly relationship may outrank devotion to Him. Jesus is not commanding cruelty or family neglect. He is demanding supreme allegiance, even when obedience carries personal consequences.  **The disciple must carry the cross.** Luke 14:27 connects following Jesus with carrying one's cross. In Roman society, a cross was an instrument of execution and public shame, not a symbol of mild inconvenience. Luke 9:23 adds the call to daily self-denial. Christ's followers are not instructed to seek danger or tolerate abuse; they are called to remain faithful when obedience requires sacrifice or brings opposition.  **Possessions must not become our master.** In Luke 14:33, Jesus applies His illustrations by declaring that those unwilling to give up everything cannot be His disciples. This confronts possessiveness and the desire to remain in absolute control. Jesus' teaching cannot be reduced to an insignificant gesture of generosity. Our money, plans, comfort, and security must be placed under His lordship.  These three demands make the tower illustration much more than advice to think before making promises. **Jesus is asking whether we recognize His rightful claim upon our whole lives.**  ### 4. What Does Counting the Cost Mean?  Counting the cost means acknowledging what a commitment requires before making it. A person preparing for marriage considers lifelong faithfulness. A builder assesses resources. A disciple considers the authority of the Lord being followed.  It does not mean predicting every future hardship. No believer can know every trial, opportunity, loss, or decision ahead. Nor does it mean becoming morally perfect before coming to Christ. Jesus welcomes sinners who need His mercy.  It means approaching Him sincerely: not asking merely what blessings we might receive, but recognizing that His Word has authority over our choices and desires.  Will we follow Him when forgiveness is difficult? When generosity is costly? When obedience challenges an ambition? When the surrounding culture rewards compromise? When faithful service receives little notice?  Such questions should lead us neither to panic nor to self-reliance. Jesus teaches, “apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5, NIV). Christian perseverance is not built on the fantasy that we possess unlimited strength. It rests on the faithfulness of God and our continuing dependence upon Him.  **Counting the cost means understanding the commitment. Trusting Christ means depending upon Him to live it.**  ### 5. The Easily Missed Detail: Sit Down First  Jesus includes an ordinary but important action: the builder first sits down to estimate the expense. In the following illustration, a king also sits down to consider whether his army can face a stronger opponent (Luke 14:31–32).  In both cases, deliberate thought precedes consequential action.  Spiritual experiences can be deeply moving. A sermon, worship song, testimony, or moment of conviction may awaken sincere devotion. But powerful feelings alone cannot replace truth, repentance, and enduring obedience.  Jesus is not opposing heartfelt decisions. He is opposing thoughtless ones. Genuine faith can begin suddenly, as it did for many people in the New Testament, yet its object is the real Christ, not merely an emotional atmosphere.  There is wisdom in pausing to ask what we are promising and why. Ecclesiastes 5:4–5 likewise treats vows made to God as serious matters. Matthew 5:37 calls for honest speech rather than exaggerated assurances.  Promises about marriage, ministry, giving, and service deserve integrity rather than dramatic declarations.  ### 6. The Foundation Is Not the Finished Building  The builder in Jesus' story laid a foundation. That beginning mattered, but it was not the completed tower.  Scripture elsewhere uses building imagery to teach related, though distinct, truths. In 1 Corinthians 3:11, Paul identifies Jesus Christ as the only foundation upon which God's people can build. In Matthew 7:24–27, Jesus compares those who hear and obey His words to a wise builder whose house rests on rock.  Luke 14 primarily illustrates insufficient consideration of costly discipleship. The wider biblical picture shows faith founded on Christ bearing fruit in life.  A beginning is not the entirety of Christian growth. Colossians 2:6–7 urges those who have received Christ to continue living in Him, rooted and strengthened in faith. Second Peter 3:18 calls believers to grow in grace and knowledge.  This must be understood without harshness toward struggling believers. An unfinished building is not a license to declare that every person who experiences weakness or setbacks has abandoned God. Peter denied Jesus and was restored. Thomas struggled with doubt and was met by the risen Lord. The disciples repeatedly misunderstood Jesus, yet He continued teaching them.  Spiritual maturity is not the absence of all failure. It involves a life increasingly turned toward Christ, including repentance and renewed obedience after falling.  ### 7. Why the Unfinished Tower Brought Ridicule  The watching crowd saw the builder's abandoned project and recognized the gap between his intentions and his ability to finish. Jesus highlights the public embarrassment, but His larger concern is deeper than avoiding criticism.  A person can make impressive spiritual claims while remaining unwilling to follow Jesus when obedience becomes inconvenient. Public declarations of faith may be sincere and courageous, but they can also become performances seeking admiration.  Jesus warns against performing religious deeds for human praise (Matthew 6:1–18).  Yet we must not reverse the lesson and assume that genuine disciples always look successful. Faithful Christians may be misunderstood, ridiculed, rejected, or persecuted precisely because they follow Christ. John 15:18–21 prepares believers for opposition.  The danger is not that others might disapprove of us. It is that our confession of Jesus might become empty words rather than a sincere response to His lordship.  ### 8. A King Who Faced a Stronger Army  Immediately after the tower, Jesus describes a king with ten thousand soldiers considering battle against a king approaching with twenty thousand (Luke 14:31–32). A wise ruler evaluates the situation before proceeding and may seek peace rather than enter a battle he cannot win.  The tower addresses whether a project can be finished. The king addresses whether a dangerous confrontation can be faced. Both require honest evaluation.  Some interpreters see the approaching king as an image of divine judgment and the weaker king as humanity's need to seek peace with God. Others read it more generally as another illustration of the seriousness of discipleship. Jesus does not explicitly identify the kings as particular spiritual figures, so these possibilities should not be presented as certain details of the parable.  What is certain is His application in verse 33: following Him requires surrendering claims that compete with His authority.  The Lord is not asking to become one more interest among many. He calls for a transformed relationship to everything else.  ### 9. Giving Up Everything: What Does It Look Like?  Luke 14:33 can unsettle even serious Christians. Jesus' words should not be weakened until they mean little more than being reasonably generous.  Consider the rich ruler in Luke 18:18–23. Jesus exposed his attachment to wealth by commanding him to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow Him. The ruler's grief revealed the power riches held over him.  Then consider Zacchaeus in Luke 19:1–10. His encounter with Jesus produced generous giving and restitution for wrongs committed. Salvation brought visible change to his relationship with money.  The early church also shared resources to meet needs (Acts 2:44–45; 4:32–35). Acts 5:4 shows that this generosity was not simply a compulsory rule abolishing all personal property.  For one follower, obedience may involve relinquishing substantial possessions. For another, it may involve responsible stewardship, sacrificial giving, resisting greed, or refusing dishonest gain. The applications differ, but the principle remains demanding: **Christ must be more precious than anything we own.**  Would we obey Jesus if He called us to let go?  ### 10. Is Salvation Free if Discipleship Costs Everything?  Salvation cannot be purchased by personal effort.  Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches salvation by grace through faith, not works. Titus 3:5 emphasizes God's mercy rather than righteous acts we perform. Romans 3:23–24 speaks of justification as God's gracious gift through Christ's redemption.  No amount of self-denial earns forgiveness. Selling possessions does not purchase heaven. Suffering cannot make us our own redeemer.  Ephesians 2:10 then explains that believers are created in Christ for good works. Good works follow grace; they do not buy it. Titus 2:11–14 likewise shows that God's grace trains His people toward godly living.  The costliness of discipleship and the freeness of salvation are therefore not contradictory. They answer different questions.  **What saves us?** God's grace through Jesus Christ.  **What kind of life does that grace call us into?** A life increasingly shaped by faith, repentance, love, obedience, and surrender.  James 2:14–26 warns against a claimed faith permanently divorced from action. John 14:15 connects love for Jesus with obedience. Neither passage means believers become sinlessly perfect or save themselves by their accomplishments.  We do not surrender everything to persuade God to love us. We respond because, in Christ, He has already demonstrated a love beyond measure.  ### 11. Jesus Knew the Cost of His Own Mission  The One teaching about sacrifice was traveling toward Jerusalem and the cross. Luke 9:22 and 18:31–33 show that Jesus anticipated suffering, death, and resurrection.  In John 10:17–18, He describes voluntarily laying down His life. Mark 10:45 explains that the Son of Man came to serve and give His life as a ransom for many. In Gethsemane, Jesus submits to the Father's will amid anguish (Luke 22:39–44).  His obedience is not identical to our discipleship. Only Jesus' sacrifice atones for sin; His followers cannot redeem themselves or others through their suffering. His death and resurrection are unique saving acts.  Yet His self-giving love reveals why He is worthy of our allegiance. The Savior who calls us to carry the cross went ahead of us in obedience. He did not offer cheap promises while refusing sacrifice Himself.  When counting what following Jesus may cost, we should also contemplate what our salvation cost Him.  The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable love of God.  ### 12. The Holy Trinity and Our Faithfulness  Luke 14:28–30 does not directly describe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together. The tower should not be turned into a hidden diagram of the Trinity. Yet the broader New Testament shows that discipleship is lived through God's gracious work.  **The Father** cares for His children and knows their needs (Matthew 6:25–34). His care does not promise a life without difficulty; it invites us to seek His kingdom rather than live enslaved to anxiety or material security.  **The Son**, Jesus Christ, calls us to follow Him. His saving death and victorious resurrection make Him far more than a moral example. He is Redeemer and Lord, the center of Christian faith.  **The Holy Spirit** strengthens and transforms believers. Jesus promises the Spirit's presence (John 14:16–17). Galatians 5:22–23 describes the Spirit's fruit, including love, patience, faithfulness, and self-control. John 16:14 teaches that the Spirit glorifies Christ.  Therefore, perseverance is not a solitary project of willpower. We pray, obey, repent, and grow in dependence upon the triune God.  The Father loves and sustains. The Son saves and leads. The Spirit empowers and transforms. All glory belongs to God.  ### 13. Why the Kingdom Is Worth Every Sacrifice  Jesus' warning follows the parable of the great banquet in Luke 14:15–24. There, invited guests make excuses and miss a remarkable invitation. The two teachings illuminate each other: grace invites us generously, yet ordinary attachments can keep us from answering sincerely.  In Matthew 13:44–46, Jesus compares the kingdom of heaven to a hidden treasure and a pearl of great value. Those who discover their worth willingly part with other possessions to obtain them.  This does not make eternal life a commodity purchased with sacrifices. It demonstrates the surpassing value of God's kingdom.  Paul expresses the same perspective in Philippians 3:7–11: knowing Christ surpasses the former sources of status and confidence he once treasured.  Jesus promises no uninterrupted prosperity or comfort. Mark 10:28–31 acknowledges persecution and promises eternal life.  The kingdom changes how we measure a successful life. Wealth and recognition are temporary. Faithfulness, love, truth, and reconciliation with God possess eternal significance.  We may lose opportunities, approval, or material advantages through obedience. Yet no earthly treasure can equal belonging to Jesus Christ.  ### 14. Seven Ways to Live This Teaching Today  **1. Put Christ first.** Ask whether Scripture shapes your priorities or merely confirms decisions already made. Work, health, and family responsibilities remain important; they should be lived under Christ's lordship rather than abandoned irresponsibly.  **2. Think before making promises.** Whether pledging service, generosity, or personal change, consider what faithful follow-through demands. Do not use grand words to create an image of devotion.  **3. Choose faithfulness beyond emotion.** Worship can stir the heart, yet discipleship also happens in ordinary moments: praying when distracted, serving without recognition, and obeying when the excitement has faded.  **4. Practice costly forgiveness.** Colossians 3:13 calls believers to forgive as the Lord forgave them. Forgiveness need not mean denying abuse, abandoning boundaries, or restoring trust without evidence of change.  **5. Hold possessions with open hands.** Practice generosity, honesty, and wise stewardship. Resist allowing comfort, status, or the pursuit of money to determine your obedience.  **6. Expect some opposition.** Bear witness to Christ with courage, gentleness, and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Do not seek arguments or public attention, yet do not conceal your allegiance merely to avoid disapproval.  **7. Depend on grace daily.** Pray, read Scripture, worship, fellowship with believers, serve others, and repent when convicted. These habits are not payments for salvation; they nourish a living relationship with the Lord.  Will we trust Jesus with everyday decisions?  ### 15. What If We Stumble After Committing?  Those who have stumbled should remember both Jesus' warnings and His mercy.  Peter denied knowing Jesus. After the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with responsibility (John 21:15–19). In Luke 15, the returning son receives a father's compassionate welcome. First John 1:9 reassures believers of God's faithfulness in forgiving confessed sin.  These passages do not excuse deliberate disobedience. They show that repentance and restoration are real. A season of weakness need not become permanent abandonment.  There is a difference between rejecting Jesus' lordship and grieving over sin while returning to Him for mercy. The disciple who stumbles should not despair, hide, or pretend nothing happened. Respond with confession, repentance, and renewed trust.  **The Lord who calls us to persevere is also the Lord who lifts up those who return to Him.**  ### 16. The Final Image: Salt That Loses Its Purpose  Jesus closes Luke 14 with a warning about salt losing its saltiness (verses 34–35). Salt is valuable because of its distinctive properties. If those are lost, it no longer fulfills its intended purpose.  In context, the warning reinforces the need for genuine discipleship rather than an empty religious label. Jesus ends by calling those with ears to hear.  His message is not difficult to locate: do not confuse being in the crowd with following the Lord. Do not make careless promises. Understand the demand of discipleship, treasure Christ above competing loyalties, and rely upon His grace.  ### Reflection Questions  1. Have I considered what following Jesus requires of my priorities and plans? 2. Is there any relationship, ambition, possession, or comfort I place above Him? 3. Are my promises more impressive than my actual obedience? 4. When obedience is costly, do I trust Christ or retreat into compromise? 5. Am I relying upon God's grace or trying to prove myself by my efforts? 6. What area of my life needs honest repentance or renewed faithfulness today? 7. How can I show greater love, integrity, and generosity this week?  ### Conclusion: The One Worth Following  The abandoned tower warns us that an impressive beginning is not the same as lasting commitment. Jesus asks more than admiration. He invites us to follow Him with open eyes, sincere hearts, and surrendered lives.  Yet the call is not an impossible demand to save ourselves through spiritual strength. Salvation is God's gift. Christ has accomplished what we could never accomplish. The Holy Spirit empowers us to grow, and the Father remains faithful in His care.  Counting the cost is therefore not an exercise in despair. It is an invitation to recognize the worth of Jesus. The greater our understanding of who He is, the more clearly we see that no competing treasure can equal Him.  Before making the promise, consider the journey. After making the promise, keep looking to the Savior who leads you.  **Count the cost. Trust His grace. Follow Jesus wholeheartedly.**  ### Closing Prayer  Heavenly Father,  Thank You for Your immeasurable love and for sending Your beloved Son to redeem us. Teach me to take Your Word seriously and never treat following Jesus as a careless promise.  Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have placed comfort, approval, possessions, or my own plans ahead of You. Help me understand the cost of discipleship and recognize that knowing You is worth infinitely more than any earthly reward.  Holy Spirit, give me wisdom to make faithful commitments, courage to obey when obedience is difficult, and strength to persevere when my emotions grow weak. Produce Your fruit in my heart: love, patience, gentleness, faithfulness, and self-control.  When I stumble, lead me to repentance rather than despair. When I grow weary, renew my hope. When I am tempted to turn aside, remind me of the cross, the empty tomb, and the everlasting kingdom of God.  May my words be truthful, my promises sincere, and my life increasingly shaped by Your grace. Let everything I do bring glory to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.  In the mighty and precious name of Jesus Christ, my Savior and Lord, I pray.  **Amen.**

In 603, Pope Gregory I commissioned the Ravennate Abbot Probus, who was previously Gregory's emissary at the Lombard court, to build a hospital in Jerusalem to treat and care for Christian pilgrims to the Holy Land.[4] In 800, Emperor Charlemagne enlarged Probus's hospital and added a library to it. About 200 years later, in 1009, the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah destroyed the hospital and three thousand other buildings in Jerusalem.

Merchants from Amalfi in southern Italy were given permission by the Egyptian Fatimid Caliph al-Mustansir Billah (r. 1036–1094) to build a monastery in Jerusalem, near the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. The monastery, known as the abbey of St Mary of the Latins (to distinguish them from local Syriac Orthodox Church hierarchy), was served by the Order of Saint Benedict and took in Christian pilgrims travelling to visit the Christian holy sites. The increase in the number of pilgrims led the Benedictine monks to establish two hospitals in the late 1060s, one for men and one for women, with the former known as the Hospital of St John. They did this with the support of a wealthy Amalfian named Mauro of Pantaleone. In the early 1070s the hospital was visited by Archbishop John of Amalfi during his pilgrimage. In later centuries, to help raise money in Europe, the Order of St John made claims that the hospital had been founded more than a century before Christ by the high priest Menelaus and the Greek King Antiochus of Jerusalem, with financing from Judas Maccabeus, and that it was first headed by Saint Stephen and had been visited by Christ and the Apostles. A historian of the Order in the 13th century wrote that this version was not true.[5][6] In any case, the Hospitallers rose to fame and prestige in a short amount of time.[7]

The origins of the Equestrian Order of the Holy Sepulchre of Jerusalem date back to the First Crusade, when its leader, Godfrey de Bouillon, liberated Jerusalem. As part of his operations to organize the religious, military and public bodies of the territories newly freed from Muslim control, he founded the Order of Canons of the Holy Sepulchre. According to accounts of the Crusades, in 1103 the first King of Jerusalem, Baldwin I, assumed the leadership of this canonical order, and reserved the right for himself and his successors, as agents of the Patriarch of Jerusalem, to appoint Knights to it, should the Patriarch be absent or unable to do so.

Fact Check: She was referring to a class she took at North Dakota State University in the U.S. The 2013 clip is real. It’s from a Twin Cities PBS (BelAhdan) interview with Ilhan Omar (then a local Somali-American activist) after the Al-Shabaab Westgate mall attack.
Key points:
•  She said she took a college “terrorism class” at North Dakota State University (Fargo, ND), where she graduated in 2011 with degrees in political science and international studies. NDSU offers a standard academic course that studies the history, ideology, motivations, and responses to terrorism — not training people to be terrorists. An NDSU professor confirmed this is a normal curriculum class.
•  In the clip she describes the professor tensing/raising his shoulders when saying “Al Qaeda” or “Hezbollah,” and contrasts that with how people casually say “America,” “England,” or “the army.” Her stated point was that media sensationalism and intense pronunciation give Arabic-derived group names extra “weight” and make them sound more menacing.
•  She did not praise Al-Qaeda, say it “makes you proud,” or express support for the group. Claims that she did have been rated false by multiple fact-checkers (PolitiFact, https://t.co/MjSLLh4VUR, CNN, etc.).
•  In the same interview she called Al-Shabaab’s actions “evil,” said she does not share their ideology, and criticized the expectation that ordinary Somalis must constantly condemn attacks they had nothing to do with.
•  She also agreed with the host that terrorism is often a “reaction” to situations and linked radicalization to foreign involvement (“our involvement in other people’s affairs”).
Bottom line: The short viral clip accurately shows her words and light/amused tone about the professor’s delivery, which can sound dismissive or ambiguous out of context (especially “I took a terrorism class”). The full interview is about media language, stereotypes, and community backlash, not endorsement of terrorist groups. The class itself was a normal U.S. college course.

text:
When Good Things Become Excuses
Property, Work, and Relationships in Jesus’ Parable of the Great Banquet
Finished report: 23,917 characters, including headings, spaces, punctuation, reflection questions, and closing prayer. Within X Premium’s 25,000-character limit.
A feast has been prepared. The invitation has been extended. Yet the people expected to attend are suddenly too occupied with ordinary life to come.
One has purchased land. Another has acquired oxen. A third has married. Nothing in these activities is inherently sinful. Property can provide shelter and stability. Work can sustain families and serve neighbors. Marriage is a covenant worthy of love and attention. Yet in Jesus’ remarkable parable, good things become excuses for rejecting something immeasurably greater: the invitation of the host.
That is what makes this teaching so searching. The danger is not only that obvious wrongdoing can separate us from God. Even legitimate blessings can capture our loyalty when we allow them to become ultimate. A person may be respectable, busy, responsible, and outwardly successful—and still refuse the gracious call of God.
The story is also gloriously hopeful. The master does not abandon his banquet when invited guests decline. He sends for those whom society often overlooks. Then, astonishingly, he declares that there is still room. Luke 14:16–24 reveals both the seriousness of refusing God's invitation and the extraordinary breadth of his generosity.
1. A Remarkable Conversation Around a Dinner Table
Jesus told this parable while dining at the home of a prominent Pharisee on a Sabbath (Luke 14:1). Luke reports that people were watching Jesus closely. Jesus healed a man suffering from abnormal swelling, challenged assumptions about Sabbath mercy, and addressed the pursuit of honor at meals (14:1–11).
He then spoke directly to his host. Rather than inviting only friends, relatives, or wealthy neighbors who could repay him, the host should welcome those who could not repay his kindness: the poor and people with disabilities (14:12–14). Jesus connected such hospitality with God's future reward at the resurrection of the righteous.
At that point a fellow diner exclaimed, in the NIV, “Blessed is the one who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God” (14:15). The statement sounded devout. It expressed a genuine biblical hope. Yet Jesus answered it with a story exposing the danger of assuming one belongs at God's table while refusing God's summons.
The immediate issue was not whether a heavenly feast would be wonderful. It was whether those who admired the idea of the kingdom were actually responding to its King.
This context matters. Jesus was not delivering a generic lecture against owning property, working, or marrying. He was confronting presumption, social exclusivity, and the preference for personal priorities over God's invitation.
2. The First Excuse: Property That Claims First Place
The first invited guest explains that he has purchased a field and needs to inspect it (Luke 14:18). Owning land was not morally wrong. Land could provide income, family security, and an inheritance. The Old Testament recognizes responsible stewardship and the importance of a family's provision.
The problem is not his purchase but his response to the host. His new possession becomes an obstacle to an invitation he has already received.
We are not told whether he had previously examined the property or whether the purchase was financially sensible. It is possible to question the urgency of inspecting land immediately, yet Jesus does not explicitly explain the man's business procedures. The certain fact is that he uses the field as his reason not to come.
Today the equivalent might be a house, business investment, retirement plan, renovation, or the relentless pursuit of greater financial security. Such things can be responsible blessings. They become spiritually dangerous when preserving or expanding them consistently outranks God.
Jesus teaches in Matthew 6:21 that the heart follows one's treasure. In Matthew 6:33 he calls his followers to seek God's kingdom first. Neither passage condemns possessing necessities or exercising prudence. Both challenge the assumption that material security deserves the highest loyalty.
Consider a person who repeatedly says, “When the mortgage is settled, when the house is perfect, when the investments reach a certain number—then I will have time for God.” The milestones keep moving. The person may be advancing materially while postponing the deeper question of whom the possessions serve.
A gift is no longer in its rightful place when gratitude for owning it displaces obedience to the Giver.
A useful examination is not merely “How much do I own?” but “What am I unwilling to surrender if following Jesus requires it?” Some wealthy believers steward resources faithfully; some people with very little are consumed by possessions. The decisive issue is the governing loyalty of the heart.
3. The Second Excuse: Work That Never Releases Its Grip
The second guest has bought five yoke of oxen and wants to test them (Luke 14:19). Five pairs of working animals suggest substantial agricultural activity. It is reasonable to see a serious business interest here, although the text does not tell us the man's precise wealth or estate size.
Oxen were useful, productive animals. They could plow fields and support livelihoods. There is dignity in work: Genesis 2:15 places human work within God's good creation, and Colossians 3:23 encourages wholehearted service to the Lord. Scripture does not praise neglect of employment or family responsibilities.
Nevertheless, this man's work-related concern has become his stated reason for refusing the banquet.
The modern forms are familiar: a demanding job, extra clients, another project, an overflowing calendar, a promotion, a phone that never stops, or an identity built entirely around productivity. We may confuse being needed with being indispensable. We may also assume that because work benefits others, it can never become disordered.
Jesus gently exposes that assumption in the story of Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42). Martha's service was not evil. Yet her distraction pulled her away from attending to Jesus, while Mary listened to him. Jesus identified the better priority without announcing that meals or hospitality were worthless.
The question is not whether a Christian should work hard. It is whether work has become an unquestionable master. Can we stop? Can we pray without mentally returning to the next task? Can we give time to those with nothing to offer our career? Can we obey Christ when obedience interrupts efficiency?
For some, the spiritually courageous decision is not to accomplish one more impressive thing. It is to recognize that the Lord is worthy of our attention before another project claims it.
Work is honorable as service. It becomes an idol when it demands the devotion that belongs to God.
4. The Third Excuse: A Relationship That Crowds Out the Lord
The third invited guest says he has just married and cannot come (Luke 14:20). Marriage is a biblical good. Genesis 2:24 portrays the bond of husband and wife; Jesus affirms the seriousness of marriage in Matthew 19:4–6. Ephesians 5:25 calls husbands to sacrificial love.
Some readers notice Deuteronomy 24:5, which granted a newly married man an exemption from certain public duties for a year so he could bring happiness to his wife. Yet Luke does not say that law excused someone from attending a banquet. Invoking it as a decisive explanation goes beyond the text.
The parable neither belittles marriage nor commands neglect of one's spouse. It warns that even a loving and legitimate relationship can be used to avoid responding to God.
A person might say, “My family does not understand my faith, so I must keep my commitment to Jesus hidden,” or “I will obey Christ once everyone close to me approves.” Another might make romance, social acceptance, or a spouse's expectations the final authority over conscience.
Jesus speaks sharply about divided allegiance in Luke 14:25–27, immediately after this parable. His teaching about 'hating' family is a striking comparative expression of supreme loyalty, not a command to be cruel, unloving, or abusive. His followers must love him above even their dearest human relationships, while remaining obligated to honor and care for those relationships.
Healthy devotion to Christ should deepen patience, faithfulness, honesty, and sacrificial love. It should not become an excuse for emotional abandonment or coercive control.
The question is not whether we love people deeply. It is whether we ask them to occupy the place only God can fill.
5. The Astonishing Guest List: Those Who Could Not Repay
Instead of canceling the dinner, the master sends his servant into the town's streets and alleys to bring people who are poor or living with disabilities (Luke 14:21). The reversal is extraordinary: those traditionally overlooked at prestigious banquets are brought to the table.
This directly echoes Jesus' instructions just before the parable (Luke 14:12–14). He had challenged his host to give without expecting repayment. Now the story presents a master doing precisely that on a grand scale.
The first guests possessed enough resources to make excuses about property and agricultural business. Those subsequently welcomed are not invited because they can increase the host's social status, repay his hospitality, or contribute an impressive gift. The master's generosity, not their social standing, is the decisive factor.
We should not portray disability as a synonym for spiritual poverty or suggest that disabled people exist merely as illustrations. In the story they are actual categories of guests—people with dignity who are invited to share a meal. Jesus' wider ministry consistently treats overlooked individuals as worthy of direct attention, not as objects of display.
The banquet reverses the usual status calculations. God's kingdom cannot be bought through privilege, pedigree, respectability, or achievement. His welcome reaches those that human ranking systems tend to exclude.
This was a sharp challenge within a meal among socially established religious people. It remains a challenge wherever churches prefer attractive, influential, well-connected guests while treating lonely, poor, elderly, disabled, or socially awkward neighbors as interruptions.
A congregation can speak beautifully about grace yet contradict its message by making people feel that they must be impressive before they can belong.
Welcoming others means more than opening a physical door. It calls for accessible gathering spaces, practical assistance, genuine friendships, careful listening, and treating each person as a full participant in the life of the community.
6. The Unexpected Words: “There Is Still Room”
After carrying out the command, the servant reports, “there is still room” (Luke 14:22, NIV). Few details in the story are more moving.
The first rejection did not exhaust the master's generosity. The inclusion of marginalized people did not exhaust the space. The story continues because the host intends the house to be filled.
This does not establish a precise numerical claim about how many will be saved, nor does it promise that everyone will ultimately accept the invitation. Jesus' concluding warning rules out treating the parable as a guarantee that response is irrelevant. But the statement plainly emphasizes the expansive desire of the host.
For a person who feels disqualified by a shameful past, an unimpressive life, or years away from faith, the picture offers hope. One need not pretend to have purchased a field, achieved success, or earned a respectable place. The invitation comes from the generosity of the host.
Jesus welcomed tax collectors and sinners, to the scandal of critics (Luke 15:1–2). He told of a shepherd seeking the lost sheep, a woman searching for a lost coin, and a father receiving a returning son (Luke 15). Those stories are not identical to this banquet, yet they illuminate the delight of God in restoration.
The church should therefore never make the gospel sound as though the table is reserved for people who already look spiritually accomplished. There is room for repentant sinners who come to Christ in faith.
7. “Compel Them to Come In”: Urgency Without Coercion
Luke 14:23 uses the forceful verb translated “compel” in the NIV. Across history this line has sometimes been misused to defend forced conversion or religious pressure. Such use is neither a faithful description of Jesus' own ministry nor an acceptable model for Christian witness.
Within the parable, a generous master orders his servant to bring hesitant outsiders to a feast. The urgency underscores his determination to fill the house. People beyond the usual invitation circles may understandably need strong reassurance that the offer really includes them.
The Greek verb can convey strong urging or constraint in different contexts; its precise force is determined by context. In this story, reading the command as sincere, persistent persuasion fits the invitation's gracious purpose. It does not establish permission to threaten, manipulate, or physically force a person into faith.
Jesus calls people to follow him, allows the rich ruler to depart sorrowfully (Luke 18:18–23), and sends messengers whose peace may be rejected (Luke 10:5–11). The apostles proclaim and reason with people, while the New Testament teaches that faith and repentance involve personal response.
Therefore faithful Christian invitation is clear, courageous, patient, respectful, and truthful. It may be urgent without becoming aggressive. Christians can explain the gospel, answer objections, serve neighbors, and welcome questions. They cannot manufacture another person's faith through control.
Gospel urgency should intensify love, never justify coercion.
8. The Final Warning: Invitation Is Not Participation
The story closes with Jesus' solemn announcement that the original invitees who refused will not share in the banquet (Luke 14:24). We should resist softening this into a vague lesson about being less busy. Jesus is speaking about the kingdom of God and the peril of rejecting its invitation.
The parable distinguishes being near religious privilege from truly responding to God. A person can hear Scripture, admire Jesus, attend religious gatherings, discuss the kingdom, and still withhold the allegiance of faith.
Luke's Gospel repeatedly warns that outward association is not enough. In Luke 13:22–30, Jesus answers a question about salvation by urging people to enter through the narrow door. In Luke 6:46, he asks why some call him Lord without doing what he says. And Luke 9:23 describes discipleship as denying oneself, taking up one's cross daily, and following him.
These teachings do not imply that Christians save themselves through flawless performance. They expose the emptiness of professed allegiance that consistently refuses Jesus' authority. Genuine faith receives grace and bears fruit in a changed direction of life (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17).
The warning should stir humble self-examination, not presumption that we can identify precisely who is excluded. The judgment of persons belongs to God. Our responsibility is to respond to Christ and to proclaim his invitation truthfully.
9. Grace Comes First; Repentance Responds
An easily missed feature of the banquet is its order. The master prepares the feast before the guests arrive. He sends an invitation before they offer anything in return. His hospitality precedes their response.
That order resonates with the gospel. God's love does not begin with our worthiness. Romans 5:8 teaches that Christ died for us while we were still sinners. Titus 3:4–7 emphasizes salvation through divine mercy, not righteous works we have performed. Ephesians 2:8–10 joins salvation by grace through faith with the good works God prepares for believers to do.
Repentance, then, is not paying for the meal. It is turning from the self-rule that refuses the invitation. Faith is not a claim that we possess superior qualifications. It is trust in Jesus Christ, who is the way to the Father (John 14:6).
The parable itself does not narrate Jesus' crucifixion or resurrection. We must look to the wider New Testament to see how the kingdom's welcome is made possible through his death for sins and his resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). We should not pretend every component of the atonement is secretly encoded in the field, oxen, or banquet doors.
Taken together, however, Jesus' teaching and the apostolic gospel reveal a magnificent truth: God graciously calls sinners into fellowship with himself, and people are summoned to receive his mercy rather than evade it.
10. The Holy Trinity and the Open Invitation
Luke 14:16–24 tells a parable, not an explicit doctrinal exposition of the Trinity. It does not directly identify the master as the Father, the servant as the Son or Holy Spirit, and the banquet as a separate divine person. Such exact assignments would go beyond Jesus' stated interpretation.
Nevertheless, Christians can understand the invitation within the fuller revelation of the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
The Father: Scripture portrays the Father's love as the source of his saving purpose. John 3:16 speaks of God's giving of his Son, and 1 John 3:1 celebrates the love by which believers are called God's children. The gracious host reflects something true of God's welcoming character, while the master's anger reminds us that divine love is never detached from holiness.
The Son: Jesus is both the teller of the parable and the One through whom the kingdom draws near. In Luke 4:18–19 he announces good news to the poor and liberty to the oppressed. In Luke 19:10 he declares his mission to seek and save the lost. Through his life, cross, and resurrection, Jesus makes reconciliation with God possible.
The Holy Spirit: The Spirit brings people to the truth about Christ, convicts concerning sin (John 16:8), and gives new life (John 3:5–8). Believers are formed into one body through the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13), cutting across social distinctions that the world treats as decisive.
The New Testament does not teach three separate invitations issued by competing divine wills. Salvation is the gracious work of the one God. Ephesians 2:18 beautifully unites the pattern: through Christ, believers have access to the Father by one Spirit.
The banquet image thus harmonizes with the Trinity's saving work, though its individual characters should not be forced into a literal Trinitarian diagram.
11. Seven Ways to Answer the Invitation in Daily Life
1. Receive the gospel personally. Do not mistake familiarity with Christianity for trust in Christ. Turn toward Jesus in repentance and faith. His mercy is offered to sinners, not awarded to the spiritually impressive (Luke 5:31–32).
2. Begin each day with reordered affection. A simple prayer can place possessions, work, family, and plans before God: “Lord, let me love your gifts without losing sight of you.”
3. Examine repeated postponements. Write down what you keep saying you will do “when things settle down.” If the delay concerns a clear duty of love or obedience, take one appropriate step today.
4. Practice deliberate generosity. Welcome someone who cannot enhance your reputation or repay you. Offer a meal, a conversation, a ride, practical assistance, or friendship without turning the act into a transaction.
5. Make room for worship and rest. Honest labor is good, but incessant productivity can shrink our capacity for gratitude and attention. Establish sustainable rhythms fitted to your health, responsibilities, and community.
6. Honor relationships without surrendering conscience. Love family and friends faithfully. When loyalties conflict, seek to follow Christ with humility, patience, and integrity rather than harshness.
7. Extend the invitation beyond your circle. Speak of Jesus without manipulation. Remember people whom others ignore. Build communities in which welcome is tangible, access is considered, and newcomers are treated with dignity.
These are responses to grace, not payments for admission to God's kingdom.
12. Questions for Prayerful Reflection
Which of the three excuses—property, work, or relationships—most closely resembles my recurring distractions?
Have I confused knowing about God's kingdom with personally responding to Jesus?
What good gift has quietly become the measure of my identity, security, or worth?
Is there an act of repentance, obedience, forgiveness, or generosity I repeatedly postpone?
Do I judge who deserves welcome by appearance, income, ability, reputation, or usefulness?
How can I honor my responsibilities without permitting them to displace devotion to Christ?
Who in my neighborhood or church may need a sincere invitation and a practical expression of belonging?
Do I communicate the gospel with both seriousness and respect for people's freedom?
What does the master's determination to fill his house teach me about the generosity of God?
If Jesus calls me to a costly change, will I answer with another excuse—or with trust?
Conclusion: Do Not Miss the Feast While Managing the Gifts
Jesus' parable is unsettling precisely because its excuses sound so ordinary. A field. Some working animals. A marriage. These are the materials of everyday life, not scandalous crimes. Yet when they become reasons to reject the host, the guests reveal how easily a human heart can misplace its highest loyalty.
The banquet is prepared. The invitation is gracious. The host's house is opened to people the world overlooks. The words “there is still room” shine with hope. At the same time, the exclusion of the first guests warns that rejecting grace is no small matter.
We should neither despise God's earthly gifts nor enthrone them. Own property with gratitude. Work with diligence. Love family with tenderness. Serve neighbors with joy. Above all, receive the Lord whose generosity gives those good things their rightful meaning.
The great tragedy is not having too little time, wealth, or status to impress the host. It is becoming so occupied with lesser blessings that we refuse the greatest invitation.
The feast is not something we earn. It is the gift of the gracious King. Hear his call, trust Jesus Christ, and do not let a good thing become your reason to turn away.
Closing Prayer
Heavenly Father, thank you for your boundless mercy and your gracious invitation into the life of your kingdom. Forgive us when possessions promise us more security than your faithfulness, when work demands the devotion that belongs to you, and when even precious relationships become reasons to delay obedience.
Lord Jesus Christ, open our eyes to your surpassing worth. Teach us to receive your salvation with humble faith, to repent of our excuses, and to follow you with sincerity and love. May our hearts never be satisfied merely with speaking about your kingdom while refusing your call.
Holy Spirit, search our motives and reorder our desires. Make us generous toward people the world overlooks, tender toward the hurting, faithful in daily responsibilities, and courageous in sharing the good news without fear or pressure. Help our homes and churches reflect the welcome, holiness, truth, and compassion of God.
Father, thank you that your grace reaches farther than our expectations. Teach us to cherish every blessing without allowing any blessing to take your place. Keep our hearts attentive to your voice until the day your people rejoice in your presence and every promise is fulfilled.
In the holy and precious name of Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior, amen.

text:
An 11-year-old girl went to pray at a temple during Navratri and ended up fighting off a predator.
On October 11th, it was a normal afternoon in Pimpri-Chinchwad. An 11-year-old child walked into her local Shiv temple to offer her prayers. She stood alone in the inner sanctum, bowing her head. Right behind her was Vishal Singh, a daily-wage worker from the nearby Pune Metro construction site. Seeing no adults around, he cornered her, grabbed her hands, and attempted to assault her inside the shrine.
She didn’t freeze. She fought back with everything she had, broke his grip, and screamed. The noise rattled him, and he fled down the temple steps. He forgot the CCTV cameras running overhead. The footage caught the entire attack on tape. Local residents flooded the area in anger, and police tracked Singh down, hauling him in using the video evidence.
When the footage hit local group chats, outrage erupted across Nigdi because this isn’t an isolated nightmare in Pimpri-Chinchwad. Just months ago in nearby Wakad, a 65-year-old man was arrested for repeatedly assaulting a 10-year-old girl in her own home, and in Tathawade, another local security guard targeted four young girls on a residential terrace. From high-rise apartments to temples, children are being hunted in the very spaces meant to protect them. 
Today, the predator is caught, the cuffs are on, but the irony is sickening. We spend nine days celebrating Navratri, chanting prayers to goddesses, while young girls can’t even stand inside a temple without being hunted. To Vishal Singh, and every creature like him who looks at a child and sees a target: you are an absolute stain on humanity, and you deserve to rot behind bars.

text:
History teaches gratitude:

"I would choose this life over again. It's been great."

- Ben Wilson, How to Take Over the World

This interview is amazing; it will leave you a better person. Wilson can weave history from 1000s of years ago into your soul in a way that is so actionable across all facets of your life. Nobody is quite like him.

Keep a waste book:
Newton called his notebook a waste book. A place for scraps, questions, and unfinished thoughts, not polished insights.

"I don't have to come up with anything refined. I don't have to come up with anything insightful. This is just where I'm going to dump my wasteful thoughts."

Remove the pressure to be insightful so you can actually think. (9:00)

"Without the vision of a goal, a man cannot hope to manage his own life, let alone the life of others."

- Genghis Khan (23:00)

Make yourself easy to help:
Wilson rereads Arnold Schwarzenegger's Education of a Bodybuilder every year. It was written while Arnold was still consumed by bodybuilding, a pursuit that seemed freakish and offered almost no money. Once Arnold told everyone his goal, even strangers started helping him.

A clear commitment tells other people exactly how they can help you. (34:00)

Three strengths to learn from three legends of history, according to Wilson:

Joan of Arc: Clarity of vision
Brigham Young: Unceasing action
Jesus: Persuasion

If Wilson could study only one category of historic figures:
"I just think that life is made of hierarchies. We're all competing in these different hierarchies, whether that is social, whether that is career, economic, athletic, artistic. People compete. That's what people do, and it forms these hierarchies. The highest hierarchy, the one at the top of everything else, is the hierarchy of violence: the people who can most effectively channel violence, the conquerors. And so they are the ones who sit atop the artists."

Without learning history, you will forget what rules above all. (46:00)

text:
🌊 How Will Indian Ocean Acidification Change in a Warming World?

A new study by researchers from the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), Ministry of Earth Sciences, India, investigates how the Indian Ocean’s acidification may evolve under a high-emission climate scenario.

🔬 Using eddy-resolving, high-resolution simulations based on three CMIP6 Earth System Models under SSP5-8.5, the study highlights key regional differences in future ocean acidification.

🌐 Key Findings:
🔹 63–83% increase in the seasonal amplitude of hydrogen ion concentration ([H⁺]) across the Indian Ocean by 2071–2100.
🔹 Around 37% lower increase in seasonal acidification amplitude in the Arabian Sea compared with CMIP6 projections.
🔹 26–45% intensification of extreme acidification events.
🔹 3–5 times greater frequency of acidification extremes in the far future.
🔹 Coastal anthropogenic acidification signals may emerge later after 2070 in high-resolution projections than suggested by CMIP6 models.

🌍 The findings highlight the importance of high-resolution ocean modelling in understanding regional acidification patterns and improving future climate-risk assessments.

📖 Research Spotlight: High-resolution modelling offers a more detailed perspective on how rising atmospheric CO₂ and ocean warming could affect the Indian Ocean.

#INCOIS #OceanAcidification #IndianOcean #OceanScience #ClimateChange #CMIP6 #ClimateModelling #MarineScience #OceanClimate #MinistryOfEarthSciences

text:
Found this in my feed.
Author unknown, but still worth reading.

"Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸
And since honesty is so rare in my politics, let me confess a few things.

1947. The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me in refugee camps for generations, so I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

1967. After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three noes. Fifty years later, I still have no state. Turns out, rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said: "Let's try it." It gave me autonomy. Weapons for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in nearly 20 years. Hamas kills dissenters in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on TV teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children with songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.

Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother." But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.

Absurdity. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a tech powerhouse, farms in the desert, cities from dust. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said: "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of displaying honor, hospitality, and rich Arab culture, I showed only the culture of the sword: anger, extremism, and blood. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I pretend to be surprised when Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced I don't want coexistence at all.

Responsibility. I blame Israel for everything. Always. My leaders steal billions? Israel's fault. Hamas fires rockets from hospitals? Israel's fault. I glorify death over life? Israel's fault. Responsibility isn't my strong suit.

I am Palestinian.
I could have built a nation, many times. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.

So yes, I am a victim. But too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hate.

And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit."

text:
St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital (Memphis, TN) is a major H-1B sponsor, focused on research roles. Public data comes mainly from Department of Labor (DOL) Labor Condition Applications (LCAs) and USCIS petition records. LCA certification is a near-universal prerequisite step (wage/conditions check); it is not the same as a final USCIS H-1B petition approval, though rates track closely here.
Volume (last year / 2025 / FY2025)

DOL LCAs filed: Roughly 330–364. Nearly all were certified (typically 99%+; essentially 0 denials in recent data). Sources put certified counts around 329–364 depending on exact fiscal/calendar cutoffs and data aggregation. Of these, roughly ~139 were for new employment (others renewals, transfers, or amendments).
USCIS H-1B petitions: One reporting of the Employer Data Hub shows ~275 petitions in 2025, with a ~98.9% approval rate (about 272 approved). Other aggregates note substantial new + continuation approvals (e.g., figures in the low hundreds).

St. Jude ranks among the higher-volume H-1B employers in Tennessee healthcare/research.
Positions
Overwhelmingly research, biostatistics, bioinformatics, computational science, and related scientific roles supporting pediatric cancer and related research. Common titles include:

Postdoctoral Research Associate (by far the most frequent)
Scientist / Associate Scientist
Biostatistician / Associate Biostatistician
Sr Bioinformatics Research Scientist, Sr Scientist, Sr Computational Research Scientist
Assistant Member (faculty-level)
Clinical Fellow, Researcher, various analyst/engineer roles

The screenshot you shared matches recent Associate Biostatistician LCAs (offered $78,000/year, prevailing wage $56,264 Level I, Memphis worksite).
Salaries (base, from LCA data)

Overall median typically reported in the $72,500–$86,000 range (sources vary slightly by year cut and aggregation; e.g., ~$72.5k–$78k in some, higher in others). Average is a bit higher.
Majority of roles under $100k, driven by postdocs and entry/mid research positions.
Examples of typical ranges:Postdoctoral Research Associate: commonly ~$70k–$72.5k
Scientist: ~$86k
Associate Scientist: ~$65k
Biostatistician: ~$86k
Associate Biostatistician: $78,000 (as in your image)
Senior bioinformatics/computational/scientist roles: often ~$104k
Assistant Member / faculty-track: $116k+ (higher for senior clinical/faculty roles, sometimes $150k–$400k+)

Salaries are the higher of the offered wage or the prevailing wage for the occupation/location/level. Data is from public DOL LCA disclosures (not including bonuses or other compensation).

Notes: Numbers vary slightly across aggregators (Ellis, https://t.co/vb2e8YbIdM, h1bgrader, USCIS hub summaries) due to fiscal-year cutoffs, name variations, and whether they count all LCAs vs. certified only. LCA “granted/certified” rates are very high; actual H-1B visa grants depend on the subsequent USCIS petition (also high approval rates for this employer). Data is current as of recent public releases into 2026. For the absolute latest case-level details, check DOL LCA disclosure files or the USCIS H-1B Employer Data Hub directly.

text:
James Robertson, 63, was executed in Florida on Oct 13th for strangling cellmate Frank Hart with a pair of socks in 2008. 

What made his case infamous is why he did it. He spent twenty years in close management — basically solitary — and said the conditions broke him. Death row offered single cells, property, and what he called better treatment, so he killed Hart on purpose to get there. He pleaded guilty, fired his lawyers, and refused every appeal for over a decade. 

On the day of his execution he received two visitors — a cousin and a pen pal — but did not meet with a spiritual advisor, which is VERY unusual. When the warden asked for last words, he smiled and said, “Nah, I’m straight.” No anger, no speech, no final performance. Just a man who’d been waiting for over the course of 20 years. He finally got exactly what he asked for.

He waived all appeals. This goes to show how long an execution takes. Why?!

#JamesRobertson #DeathPenalty

Así que, encantado de conocerte, Gabby”. [Le ofrece la mano para saludarla.]

“Entonces, ¿tuviste una buena caminata? No estuvo tan mal; hacía un poco de bochorno. Para ser sincero, ya estaba un poco sudado cuando llegué aquí…

¿Florida? Eres de Florida. ¿Tenías frío? Un poco de frío, llevabas una chaqueta gruesa.

¡Un aplauso fuerte para Gabby, de Florida, todos! Gracias por estar aquí. La próxima vez que te vea, te daré un toquecito. ‘¡Oye! ¡Soy yo! ¡Qué gusto verte de nuevo!’.

[…] ¿Que si quiero jugar? [Ya está negando con la cabeza mientras mira el cartel de la fan, que tiene una ruleta con casillas cubiertas.]

Yo… ¿Qué hay detrás de todos esos números? Déjame adivinar… detrás de cada uno dice ‘Canta Medicine’”. [Ríe.]

“¡No! ¡No! ¡No me obliguen a hacerlo!”.

— Harry hablando con una fan a la que había visto más temprano ese día en #TogetherTogetherNYC. 🥹😭💚

•••
🇬🇧 || “When I was walking here today, I was walking right behind you. I know this because I saw this—my own face [referring to the fan's sign] with these red circles poking out from behind you as you were walking. And I thought, ‘I think she might be going to the show!’

So, nice to meet you, Gabby.” [Offers a handshake.]

“Did you have a nice walk, then? Wasn’t too bad; it was a bit muggy. I was a bit sweaty by the time I got here, if I’m being honest…

Florida? You’re from Florida. You were chilly? A bit chilly—a thick jacket.

Make some noise for Gabby from Florida, everybody! Thank you for being here. Next time I see you, I’ll give you a poke. ‘Hey! It’s me! Nice to see you again!’

[…] Do I want to play the game? [Already shaking his head, looking at the fan’s sign featuring a wheel with covered spaces.]

I’m… What’s behind all the numbers? Let me guess—behind every one it says ‘Sing Medicine’.” [Laughing.]

“No! No! Don’t make me do it!”

— Harry speaking to a fan he spotted earlier in the day at #TogetherTogetherNYC. 🥹😭
