text:
Vaping Damaged Lungs And Weakened Virus Defenses In Just Days, Research Shows | StudyFinds

In a Nutshell

- Brief e-cigarette vapor exposure damaged the protective lining of human lung cells and triggered a stress response that led to cell death.

- In hamsters, signs of lung cell stress and incomplete cellular repair were still present ten days after vaping exposure ended, even though the animals looked and acted healthy.

- Hamsters pre-exposed to vapor had higher coronavirus levels in their airways and lower activity of genes that normally help fight viral infections.

---

It took only five days. Five days of vaping was enough to leave lung cells struggling to repair themselves more than a week after the last puff, and hamsters given the same short exposure still showed weaker antiviral defenses ten days on, even though the animals looked completely healthy.

Researchers from National Jewish Health, the University of Colorado, and Colorado State University, writing in the journal JCI Insight, wanted to know what vapor from e-cigarettes actually does to the deepest, most delicate parts of the lungs: the tiny air sacs and blood vessels where oxygen moves into the bloodstream. Working with human lung cells in the lab and with hamsters exposed to vapor from a popular nicotine vape product, they found that even brief exposure sets off a stress response that damages the lungs’ protective lining, jams up the cells’ internal cleanup system, and leaves hamsters carrying higher levels of a coronavirus after infection.

Timing is what stands out here. This wasn’t the result of years of heavy use. Human cells showed damage after just 24 hours of lab exposure. In hamsters, five days of vaping was enough to trigger changes in lung gene activity and immune defenses that stuck around long after the vaping stopped. A separate round of experiments showed those weakened defenses carried real consequences when a virus arrived.

How Scientists Tested Vaping’s Effect on the Lungs

Researchers started small, growing human lung cells in lab dishes, including cells that line blood vessels in the lungs and cells that line the small airways deep in the chest. They also used thin slices of real human lung tissue donated for research. These cells and tissues were exposed to vapor from a commercial nicotine vape product, at levels meant to mimic what a casual vaper might breathe in.

That exposure weakened the protective barrier these cells form, in some cases almost immediately. Researchers measured this by tracking electrical resistance across a layer of cells, a way of testing how “leaky” the barrier becomes. Higher vapor levels caused more damage, and the effect appeared in both blood vessel and airway cells.

To understand why, the team found that vaping activated a stress pathway inside cells called JNK signaling, which normally kicks in when cells encounter chemical irritants or other damage. Once triggered, it set off a chain reaction. Cells tried to clean up the damage through a process called autophagy, a kind of internal recycling system, but the process got stuck partway through. Instead of finishing the cycle, waste material piled up inside the cells, growth slowed, and some cells died off. When researchers blocked the JNK pathway with a drug, the barrier damage and the stalled cleanup process both improved, pointing to this pathway as a central driver of the injury.

Why Vaping Damage Lingers in the Lungs

To see whether this damage sticks around, researchers used golden Syrian hamsters, chosen because their small airways more closely resemble human lungs than a mouse’s and because they respond to respiratory viruses similarly to people. Researchers exposed the hamsters to vapor once a day for five days in a row, then left them alone for ten days before examining their lungs on day 15.

By that point, the hamsters looked completely normal. Their weight was stable, and the microscope showed no visible signs of illness or lung inflammation. But a closer look told a different story. Lung tissue showed a fourfold increase in a protein called p62, a marker that builds up when a cell’s cleanup process doesn’t finish properly, the same stalled process seen in the human cell experiments. This buildup appeared in both blood vessel and airway linings. Researchers also found cell death still happening in lung blood vessels a full ten days after the last vaping exposure.

Gene activity in the hamster lungs supported this: researchers counted roughly 200 genes turned up and about 300 turned down compared with unexposed animals, though many of these changes still need further confirmation. Many of the shifts pointed to the same JNK stress pathway identified in the lab dish experiments, along with signs of tissue remodeling and changes in immune-related genes.

Vaping Leaves Lungs Weaker Against Viruses

Given these immune changes, researchers next tested whether prior vaping affected how hamsters handled a real viral infection. Animals were exposed to vapor for five days, then infected with SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, a few days later. Some animals were also given the flu virus beforehand to mimic a real-world scenario in which someone catches two respiratory illnesses close together.

Hamsters that had been exposed to vaping beforehand carried notably higher levels of SARS-CoV-2 in their airways than unexposed animals. Vapor exposure downregulates several genes involved in fighting viral infections, while increasing molecular signals tied to tissue remodeling and inflammatory pathways, even though the physical damage visible under the microscope was severe across all infected animals regardless of whether they had vaped.

Weight loss, a measure of how sick the infected animals became, told a more complicated story depending on sex. Female hamsters pre-exposed to vapor lost far more weight after SARS-CoV-2 infection than females that hadn’t vaped. Male hamsters showed the opposite pattern, losing less weight if they had been pre-exposed, though researchers caution that each sex group was small and this finding needs confirmation in future work. A prior flu infection seemed to offer some protection against the SARS-CoV-2 infection that followed, a known effect called viral interference, while vaping appeared to work against the body’s defenses, leaving more virus in the airways.

Why Vaping’s Lasting Lung Damage Matters

A few days of vaping left a mark on the lungs that outlasted the exposure itself, and that mark included a weaker ability to fight off a respiratory virus. A stress response that lingers quietly without obvious symptoms, paired with a dulled antiviral defense, complicates the common idea that vaping is harmless as long as someone isn’t coughing or wheezing. Lungs can look fine on the outside while cells inside are still working through an incomplete cleanup job, and animals that appear perfectly healthy can still be more vulnerable when a virus comes knocking.

Nope,

Afghanistan’s terrain strongly favors the defender: mean elevation ~1,880 m, highest peak (Noshaq) 7,492 m, extensive Hindu Kush ranges with peaks over 6,000–7,000 m, glaciers, narrow valleys, and harsh high-altitude winters. 

Combined with being fully landlocked, this creates extreme logistical bottlenecks and channels attackers into predictable kill zones - exactly why both the Soviets and the U.S. struggled.

Yemen is different. Highest peak (Jabal an-Nabi Shu’ayb) is only 3,666 m, mean elevation ~1,000 m. The western highlands offer some cover, but the country also has ~1,900 km of coastline, broad coastal plains, and large desert areas that are far more open to air power, mobility, and conventional operations. 

Saudi Arabia also shares a direct land border, avoiding the extreme supply-line problems of a landlocked high-mountain theater.

Rugged terrain helps insurgents in both places, but Afghanistan’s combination of extreme altitude, isolation, and scale is in a different category. 

Yemen’s mixed geography does not impose the same structural penalty on an attacker.

🚨WHY FULL FILE DISCLOSURE FALLS SHORT OF JUSTICE FOR EPSTEIN SURVIVORS

Instead of parading around Capital Hill, maybe Congress members (former & current) should have looked at the process they could have actually helped.
This proves it was all grandstanding, not assistance.

▶️Congress could pass federal legislation to permanently eliminate the statute of limitations for adult trafficking survivors.
▶️Civil attorneys could use the newly exposed records to launch new lawsuits against the financial enablers.
▶️State governors could sign absolute bans on child marriage to permanently shut down legal loopholes for abusers.
▶️The Department of Justice could look into the unredacted files to indict living co-conspirators under federal child sex trafficking laws.  The hurdle for the Department of Justice is no longer the clock, but ACTIONABLE EVIDENCE.

Following the recent mass release of millions of pages of unredacted Department of Justice files under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, public demands for immediate accountability have reached a fever pitch. However, legal experts warn that total transparency does not equate to judicial resolution. For the survivors of the decades-long trafficking ring, the true path to justice lies not in public document dumps, but in targeted civil litigation, legislative reform, and corporate accountability.

The unsealed records offer a meticulous blueprint of a systemic failure spanning three decades, detailing early ignored FBI tips from 1996, the highly controversial 2007 Florida Non-Prosecution Agreement, and the complex network diagrams of high-profile enablers. Yet, from a legal standpoint, raw investigative files are not a substitute for due process. Because Jeffrey Epstein’s 2019 jail suicide permanently terminated criminal proceedings against him, and because strict statutes of limitations protect many living associates from decades-old state charges, the criminal justice system faces severe institutional gridlock.

Furthermore, historical context reveals how deeply systemic loopholes protected abusers during the core era of the crimes (1996–2005). During those years, child marriage was legal in all 50 states. In key operational hubs like New York, Florida, and New Mexico, adults could legally marry minors via parental consent or unchecked judicial waivers. These marriages routinely triggered marital exemptions within statutory rape codes, effectively shielding abusers from felony prosecution. While modern legislative updates have restricted these loopholes, the legal system cannot retroactively apply current criminal laws to past conduct.

Consequently, legal recourse for survivors has shifted entirely away from prosecutors' offices and into civil courtrooms. Survivors have bypassed criminal dead-ends by utilizing temporary "look-back windows" established by state Child Victims Acts, which artificially revive expired statutes of limitations. 

Rather than waiting on federal indictments, victims have successfully pursued multi-million dollar third-party liability lawsuits against the major financial institutions and territorial governments that facilitated the enterprise. 

Moving forward, survivors and advocacy groups maintain that true recourse means converting the newly exposed data into actionable civil filings, stripping enablers of their wealth, and permanently outlawing the remaining legal loopholes that allowed the abuse to occur.

TAXPAYER COST
There is no official, unified figure for the total amount of US taxpayer dollars spent on the Jeffrey Epstein cases from start to finish. Because the investigations spans three decades and is fractured across dozens of separate budgets—including local Florida law enforcement, various state prosecutor offices, the FBI, the federal Bureau of Prisons, and multiple congressional committees—a single comprehensive receipt does not exist.

However, recent disclosures highlight specific taxpayer expenditures tied to the case:
▶️The Unredaction Mandate: 
According to Department of Justice insiders, reviewing and processing the millions of pages of records mandated by the Epstein Files Transparency Act has cost the agency between $4 million and $5 million in direct legal overhead and overtime pay alone.
▶️Grand Jury Requests: 
Administrative actions to prepare and process related grand jury testimony for release cost taxpayers an additional $167,000.
▶️The Opportunity Cost: 
These figures do not account for the tens of millions of dollars utilized in the multi-decade federal sex trafficking investigations, court trials (such as Ghislaine Maxwell's prosecution), or the heavy administrative cost of ongoing congressional oversight probes.

text:
Mothers are ALWAYS the best right?

In June 2008, 2-year-old Caylee Anthony vanished in Orlando, Florida.

Her mother, Casey, never reported her missing. For 31 days, she just kept living as if nothing had happened.

Whenever Caylee's grandparents asked to see her, Casey had an excuse. She told them Caylee was with a babysitter and doing fine. But no one had actually seen the little girl.

During that time, Casey went to nightclubs, spent time with her boyfriend, and even got a tattoo reading “Bella Vita.”

On July 15, Caylee’s grandmother finally called 911. She said her granddaughter had been missing for a month and that Casey's car smelled like a dead body had been inside it.

When police began investigating, Casey claimed the nanny had kidnapped Caylee. That story was false. She also claimed she worked at Universal Studios and even walked detectives into the building before admitting she had no job there.

In December 2008, a utility worker found Caylee's remains in the woods, less than half a mile from her home.

Casey was charged with first-degree murder, and prosecutors asked for the death penalty. They argued that Casey had suffocated Caylee with duct tape because she wanted freedom from motherhood.

Her defense offered a different explanation: Caylee had drowned in the family pool, and Casey’s father had helped hide her death. He denied it. 

But the prosecution had a big problem. Caylee's body had been outside for months, so no one could say exactly how she died. There was no weapon, no witness and no confession.

In July 2011, the jury found Casey not guilty of killing her daughter. She was convicted only of lying to police. With credit for the time she had already spent in jail and good behavior, her sentence was almost over.

Twelve days later, she walked free.

text:
@grok Among the eight countries shown, the practical answer for the safest and most affordable place to settle, once ordinary daily conditions are included, is a smaller or mid-size city in a lower-tax US state such as Texas or Florida.
National indexes alone ranked Canada highest on the combination of 2026 GPI safety (14th) and moderate Numbeo cost-of-living. That ranking treats each country as uniform and omits local variation, after-tax disposable income, routine healthcare waits, energy costs, and the ability to choose a specific location. When those factors are added, the ordering changes.
Canada’s national violent-crime rate is lower than the US average, yet many smaller US cities in Texas and Florida post rates competitive with or below Canadian city averages. Those same places typically have lower housing costs than Canadian major metros, no state income tax, and higher average purchasing power. Insured residents also obtain non-emergency imaging and specialist care far faster than Canada’s median waits of roughly 18 weeks for MRI and 28.6 weeks from referral to treatment. Energy costs are generally lower than in Germany or Switzerland. The US further allows internal relocation across climates and job markets without leaving the same national system.
Switzerland and Iceland rank highest on pure safety and quality-of-life composites but have the highest living costs. Germany and Australia offer solid middle paths with good safety and shorter routine waits than Canada, yet narrower internal choice and (in Germany’s case) higher energy prices. Israel and Russia rank poorly on safety due to conflict or geopolitical conditions. Canada remains competitive on national peace metrics and financial protection against catastrophic medical bills, but its combination of housing pressure in desirable areas, higher effective taxes in many provinces, and long waits for ordinary care makes it less advantageous for daily living than carefully chosen US locations.
The original reply answered only the narrow national-index version of the question. For an individual who can select location and obtain insurance, the broader set of everyday factors points to smaller cities in lower-tax US states as the stronger balance of safety and affordability among the options shown.

text:
The Windover Bog People
Titusville Florida, archaeologists uncovered 167 human bodies dating back over 7000 years.
Remarkably, 91 skulls still contained preserved brain tissue, likely because the deceased were buried within 48 hours, preventing rapid decomposition in Florida’s heat. The bodies were carefully placed: on their left sides, heads west, faces north, often in fetal positions, and staked underwater to prevent floating.
The site reveals a compassionate community: children clutching toys, a 50-year-old woman with healed fractures cared for over years, and a 15-year-old boy with spina bifida nurtured despite his condition.
Thirty types of edible and medicinal plants were also found, including elderberry, nightshade, and holly, suggesting herbal remedies. Windover offers an extraordinary glimpse into the empathy, healing, and sophisticated burial rituals of these ancient people.

#TheLostTribe #AisCoast

text:
I'd separate the queue of unsold homes from the prices of homes that actually trade

The 62.6% gap compares active listings with a modelled estimate of active buyers, using sales and buyer search time to infer the buyer side

A bigger queue gives buyers more room to negotiate, while owners with equity and flexibility can wait or withdraw their listings, letting inventory build before prices adjust

Geography matters too: Miami had 158.9% more sellers than buyers in September, while San Francisco had 10.6% fewer sellers than buyers, so a national number bundles very different negotiations together

I'd also check what the price statistic measures, since a median sale price moves with the mix of homes sold, while a repeat-sales index tracks changes in the same properties over time

For a particular house, I'd watch recent comparable sales, days on market and price cuts in that neighborhood before using the national gap to set an offer

text:
Mark Zuckerberg was 22 when Yahoo offered $1 billion for Facebook. His own team wanted him to take it.

He went to Steve Jobs instead.

Jobs told him to go to India.

Not to a conference. To a specific temple - the one Jobs himself had visited years earlier, when he was trying to work out what Apple was supposed to be.

Zuckerberg travelled for almost a month. He says it "reinforced for me the importance of what we were doing."

He came back and said no to Yahoo.

Then came the part nobody puts in the motivational version. Years later he described it himself:

"A huge amount of the company quit because they didn't believe in what we were doing."

"The whole management team was gone within about a year after that."

Think about who those people were. Facebook was two years old with around 10 million users. Anyone holding stock was being handed life-changing money and told to hand it back for a maybe.

They weren't stupid. They were wrong. Those are different things, and at the time nobody could tell which one they were.

Today Meta is worth more than a thousand times what Yahoo offered.

Yahoo offered a billion dollars. Jobs offered an address.

The people who walked out were right about the risk and wrong about the outcome.

Would you have stayed?

The video below is Zuckerberg telling this story out loud - he opens it by saying he's never told it publicly before.

If you liked this one, follow - I've got a lot of these.

text:
Texas has a ton of state parks that are worth a visit on your travels, some suggestions using Grok:     
                   📷📷📷30 sourcesTexas Hill Country (the central Texas region of rolling hills, spring-fed rivers, and limestone country roughly between Austin, San Antonio, and Fredericksburg) has one of the densest and most scenic collections of state parks and natural areas in the state.⁠ExploretexasstateparksHere are the main ones managed by Texas Parks & Wildlife Department (TPWD):Top Highlights
📷Enchanted Rock State Natural Area (near Fredericksburg) — The iconic pink granite dome. Summit hike with panoramic views, rock scrambling, camping, and dark-sky stargazing. One of the most recognizable spots in Texas.📷Pedernales Falls State Park (near Johnson City) — Broad limestone falls and river slabs, hiking/biking/horse trails, camping, and swimming. Strong all-around first visit.📷Garner State Park (on the Frio River near Concan) — Classic summer destination with clear river swimming and tubing, popular Old Baldy hike, extensive camping (including cabins), and a historic pavilion. Very busy in warm months.Guadalupe River State Park (near Spring Branch) — River access for swimming, limestone cliffs, cypress trees, trails, and camping. Frequently paired with nearby Honey Creek State Natural Area.Full List of Notable Hill Country State Parks & Natural Areas
Blanco State Park — Small, easy-access park on the Blanco River; swimming, camping, CCC history.
Inks Lake State Park (near Burnet) — Lake swimming (Devil’s Waterhole), boating, fishing, camping, and cabins.
Colorado Bend State Park — Rugged backcountry with Gorman Falls, caves/springs, hiking, and mostly primitive camping.
Hill Country State Natural Area (near Bandera) — Large former ranch (~5,000+ acres) with multi-use trails (hike/bike/horse), primitive camping, and solitude.
Government Canyon State Natural Area (near San Antonio) — Extensive trails, canyon scenery, and Cretaceous dinosaur tracks.
Lost Maples State Natural Area — Best known for fall color (bigtooth maples), canyon hiking, and camping.
Lyndon B. Johnson State Park & Historic Site (near Stonewall) — Living history farm, bison, trails, and Pedernales River access; adjacent to the LBJ Ranch.
Longhorn Cavern State Park (near Burnet) — Guided cavern tours through limestone formations.
South Llano River State Park — Spring-fed river, strong birding (including wild turkeys), camping, and dark skies.
Old Tunnel State Park — Tiny park famous for seasonal Mexican free-tailed bat emergences from an old railroad tunnel.
Honey Creek State Natural Area — Guided-access spring-fed creek preserve (typically entered via Guadalupe River SP).
Kickapoo Cavern State Park — More remote cave tours, bats, and rugged western Hill Country terrain.
Albert & Bessie Kronkosky State Natural Area (near Pipe Creek/Boerne) — Under development; expected to open in late 2026 with trails, camping, and conservation focus. Not yet open to the public.
Some lists also include McKinney Falls State Park (near Austin) for its waterfalls and easy access.Practical Tips
Fees: Typically $5–8 per adult (kids 12 and under free). A Texas State Parks Pass offers good value for frequent visitors.
Reservations: Strongly recommended for camping and popular day-use (especially weekends, spring wildflower season, summer river parks, and holidays). Book via the TPWD website or (512) 389-8900.
Best seasons: Spring (wildflowers, mild weather) and fall (hiking, foliage at Lost Maples). Summer is ideal for river/lake parks; winter is quieter for hiking.
Check current conditions, trail status, and alerts on the official TPWD site (https://t.co/10LCELUoKQ), as weather can close trails or affect river levels.
For the most up-to-date maps, fees, and reservations, start at the Texas Parks & Wildlife Department state parks page. The Hill Country parks pair well with scenic drives through towns like Fredericksburg, Boerne, and Johnson City.

text:
I recently spent an evening with a traditional Georgian family, and it completely redefined how I understand hospitality 🇬🇪✨
Everything you’ve heard about Georgians welcoming strangers isn’t an exaggeration. The moment I walked through the door, I was treated like a VIP.
Here are a few moments that stuck with me:
1. The Supra (Feast) 🍷🍽️
The table was literally overflowing. Cooking a spread like that would take me two solid days, but to them, this is just Tuesday. They genuinely love good food, gathering people, and celebrating life over dinner almost every single day.
2. The Wine 🍇
They grow their own grapes and make their own wine. I’m usually pretty sensitive to alcohol, but I woke up feeling completely refreshed. Pure, organic, homemade fermentation with zero additives makes all the difference!
3. The Definition of "Family" 🫂
In Georgia, the family circle expands to include everyone. Over the course of the evening, neighbors and friends just walked in unannounced. No formal invites needed — doors are permanently open. I met more than 20 people in a matter of hours!
4. The Next-Level Care 😅📦
When it got late, they flat-out refused to let me travel back at night and insisted I sleep over. The next morning, before driving me home, they packed half their fridge for me to take. You simply do not leave a Georgian household empty-handed (and they already made me promise to return for mandarin season 🍊).
5. The Location 🏔️🌊
A countryside home tucked into the mountains, with a clear view of the sea in the distance. The mountain air is so crisp that a week out there feels like it could recharge your lungs for an entire year in the city.
I’m still processing the whole experience. Coming from Ukraine, I’m no stranger to warmth, but the effortless, unconditional generosity Georgians offer to literally anyone who walks in is rare.
It’s a powerful reminder of how rewarding it is to move through the world with an open door and an open heart ❤️

Juror Atticus Haygood Henslee Answers the Accusations Against Him in the Leo Frank Murder Trial

October 7, 1913: The Defense Accuses Two Jurors of Prejudice, Henslee Challenges the Affidavits, and the State Prepares Its Answer

On Tuesday, October 7, 1913, The Atlanta Journal published an important statement from Atticus Haygood Henslee, one of the twelve jurors who had convicted Leo Max Frank of murdering thirteen-year-old Mary Phagan in Atlanta, Georgia. Henslee was answering accusations made by Frank's defense attorneys, who claimed that he had already decided Frank was guilty before taking his oath as a juror.

The controversy had developed more than five weeks after the guilty verdict. Frank's attorneys were gathering sworn statements from people who claimed they had heard Henslee and another juror, Marcellus Johenning, express prejudice before the trial began. If the defense could establish that either man had entered the jury box with a fixed opinion of Frank's guilt, it hoped to persuade the court to set aside the verdict and order another trial.

Henslee rejected the accusations. He acknowledged discussing Frank's guilt with several men in Sparta, Georgia, but insisted that the conversation occurred on September 2, 1913, eight days after the guilty verdict. His accusers maintained that he had expressed those opinions before the trial.

The dispute centered on a simple but important question: Were the witnesses remembering conversations that occurred before Frank's trial, or were they remembering conversations that occurred after his conviction and assigning them earlier dates?

That disagreement became one of the leading controversies surrounding Frank's motion for a new trial (The Atlanta Journal, 1; The Atlanta Journal, 2).

The Background: Mary Phagan's Murder and Leo Frank's Conviction

Mary Phagan was thirteen years old when she was murdered on Saturday, April 26, 1913. She had traveled to the National Pencil Company factory at 37–41 South Forsyth Street in Atlanta to collect wages she had earned before being laid off from her job.

Her body was discovered early Sunday morning, April 27, in the factory basement. The discovery led to a police investigation, a coroner's inquest, and eventually a murder prosecution against Leo Max Frank, the factory's superintendent.

On Saturday, May 24, 1913, a Fulton County grand jury indicted Frank for murder. His trial opened on Monday, July 28, 1913, in Fulton County Superior Court, with Judge Leonard Strickland Roan presiding.

Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey directed the prosecution, assisted by Edward A. Stephens. Frank's principal defense attorneys included Luther Zeigler Rosser and Reuben Rose Arnold.

The trial lasted approximately four weeks and attracted enormous public attention. Witnesses testified about Mary's movements, the factory, physical evidence, and the conduct of Frank and other employees. One of the prosecution's most important witnesses was James Conley, a factory janitor whose testimony implicated Frank.

On Monday, August 25, 1913, the twelve jurors returned a unanimous verdict finding Frank guilty of murder. Judge Roan sentenced him to death the following day.

The verdict concluded the trial, but the legal battle continued. Frank's attorneys challenged numerous rulings, portions of the testimony, the conduct of the proceedings, and eventually the qualifications of two jurors (Frank v. State, 5).

The Defense Turns Its Attention to the Jury

Following the conviction, Frank's attorneys prepared an amended motion for a new trial containing 115 grounds, or asserted reasons, for setting aside the verdict.

Among those grounds were accusations directed against Atticus Haygood Henslee and Marcellus Johenning.

Henslee was a traveling salesman associated with the Franklin Buggy Company of Barnesville, Georgia. His work required him to travel among Georgia towns, where he met merchants, customers, and other traveling salesmen. Those journeys became central to the accusations because several people claimed to have heard him discuss Frank's guilt while traveling on business.

Johenning was employed in Atlanta and worked in an industrial setting associated with the Hodges Broom Company. His alleged prejudice became a separate issue after acquaintances claimed that he had expressed an opinion about Frank's guilt before serving on the jury.

Ground 73 of the amended new-trial motion challenged Henslee's impartiality. Ground 74 challenged Johenning's.

The defense gathered affidavits, which are written statements sworn to be true. The object was to demonstrate that the two men had expressed opinions before the trial and were therefore unqualified to serve as impartial jurors.

These were serious allegations. A murder defendant was entitled to a jury willing to decide the case from the evidence presented in court rather than from an opinion already firmly established.

The defense, however, still had to establish that the alleged prejudicial statements had actually been made and that they demonstrated disqualifying bias at the relevant time (Georgia Supreme Court Records, 6).

The Men Who Accused Henslee

By early October 1913, the defense had obtained statements from several men in different Georgia communities.

Among the accusers were Shi Gray, John M. Holmes, and Johnson of Sparta, Georgia. The October 5 newspaper report identifies Johnson as T. M. Johnson, while another contemporary report identifies him as S. M. Johnson.

Other witnesses included R. L. Gremer and Mack Farkas of Albany, Georgia, Julian A. Lehman of Atlanta, C. P. Stough, and Samuel Aron.

The newspaper accounts attributed several harsh statements to Henslee, including declarations that Frank was guilty and deserved to be hanged.

Samuel Aron's affidavit was among the most serious. Aron alleged that he had heard a man, whom he later identified as Henslee, express hostility toward Frank as a Jew and say that he would hang him if selected for the jury.

Henslee denied the accusations of prejudice.

An important limitation in Aron's allegation was that he described identifying Henslee afterward. That created a question about the reliability of the identification, in addition to the question of whether the alleged conversation occurred.

The defense considered these statements evidence that Henslee had already decided the case. Henslee maintained that his accusers were mistaken or that their accounts were false.

The affidavits created a conflict that the court would eventually have to resolve (The Atlanta Journal, 2; The Atlanta Journal, 3).

The Three Sparta Witnesses and the Disputed Dates

The dispute involving Shi Gray, John M. Holmes, and Johnson became especially important because Henslee acknowledged knowing the men and visiting their office.

He did not deny that a conversation about Frank had occurred. Instead, he disputed when it occurred.

According to Henslee, he visited the office on June 27, 1913, but the Frank case was never mentioned. He maintained that the conversation his accusers remembered occurred on Tuesday morning, September 2, after Frank had already been convicted.

During that September visit, Henslee said he met several acquaintances of the three men, discussed the case openly, and expressed his opinion that Frank was guilty.

Henslee acknowledged that he had also described Frank as a pervert, an opinion he said he had formed from James Conley's testimony.

This admission is important. Henslee was not claiming that every statement attributed to him had been invented. He acknowledged expressing strong opinions. His defense was that those opinions had been expressed after the verdict.

He insisted that the Sparta men had confused the dates.

"They got their dates wrong, that's all."

There was another chronological problem. One account placed the conversation on July 27, 1913, the day immediately preceding the opening of the trial. Henslee later maintained that he had received his jury summons in Atlanta on July 25 and had not traveled to Sparta between that date and the conclusion of the trial.

That explanation, if supported by the travel and summons records, would undermine the claim that he had discussed the case with the Sparta men after being summoned but before the trial.

The opposing accounts made the precise date of the conversation more important than the mere fact that Henslee had discussed Frank's guilt (The Atlanta Journal, 1; The Atlanta Journal, 4).

Henslee's Reply to the Sparta Men

In his October 7 statement, Henslee adopted a comparatively restrained tone toward Gray, Holmes, and Johnson.

He said he regretted that men he respected had signed statements accusing him of prejudging Frank.

He also rejected the suggestion that he had publicly branded them all liars.

Instead, Henslee described their statements as mistaken recollections.

He said he had known the men and their families for years and held them in high esteem. He even stated that he would gladly defend them personally if necessary.

This approach was significant because the defense had obtained statements from people who claimed personal knowledge of Henslee and his conversations. By acknowledging their acquaintance and disputing their dates, Henslee offered an explanation that did not require him to accuse every opposing witness of deliberate dishonesty.

Yet that explanation still needed to be tested. The question was whether independent evidence supported his account of the September 2 visit or the earlier conversations alleged by the defense.

Julian A. Lehman and the Railroad Conversation

Henslee's response to another accuser was much more forceful.

Julian A. Lehman, associated with the Atlanta firm Floyd & Lehman, alleged that he had encountered Henslee on a train between Atlanta and Experiment, Georgia, during June 1913.

In the October 4 newspaper account, Lehman attributed to Henslee a statement declaring Frank guilty and saying he deserved to have his neck broken.

Henslee denied making the statement.

He maintained that on June 2, 1913, he was traveling between Edison and Arlington, Georgia, and on June 6 he was traveling between Tifton and Ashburn.

These locations were important because they offered a potentially verifiable answer to Lehman's allegation. Henslee was identifying particular railroad journeys rather than relying exclusively on a general denial.

He further asserted that the Franklin Buggy Company's business records in Barnesville could establish his whereabouts.

The existence, contents, and reliability of those records would be necessary to determine how strongly they supported his account.

A business record showing Henslee working in another part of Georgia on the alleged date could substantially undermine Lehman's recollection. But a claim that records existed was not equivalent to independently verifying them (The Atlanta Journal, 1; The Atlanta Journal, 2).

October 4, 1913: Henslee Confronts Lehman

On Saturday, October 4, Henslee personally visited Lehman at his Atlanta business.

He acknowledged making the visit in his published statement and described telling Lehman that he intended to seek a grand jury indictment against him for attempting to portray Henslee as a perjurer.

This was a much sharper response than the one he directed toward the Sparta witnesses.

It also introduced another issue into the controversy. A person falsely accused of misconduct could reasonably seek to defend his reputation through lawful means. At the same time, an accused juror personally confronting an opposing witness with the prospect of criminal prosecution could raise questions about pressure or intimidation.

The newspaper report preserves Henslee's own description of the encounter, but does not establish whether his threatened legal action was justified or whether Lehman altered his testimony because of it.

The episode deserves attention because it reveals the intensity of the fight over the affidavits. Both sides understood that the credibility of the witnesses could influence the decision on Frank's motion for a new trial.

The Second Juror: Marcellus Johenning

Although the October 7 article concentrated on Henslee, Marcellus Johenning was also facing accusations of prejudice.

Statements against Johenning involved H. C. Loevenhart, Jennie G. Loevenhart, and Mariam Loevenhart, whose surname appears with variant spellings in contemporary accounts.

The allegations concerned conversations in which Johenning supposedly expressed an opinion of Frank's guilt before the trial.

Johenning rejected the charge that he had entered the jury box prejudiced.

In a later response reported by The Atlanta Journal on October 21, Johenning acknowledged having discussed Frank's prospects with members of the Loevenhart family. His explanation was that he had commented on the unfavorable impression created by newspaper coverage and had not declared Frank guilty.

That raised another issue for the court: whether expressing concern about a defendant's prospects, or repeating what newspapers seemed to suggest, established a fixed opinion of guilt.

The defense sought to show that Johenning's mind was already made up. Johenning maintained that he had remained impartial.

The dispute against him was considered separately from the accusations involving Henslee (The Atlanta Journal, 4; Frank v. State, 5).

What the Other Jurors Said About Henslee

An important part of the prosecution's answer involved affidavits from men who had served alongside Henslee and Johenning.

These included F. E. Winburn, W. M. Jeffries, W. F. Medcalf, A. L. Wisbey, A. Townsend, J. T. Orsburn, and C. J. Bosshardt.

The jurors described their observations of Henslee and Johenning during the trial and deliberations. Their accounts generally maintained that neither man had displayed prejudice during the proceedings.

One detail was especially important.

According to the affidavits, Henslee initially cast a doubtful ballot during jury deliberations. Fellow jurors described him as discussing the evidence and explaining the uncertainty behind his position.

If accurately reported, that conduct was difficult to reconcile with the image of a man who openly entered deliberations determined to convict regardless of the evidence.

Nevertheless, a juror's conduct during deliberations cannot conclusively establish what opinions he may have expressed months earlier. The affidavits were valuable evidence of how fellow jurors observed Henslee acting, but they did not automatically disprove every account of a prior conversation.

The defense affidavits and the counter-affidavits had to be weighed together (Georgia Supreme Court Records, 6).

Judge Leonard S. Roan Rejects the Juror-Bias Claims

On Friday, October 31, 1913, Judge Leonard Strickland Roan denied Leo Frank's motion for a new trial.

The ruling followed the presentation of arguments and opposing affidavits. Roan had to decide whether the defense had established sufficient legal grounds for disturbing the verdict.

The accusations against Henslee and Johenning did not persuade him to order a new trial.

The defense appealed.

On Tuesday, February 17, 1914, the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the trial court's decision by a vote of four to two.

The court addressed the juror-bias allegations directly in paragraph 18 of its opinion in Frank v. State, 141 Georgia 243.

Its reasoning is important because it explains exactly how the conflicting evidence was treated.

The court acknowledged that the defense had presented evidence tending to show Henslee had expressed strong prejudice against Frank before the trial.

It also acknowledged Henslee's sworn denial and his statement that he had remained impartial.

The court explained that when a juror's impartiality was challenged during a motion for a new trial, the trial judge was responsible for resolving the factual dispute. An appellate court would ordinarily leave that determination undisturbed unless the judge had abused his discretion.

After considering the conflicting evidence, the Supreme Court found no such abuse.

The court reached the same result concerning Johenning.

That was the legal outcome. Judge Roan rejected the accusations as grounds for ordering a new trial, and the Georgia Supreme Court sustained his ruling.

The decision did not establish that every witness against Henslee was dishonest. It established that the conflicting evidence did not justify overturning Roan's decision (Frank v. State, 5).

What the October 7 Newspaper Report Adds to the Historical Record

The Atlanta Journal's October 7 report deserves attention because it captures the dispute while the prosecution and defense were actively preparing their competing cases.

Henslee's response was detailed. He identified the Sparta witnesses, acknowledged the September 2 conversation, disputed the earlier dates, answered Lehman's railroad allegation, described his business travels, and stated that records could support his account.

He also openly admitted confronting Lehman over the affidavit.

Those details allow researchers to examine the accusations more carefully than would be possible from a brief statement that the defense charged two jurors with prejudice.

They also illustrate why chronology is so important in historical research. A statement made on June 27, July 27, or September 2 could carry a very different meaning in a case whose trial began July 28 and ended August 25.

The substance of a remark is important, but its date can determine whether it is evidence of a previously formed opinion or a judgment expressed after a completed trial.

The historical record should therefore preserve both the accusations and the answers, along with the court's actual decision.

Henslee faced sworn accusations of prejudice. He denied the charges and disputed the dates. Fellow jurors defended his conduct. Judge Roan rejected the new-trial challenge, and the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed that decision.

The accusations were serious enough to require judicial consideration. They were not sufficient to secure a new trial.

The Atlanta Journal,

Tuesday, 7th October 1913,

PAGE 7, COLUMN 3.

(Special Dispatch to The Journal)

VALDOSTA, Georgia, Oct. 7

Solicitor General Hugh Dorsey and Assistant Solicitor Ed Stephens of Atlanta, are spending this week in Valdosta, preparing the answer to the motion for a new trial which was made by the lawyers for Leo Frank in Atlanta recently.

While Judge Thomas is holding court in Moultrie, Attorneys and Stephens are occupying his office in the county court house, where they have the advantage of his library and can carry on their work without interruption.

PAGE 7, COLUMN 4

HENSLEE ANSWERS

PERJURY CHARGES OF FRANK DEFENSE

Fight for New Trial

Now

Hinges on Charges

Juror Was Prejudiced Before He Took Oath

The fight for a new trial for Leo M. Frank now hinges apparently around A. H. Henslee, one of the jurors, who has been attacked by the defense as prejudiced before he took the oath of a juryman.

Although Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey and his assistant, E. A. Stephens, are both in Valdosta, studying the legal phases of the case, they are keeping the telegraph wires hot in their efforts to sustain Henslee.

The attack of the defense on Juror M. Johenning has not been as vigorous and is not considered of great importance.

The attack on Juror Henslee has become the paramount issue in the fight for a new trial for Frank, standing way above the 114 other points made in the motion of Attorneys Luther Z. Rosser and Reuben R. Arnold.

Solicitor Dorsey, when he left Atlanta for the south Georgia town, declared that he would make every effort to be ready with his answer to the motion on next Saturday, when the argument of the case is slated to commence before Judge L. S. Roan, of the Stone Mountain circuit.

While a tremendous amount of work lies before the solicitor general, it is believed that he will announce "ready" when the case is called, and he is certain to introduce many affidavits and depositions in an effort to sustain Henslee and Johenning.

Henslee has written a card to The Journal in which he makes clear his position in regard to the attacks made on him by the sworn statements of three Sparta citizens and one Atlanta man.

The juror's statement is as follows:

"Editor The Journal:

Replying to your article in today's issue, October 6, 1913, in reference to Messrs.

Holmes, Johnson and Gray, I will say I am sorry to think that they would go ahead and make such a statement over their signatures that I discussed and tried Leo Frank in their office on July 27."

"Having read their depositions, in solicitor Hugh Dorsey's office. I will say that I spoke of the case freely, and met there many friends in the office on September 2, which was Tuesday morning."

FRANK NOT MENTIONED.

"I am sorry to think they would express themselves and dare their deposition as they did, either July 27 or June 27.

I will say that I was in this office on June 27, but the Frank case was never mentioned."

"As for branding them all liars, I have never done so, but they have miscalculated the date."

"I did willingly express myself freely regarding the Frank case on September 2, which was after Frank was convicted, Tuesday morning, met many of their friends to whom they introduce me, and did say and express to these friends and to them, that Leo M. Frank, judging from the evidence of Jim Conley, was really a pervert."

"I made a statement to one of the Atlanta papers that I almost positively knew that the depositions received from Sparta, Ga., would not contain anything that I had said prior to the case that they would be similar to those from Blakely, Ga."

"Regarding the statement that they knew me and my family for years, I wish to state that I hold these gentlemen in the highest esteem, as men whom I believe would defend and honor me and my family regardless of public sentiment."

"I wish to state further, however.

that after reading their depositions in Solicitor Dorsey's office.

I am surprised that men of their intelligence should come out in a newspaper and request a reply in such a way as they have. As to branding them liars I have never done 80. They got their dates wrong, that's all."

"In conclusion considering this as a reply to each one of them personally.

instead of branding them as liars, I would gladly defend them at all times."

"Mr. Julius A. Lehman, of the firm of Floyd & Lehman, of the city of Atlanta, makes an affidavit.

I understand, to the effect that I stated to him, on either June 2 or 6, while on the train between Atlanta and Experiment, Ga., that I believed Frank guilty.

This statement also, I brand as false, as on June 2, 1913, I was on the train between Edison and Arlington, Ga.

On June 6, I was on the train between Tifton and Ashburn, Ga."

"Regarding his statement and affidavit, I brand them as absolutely false, and, furthermore, I wish to state that I called on Mr. Lehman personally on Saturday afternoon, October 4, at his place of business, and stated to him, personally, that the only reason I came by was to inform him that I would get a bill of indictment against him when the next grand jury convened in Fulton county for trying to make me out a perjurer. That was all I had to say to him, and I then left his place of business."

"Regarding all of the foregoing statement, I will say that the proof is on record at the Franklin Buggy company's place of business in Barnesville, Ga."

(Signed)

"Atticus Heygood HENSLEE,

"Barnesville, Georgia."

text:
Undercover video exposes program promoting DEI at Mizzou despite pledge to dismantle it | Jennifer Kabbany, The College Fix

A diversity, equity, and inclusion program continues to be offered at the University of Missouri despite campus leaders saying they would voluntarily shut down DEI programs amid pressure from Republican lawmakers.

An undercover video from the activism group Accuracy in Media shows two staffers talking about a program called “The Bridge” that facilitates DEI programming.

“We have something called The Bridge, and they’re really focused on DEI, like inclusion and stuff like that,” one staffer said. “We run a lot of events and programming, like open discussions and forums.”

Another employer in the video said: “All of our events and things we do are focused on expanding multicultural perspectives on, like, social justice issues. … We’re still trying to do the work. It’s just … everything’s going to be done under, you know, different wording.”

The Bridge’s webpage has been taken down, with a “page not found” notice showing in its place. A Google cache description states it included a “multicultural lounge and brave space designed to expand perspectives on social issues through learning, training, and service.”

The nearly four-minute, edited video has a time-date stamp of Dec. 12, 2025, but was released this week as part of a parade of undercover videos focused on DEI activities on campuses in Missouri released by AIM over the last two months.

In July 2024, the University of Missouri announced it was closing its Diversity, Equity and Inclusion office. In 2023, the University of Missouri System also stopped requiring applicants to pledge allegiance to DEI by banning mandatory diversity statements. Universities took steps to dismantle DEI in response to GOP pressure from state lawmakers and the Trump administration.

Responding to the latest video, Mizzou posted on X on Oct. 13: “The video was taken last year as Mizzou was eliminating its DEI programs. Mizzou voluntarily eliminated all DEI programs and DEI requirements in the curriculum. Mizzou has complied with all federal directives to end DEI research projects.”

“We do not discriminate or provide preferential treatment on the basis of race, color, or national origin, etc. We will continue to inform our faculty, staff and students to be aware of our policies and to be in compliance with state and federal laws and guidelines regarding DEI,” the statement continued.

Mizzou added that the two staffers seen in the video “will be investigated and appropriate actions will be taken if they are found to have violated our policies or federal and state laws.”

As The College Fix reported earlier this month, a Mizzou professor was also secretly recorded admitting that diversity, equity, and inclusion activities persist at the university, and that anti-DEI directives “haven’t hit the curriculum.”

After the video was released, the scholar stated: “I apologize for my mistake. The video was taken last year as Mizzou was eliminating its DEI programs. I am fully aware that Mizzou no longer has DEI programs and does not conduct DEI research.”

And at the end of August, The College Fix reported on a University of Missouri Kansas City employee who was suspended after the individual was caught in an undercover video saying the school continues to practice diversity, equity, and inclusion under a different name.

An undercover video posted in late September from AIM also showed an employee saying there was a DEI name change to shield the school from scrutiny.

text:
☕️ SPY Morning Market Prep - Thursday, October 15

Yesterday, CPI gave sellers control. This morning’s PPI report isn’t giving buyers much relief.

Producer prices rose 1.3% for the month versus 0.6% expected, while core PPI came in at 0.7% versus 0.3% expected. Retail sales also beat expectations, rising 0.8% versus 0.3%, and initial jobless claims were essentially in line at 199,000 versus 200,000.

My takeaway, inflation pressure remains uncomfortable, spending is holding up, and this claims report doesn’t show a sudden jump in layoffs. That keeps further rate hikes in the conversation.

After yesterday’s CPI, October hike odds briefly approached 50% before retreating. This morning’s reporting had them around 27% before PPI, so don’t mistake that for the odds after today’s release. Expectations can move quickly, especially with Warsh speaking tonight.

The backdrop is cautious. Technology and AI related stocks were already under pressure, and another inflation surprise adds to that uncertainty. But sentiment can change during the session. Bad news can produce a sustained selloff, a sharp recovery, or a frustrating day of going nowhere after the initial move.

That’s why I’m watching the reaction.

📍 Where we are on SPY

The chart has SPY near 767.40, sitting just above the marked demand around 766.50-767. Overhead, 768 and 769 are the first recovery levels, with the more important supply area around 769.50–770.

There is a lot of real estate between 770 and 775. Yesterday’s selloff moved through that area quickly, leaving relatively little consolidation on this chart. That makes a recovery through it worth watching, but only after buyers prove they can clear and hold 770.

We also have room below. Losing nearby demand would bring the lower descending trendline around 765 into focus, followed by 764. Beyond that, 762 and 760 are deeper checkpoints. They are not automatic targets just because the chart looks open.

🟢 The bullish case

I want to see buyers defend demand, reclaim 768–769, and then deal with that 769.50–770 supply zone.

A break above it, a controlled pullback, and a higher low would make the recovery toward 775 more interesting. Above 775, 776 and the upper descending trendline become the next test.

I’m not interested in chasing the first green candle after a large selloff. A bounce into resistance is one thing. Reclaiming that resistance and establishing support is another.

🔴 The bearish case

If rebounds keep failing beneath 769–770 and price continues making lower highs, sellers still have the stronger structure.

A break below 766.50, followed by a failed reclaim, would put 765 and 764 on my radar. If selling continues through those areas, I’ll reassess the deeper levels as we approach them.

The temptation will be to see hot inflation and immediately chase puts. I’d rather wait for the bounce, rejection, and confirmation than enter an extended move directly into support.

🟡 The scenario that can quietly become expensive

Demand holds, supply holds, and SPY rotates between roughly 766.50 and 770.

Big headlines don’t guarantee clean follow-through. If price keeps crossing VWAP and neither side can hold a break, forcing an options trade can turn into a slow bleed.

🔎 What could change the read?

I’m watching the 2-year Treasury yield, the dollar, QQQ, and market breadth alongside SPY.

Rising yields and a stronger dollar, combined with continued tech weakness, would reinforce the pressure. A recovery with improving participation would deserve attention.

But falling yields alone aren’t enough. They can also reflect investors seeking safety. I want to see what stocks actually do with that move.

⏰ Key times today (all Eastern)

9:30 a.m.: Cash open. Does the overnight weakness carry into regular trading, or do buyers absorb it?

9:45–10:00 a.m.: Assess the opening range and whether the first move is holding.

10:00 a.m.: Business inventories.

10:30 a.m.: Natural-gas storage, primarily relevant to energy.

12:00 p.m.: Oil inventories. This week’s holiday moves the release to noon today. Energy matters with inflation already front and center.

3:00–4:00 p.m.: Watch whether the day’s move holds into the close or starts unwinding.
After the close, Hammack speaks at 4:30 p.m. ET, and Warsh’s IMF discussion is scheduled for 11:30 p.m. ET
That matters if you’re considering overnight exposure.
My starting lean is cautious while SPY remains below 770. That doesn’t mean I’m committed to puts. If buyers reclaim the levels and build the structure, I need to be willing to adjust.

The market offers hundreds of opportunities. We don’t need to catch every move. We need to be selective enough to protect our capital and keep showing up for the opportunities that fit our process. Before entering, know your position size, what invalidates the trade, how much you’re willing to lose, and where you plan to exit. And never trade because you “need the money.” That pressure makes it much easier to turn a manageable loss into an emotional decision.

Preparation > Prediction.

text:
There's a well-known long running Shopify app offering search & filtering functionality that was bought out not long ago, and its new private-equity investor backed owners decided to start charging stores ludicrous prices purely based on their GMV, rather than on features or actual app usage as it was before. 

For one of our stores, the app's pricing went from $29, to $58, to $699 in a matter of months.

The store is doing well, but not because of the app - far from it. The app's own analytics literally attributes £0 revenue in their own 'app impact' report. Its a brand that's being going many years, and built up a loyal recurring subscriber base and recurring revenue, the vast majority of whom don't even visit the part of the site that this app operates on. In fact, on that store, we barely use any of this apps' features. We just went with it for a consistent tech stack, as all our other stores use it too. We will be costing them next to nothing to operate - its a small catalogue, and we barely ever speak to their support aside from some initial setup they had to do at their end.

After I argued this case with them, they offered a reduced charge of $300 on the basis they'd stopped counting the recurring revenue. One of our other stores, which is much larger and also has recurring revenue, only pays $69/mo for the same app on a grandfathered plan with more features (yes its a retired plan but it just shows what they used to charge, and that's how that app actually built up a great reputation - offering good value). They refuse to offer that pricing to our smaller store, or do a multi-store deal.

This whole concept of buying up successful apps that built their reputation on offering great value and features, only to then start charging extortionate prices on them while offering less for it, is simply not going to work and is absolutely bonkers tactics in this new age of rapidly growing AI-backed competition. They fail to realise, such stores have many other apps they work with, its an ecosystem, and if they all started charging like that, it simply wouldn't be viable. They somehow forget how much Shopify charges for their plans, and how ridiculous it looks when your app (which offers a small portion of what Shopify does) is trying to charge similar amounts, if not more. 

In years to come, these private-equity backed apps will fail, after pumping in investors money, jacking up prices, and wondering why all their customers left. I used to recommend this app to everyone, now I do the opposite. We work on 5 Shopify Plus stores, and I'm now thinking what we do to migrate them all away from that app, and I'm sure others will be too.

Luckily, not all apps are doing that, because some understand that you can't get away with charging whatever you want to exploit a merchants success, you instead have to prove your own value and offer more, not less. This is why I admire what @celispj is doing with https://t.co/dBPByYttg1 and their latest email app too. He gets it. They don't charge Shopify Plus customers more 'just because', in fact everyone pays the same. They don't charge on merchants success. Others out there need to learn and stop taking the piss, or risk extinction.

Usual disclaimer: these are my own personal opinions, not those of anyone I work with or for.

Here is a simple plan to help you build a strong ETF portfolio on @EasyEquities 
You do not need to hold many ETFs. Starting with two is fine. As you build more knowledge and confidence, you can add more, but try to keep the total under five and stay consistent. Pay attention to the overlaps so you do not accidentally end up with too much of the same thing.

If you want broad global equity exposure, Satrix MSCI World gives you access to large and mid-cap companies across developed markets, mainly the US, Europe, Japan and others. It is a simple way to own a slice of the global stock market outside emerging markets. Note that it has significant overlap with both the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100 because US companies make up a large portion of the World index.

If you want only technology or the Nasdaq, Satrix Nasdaq 100 gives you access to the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq. It is heavily weighted toward big technology and growth companies such as Applee, Microsoftt, NVIDIA and Amazon. This ETF has a high overlap with the S&P 500 because many of the same large US tech stocks appear in both.

If you want the US market, Satrix S&P 500 gives you access to the 500 largest companies listed in the United States across all sectors, not just technology. It overlaps heavily with both the MSCI World and the Nasdaq 100, so holding all three together can create more concentration in US large-cap stocks than you might expect.

If you want emerging markets, Satrix MSCI Emerging Markets gives you access to large and mid-cap companies in places such as China, India, Taiwan, Brazil, South Africa and others. It offers higher growth potential but also higher risk and volatility. There is limited overlap with the developed-market ETFs above, which makes it a useful diversifier if you want exposure outside the US and Europe.

For South African equities, Satrix Top 40  gives you access to the 40 largest companies on the JSE by market capitalisation, while Satrix RAFI 40 gives you access to the 40 largest South African companies weighted by fundamental factors such as sales, cash flow, book value and dividends rather than pure market size. These two overlap with each other and also appear inside the Emerging Markets ETF, so owning both plus STXEMG increases your South African weighting.

That is the power of ETFs. You can target exactly what you want without having to pick individual stocks yourself. One investment gives you a ready-made basket of companies that fit the theme. Just remember that an ETF is only as good as the assets inside it. Choose the ones that match your goal, stay consistent, and watch the overlaps.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Tucker Carlson Show: Tucker Responds to Trump’s Plan to Livestream an Execution and His Anti-Christian Death Cult

Overview
Tucker Carlson treats Pete Hegseth’s comments about a public firing-squad execution as a signal worth taking literally rather than dismissing as ordinary political rhetoric. Carlson separates the question of whether Nidal Hasan deserves punishment from whether the state should stage a killing as a public spectacle. His central argument is that public executions degrade the society that watches them, and that this degradation is not an isolated incident but part of a broader callousness toward human life. From there, the discussion widens into a larger claim: that neoconservatism is fundamentally anti-Christian, that it worships violence and treats killing as a kind of blood sacrifice, and that abandoning the belief in God-given human equality imperils everyone. The thread running through it all is fear as a tool of rule, the loss of empathy through war and propaganda, and a closing argument that the Sermon on the Mount offers the only real off-ramp from mutual annihilation.

Key Themes
- Hegseth’s public-execution remarks should be parsed as a serious policy signal, not brushed off as loose talk, because no moral outcry followed and no Rubicon was crossed in the minds of those in power.
- Carlson separates Hasan’s guilt from the propriety of a public spectacle, arguing the killing harms spectators the way pornography, snuff films, and exploitative material harm viewers.
- Charles Dickens’s 1849 account of a London public execution is used as historical evidence that public killings degrade a crowd and stir dangerous instincts rather than deliver justice.
- Neoconservatism is framed as anti-Christian: an attack on the belief that every person has a soul and that moral limits constrain power, with indifference to Ukrainian deaths cited as evidence that killing is the point.
- Dehumanizing language trains people to accept violence against fellow citizens, from calling opponents “scum” to celebrating a botched execution of a paralyzed inmate.
- The American project rests on rights being God-given and inalienable, not granted by government; when leaders stop seeing others as human, the social contract changes and everyone is at risk.
- Fear is presented as the main alternative to government by consent, and Christianity is uniquely destabilizing to fear-based rule because the cross signals that believers do not fear death.
- The Sermon on the Mount is framed as the off-ramp: refusing violent retaliation, refusing to keep grudges, and recognizing God provides for one’s enemy.
- Repeated language makes the unthinkable socially real, and current nuclear doctrine changes and threats against Iran are read as preparing the ground for a first strike.

Detailed Summary
Pete Hegseth described Nidal Hasan as a case for public execution, tied to deterrence, punishment, and a World War II-style sense of winning. Hasan was an Army major and admitted mass murderer who killed 13 people and wounded about 30 others at Fort Hood. Hegseth said Hasan would be executed by firing squad at Fort Hood on a Thursday at 1:00, the same time as the attack, with soldiers using rifles, and suggested people could watch. He said firing-squad executions had not been used since World War II. Carlson notes Hasan has been imprisoned for more than a decade and asks what executing a long-imprisoned inmate actually wins.

Carlson splits the question in two: whether Hasan deserves punishment, which he does not dispute, and whether the United States should conduct public executions at all. He accepts Hasan’s guilt and the severity of the crime but challenges the public spectacle. His claim is that public killings harm society by encouraging bloodlust and degrading viewers, comparing the effect to pornography, snuff videos, and child sexual abuse material. The state staging a killing for an audience does something corrosive to the audience, not just to the condemned.

Carlson cites Charles Dickens’s 1849 essay after attending a public execution in London. The case involved a husband and wife who had murdered the wife’s former boyfriend, stolen his money, and buried him under kitchen stones. Dickens described the crowd as degraded and the spectacle as an incitement to dangerous instincts. Parliament ended public executions in Britain in the late 1860s, roughly 20 years after Dickens’s campaign. Carlson uses this as evidence that the degradation of spectators is a known historical outcome, not a hypothetical.

Carlson notes the last public executions in the United States were in the 1930s, in Europe about 100 years ago, and in Britain about 150 years ago. He questions why the administration is resurrecting public execution now and notes uncertainty over whether it will actually happen. Reporting indicates the president did not know Hasan was in a wheelchair and had been a paraplegic since being shot during the attack.

Markwayne Mullin endorsed public execution. Carlson describes him as head of Homeland Security, a committed neoconservative, a major buyer of ammunition, and a commander of armed federal employees. Carlson also says Mullin is part-owner of a company, though that thought cuts off. The endorsement is treated as evidence of callousness toward human life, not an outlier.

Carlson argues the defining feature of neoconservatism is a worship of violence. He treats support for public execution as proof of a broader indifference to human life. Charlie Kirk’s death-penalty clip is used to claim that government power may be turned against its users; Kirk called those who would use such power “Bolsheviks.” The speaker argues the Bolshevik Revolution was fundamentally a revolution against Christianity and the Christian order, replacing God with money, power, and violence as blood sacrifice.

Conservatism is defined as rooted in equality: God created every person, giving inalienable rights and equal moral value despite differences in ability or appearance. The speaker says this moral foundation is eroding, producing callousness toward human life and peril for everyone when leaders no longer see others as human. The American project depends on the idea that life is inherently valuable because it was not created by humans. Police can pull someone over for a broken tail light but must be polite and cannot violate rights because they did not grant those rights.

The speaker says that in 1985 or 1995, a secretary of defense announcing a public firing-squad execution would have caused an outcry as degrading, even among death penalty supporters. No such outcry followed Hegseth’s remarks, and no moral Rubicon was crossed in the minds of those in power. The two-party adversarial system is designed to keep parties honest, but no major Democratic pushback or street protests demanded accountability. Governor Maura Healey of Massachusetts announced passage of a bill to protect and strengthen abortion protections, described by the speaker as allowing abortion up to birth.

Healey is quoted saying abortion is on the ballot in Massachusetts and around the country, and that she stands with women while her opponents do not. The speaker frames this as notable because she describes the bill plainly as abortion rather than using euphemisms like health care or reproductive freedom. Bill Clinton’s “safe, legal, and rare” formulation is cited as past pro-choice euphemism. The speaker says there are about a million abortions a year in the United States and claims that is not enough for current advocates. Only a small group of evangelicals and passionate Catholics reacted to Healey’s announcement, while most people did not.

Charlie Kirk is credited with the idea that “bullsheism” replaces the Christian social order. Marxism is described as absurd and something no one cares about, unlike this newer current. The speaker says war accelerates the process by killing innocents and desensitizing the public through repeated exposure. Trump’s comment that civilians die in war is called callous. Netanyahu is described as giving gassy speeches claiming everyone wants to kill Israel. The speaker claims Israel is now the least popular country in the world after committing genocide, blowing up southern Lebanon, and leveling churches, and suggests an alternate path where Israel sought peace with its neighbors 60 years ago instead of permanent occupation.

Fear-based rule is presented as the main alternative to government by consent: leaders who cannot rule by consent use terror to control the population. The United States is described as inherently one of the safest countries due to geographic isolation by the Atlantic and Pacific oceans; claims that it is under constant threat are framed as a tool for control. Christianity is argued to be uniquely destabilizing to fear-based rulers because its central symbol, the cross as a torture device, signals that believers do not fear death. Crucifixion is described as a gruesome public torture designed to terrify; Jesus’s followers embraced the cross as a symbol of fearlessness rather than running from it. Paul wrote many New Testament letters while chained in prison and they were cheerful.

The speaker claims the goal of Bolsheviks, the French Revolution, the Spanish Civil War, the Russian Revolution of 1917, and the AI revolution is to extinguish Christianity specifically. Trump is quoted explaining he is building a ballroom with a drone port on the roof for military safety. The 9/11 files are said to be classified forever. After January 6th, the speaker says the government would have been wrong to respond by murdering unarmed Americans in the Capitol. Former DC police officer Michael Fenone says Lindsey Graham told responding officers they should have shot them all in the head. The speaker says Graham’s alleged statement should have triggered investigation by the Republican Party, Congress, or courts, but nobody even noticed.

A Fox News clip features a guest praising Ukrainian drone innovation as phenomenal for taking out Russia’s war machine; the speaker cites that only as valuing drone technology over dying soldiers. The same clip references 30,000 young men dying on each side every single month. The speaker says if war advocates don’t care about Ukrainian deaths, it’s fair to assume they eventually applaud them. On the Christina Pike execution case, the speaker says the prison failed twice to execute her and notes moral opposition to executing women while calling liberals hypocritical for supporting it. Glenn Beck’s commentary on the botched execution is quoted as callous, mocking Pike for being paralyzed and confused, and urging authorities to do it again. The speaker cites historical botched executions in England, America, and Australia where crowds pressured authorities to stop after repeated failures, sometimes resulting in release, framing that as a civilized response.

The speaker argues that conservative rhetoric mocking or dehumanizing a paralyzed female inmate reflects a broader callousness and self-righteousness distinct from a debate about the death penalty itself. A central claim is that dehumanizing language about opponents as not fully human trains people to accept violence against fellow Americans. A Trump rally where a protester holding a “release the Epstein files” shirt is called scum by Trump, and someone in the crowd says “just punch her in the face,” is cited as an example of leaders encouraging violence. The speaker contends that conservative leadership has internalized a repulsive and untrue lie of feminism, that the sexes are identical, by failing to condemn violence against women and by sending women to front lines. Trump’s Truth Social post of videos showing people being killed by wild animals is described as intended to desensitize the public to cruelty, suffering, and death. Tulsi Gabbard’s video about the horrors of nuclear war drew outrage from Trump and neoconservative figures like Ben Shapiro, which the speaker says reveals a militant death cult program opposed to restraint.

The speaker argues that accusations of Gabbard being fringe for warning about nuclear war reflect a larger inversion: anti-nuclear-extermination views are actually majority opinion, while open advocacy of nuclear exchange is the fringe position. Ben Shapiro is characterized as unintentionally revealing truth: his outrage at Gabbard’s criticism of nuclear weapons is framed as evidence that neoconservatives want a nuclear exchange and are changing U.S. nuclear doctrine to make a first strike easier. A central argument is that repeated language can make previously unthinkable ideas socially real, with gay marriage and transgender identity cited as examples of rapid shift from widespread opposition or disbelief to broad acceptance. The speaker claims current U.S. nuclear doctrine changes are not for retaliation but to enable a first strike against a non-nuclear-armed nation, risking global annihilation. Trump’s U.N. remarks about annihilating the Islamic Republic are interpreted as a nuclear threat because no conventional weapon could achieve the described destruction. The speaker frames dehumanization, political hatred, and acceptance of brutality as preparation for nuclear war, and proposes the Sermon on the Mount’s nonviolence and recognition of shared humanity as the only off-ramp.

The Sermon on the Mount is framed as an off-ramp from cycles of blood grudges: refusing violent retaliation, refusing to keep grudges, and recognizing that God provides sun and rain to one’s enemy. The speaker argues that shared humanity, enemy included, is not liberal clap trap but the only thing preventing mutually assured annihilation. The speaker claims society is heading toward that annihilation, enabled by every institution in American life. The country is described as founded on true equality, not of ability or outcome but of humanity, and abandoning that principle leads to catastrophic ends for everyone.

text:
Ishmael, the main character and narrator of the novel, is not a sailor by profession, but neither is he entirely bereft of naval experience.

In fact, Ishmael is of an odd psychological character: though a schoolmaster, he frequently feels a restlessness that demands he leave his normal, simple life and go to sea. When the novel opens, Ishmael is in precisely this state of mind: he is wandering Nantucket, Massachusetts, looking for a ship that will hire him. He meets a friend, Queequeg, who is a member of an island tribe and offers a shrunken head to Ishmael as a gift.

It turns out that Queequeg is a skilled whale harpooner, and he and Ishmael both hire themselves out to a ship called the Pequod. At first, nothing seems to be especially extraordinary about the Pequod, except that several people mention the weird reputation of the ship and its captain, Ahab. But that doesn’t dissuade Queequeg or Ishmael — after all, seamen are eccentric, and neither man is willing to give up the voyage now that they have found it. Unfortunately, they are about to discover that they should have listened to the skeptics of Nantucket…
