text:
The 6abc post marks the anniversary of an event that accelerated the shift toward continuous, emotion-driven cable news coverage in the late 1980s.[](<https://t.co/UL4bt3DoA5>)

Jessica McClure, then 18 months old, fell into an abandoned well in Midland, Texas, on October 14, 1987, and remained trapped for approximately 58 hours before rescuers extracted her via a parallel shaft and horizontal tunnel. Networks interrupted prime-time programming for live updates, and CNN’s sustained coverage drew millions of viewers—an early demonstration of how real-time reporting of a single, high-stakes human story could command national attention for days. The rescue succeeded, but it also foreshadowed the later saturation of individual crises in 24-hour news cycles. One of the paramedics who brought her to the surface later died by suicide after struggling with the aftermath of the operation.[](<https://t.co/xZhIDtWcpL>)

Jessica McClure Morales has stated she retains no personal memory of the incident. She married, raised children in the Midland area, and largely stayed out of the public eye while a trust fund established from public donations was later reduced by the 2008 financial crisis. In April 2026, Midland County authorities arrested her on a Class A misdemeanor charge of assault causing bodily injury involving family violence after deputies responded to a domestic disturbance at her home; she was released on bond. Affidavit details reported by multiple outlets describe an altercation with her husband that involved alleged contact to the neck and occurred in the presence of an infant grandchild. Public records do not indicate a subsequent conviction or jail sentence, and the case disposition has not been widely reported.[](<https://t.co/4PCaCXF8c1>)

The anniversary coverage continues because the original story offered a rare instance of collective, non-partisan focus on a successful rescue rather than a tragedy. Canada: One of the World's Most Diverse Travel Destinations

Canada is the second-largest country on Earth, stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific and north into the Arctic. It combines cosmopolitan cities, dramatic mountain scenery, pristine lakes, rich Indigenous heritage, French and British influences, and some of the world's most accessible wilderness. Canada appeals equally to luxury travelers, adventure seekers, couples, multigenerational families, and outdoor enthusiasts.

Does Canada Cater More to Adults or Families?

The answer is both.

Excellent for Couples and Adults

Canada is ideal for:

Luxury rail journeys through the Rockies
Wine tasting in British Columbia and Ontario
Fine dining in Montreal, Toronto, and Vancouver
Northern Lights experiences
Luxury wilderness lodges
Glacier helicopter tours
Scenic cruises and wildlife expeditions
Outstanding for Families

Canada is particularly family-friendly because of:

Exceptional safety standards
Family-oriented national parks
Wildlife viewing experiences
Interactive museums and cultural centers
Ski resorts with children's programs
Easy self-drive vacations
Clean cities and excellent infrastructure

Overall: Canada is one of the rare destinations that serves luxury couples, active adults, and families equally well.

Brief History

Canada's story begins with Indigenous Peoples who inhabited the land for thousands of years before European exploration. Indigenous cultures remain a vital part of Canadian identity today.

Key historical influences include:

Indigenous First Nations, Inuit, and Métis peoples
French settlement beginning in the 1600s
British colonial expansion
Confederation in 1867
Development through immigration from Europe, Asia, the Caribbean, Africa, and the Middle East

The result is one of the world's most multicultural societies.

The Canadian People and Culture

Canadians are generally known for:

Politeness
Inclusiveness
Diversity
Respect for nature
Strong community values

Major cultural influences include:

Indigenous traditions
French Canadian culture (especially Québec)
British heritage
Modern multicultural communities from around the world

Canada is officially bilingual:

English
French

Montreal and Québec City offer a distinctly French atmosphere unlike anywhere else in North America.

What Makes Canada Unique?

Several things make Canada stand apart:

Nature on a Massive Scale
Rocky Mountains
Banff and Jasper National Parks
Thousands of lakes
Arctic wilderness
Atlantic coast fishing villages
Indigenous Heritage

Indigenous tourism experiences, art, cuisine, storytelling, and cultural programs are increasingly becoming highlights for visitors.

Four Distinct Seasons

Visitors can:

Ski in winter
See spring blossoms
Enjoy summer hiking
Experience spectacular autumn foliage
Multicultural Cities

Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal rank among the most multicultural metropolitan areas in the world.

Top 5 Must-Do Canadian Experiences
1. Visit Banff & Lake Louise (Alberta)

Often considered Canada's signature vacation experience.

Highlights:

Turquoise glacier lakes
Luxury mountain resorts
Gondolas
Wildlife viewing
Scenic drives

Ideal for: couples and families.

2. Ride the Rocky Mountaineer

One of the world's finest luxury rail journeys.

Highlights:

Glass-domed rail cars
Gourmet dining
Mountain scenery
Five-star service

Best for adults and luxury travelers.

3. Experience Québec City & Montreal

North America's most European destination.

Highlights:

Historic architecture
French cuisine
Cobblestone streets
Festivals
Art and culture

Perfect for couples and cultural travelers.

4. See the Northern Lights

Best regions:

Yukon
Northwest Territories
Northern Manitoba

Highlights:

Aurora Borealis viewing
Winter wilderness lodges
Dog sledding

Among the world's premier aurora destinations.

5. Explore Vancouver & the Pacific Coast

Highlights:

Mountains and ocean together
Whistler Resort
Whale watching
Coastal cuisine
Luxury waterfront hotels

Ideal for both families and adults.

Canadian Cuisine

Canadian food is heavily influenced by regional ingredients and multicultural traditions.

Signature Foods
Poutine

French fries topped with cheese curds and gravy.

Maple Syrup

Canada produces the majority of the world's maple syrup supply. Québec's maple traditions are especially famous.

Atlantic Lobster

Particularly celebrated in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.

Indigenous Cuisine

Features ingredients such as:

Wild game
Berries
Bannock
Salmon
Ice Wine

Ontario's Niagara region is world-famous for producing premium ice wine.

Montreal Bagels & Smoked Meat

Regional specialties unique to Québec.

Best Time to Visit
First-Time Visitors
Mid-June Through Mid-September

Generally considered the best overall period because:

Warm temperatures
All attractions open
Long daylight hours
Peak scenery
Best national park access
For Fall Colors
Mid-September to Mid-October
Fewer crowds
Spectacular foliage
Slightly lower hotel rates
For Winter Activities
January through March
Skiing
Northern Lights
Winter festivals

Summer Travel (June-August)

Book:

Airfare: 4-8 months ahead
Luxury hotels: 6-10 months ahead
Rocky Mountaineer: 8-12 months ahead
Fall Travel

Bottom Line

For many American travelers, Canada offers a compelling combination of European-style culture, world-class luxury hotels, extraordinary wilderness, and easy access without a long-haul flight. Couples often gravitate toward Banff, Lake Louise, Vancouver, and Québec City, while families love the national parks, wildlife experiences, and family-friendly resorts. The Big Ten is going to get smoked by the SEC on their next TV deal.  How so?  First, the SEC's primary ABC/ESPN agreement was a 20-year agreement signed in 2013, that runs from July 2014 - June 2034.  That contract contains every single game, across every single sport, including 97 of the SEC's 112 annual football games.  ABC/ESPN bought the additional 15 football games in 2020, which had previously been aired by CBS.  That 15-game contract runs from July 2024 - June 2034.

Further, NEITHER deal includes the market value of Texas or Oklahoma.  Both the 2013 & 2020 have a pro rata clause.  So, when Texas & Oklahoma joined the conference, ABC/ESPN simply increased their annual payout by 2 shares.  Neither contract was re-priced based on TX & OU's market value.  

Contrast that with the Big Ten.  Their Fox/NBC/CBS contracts were signed in 2022, & included the market value of USC & UCLA.  Oregon & Washington joined on a partial pro rata.  But, neither have significant TV $ value, which is why NBC & CBS refused to increase their payout to the B1G to account for the additions of Oregon & Washington, & why their TV ratings are middling relative to SEC programs.

So, as of this moment in time, the SEC is playing on a contract based almost entirely on 2013 TV values *AND* without Texas & OU included.  So what do you think happens when, after more than a decade of dominating the Big Ten in TV ratings, the SEC's outdated TV contract comes to market & they're paid a current market value *AND* Texas & OU are added to the valuation?  The only reason the Big Ten *barely* outpaces the SEC now is b/c they're playing on a 2022 valuation, rather than the SEC's 2013 valuation, & their contract includes USC & UCLA's, but the SEC's doesn't include Texas & Oklahoma.🫡

text:
**Alyona Yarushina’s Cover of “Another Day in Paradise”: Vocals, Production, and an Unyielding Pursuit of Excellence**

In a crowded field of online covers, Alyona Yarushina’s version of Phil Collins’ 1989 classic “Another Day in Paradise” stands out for its emotional clarity, technical control, and fully independent craft. Released on her YouTube channel in late June 2026 (https://t.co/TfUJzKxpHK), the performance has drawn tens of thousands of views and comments praising its soul, empathy, and sense that the song has been “reborn” in her voice. It is a clear example of an artist who prioritizes serving the material over spectacle.

Follow Aly on X at @AlyonaYarushina
Patreon: https://t.co/oeKbEiGZ0J
YouTube: https://t.co/X8Aw2rS2RD

Yarushina treats the song’s themes of indifference and human need with restraint and warmth rather than dramatic overstatement. Her tone is textured and lived-in, moving fluidly between intimate, almost conversational verses and fuller choruses. Listeners note the empathy in her delivery—one commenter described it as sung “with true soul and empathy,” while others say Phil Collins would be proud or that the track feels renewed through her interpretation.

What distinguishes the performance is the absence of processing shortcuts. Across her catalog, Yarushina is known for singing without autotune, preserving natural texture and dynamics. Formal training underpins the control: years of piano study, choir conducting, and university-level vocal work produce precise pitch, clear diction, and seamless shifts in intensity. Her documented range supports both lower, warmer lines and higher, more expansive passages without strain. On this ballad, the voice stays in service of the lyric—vulnerable where the story requires it, steady and resonant where the chorus needs weight—creating a reading that feels personal rather than imitative.

The entire track is the work of one person. Yarushina acts as arranger, pianist, multi-tracked vocalist, mixer, and masterer, recording in her home studio (typically using Logic Pro). Piano frequently anchors the arrangement, providing a supportive bed that leaves space for the lead vocal. Her own layered harmonies and backing vocals add depth without clutter. The resulting mix is clean and professional—warm, balanced, and intentional—matching the polished standard of her broader catalog of more than 1,200 self-produced videos.

This approach is deliberate. Instruments frame the voice and the song’s message rather than competing with them. High-resolution WAV and MP3 versions of such recordings are offered to supporters, reflecting a commitment to delivering finished, high-quality audio rather than quick uploads.

Born June 1, 1984, in Chelyabinsk, Russia, Yarushina grew up inside music. Her father, Valeriy Yarushin, led the influential Soviet-era folk-rock band Ariel; her mother taught piano. She studied piano from a young age, trained as a choir conductor, and completed university studies as a vocalist and performer. In 2004 she won the Grand Prix at the International Hopes of Europe competition with Whitney Houston’s “I Have Nothing.” She later performed with the Led Zeppelin tribute Plumbum Dreams and took her own Beatles arrangements with Back from the USSR to Beatles Week in Liverpool.

Since launching her YouTube channel (@ AlyonaY) in 2008, she has built a catalog spanning classic rock, power ballads, and more—Queen, Heart, Led Zeppelin, Whitney Houston, and many others—reaching roughly 412,000 subscribers and over 100 million views. Copyright claims routinely limit ad revenue on the platform, so she has developed Patreon (https://t.co/mhgd4RDa6y) as what she calls her independent record label. With more than 1,000 members, the page offers exclusive posts, behind-the-scenes material, early access, and downloadable high-quality files, directly funding continued work.

Tawana Houston, the mother of Javon Hadley and mother in law of Demoree Hadley, has submitted a 13 page sworn declaration containing 124 numbered paragraphs in support of Demoree’s opposition to Desiree Perez’s motion to strike portions of her declaration.

Houston states that she has known Demoree for approximately 14 years, considers her a daughter and has maintained a close relationship with her throughout the events underlying this litigation.

Several portions of her testimony stood out.

Demoree’s Mental Health and Alleged Behavioral Changes

Houston disputes Perez’s characterization of Demoree’s deteriorating mental health. She states that throughout their relationship, she never personally witnessed Demoree abusing drugs or alcohol, expressing suicidal thoughts, experiencing hallucinations or exhibiting behavior that caused her to believe Demoree needed psychiatric hospitalization.

She also disputes allegations about Demoree’s deteriorating appearance and hygiene, describing her as consistently well groomed, intelligent, responsible and composed.

James Fondo and the Landscaping Business

Houston provides a detailed account of Javon and Demoree’s dealings with James Fondo and his son, James Michael Fondo, dating back to approximately 2018.

She states that Fondo approached the couple about purchasing landscaping contracts through B Cool Lawn Maintenance and that Perez offered to assist with reviewing business proposals and documents.

Houston alleges the couple eventually became suspicious of the arrangements, particularly after discovering that an LLC Perez allegedly created for their landscaping business excluded Javon from the ownership paperwork.

She states:

“It was not until years later we all discovered the meetings with James Fondo and his Son, were not legit and were attempts of Desiree Perez to harass my Son and Daughter in law and control my Daughter in law.”

text:
AI is creating a 'human premium' for art created by people | Ros Atkins, BBC

A few weeks back, in a former bank building that's now a music venue in Falmouth, Cornwall, I was DJ-ing at a night I run called Rave Machine. It was a noisy, high-energy, sweaty affair, just as a night's dancing should be.

All of the elements - the crowd, performers, staff, music, the journey home - connected to create something special, a one-off. It was also completely human.

Something, in theory, well out of reach of what technology could possibly offer.

In the DJ world, though, technology has already changed the equation. In the 1990s, a DJ had to not only pick the tracks, but also thread them together armed only with vinyl records, a pair of turntables and a mixer. Now, much more assistance is on offer, including software that will sync beats on different tracks should you ask it to (I don't). Apple Music and Spotify have an AI tune-mixing option too.

If you were out dancing, would it matter to you if a DJ was, well, not really DJing? If you loved the music being played, would you care if technology was doing the work?

It's a question that generative AI - the type of AI that creates content - is asking of us all. One of the thrills of that night in Falmouth was seeing our special guest, Andy Cato from Groove Armada, artfully weaving an array of tracks. How would I feel if a DJ was just pressing play? (And that does happen).

I mention all of this because that experience in Falmouth connects to a far broader question: whether we actually care if a piece of art has been created by a human, be that a painting, song, book, poem, or any other type of art.

Renaissance frescoes and chess champions

The music platform Deezer says 44% of tracks uploaded to it are AI-generated. Its research also found that 97% of listeners couldn't tell what was AI-generated and what wasn't. But here's a third statistic: more than half of those surveyed said they did care if it was made by AI. They want humans to be involved.

Daniel Susskind, an economics professor at King's College London, says many of us place huge value on the human role in making art. It's what makes the creative process different from more functional, practical tasks, he thinks.

"I was once in a room of accountants, and one of them stood up and said, 'My clients come to me for the personal touch, the human process'," he remembers. "And I said, 'That isn't why they come to you, they come because they want their taxes done properly'."

But it's different with art, he says. "If I walk into the Sistine Chapel and look at the ceiling, I think not only is that extraordinarily beautiful, but isn't it amazing that a human hand, flesh and blood like my own, came up with that. A mind like mine dreamt that up," he says.

As Susskind describes it, what we value isn't just the destination, it's the knowledge that a human - one of us - got us there. We can wonder at that achievement.

Of course, it could be argued that computers and AI software were themselves created by humans. If Susskind feels awe walking into the Sistine Chapel, others might experience awe of a different type using a chatbot like ChatGPT.

Susskind points to another example, this time a chess match in 1997, when a world champion, Garry Kasparov, lost for the first time to a computer, Deep Blue. At the time, there were fears the computer's success would mean our interest in chess would wane. In fact, chess is more popular than ever, played by millions.

"It wasn't simply the moves on the board that people care about. It's the fact that it's a human being sitting behind them, moving those pieces along that matters," Susskind argues.

And some think that the advent of AI has actually placed extra value on things created by people. You might call that a human premium.

Human touch

Kyle Chayka, a journalist at The New Yorker focused on technology, says AI writing is now widely considered to be "generic, obsequious and banal". As a result, he says, "I think readers are coming to value very obviously personal writing, and maybe even writing that's messier, less structurally sound or composed or perfected, than they maybe once would've desired."

Chayka goes on: "I think illustration and graphic design is going in the same direction, where the average is too easily accessible, and so designers are leaning into being weirder and more eye-catching and more unusual, trying to find things that AI can't generate so easily."

In response to the surge in AI-created content, academics are racing to develop a universally recognised symbol to denote something that is "human made" (similar to the "Fairtrade" label that emerged in the 1980s). Labels like "AI-free" are already appearing on covers of some books, films, and albums.

For C Thi Nguyen, a philosophy professor at the University of Utah, it's a question of our underlying values.

He says you can often work out your values by following what he calls a "why chain". If you like something or want to do something, ask "why?". If the answer is to make money or be successful, keep asking 'why?' When the process ends, that will be what you really value, he explains.

The question, he says, is whether human involvement and shared human experience will keep its place at the end of the "why chain".

Author John Lanchester is optimistic. He thinks the value of what only humans can do will prevail. In fact, he sympathises with the idea of a 'human premium'.

"If you commodify one kind of thing, the things you can't commodify start to seem more important," he tells me.

The algorithmic loop

All of that might sound heartening for people hoping that humans will remain central to the creation of culture.

But I'm not so sure. The amount of AI-generated content is increasing so quickly that we may soon struggle to distinguish what has or hasn't involved AI.

You may well have seen coverage of the AI 'actor' Tilly Norwood, made last year by a company that bills itself as the world's "first AI talent studio". The Screen Actors Guild in the US was not impressed. "It has no life experience to draw from, no emotion, and, from what we've seen, audiences aren't interested in watching computer-generated content untethered from the human experience," they wrote.

I'm not saying AI will replace actors - of course not. But what feels untethered and strange now, may not, in some situations, feel so strange in time.

It's also worth remembering that long before Large Language Models went mainstream, we'd already allowed technology to shape our cultural tastes.

As recently as the 2000s, we still sought out lots of the culture we consumed. We'd buy a book, a cinema ticket, an album. Sometimes we still do.

But increasingly, culture just arrives - in an endless stream, sorted and served by an algorithm that is constantly predicting our tastes.

At first glance, this sounds convenient. The work's being done for us. But as the role of the algorithm goes up, so the role of humans goes down.

"There's the mythical figure of your big brother's friend or something, who passes on good music taste to you," says Chayka, whose book Filterworld explores the impacts of algorithms on culture. "And now we rely on algorithmic recommendations to do that same thing for us. To introduce us to new things."

I recognise this from my own habits. Back in the 1990s, when I started collecting dance music, I'd find new music through record shops and recommendations from people I trusted. I can still do that, and do. But these days the algorithm's doing a lot of that work for me - and it can be really helpful. I'll find tunes I wouldn't have discovered otherwise.

To an extent, I am letting technology guide me.

Chayka thinks algorithms have made us lazy, and "prevent us from going deeper" in our cultural taste. Sometimes we might find a piece of art that requires work - a long, difficult book, perhaps, or a weird-seeming movie. "It might alienate us initially, but eventually it inspires us," Chayka says.

"I think that kind of culture has fallen by the wayside in favour of culture as content to consume that's not going to change your life, it's just going to turn your brain off for a few hours."

And it's a self-reinforcing loop; creators adapt their work as they seek out the attention the algorithm can provide.

And here's the key point: this shift - to discovering culture via algorithms - is one we've already largely accepted. So when AI starts making books, films, and music in large numbers - might we just shrug and accept that too?

Calculator backlash

Back in 1986, in Washington DC, protesting teachers lined the streets outside a convention centre. They weren't angry about their wages or budget cuts. In this case, the object of their ire was the calculator. Maths teacher John Saxon had taken up the cause. "The kids are not learning their math facts because they're becoming calculator hooked," he proclaimed. " If they had given me a black box, I wouldn't know that… six times eight's 48 'cause it rhymes, and seven times nine is 63 'cause it does not."

We all have our ways of remembering times tables.

Needless to say, this is an argument that Saxon lost. But some of those arguments feel familiar.

Of course, some things are definitely out of range of technology, at least for now. Think of my sweaty DJ night in Falmouth a few weeks ago, with 250 other ravers.

Alex Mahon says she's noticed an uptick in appreciation for in-person experiences like these - perhaps as a backlash to the amount of our lives now spent on a smartphone screen.

She's chief executive of Superstruct Entertainment, one of the world's leading festival and live entertainment groups.

"People want to go to more live things," she says. "They want to have things that are unforeseeable… unpredictable. The special moment is live. The excitement, the discovery is hearing it in person with others."

In the case of culture, when is it OK to outsource to technology, and when is it not? The more I look at this, the less I'm sure we can assume what choices we'll make.

Each of us will have to decide when it matters if something is made by a human.

text:
The Utah high school football season wrapped up for our school (West Jordan) yesterday. 

I went to high schools I had never been to before, and one thing I appreciated was the variety of PA announcers.

Here are my thoughts:

Riverton Silverwolves - every single tackle was "by a pack of wolves!" It didn't matter if it was one player, or the entire defense that made the play.

West Jordan Jaguars - Solid. Wanted people to respond to the call "And that's another Jaguar..." (first down!). His timing for this call was interesting though--he'd often do it after a kickoff. It was technically true a first down was achieved, but an unexpected place for the call to happen.

Cyprus Pirates - A pro. Knew football, when and what to announce. Had a good cadence. Never overstayed his welcome.

Granger Lancers - Legend. I have no knowledge, but my guess is that he's been doing this for a long time. Probably a volunteer, and they offered to pay him, but he refused because he does it for the love of the game. Absolutely no issue pronouncing Polynesian names. He noted which West Jordan player had made a play more than any other announcer.

Kearns Cougars - Ah, good ol Kearns. I believe a student was the PA for the game. Every two minutes, they would encourage everyone in the stadium to get food at the concessions. Every two minutes. A good-natured person who would often make announcements when the ref was announcing a penalty.

New! @NavalWarCollege/@ChinaMaritime Note 25—“Precluding the Powerful Enemy: A New PLA Concept for a #Taiwan Conflict”

https://t.co/BMdbo8zCfM

From #CMSI Director CAPT @ChrisHSharman, @USNavy (Ret.):

#China PLA Watchers: What does the PLA think it must do to dissuade the United States from intervening in a Taiwan conflict?
And if deterrence fails, how does it plan to stop the @DeptofWar from contributing to Taiwan’s defense?

The PLA has a term for this 2-part challenge: preclusion or shezu (慑阻). The concept combines deterrence and denial into a single approach for countering U.S. military intervention in a Taiwan conflict.

The term has appeared with increasing frequency in PLA reporting & academic writing since 2022.

So what exactly is preclusion? Moreover, what can this emerging PLA concept tell us about PLA strategy?

To find out, download China Maritime Studies Institute’s (CMSI) Note #25 authored by Professor Ryan Martinson/@rdmartinson88.

This note offers unique insights into a new PLA concept for a Taiwan conflict. Certainly worth your time!

Key Takeaways:
⚓  In recent years, the PLA has employed a new concept—“preclusion” (shezu)—that captures the 2 related missions of deterring and denying U.S. military intervention in a Taiwan conflict.
⚓  While the precise origin of the term is unknown, as early as 2019 it appeared in an internal PLA article written by a PLA Navy admiral with direct responsibility for commanding forces in a Taiwan campaign. This early use of the concept suggested that “deterrence” (慑) & “denial” (阻) were 2 steps in a 3-step graduated PLA response to U.S. military intervention.
⚓  Since the intensification of PLA operations around Taiwan that began in 2022, the term has frequently appeared in both PLA reporting & academic writing.
⚓  In Chinese military strategy, “preclusion” would seek to combine defensive operations on “interior lines” & offensive operations on “exterior lines.” The former would rely on shore based cruise & ballistic missiles “to use the land to control the sea,” while the latter would favor long-range air & naval operations to envelop the approaching enemy.
⚓  The “preclusion” concept is essential to PLA thinking on “cognitive warfare,” which seeks, among other aims, to deprive the adversary of the will to intervene on Taiwan’s behalf.
⚓  Precluding U.S. military intervention in a Taiwan conflict is an apparent driver of the PLA Navy’s development & employment of carrier strike groups. It is the core focus of PLA Air Force training & operations beyond the First Island Chain.

text:
‘Everyone Should Be Furious’: Lithium-Ion Battery Fires Are Up 41% As Public Fix Stalls

14OCT2026
By Sophia Lebowitz
https://t.co/ejrQtkF8NO

Lithium-ion batteries [fires] are up 41 percent from last year — "Every single New York City resident should be furious," said one advocate.

Fires caused by the lithium-ion batteries used in e-bikes are up 41 percent this year as the city slow-walks safe, outdoor charging and storage initiatives that have been in the works since 2023 — but there’s one bright spot: most fires now happen outside of apartments.

The rise in the raw number of fires isn’t new. In fact, the number of lithium-ion battery fires has grown every year since the Fire Department started counting them in 2020. But in the first three-quarters of 2026, the rate of increase is widening, indicating some shortcomings of the city’s many initiatives to combat battery fires.

“The New York City bureaucracy is obviously failing at its mission of preventing fires,” said Baruch Herzfeld whose company, Popwheels, offers subscription-based battery swapping to delivery workers. “Every single New York City resident should be furious.”

Lithium-ion batteries are particularly flammable. If the battery is overcharged or damaged it can easily enter into a “thermal runaway” reaction; the heat generated by the reaction causes an explosion followed by a self-sustaining fire and an expulsion of hot gases. A battery can explode when it is over-charged, damaged or hit.

E-bikes began proliferating after the state legalized them in 2020 — and an increase in battery fires soon followed. In 2023, just as many of the cheap, uncertified batteries were reaching the end of their useful life, 18 New Yorkers died in battery fires.

So far this year, five people have died in fires. That may sound like a contradiction given the increase in fires this year, but fewer deaths from more fires can be explained simply: This year, 61 percent of battery fires were determined by the FDNY to be “non-structural,” meaning they occurred outside of an apartment, business or home. By comparison, in 2023, just 33 percent of fires were ruled “non-structural.”

The greatest increase in fires this year has been in an undefined category the FDNY calls “other,” which the agency says is selected when a fire “only requires a first-alarm response” and a full investigation isn’t done. This indicates to experts that a large swath of batteries are reaching the end of their usable life and simply exploding due to age or damage.

One former official said the unspecific category was what the investigators used when a battery exploded in a garbage truck. 

“There’s a huge increase in Sanitation truck fires,” said John Orlando, a retired FDNY official who supervised the Lithium-Ion Task Force from 2022 through 2024. “That’s the ‘other.’ We were tracking them back in 2023, so that incident classification ‘other’ is a sanitation truck for us.”

There have been a total of 87 lithium-ion fires in garbage trucks this year according to FDNY. Seventy six were in DSNY sanitation trucks, up from 55 in all of last year, according to the Department of Sanitation.

Early efforts by the city to curb fires focused heavily on charging safety. But it turned out that 59 percent of the lithium-ion battery fires in 2023 started when those batteries were not charging, according to the city. But given that this year, most fires occurred outside or in sanitation trucks, the biggest battle is not with charging, but with disposal.

“There’s no comprehensive plan to deal with the battery life cycles,” said Herzfeld. “There’s a fictitious belief that battery fires don’t happen unless batteries are charging. People are basing their safety guidelines on something that’s not true.”

Another expert who analyzed the recent FDNY data dump said the acceleration in fires this year can be tied to batteries dying en masse.

“From 2023 to 2024 to 2025, [the number of fires] is almost a flat line. [But] now the rate of change is increasing and batteries are reaching the end of their life,” said Adrian Kombe, whose company, Nomoto, is developing a safety device that detects warning signs of battery failure. 

Orlando said despite FDNY’s best efforts to educate e-bike users, most don’t really think about the battery’s end of life. Like people, lithium-ion batteries age a tiny bit with every “cycle” of charge. If a delivery worker is recharging a battery multiple times every day, the battery will age rapidly, creating an ongoing cycle of batteries reaching the end of their life and becoming a higher risk.

“There’s a part of the consumer that thinks, ‘Oh, it’s just a battery, we throw this in the regular waste bin,’” he said. “I don’t think there’s enough information. It’s in the booklet, but who reads through the whole booklet? Or who looks at the booklet two years later if you still have it, or three years later, when the battery’s not working and you have to get rid of it?”

The fires this time
One recent fire in Corona, Queens at a Fly E-Bike shop, a company known for poor battery safety, is emblematic of the growing trend. 

Sal Lopez, who works at the store a few days a week, said the fire started from a battery in a customer’s bike that was left at the shop, not from one that was charging. Customers often call asking if they can dispose of their old batteries at the shop, but the shop doesn’t permit it. 

“They have to take it with them,” he said of customers coming in with old or damaged batteries. Most of the store’s customers are delivery workers, he added. “There should be a place to dispose of [the batteries]. Sometimes people call or ask, they want to leave it or want to find out where to throw it out.”
 
In this case, the sprinkler system suppressed the blaze for long enough to everyone escape safely. But witnesses expressed horror at how quickly the blaze spread.

“It was really fast,” Elias Castañeda, a mechanic at another bike shop on the street that only services traditional bikes, said in Spanish of the fire. Regular bikes cause “less problems” and have “less risks.”

The FDNY acknowledged the increase in fires, but said the increase in non-structural fires shows that a key part of the safety messaging is working.

“The FDNY has shared consistent safety messaging with the public about storing and charging these devices outside where possible. The number of ‘structural’ versus ‘non-structural’ fires leads us to believe that message is being received,” said spokesperson Clare Bourke.

But fires that spare the lives of those around them still scare residents and damage property.

On May 29, an e-bike battery sparked a blaze in a residential building in the Navy Yard section of Fort Greene, and smoke “spread throughout” the entire floor and went into “all the apartments,” said one neighbor.

“When I did look through the peep hole I couldn’t see anything — too much smoke,” said Anette Diaz. “Once the smoke went a little bit, I saw that everything was burnt up. … Everything was destroyed and there was a big hole in the wall.”

Another fire at the Albany Houses in Brooklyn in August killed 18-year-old Caleb Matthews. His mother told Eyewitness News that the fire was caused by an e-bike battery exploding while charging. She urged the city to act.

Federal inaction
The city and state passed laws when regulating the sale of e-bikes and their batteries, requiring a UL certification, the gold standard for safety. The city also created a lithium-ion battery task force to educate delivery workers and other e-bike users about battery risk. But federal regulation around e-bikes and e-scooters is lax, so it is easy to get risky batteries online.

“Even though we put all the regulations in place [and] were able to shut down bad actors in the retail space, it’s still not illegal for somebody to buy a cheaper uncertified bike. You can still get it direct-to-consumer,” said Orlando.

The online marketplace for e-bikes is often referred to as the “Wild West.” Whether it’s over-powered illegal “e-motos” that have high speed capacities and are falsely marketed as street-legal e-bikes, or shoddy batteries, it’s hard to know what you’re buying online. 

“At the end of the day, we’re still just a local fire department, so any ordinance we pass is just for New York City, so we really need the federal government because this stuff is just coming in unfettered, or or the components are coming in unfettered through the borders and through shipping,” Orlando said. 

The Consumer Product Safety Commission, the federal agency that regulates goods shipped to the United States, has proposed rules to deal with the e-bike and e-scooter battery problem, which is not unique to New York City. The domestic e-bike market grew 31 percent between 2018 and 2024, according to the document. If the rule is adopted, UL certification would be required at the federal level. 

What has the city done?
The city’s plan to tackle lithium-ion battery fires was laid out in the “Charge Safe, Ride Safe” action plan issued by the Adams administration in 2023. But most of the initiatives detailed in the plan have either stalled or never made it past a pilot phase. Part of this is because the FDNY regulations are so strict.

“If I want to install a battery cabinet in New York City, it takes me a year and a half. If I want to install one in Philadelphia, Jersey City, two weeks,” said Herzfeld, whose company was a part of the city’s successful public battery-charging pilot program.

Last year, Streetsblog reported that the department changed the type of UL certification required for outdoor cabinets before there was even a way to get said certifications. The department later softened those rules and extended its deadline for compliance, allowing companies to continue using a “letter of no exemption” as proof of safety. But that extension ended on Oct. 1, Herzfeld said. Now it is again impossible for his company to get approval for new sites because that new UL certification is still out of reach.

“It should not be this hard to get life-saving equipment into outdoor parking lots. We should all be embarrassed.”

The pilot ended in 2024. Now, two years later, the Department of Transportation just closed its feedback portal to help it decide where to place 25 permanent battery-swapping cabinets, though they won’t be up and running until 2027 at the earliest.

As part of the action plan, the DOT started allowing businesses and landlords to apply for a permit to install battery charging cabinets on public sidewalks last February. But because of the FDNY’s location requirements, this is nearly impossible, too. To date, zero 
applications have been approved, but “several” are pending, according to an agency spokesperson. 

For delivery workers, who are one of the largest groups of e-bike users in the city, thinking about properly disposing of a battery can be low on the list of priorities when their livelihood is being threatened by a precarious work arrangement. The risk of getting your account deactivated takes precedence over everything.

“We have literally over 100 workers every single day showing up at our center because they’ve been deactivated, and everything else takes a backseat to ‘I’ve lost my job and can’t make a living and can’t deliver,’” said April Herms, the deputy director of the Worker’s Justice Project, which organizes the Los Deliveristas Unidos.

Even at the Worker’s Justice Project headquarters in Williamsburg, where hundreds of delivery workers flock on their bikes to use the organization’s many services, building an outdoor charging cabinet was impossible. There was no place on the large corner lot that fit all of FDNY’s rules, the DOT told Herms. 

“At some point the policy needs to meet the reality because if it doesn’t then what happens is you still have people charging indoors because they don’t have any options. Effectively the FDNY policy is don’t charge inside, don’t charge outside. In fact, just don’t have these batteries,” said Herms.

DOT said it is eager to get its public e-bike charging program off the ground. It also said that Question 1 of the mayor’s charter revision ballot proposals would streamline the process by which landlords apply for permission to install sidewalk cabinets.

“Battery swapping is an important solution to support safe, certified electric micromobility, and DOT is eager to advance it through our Public E-Bike Charging Program and the revocable consent process,” said agency spokesperson Vin Barone.
— With Sam Brule

Note on methodology: Streetsblog analyzed two datasets from FDNY and combined them based on multiple factors. The data only includes fires where the investigations were closed, some recent battery fires still have open investigations.

Sophia Lebowitz
Before joining Streetsblog, Sophia Lebowitz was a filmmaker and journalist covering transportation and culture in New York City.

text:
This sailor escaped a sunken submarine—then hid for 18 months.

On 6 December 1941, during WW2, Royal Navy stoker John Capes was trapped aboard HMS Perseus after it struck a mine off the Greek island of Kefalonia.

He was travelling as a passenger, catching a lift back towards his ship.

The explosion knocked out the lights and sent the submarine plunging to the seabed.

Capes survived in the rear, where air remained trapped.

With a working torch, he searched the wreckage and found three badly injured sailors still alive.

He brought them into the stern compartment, where an escape hatch offered a way out.

Then he fitted them with breathing equipment designed for escaping submerged submarines.

Opening the hatch meant deliberately flooding the space around them until the pressure inside matched the sea outside.

But the valve he needed had a bent spindle and would not move.

Capes found another way to let seawater in, through a device normally used to send smoke signals to the surface.

As the water rose, the space left for breathing shrank.

He worked his way into the escape trunk beneath the hatch and loosened its fastenings.

The lid opened, releasing a great bubble of air.

Capes could have started upwards.

Instead, he went back into the compartment for the injured men.

He helped all three through the escape route before following them out.

When he reached the surface, he could see none of them.

His lungs hurt, the sea was rough, and the submarine had disappeared beneath him.

He spotted a pale line of shore and began swimming towards it.

Using his breathing bag for support, he kept going for hours until he reached the rocks and crawled onto a beach.

Islanders found him the next day.

Kefalonia was occupied, so reaching land had brought him into another kind of danger.

Local people sheltered him for 18 months, moving him between houses to keep him hidden from the occupying forces.

A boat finally carried him to safety in Turkey.

His account of escaping the submarine met with disbelief, although he received the British Empire Medal.

In 1997, a Greek team led by diver Kostas Thoctarides located Perseus in 52 metres of water.

The rear escape hatch was open, and objects inside matched details of Capes’s account.

Capes had died in 1985.

His daughter Julie lived to hear that the wreck had supported the story her father had told.

text:
Happy birthday to former Norman, University of Arkansas and NFL kicker Bill McClard, born on this day in 1949 in Purcell.

McClard attended Norman High School, earning All-State recognition as a senior after kicking three field goals in excess of 50 yards.

In an article that appeared in The Oklahoman in 1967, McClard said he got his kicking start in his back yard, where there were two telephone poles about ten feet apart.

At Norman, McClard did not get a lot of opportunities to kick as the Tigers did a lot of scoring and converting two-point conversions under head coach Gene Corrotto. But when he did get the opportunity, it was noteworthy.

In a late-season victory over Ardmore as a senior, McClard had field goals of 50 and 56 yards. On a third-quarter 58-yard attempt, his kick hit the upright. His 56-yard kick would have tied what was the NFL record at the time.

McClard earned All-State honors from the Oklahoma Journal and also earned special recognition from the Tulsa World as an offensive tackle in 1967.

The attention earned him offers from OU and Arkansas and he chose the Razorbacks, where he set a then-NCAA record 60 yarder in 1970. He was named All-American by the American Football Coaches Association in 1970 and by the Sporting News in 1971.

In the 1972 NFL Draft, McClard was selected by the San Diego Chargers in the third round with the 61st overall pick. He played one season in San Diego and three with the New Orleans Saints, making 26 of his 51 field goal attempts in the NFL, with a long of 52 coming against the Denver Broncos in 1974. He was 2-of-2 from 50-plus yards that season. He also hit 31 of 32 extra points.

Following his retirement from the NFL, McClard became a commercial real estate broker in northwest Arkansas.

▫️🌏 Chinese Protein Producers Expand Globally, Threatening International Food Industry Rivals▫️

🌍 China Expands Into Global Food Markets: Chinese protein producers are increasingly targeting international supermarket shelves, using competitive pricing, expanding production capacity, and improving quality controls to challenge established food suppliers.

🏭 Excess Production Capacity Fuels Expansion: China's food processing industry has developed substantial manufacturing capacity, allowing producers to pursue overseas customers as domestic competition intensifies. Export growth offers companies an opportunity to utilize factories more efficiently and increase revenue.

💰 Aggressive Pricing Challenges Global Competitors: Chinese manufacturers are pursuing a strategy similar to the country's expansion in steel, solar panels, and electric vehicles. Large production volumes and lower prices can pressure international competitors, particularly those facing higher labor, energy, and operating costs.

🥩 Protein Products Become a New Export Opportunity: Chinese suppliers are seeking opportunities across processed meat, seafood, and other protein categories. Their ability to offer competitively priced products could attract supermarket chains, food distributors, and restaurant suppliers looking to reduce procurement expenses.

🛡️ Food Safety Reputation Remains a Major Obstacle: China's history of food contamination scandals continues to create concerns among international consumers and regulators. Exporters must demonstrate compliance with strict food safety requirements, product testing procedures, and traceability standards to establish credibility in foreign markets.

🛒 Supermarkets Face New Competitive Choices: Retailers could benefit from lower wholesale prices and a broader supplier base. However, sourcing decisions also involve food safety certifications, import regulations, supply chain reliability, and consumer confidence.

⚖️ Trade Tensions Could Spread Into Food Markets: If Chinese protein exports expand rapidly, domestic producers in importing countries could face stronger price competition. Industry groups may seek trade investigations or additional import restrictions, although any government response would depend on evidence of unfair trading practices or other legal grounds.

📉 Global Food Industry Faces Potential Disruption: China's growing export ambitions could reshape competition in international protein markets. The extent of that disruption will depend on whether Chinese producers can maintain low prices while consistently meeting overseas safety standards and winning consumer trust.

A bipartisan group of eight US states is suing OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT. 

The states include Iowa, Kansas, Arizona, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Idaho, and Montana. 

Officials accuse the artificial intelligence company of violating consumer protection laws and endangering public health. 

They claim that OpenAI marketed its chatbot as safe while secretly knowing it could cause severe mental and physical harm to minors.

The lawsuits claim that ChatGPT acts as a "fake friend" to gain the trust of young users. According to the states, the software has coached children to commit suicide and engage in self-harm. 

It also allegedly reinforces dangerous delusions, 

offers unsafe medical advice, and helps users plan real-world violence like mass shootings. 

Because of these extreme safety failures, the states are demanding that OpenAI radically change how its software works for children and give up all profits made from young users.

This coordinated legal action is the largest state-led assault OpenAI has faced regarding child safety. 

It follows a similar lawsuit filed by Florida's attorney general. 

The heavy legal pressure arrives at a critical time for OpenAI, 

as the tech firm is actively preparing to transition into a public company. 

Beyond this child-safety case, 

OpenAI is already fighting dozens of separate lawsuits claiming its technology assisted in mass shootings or wrongful deaths.

text:
French author goes viral with post warning Americans not to vote Democrat—or else America will end up like debt-ridden, riot-torn France | Human Events Media Group, Human Events

A post from a French author has gone viral, garnering more than 2.2 million views on X, after he issued a warning to Americans who are planning to vote for Democrats. "I’m French. I want to talk to Americans who are about to vote Democrat. Not to insult you. To warn you. I come from your future," Brivael Le Pogam began.

His post comes as France is facing weeks of riots, thousands of arrests, arson, and mayhem in what began as student protests seeking better conditions for education. Those riots have spread to unions and teachers and on into Belgium.

He said that France bought into the "progressive politicians promise" of free everything, including "healthcare, free college, generous welfare, strong unions, heavy regulation, high taxes on the rich, a state that takes care of everything." As a result, he said the costs and spending rose to nearly 60 percent of the nation's gross domestic product, "one of the highest on the planet."

While acknowledging that "on paper, it's the dream," he said that "from the inside," things are crumbling. Massive debt is threatening to bankrupt the nation, and the services so generously provided are not working.

"France hasn’t passed a balanced budget since 1974," he wrote. "Our debt is above 3,300 billion euros. Interest on that debt is becoming one of the biggest items in the national budget. Our hospitals are collapsing despite record funding. Our schools rank lower every year. Young people with degrees can’t afford an apartment in the city they were born in. Our best engineers leave for London, Zurich and San Francisco. And the rich you wanted to tax? They left too, and took the jobs with them. The promise was protection. The result is stagnation."

The French voted for great things, he said, "Every single step sounded generous, compassionate, reasonable. One more program. One more regulation. One more tax to fund it. Each step alone makes sense. Fifty years of them, and you wake up in a country that can no longer build a nuclear plant on time or keep its streets safe."

He said that he loves America "because it's the one place on earth where people still believe they can build something from nothing. I came to Silicon Valley as a self-taught kid and it changed my life. That spirit is the most precious thing your country has. Before you vote, ask yourself one question: is the program you’re voting for making America more like America, or more like France? Trust me. You don’t want to be France."

In a follow-up post, he addressed critics who said to him that "Democrats aren't socialists. America will never be France." He walked through his claims, backing them up with data.

"Start with a simple observation. Look at what has gotten cheaper in America over the last 25 years: TVs, phones, software, clothes, toys. Now look at what has exploded: college tuition, healthcare, childcare, housing. What separates the two lists? The first lives in competitive markets. The second is exactly where government is most involved: subsidies, mandates, licensing, zoning, regulation," he noted.

He went on to say that those items that are horrendously, prohibitively expensive are the ones "where the market has already been replaced by the state. And the solution you're being offered is more of the same."

The big free programs, he said, are just making things worse. "Then the failure of that program becomes the argument for the next one. People who lived under communism in Poland learned to recognize the lie and the mask the lie wears. The lie never presents itself as a lie. It presents itself as compassion," he said.

"In France we are at the end of that road," he said in conclusion. "Debt we can never repay. Young people who can't afford a home. Our best people leaving. And every few years our cities burn. Nobody voted for this. They voted for one more generous promise, fifty years in a row." The bill on those promises is now coming due, and France can't pony up the cash.

"If you're a Republican," he urged, "share this with the Democrat in your life. Not to win an argument. To start a conversation. If you're a Democrat, I'm not asking you to switch teams. I'm asking you to look at the pattern. Wherever the state took over, life became unaffordable. Don't fix the failures of government with more government. Stay American. Ask for less state, not more."

text:
I and all Muslims advocate for the proliferation of Islām in all lands across the earth. This is one of the obligations enjoined on us by Allāh سبحانه وتعالى.

Islām is spread by both jihād and daʿwah. Jihād is armed struggle by Muslims against the disbelievers to make the word of Allāh the highest. Daʿwah is calling to the true religion by word.

That said, all four schools of Islāmic jurisprudence have agreed that a Muslim who enters a land of the disbelievers with a guarantee of safety from its authorities is obligated to return that guarantee, and breaking it is a form of hideous treachery. This applies to modern visas and passports, as anyone who enters a land of the disbelievers with a visa or passport is at least implicitly welcomed and protected by the authorities of that land.

Imām ash-Shāfiʿī stated in Al-Umm:

“So if they, or some of them, grant him security and admit him into their lands according to what is customarily recognized among them as granting him protection, while they are capable of doing so, then it becomes binding upon him that they should be safe from him — even if he did not explicitly state that.” 

It is not prohibited for a Muslim to treat the disbelieving population of the land he resides in with justice and kindness; instead, it is a praiseworthy act that can help achieve the purpose of inviting others to Islām. Allāh سبحانه وتعالى says in the Qurʾān:

لَّا يَنْهَىٰكُمُ ٱللَّهُ عَنِ ٱلَّذِينَ لَمْ يُقَـٰتِلُوكُمْ فِى ٱلدِّينِ وَلَمْ يُخْرِجُوكُم مِّن دِيَـٰرِكُمْ أَن تَبَرُّوهُمْ وَتُقْسِطُوٓا۟ إِلَيْهِمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُقْسِطِينَ

“Allah does not forbid you from dealing kindly and fairly with those who have neither fought nor driven you out of your homes. Surely Allah loves those who are fair.”

If the authorities of that land prevent Muslims from practising or spreading their religion, it is prohibited for a Muslim to continue to reside there and it becomes an obligation for him to leave. I’m not aware of any difference of opinion among Muslim scholars on this point.

Jihād against the disbelievers is not committed through treachery or killing non-combatants. These are explicitly prohibited in our religion.

Rabāḥ ibn Rabīʿ reported in Sunan Abī Dāwūd:

When the Prophet ﷺ saw people gathered around something, he sent a man to investigate. He returned and said:

“A woman has been killed.”

The Prophet ﷺ said:

“She was not one who would have fought.”

Then he instructed Khalid ibn al-Walid:

“Do not kill women or hired workers (or servants).”

Rather, jihād against the disbelievers is done through an external force, usually a state, that first invites a group of disbelievers to Islām, offers them the jizyah if they refuse, and fights them if they refuse even that. 

Furthermore, war is not the only state of relations between a Muslim state and a disbelieving state. It is permissible for a Muslim state to sign a peace treaty with a disbelieving state and engage in diplomacy, trade, or any other type of cooperation if there’s a need for or benefit in it.

I and all Muslims strive for the instatement of Sharīʿah. We believe that the Sharīʿah would solve many of the social and economic ills present in the modern world. However, its implementation must follow the guidelines outlined above. It’s not permissible to commit disobedience to Allāh with the aim of achieving a greater good. This is the belief of communists and their like, not of the Muslims.

I have tried to answer your question honestly, to the best of my knowledge and ability, without watering anything down. Take from this as you will.

text:
The ticket at the window

In an order dated 6 October, the Supreme Court has directed Indian Railways that from 27 October 2026, tickets bought at station counters must be covered by insurance "in the same manner as tickets purchased online". At present, online e-tickets offer optional cover of up to ₹10 lakh for about 45 paise; the terms for counter tickets are yet to be notified.

It is a small change, the kind very few people will notice. But it stayed with me.

For a long time, travel in India was not something you could simply count on. It came as a state legacy that barely worked, where privilege and connections decided who got a seat, a berth or a little consideration. For those with the least, there was rarely an alternative, and almost never any thought for their dignity.

Many of us now take it for granted that the system will at least treat us as equals. For vast numbers of people, that basic courtesy has never been a given. The person queuing at the window, without an app or a card, has quietly been second in line by default.

So when an order closes even a small part of that gap, it deserves to be noticed. Not because it fixes everything, since the details and how claims will work are still to come, but because of the principle behind it: dignity shouldn't depend on how you book your ticket.

Real progress is often like this. Not the big announcements, but the quiet corrections that finally include the people who were always left out.

SPIRITUAL BATH (GHUSL)
Praise be to Allah (Subhanahu wa ta’ala).

Is Ghusl sufficient with no need for wudoo:
Shaykh ‘Abd al-‘Azeez ibn Baaz (may Allaah have mercy on him) said, as it says in Majmoo’ Fataawa Ibn Baaz (10/173-174): 

If it is ghusl from janaabah, and the person doing ghusl intends to remove both major and minor impurity, then it is sufficient for both, but it is better for him to wash his private parts, then do wudoo’, then complete his ghusl, following the example of the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allaah be upon him). The same ruling applies to women following menses and nifaas. 

But if the ghusl is for another reason, such as ghusl for Jumu’ah or ghusl to cool oneself off or to clean oneself, then it is not sufficient with no need for wudoo’ even if one intends that, because the parts are not washed in sequence, which is one of the essential parts of wudoo’, and because there is no major impurity where minor impurity may be included in the intention (to purify oneself), as is the case with ghusl from janaabah. End quote.  

He also said in Majmoo’ al-Fataawa (10/175-176): 

The Sunnah for the one who is junub is to do wudoo’ and then do ghusl, following the example of the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allaah be upon him). If he does ghusl from janaabah with the intention of purifying himself from both types of impurity, both major and minor, then that is sufficient, but it is not the best way.  But if the ghusl is mustahabb, such as ghusl for Jumu’ah or to cool down, then it does not count instead of wudoo’, rather it is essential to do wudoo’ before or after, because the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allaah be upon him) said: “Allaah does not accept the prayer of any one of you if he breaks his wudoo’ unless he does wudoo’.” Saheeh – agreed upon. 

And he (peace and blessings of Allaah be upon him) said: “No prayer is accepted without purification.” Narrated by Muslim in his Saheeh. 
Ghusl that is mustahabb or permissible is not counted as purification from minor impurity unless it is done as prescribed by Allaah in the verse (interpretation of the meaning): 
“O you who believe! When you intend to offer As-Salaah (the prayer), wash your faces and your hands (forearms) up to the elbows, rub (by passing wet hands over) your heads, and (wash) your feet up to the ankles”
[al-Maa’idah  5:6]. 

But if it is ghusl to purify oneself from janaabah, menses or nifaas, and one intends to do both types of purification, then the minor is included with the major, because the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allaah be upon him) said: “Actions are but by intentions and each man will have but that which he intended.” Saheeh – agreed upon. End quote. 
Shaykh Ibn ‘Uthaymeen (may Allaah have mercy on him) said in Liqa’ al-Baab il-Maftooh (no. 109, answer 14): 

If he does ghusl with the intention of wudoo’, but he does not do wudoo’, that is not sufficient with no need for wudoo’ unless it is ghusl from janaabah. If it is ghusl from janaabah then ghusl is sufficient with no need for wudoo’, because Allaah says (interpretation of the meaning): “If you are in a state of Janaaba (i.e. after a sexual discharge), purify yourselves (bathe your whole body)” [al-Maa’idah 5:6], and He did not mention wudoo’. 
But if he does ghusl to cool off or he does ghusl for Jumu’ah or some other ghusl that is mustahabb, then it is not sufficient because that ghusl is not aimed at removing impurity. 
So the basic principle is that if the ghusl is aimed at removing impurity – i.e., janaabah, or menses in the case of a woman – then it is sufficient with no need for wudoo’, otherwise it is not sufficient with no need for wudoo’. End quote. 
And Allaah knows best.

text:
Palestinians are Enemies of the Jewish State 

For seventy eight years the core of the Palestinian national movement has sought the elimination of Israel as a sovereign Jewish state. The war of 1948 ended with armistice lines that left Israel in control of more territory than the partition plan had assigned. Palestinian leadership and the Arab states continued to refuse recognition and maintained a state of belligerency. 

An enemy is a party whose objective is the destruction of your nation rather than the adjustment of its borders or policies. A partner in a conflict is a party that disagrees on territory or rights and is willing to settle the disagreement through negotiation without the systematic use of violence against the civilian population or the institutions of the state.

The historical record places the Palestinians in the first category as an enemy of Israel. In November 1947 the United Nations General Assembly voted to partition the remaining territory of the British Mandate into a Jewish state and an Arab state. The Jewish leadership accepted the plan while the Arab Higher Committee and the governments of the neighboring Arab states rejected it and launched a war to prevent the Jewish state from coming into being.

The Arab states that invaded in 1948 did so under the banner of preventing a Jewish state and many of their leaders spoke openly of driving the Jews into the sea. Palestinian fighters participated in the fighting and in subsequent years the idea of return was framed not as resettlement in a new Arab state but as the reversal of the Jewish victory and the restoration of Arab majority rule over the entire territory.

In the 1960s and 1970s Palestinian organizations based in Jordan, Lebanon, and elsewhere carried out airline hijackings, the murder of diplomats, and the attack on Israeli athletes at the 1972 Munich Olympics. Their stated purpose was to end the Zionist state.

These attacks were accompanied by a political program that rejected any Jewish sovereignty. Maps produced by Palestinian organizations showed the entire area as Palestine with no Israel. Speeches by leaders described the Jews as colonial invaders whose presence would be temporary and whose removal would restore justice to the land.

The Palestine Liberation Organization under Yasser Arafat adopted a charter that called for the liberation of all of Palestine and the elimination of the Zionist entity. Even after the organization formally amended some articles under American pressure in the 1990s the practical policy of rejecting Jewish national rights remained in place. 

Generations of Palestinian children have been taught that the land is theirs alone and that martyrdom in the struggle against Israel is the highest aspiration. This educational system makes a future generation of negotiators who accept Israel unlikely.

The First Intifada that erupted in 1987 mobilized large numbers of Palestinians in the territories captured in 1967. The uprising was presented as a popular revolt against occupation yet its leaders rejected offers of autonomy that would have begun a process toward self government without ending the Jewish state.

The Oslo process of the 1990s transferred administrative control of major Palestinian population centers to the newly created Palestinian Authority. When Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak offered a Palestinian state on most of the West Bank and Gaza with a capital in parts of Jerusalem at the Camp David summit in 2000 the proposal was rejected. The Second Intifada followed within weeks and more than one thousand Israelis were killed and thousands more wounded before the construction of the security barrier and military operations reduced the number of successful attacks.

A further offer by Prime Minister Ehud Olmert in 2008 that included additional territorial swaps and a shared arrangement for Jerusalem was likewise turned down without a counter offer that accepted the permanence of a Jewish state. Hamas, which won elections in Gaza and seized full control there in 2007, has never hidden its objective. Its original charter quotes religious texts calling for the killing of Jews and states that the land of Palestine is an Islamic endowment that cannot be relinquished.

Years of rocket fire from Gaza, the construction of attack tunnels, and the diversion of construction materials into military infrastructure prepared the conditions for the assault of October 7 2023. On that morning thousands of fighters crossed the border, murdered civilians in their homes, raped women, and abducted more than two hundred hostages. The attack was planned over years and celebrated by Hamas leaders as a historic achievement that would lead to further stages of the struggle.

Public opinion surveys conducted by the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research in the aftermath showed that a majority of respondents in both the West Bank and Gaza viewed the attack as justified. These findings are consistent with earlier polls that have repeatedly found majorities opposed to recognizing Israel as the nation state of the Jewish people and supportive of armed struggle as the primary means of advancing Palestinian goals.

Successive Israeli governments have negotiated, withdrawn from territory, and released prisoners in exchange for commitments that were later broken. The pattern has been that periods of relative calm are used to rebuild military capacity and that every political concession is followed by demands for further concessions rather than by acceptance of a final status that leaves Israel intact as a Jewish and democratic state.

The meetings between Israeli leaders and Palestinian representatives over decades produced temporary arrangements and limited security cooperation in certain periods. They did not produce a Palestinian leadership prepared to abandon the demand that Israel disappear or be reduced to a non Jewish entity within borders that would leave it unable to defend itself.

This record establishes the Palestinians as an enemy of Israel in the precise sense that their dominant political movements seek the destruction of the Jewish nation state. The distinction guides the necessary response. Security requires the ability to prevent the concentration of forces that can carry out mass attacks, the denial of international legitimacy to groups that pursue eliminationist goals, and the maintenance of defensible lines until a Palestinian leadership emerges that is prepared to live alongside Israel rather than in its place.

The Jewish people returned to sovereignty in their land after centuries in which they lacked the means to defend themselves against those who sought their destruction. The present generation carries the responsibility of ensuring that the state created for that purpose continues to exist. Understanding the nature of the adversary is the necessary starting point for that task.

text:
Trump Targets Permit Delays As America’s Power Grid Faces Growing Risks | Matt Margolis, PJ Media

President Donald Trump is pushing federal agencies to clear the path for pipelines and power lines as Congress continues debating energy-permitting reform. Considering the condition of America’s electrical grid, the more troubling question is why removing needless delays has taken so long.

At an October 13 meeting in Washington, administration officials described efforts already underway at the Army Corps of Engineers, the EPA, and the Interior Department. Their aim is to shorten the approval process for energy infrastructure that can spend years waiting for federal permission before construction even begins.

Lee Forsgren, the Army’s senior civil works official, said individual Corps permits can take a year and frequently two. The agency is preparing proposals to expand nationwide permits, a streamlined option for activities with minimal environmental effects. Forsgren floated allowing certain projects to disturb up to two acres, rather than the current half-acre limit, and said the agency aims to complete eligible permits in roughly 45 days.

From Conservative Daily News:

“A lot of it is transmitting that energy across our country, whether it’s power lines, whether it’s pipelines, and I think that is now the greatest opportunity, and unfortunately, happens to be one of the areas of greatest … litigation in the country,” Interior Deputy Secretary Kate MacGregor said on the panel.

The permitting system so often ends in litigation that companies cannot assure shareholders when a project will be delivered, MacGregor said, adding that “we need aggressive action.”

“What you need is the strength and durability of these decisions to last beyond just one administration,” she said of the discussion over judicial review of permits.

Those are proposals and goals, not a promise that every pipeline or transmission project will suddenly receive a 45-day approval. Still, Trump’s team is doing something useful: examining which federal hurdles actually protect the public and which merely keep construction plans trapped in Washington.

The Corps already reissued 56 existing nationwide permits and added one new permit in January. Eligible projects still face applicable conditions, but the system offers a path around the longer individual permitting process when their environmental effects qualify as minimal.

The urgency is documented by Trump’s own Energy Department. Its July 2026 draft National Transmission Needs Study found a pressing need for additional power lines as electricity demand rises from data centers, factories, and other major users. Aging transmission equipment and changes in electricity generation add further pressure.

This is about more than convenience. The people who manufacture essential supplies, run hospitals, farm, and keep businesses open need dependable electricity. America’s ambitions in artificial intelligence and domestic manufacturing also require enough generation and transmission to deliver power where it's needed. Announcing another factory or data center accomplishes little if the electricity can’t reach it.

Independent reliability experts have sounded similar alarms. A 2026 assessment from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation documented an 11-gigawatt increase in projected summer peak demand from the previous year’s assessment. Record additions of generation and batteries helped, but some regions remained exposed to shortages under difficult conditions.

Security makes the situation even more serious. Federal watchdogs warn that aging infrastructure and increasingly connected grid controls create vulnerabilities. Foreign adversaries, including China and Russia, pose cyber threats to critical infrastructure. A sophisticated attack could cause an outage with consequences far beyond an inconvenient evening without electricity.

Faster permits won’t install cyber defenses or replace every worn transformer. They can, however, help builders expand and reinforce the physical network. Security upgrades and responsible maintenance must accompany that construction. America needs an electrical system that can handle tomorrow’s demand and withstand tomorrow’s threats.

The EPA and Army are also reconsidering the federal definition of protected waters, with a September proposal that took public comments through October 9. Clear boundaries can help property owners and energy developers understand which projects require federal review, while retaining meaningful water protections.

Congress still has a role. Lasting permitting reform would reduce uncertainty for projects whose financing and construction extend across presidential administrations. But nothing prevents the executive branch from improving processes within its existing legal authority today.

Trump deserves credit for recognizing that the energy system supporting American life can’t be modernized on a government calendar that treats years of delay as normal. Success will be measured by permits issued, projects completed, and a grid better prepared to keep the lights on.

His administration has made a welcome start; now the country needs results.
