text:
Days ago, 94-year-old Guan Dongxiang (官冬香) in Shangrao (上饶) of east China's Jiangxi Province reached out and shook hands with an American visitor.

84 years ago, she was just nine years old. An American pilot had fallen from the sky, wrapped in his parachute. Her father brought him to safety. He reached into his pocket, pulled out a handful of candies that looked like little beans, and placed them in her hand.

"It was sweet. I can still remember the taste to this day," she recalled.

The little girl could never have imagined that 84 years later, descendants of American airmen would cross the Pacific Ocean and travel all the way to her village in China, searching for the people who had saved their fathers' lives during the war.

But behind this small, heartwarming memory lies one of the most remarkable and tragic chapters of China-US cooperation during WWII.

To understand how it all happened, we have to go back to April 18, 1942.

On that day, Lieutenant Colonel James Doolittle of the US Army Air Forces led 16 B-25 bombers on an audacious air raid against Tokyo, Nagoya, and other Japanese cities. The bombers took off from the USS Hornet, an American aircraft carrier.

The mission was launched in retaliation for Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. It was also the first American air raid on the Japanese mainland since the Pacific War began.

At the time, Allied forces had suffered a series of defeats across the Pacific, and morale was low. The raid demonstrated that Japan's home islands were not beyond the reach of American bombers, delivering a much-needed boost to morale in the United States and among its allies.

But for the 80 airmen who took part in the mission, completing the bombing raid was only the beginning of a dangerous journey.

The B-25 bombers were too large to land on an aircraft carrier. Before the mission, even taking off from a carrier had been considered nearly impossible for aircraft of that size. American engineers modified the planes, adding extra fuel tanks to extend their range.

The plan was to strike Japan, then continue westward to China, where they would land at airfields near Quzhou (衢州) in Zhejiang Province.

On April 2, the USS Hornet quietly departed from the San Francisco Bay Area. On April 14, it joined the USS Enterprise in the North Pacific, and the two carriers headed toward Japan.

But when the American fleet was still about 600 nautical miles from Tokyo, it was spotted by a Japanese patrol vessel.

Fearing that the Japanese might launch a counterattack, the American commander decided to send the bombers off earlier than planned.

That decision meant the planes would have to fly a much greater distance to reach China, pushing their fuel supplies to the limit.

To make matters worse, communication and coordination with Chinese airfields had been disrupted by the unexpected early launch. Some American bombers that managed to reach the vicinity of their intended landing sites were reportedly mistaken for Japanese aircraft. With runway lights turned off, they were unable to land.

Of the 16 bombers, only one managed to land in the Soviet Union, near Vladivostok.

The crews of the other 15 were forced to abandon their planes.

Of the 75 airmen aboard those planes, one died during a parachute descent, two drowned at sea, and eight were captured by Japanese forces.

Of the eight airmen captured by Japanese forces, three were executed. The remaining five were told that they, too, would be executed if Japan lost the war. One of them later died from abuse and mistreatment in captivity. Of the four who survived, one was near death by the time Japan surrendered in August 1945.

The other 64 airmen escaped capture with the help of Chinese civilians and soldiers, who sheltered them, provided food and medical care, and escorted them to safety. Some returned to the United States, while others stayed in China and continued fighting Japan.

At first, Doolittle himself feared that the mission had been a failure. Fifteen of the 16 bombers had been lost, and he worried that he might face a court-martial when he returned home.

But after reaching Chongqing (重庆), China's wartime capital, he learned from news reports that Americans were celebrating the raid. He and his fellow airmen were being hailed as heroes. Doolittle was subsequently promoted to brigadier general.

On April 21, when FDR was asked at a press conference where the bombers had taken off from, he jokingly replied, "Shangri-La."

But for the airmen who had bombed Japan and then flown toward China, the most urgent challenge was simply surviving in unfamiliar mountains and finding a way to safety. They owed their survival to complete strangers in China.

One of those fortunate airmen was James Macia, aboard Plane No. 14.

All five crew members of his plane parachuted into the Shangrao area, where they were rescued by Chinese villagers.

James was the third crew member to jump. As he descended, powerful winds tore away his backpack and the supplies attached to his flight jacket.

He eventually landed on a mountaintop in what is now Guangfeng District of Shangrao.

Wrapped in his parachute, he spent the night alone in the cold, damp mountains. When local villagers found him, they brought him eggs, honey, and other food. They also built a fire to help dry his wet clothes.

Once he had regained his strength, the villagers escorted him to a local government office, where he was reunited with the rest of his crew.

But one particular memory stayed with James for the rest of his life.

Among the Chinese villagers he encountered was a young man with his trouser legs rolled up, smiling at him.

James never learned his name. He never found out what happened to him, or whether he even survived the war. But even in his final days, James could still remember that smile.

Over the years, James often told his son, Thomas Macia, about the Chinese people who had saved his life. Those memories stayed with Thomas long after his father passed away.

Determined to learn more about this chapter of his father's life, Thomas traveled to Shangrao in 2018 to retrace his footsteps. During his visit, he met a local university professor who studied history.

A few years later, Thomas discovered two yellowed photographs in his father's old photo albums. One showed a young Chinese girl with short hair standing behind Jack Sims, his father's colleague at Plan No. 14. Her mouth was wide open, and her eyes were filled with surprise.

The other showed more than a dozen Chinese villagers standing in front of a farmhouse.

Thomas sent the photographs to the Chinese professor, who followed the clues and eventually located the descendants of Guan Wenqing, a villager who rescued Sims.

And the wide-eyed little girl standing behind the American pilot?

She was Guan Wenqing's daughter, Guan Dongxiang.

"I was only nine years old when I first saw an American pilot who had parachuted into our village," she recalled.

Sims had landed on a mountainside, where he spent the night wrapped in his parachute. He was not discovered until the following morning, when Guan Wenqing found him and helped him down the mountain.

The Guan family first made him some noodles, but he struggled to use chopsticks. So they offered Sims two roasted sweet potatoes instead. He was very happy and ate them both, Guan Dongxiang recalled.

"Then he reached into his pocket, pulled out a handful of candies that looked like little beans, and shared them with us. None of us had ever seen anything like them before, so nobody dared to eat them. I was the first to try one." The old lady said.

But helping American airmen in wartime China involved far more than offering food and shelter. It also meant putting one's own life at risk.

By 1942, many cities, major transportation routes, and coastal areas in eastern China had already fallen under Japanese occupation.

Some American airmen landed in Japanese-controlled territory or areas where Japanese troops were operating. If discovered, the airmen risked being captured, while the local people who helped them could face brutal retaliation.

Yet despite the danger, many Chinese villagers chose to help these American airmen who had fallen from the sky, even though they could not understand a word they were saying.

But this extraordinary rescue effort came at a devastating cost. Following the Doolittle Raid, Japan launched the Zhejiang-Jiangxi Campaign. The operation was intended to "punish" Chinese civilians and soldiers who had helped rescue American airmen, while also destroying airfields in eastern China that could potentially be used by American bombers again.

Japanese forces burned villages, massacred civilians, and conducted biological warfare.

The Chinese villagers had offered eggs, honey, and noodles. What followed was the burning of entire villages, biological warfare, and mass killings.

250,000 Chinese died. That is nearly 4,000 Chinese civilian deaths for every American airman rescued.

The young Chinese villager who helped rescue James Macia has never been identified. No one knows what happened to him afterward. It is possible that he, too, lost his life during the Japanese reprisals.

84 years ago, Chinese villagers reached out to American airmen in the midst of war.

84 years later, across generations and across the Pacific Ocean, those hands have come together once again.

text:
Actually, that never happened; the Bible is the most reliable that exists. There are thousands of ancient manuscripts, archaeological confirmations, fulfilled prophecies, and a historical and textual coherence that no other ancient book possesses. There was never any leader ordering the burning of divergent copies, because it was preserved and copied by independent communities over centuries, without a centralized control that eliminated variants, and yet the text remained stable.

A war-band can take a peninsula and still not own its own story. Muhammad died in Medina in June 632. Within a generation his men were not reciting one fixed text. According to the Sunni canon itself—Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 and 5102—Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, campaigning in Armenia and Azerbaijan under the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan (r. 644–656), heard Syrian and Iraqi soldiers accusing one another over variant readings of the Qur’an and feared schism. Uthman ordered Zayd ibn Thabit and a small committee to produce one official recension from the sheets already gathered under Abu Bakr after the battle of Yamamah (c. 632–633), sent copies to the main garrison cities, and commanded that other written collections be burned. That is not how a father handles truth. That is how a commander handles a riot in camp. The man of the raid had offered fighting men what fighting men already priced—women, spoil, rank, a paradise with the smell of victory on it—and he got his army: Hijrah 622, Badr 624, the taking of Mecca in 630, a community armed enough that, after 632, it walked out of Arabia and broke the near frontiers of Byzantium and Ctesiphon. He did not get control of the wording. The sword can gather a host. It cannot keep ten mouths from rewriting the banner. When the banner starts a fight, the caliph does not repent. He lights a fire under the other pages (Bukhari 4987).

text:
Around 965, a Jewish traveller from Muslim Spain named Ibrahim ibn Yaqub journeyed through Central Europe. 

Originally from Tortosa, in present-day Catalonia, he left one of the earliest surviving descriptions of the emerging Polish state. His account, preserved by the 11th-century Arab geographer al-Bakri, offers a rare contemporary glimpse of Mieszko I's realm.

Ibrahim describes Mieszko's country as extensive and prosperous, with ample food and resources. This wasn't a marginal tribe; it looked like a substantial territorial power.

He reports that Mieszko maintained a permanent force of 3,000 armoured warriors. This wasn't a part-time peasant militia; it was a professional force supported by the ruler. He even claimed that 100 of Mieszko's men could defeat 1,000 ordinary fighters. That implies training, organisation, and resources on a substantial scale.

Ibrahim also notes the financial system behind that army. Mieszko collected revenues from his subjects and distributed the proceeds to his warriors. He equipped them with horses, weapons and clothing. This suggests a level of centralised administration that went well beyond tribal structures.

Perhaps most surprisingly, he writes that Mieszko supported not only his soldiers but also their families, providing for children from birth and arranging marriages with financial support. That suggests a system designed to secure loyalty across generations.

Ibrahim also sketched Poland's place among its neighbours: the Rus' to the east, the Prussians to the north, and the Veleti as enemies. He described other peoples and places in the region, from Prague's commercial importance to the Veleti's political organisation. However, we cannot be sure that he personally visited Mieszko's lands. His information may have come partly from other travellers and informants.

Still, his description is extraordinary. By the 960s, Poland already possessed a functioning military-fiscal monarchy. That suggests Mieszko inherited developed institutions rather than creating them from scratch. Whoever his predecessors were, named or unnamed, they must already have begun building a territorial state.

text:
The History of the Superstrat, 1954–2026

The Superstrat evolved as guitarists modified Fender’s 1954 Stratocaster for greater output, tuning stability and upper-fret access. Its foundation was the contoured body, bolt-on neck, 25.5-inch scale, three single-coil pickups and synchronized vibrato.

During the 1970s, Southern California players combined Strat-style bodies with aftermarket humbuckers, replacement necks, larger frets and upgraded hardware. Wayne Charvel opened his repair shop in 1974; pickup makers supplied the hot-rod movement.

Eddie Van Halen’s Frankenstein, assembled around 1977, became its defining symbol. The early black-and-white guitar featured a Strat-derived body, bridge humbucker, maple neck, minimal controls and Fender-style vibrato. Red stripes and the Floyd Rose came later. Van Halen’s 1978 debut popularized the concept.

Grover Jackson acquired Charvel’s business in 1978. San Dimas guitars brought bolt-on necks, humbuckers, jumbo frets and specialized bridges into production.

Floyd Rose developed a double-locking vibrato in the late 1970s, receiving his foundational patent in 1979. Locking strings at the nut and bridge reduced tuning problems during extreme pitch changes; bridge fine tuners followed. Kramer’s wooden-neck Pacer, introduced in 1981, helped bring locking systems to a larger market.

The 1984 Jackson Soloist advanced the design with neck-through construction, 24 frets, compound-radius fingerboards and sculpted upper-fret access. It demonstrated an alternative to bolt-on construction.

In 1987, Ibanez introduced Steve Vai’s JEM777 and the RG550. The JEM combined HSH pickups, 24 frets, an Edge double-locking vibrato, recessed bridge routing and its monkey grip. The RG550 adapted similar features to a less elaborate design. Fender expanded its range with the HM Strat in 1988.

Pickup arrangements evolved from a bridge humbucker to HH, HSS and HSH configurations. Coil splitting and expanded switching added flexibility. Fingerboards moved beyond Fender’s vintage 7.25-inch radius toward flatter and compound surfaces. Thin neck profiles, jumbo frets and 22- or 24-fret layouts became common, but none was mandatory.

The Ibanez Universe extended the concept to seven strings in 1990. ESP, Hamer, Yamaha, Washburn and others developed their own interpretations. The engineering endured.

Modern Charvel, Jackson, Ibanez and other Superstrats offer roasted maple necks, stainless-steel frets, refined neck joints, locking tuners, improved tremolos, hardtails and flexible electronics. Their legacy is not one silhouette or pickup layout, but the transformation of Fender’s adaptable original into an enduring family of high-performance guitars.

text:
The Country School Children of Oklahoma, 1936. During the Dust Bowl years of the Great Depression, thousands of rural children across Oklahoma continued walking miles to small country schools despite drought, poverty, and constant uncertainty at home. Families who had lost crops, livestock, and savings still believed education might offer their children a future beyond the hardship surrounding them.

The Harper children lived on a struggling farm outside Enid where dust storms regularly covered fields, fences, and even the inside of the farmhouse with layers of dirt. Their father searched for temporary work hauling grain while their mother patched clothes from flour sacks and stretched meals with beans, potatoes, and cornbread. Yet every morning before sunrise, the children still prepared for school.

Most arrived wearing worn shoes or none at all during warmer months. Lunches often contained little more than biscuits, cold potatoes, or leftover beans wrapped in cloth. Inside the one-room schoolhouse, a single stove heated the classroom during winter while students of different ages shared books and supplies because many families could not afford their own.

Teachers became important figures in struggling rural communities. They not only taught reading and arithmetic but also helped feed hungry children, organized clothing drives, and visited families whose farms had been damaged by drought or illness. 

For many students, school provided one of the few stable routines left during the Depression years. One former student later remembered: “We didn’t know if the crops would survive, but our parents still made sure we walked to school every morning.

text:
CNN Captures and Isolates its Audience
ᵂʳⁱᵗᵗᵉⁿ ᵇʸ ᴳʳᵉᵃᵗᵉʳ ᴼʳᵉᵍᵒⁿ | ᵀʰᵉ ᴿᵉᵖᵘᵇˡⁱᶜᵃ ᴮᵃᶜᵏᵗʳᵃⁱˡ

CNN’s institutional pattern of selective reality construction and progressive moral framing does not merely report events. It organizes them into a coherent moral story that offers viewers identity, certainty, and a clear sense of who the threats and heroes are. Once a person accepts the frame, subsequent coverage functions less as neutral information and more as confirmation that their existing moral map is correct.

The loop captures people by aligning three things at once: an emotionally resonant threat narrative, continuous validation from the remaining audience and peer institutions, and reduced exposure to corrective information. Viewers who share the progressive moral priorities receive stories that confirm their judgments, reward their attention with moral clarity, and treat dissent as evidence of bad faith rather than legitimate disagreement. Over time the audience sorts itself. Those who reject the frame leave. Those who accept it stay, deepen their identification with the network’s worldview, and supply the engagement metrics that reinforce the same selection and framing choices. The result is not mass hypnosis but a self-reinforcing enclosure: the institution supplies the preferred reality, the core audience validates it, and both sides treat the shrinking external reach as proof of their own correctness rather than a signal to revise.

Those who accept it stay, deepen their identification with the network’s worldview, and supply the engagement metrics that reinforce the same selection and framing choices. The result is not mass hypnosis but a self-reinforcing enclosure: the institution supplies the preferred reality, the core audience validates it, and both sides treat the shrinking external reach as proof of their own correctness rather than a signal to revise.

cc: @CNN 

CNN as an institution operates a negative Authoritarian Feedback Loop (AFL / DAVR) because its core operating cycle systematically prioritizes internal ideological consistency and moral signaling over open, corrective engagement with conflicting evidence. The loop is not absolute fabrication on every story. It is a structural preference hierarchy: certain facts, contexts, and actors are amplified or softened according to how well they fit a progressive moral frame, while counter-evidence is down-weighted, delayed, or pathologized. This produces measurable external costs in audience size and trust outside the core progressive base.

Driver  

The initiating force is a settled institutional worldview in which progressive moral categories (threat from the right, institutional legitimacy of expert and elite consensus, protection of marginalized groups as defined by the network) function as the primary filter for what counts as newsworthy and how it must be framed. This is reinforced by economic incentives: the remaining high-engagement audience rewards intensity and moral clarity aligned with that worldview. Historical path dependency from the late 20th and early 21st century prestige-media shift supplies the cultural starting point. New ownership under Skydance does not automatically reset the driver; culture and selection effects change more slowly than ownership.

Action  

Selective reality construction appears as consistent patterns of omission, framing intensity, and language choice. High-salience political topics receive intensive coverage when they can be cast as confirmation of the preferred threat model and lighter treatment or softer framing when they complicate it. Progressive moral framing supplies the evaluative language: actors and events are positioned on a moral hierarchy before the full empirical picture is presented. Straight factual reporting still occurs, especially on non-political breaking news, sports-adjacent, or low-ideology topics. The institutional default, however, is narrative fit. When a story can be told in a way that validates the in-group moral position, that version is the one most likely to be selected, expanded, and repeated.

Validation  

Internal validation comes from newsroom consensus, peer-media amplification, and engagement metrics from the retained progressive audience. External critique is frequently interpreted as evidence of the critic’s bad faith rather than as data requiring correction. This is classic cognitive-dissonance reduction at institutional scale. Awards, professional status within legacy circles, and the absence of strong internal penalties for narrative-aligned errors further stabilize the loop. Viewpoint diversity that actually alters output remains limited; presence of occasional dissenting voices does not equal power to override the default frame.

Reinforcement  

Audience sorting is the clearest reinforcer. Viewers who reject the progressive moral frame leave; those who accept it stay and reward the product. Hiring and socialization reproduce the worldview. Trust data show large partisan gaps: CNN retains higher trust among Democrats and substantially lower trust among Republicans and many independents. Ratings declines from the 2017 peak through 2025 are consistent with the loss of broader audiences. The loop strengthens because the remaining feedback is positive from the core and negative from outside, and the institution has historically treated the negative feedback as the audience’s problem rather than a signal for structural correction.

Strongest negative frameworks  

Objective Reality Anchoring Model (ORAM) scores most negatively because the cycle of grounding perception, validation, correction, and stabilization is systematically tilted. Perception is filtered; validation privileges narrative coherence; correction of high-salience errors that damage the preferred frame is slow or partial; stabilization occurs around the model rather than around the fullest available evidence.

Moral Reasoning Framework (MRF) is strongly negative because moral input is pre-sorted through progressive justice categories. Evaluation treats deviation from those categories as moral failure. Decision and impact therefore favor in-group moral signaling over consistent application of evidence standards that would sometimes cut against the preferred side.

Political Analysis Framework (PAF) is strongly negative because institutional position has remained left-of-center across multiple ownership and leadership changes. Strategy has emphasized narrative dominance and moral framing. Feedback from electoral outcomes, trust surveys, and audience exit has produced limited strategic recalibration of the core product.

Cultural Dynamics Framework (CDF) is strongly negative because origin, transmission, adaptation, and institutionalization of the progressive moral frame are advanced. The culture is self-sustaining through selection and socialization. Adaptation has intensified the frame rather than broadened it.

Systems Analysis Framework (SAF) is strongly negative because the input-processing-output-feedback system is relatively closed. Inputs (ideology plus audience economics) are processed through a newsroom culture that outputs framed coverage. Feedback that would require revision of the model is attenuated. The system remains stable at a reduced scale.

Nuance and limits
 
Factual reporting still occurs. Not every segment or article is low-quality or false. On many non-political topics the network functions as a conventional news organization. The institutional default, however, prioritizes narrative fit and in-group validation when the stakes are political or cultural. This is distinguishable from random error or ordinary commercial bias. It is a patterned preference that survives leadership changes and is visible in coverage intensity, language, and correction speed.

Audience and trust data confirm the external costs. Significant declines in total-day and primetime viewership from the mid-2010s peak, combined with polarized trust measures, indicate that the loop extracts a real price in reach and credibility outside the core base. Whether the October 2026 ownership transition and the forthcoming Editorial Independence Board will alter the reinforcement stage depends on observable changes in correction patterns, story selection, and framing balance on contested political topics. Statements of editorial independence are not themselves evidence that the loop has broken.

text:
Californians are unhappy with how their state is governed, and many support reforms that challenge progressive orthodoxy: mandatory treatment for people living on the streets, greater accountability for public-sector workers, and tougher controls on government waste. But that frustration hasn’t translated into a willingness to elect Republicans. Voters want different results while remaining resistant to candidates associated with the Right.

That disconnect protects establishment Democrats from accountability and gives the far Left an opening. When voters want change but consider Republicans unacceptable, socialist challengers can present themselves as the only alternative—even when their policies don’t match what those voters actually want. Democratic victories therefore shouldn’t automatically be interpreted as endorsements of progressive governance, nor should enthusiasm for socialist candidates be mistaken for enthusiasm for socialism.

Achieving meaningful reform would require a coalition that crosses partisan lines, likely through relatively pragmatic Democrats who can reach voters Republicans simply cannot. San Francisco’s Daniel Lurie offers one example. Conservatives have to decide whether they care more about advancing Republicans or changing how California governs, while reform-minded liberals have to decide whether they’re willing to confront the unions, activists, and politicians obstructing their stated goals.

California has no shortage of voters who understand that something is broken. What the Golden State lacks is a durable political vehicle for fixing it.

Lecture: 
Murphy’s Law, 
Chaos, 
and the Unraveling of a Carceral Psychiatric Project

Students of
 law, 
political science, 
psychiatry, 
and social anthropology: 
consider a concrete episode 
from California’s carceral system 
around 2014. 

Under federal court pressure, t
he state planned 
a 40-bed psychiatric hospital unit 
inside San Quentin 
for death-row inmates 
identified as requiring 24-hour inpatient care. 

Roughly three dozen men
with severe mental illness 
were to be moved into a retrofitted medical facility. 

Staff were hired or recruited
—some relocating from other states, 
securing leases 
or buying homes near the prison. 

Then the specialized project 
was halted 
by shifting legislative 
and executive priorities. 

Personnel were dispersed. 

Years later,
 under a gubernatorial moratorium 
and transfer program, 
the segregated death row itself 
was emptied; 
condemned inmates 
were moved into general-population yards 
at other institutions. 

The hospital plan 
and the people 
who had ordered their lives around it 
simply dissolved.

This is not an abstract policy failure. 
It is a human one, 
and it maps cleanly 
onto three conceptual lenses.

Murphy’s Law 
states that anything that can go wrong 
will. 

In institutional design 
it is less a joke 
than a structural prediction. 

A specialized psychiatric unit 
for the condemned 
required alignment among 
courts, 
the Department of Corrections, 
legislative budgets, 
professional licensing boards, 
local housing markets,
 and the everyday labor of 
psychiatrists, 
nurses, 
and support staff. 

Any one of those elements could fail. 

In practice, 
several did at once: 
court-ordered timelines 
collided with later political shifts 
that redefined the entire purpose 
of the facility; 

hiring authority 
was granted 
and then withdrawn; 
people who had already moved 
discovered their positions no longer existed. 

The law is not that planners are incompetent. 

It is that complex, 
multi-actor systems 
contain latent failure points 
that become visible 
only when pressure is applied. 

The personal costs
—abandoned mortgages, 
broken contracts, 
professional reputations
—were predictable 
once the number of interdependent variables 
exceeded the capacity 
of any single office to control them.

Chaos theory 
supplies the second frame. 

Small changes in initial conditions 
produce large, non-linear outcomes. 

A single legislative or executive decision
—reclassifying the housing 
of condemned inmates, 
redirecting capital funds, 
altering the legal status 
of segregated death row
—functioned as a perturbation. 

The effects cascaded 
far beyond the prison walls. 

Psychiatrists and allied staff 
who had uprooted families 
found themselves unemployed 
after the move. 

Inmates previously concentrated 
in one specialized environment 
were scattered across the state,
altering both the continuity of their care 
and the risk profiles 
of the general-population yards 
that received them. 

Professional hierarchies 
inside the institution itself 
were already fragile; 
the Facebook recollection 
from October 2014 
of a social-worker CEO’s 
treatment of a chief psychiatric resident, a
nd the subsequent erosion 
of ordinary collegial courtesies 
among licensed staff, 
illustrates how local interpersonal dynamics 
can amplify the larger shock. 

In chaotic systems, 
the butterfly is not metaphorical. 

A memorandum 
or a statute change 
can empty a staffing roster 
and a set of cells 
with equal speed.

Self-organizing systems 
offer a third perspective. 

Complex adaptive systems 
generate order without central design
—markets, 
ecosystems, 
informal professional norms. 

Prison mental-health operations 
are only partly designed; 
much of their daily functioning 
depends on tacit understandings 
among 
clinicians, 
custody staff, 
and administrators. 

When those understandings collapse 
(professional courtesy 
giving way to hierarchy 
and retaliation), 
and when 
the formal plan 
for a specialized unit 
is withdrawn, 
the system does not simply stop. 

It reorganizes around 
whatever remains: 
general-population housing, 
residual medical beds, 
whatever outpatient capacity 
can be improvised. 

The reorganization is real, 
but it is not necessarily therapeutic or just. 

Staff who had organized their lives 
around the promised unit 
are left outside the new equilibrium. 

Inmates whose care 
had been concentrated 
are redistributed 
according to security classifications 
rather than clinical need. 

Order emerges, 
yet the costs of the transition 
fall on those least able to absorb them.

For law students 
the episode raises questions of 
reliance, 
due process, 
and the limits of court-ordered remedies. 

A federal judge 
can mandate inpatient capacity; 
a later legislature 
or executive can reallocate 
the population and the budget. 

What duties, 
if any, 
does the state owe to professionals 
who acted in reliance 
on the earlier mandate? 

For political scientists 
the case is a study 
in policy discontinuity 
and the power of a single office 
to redefine the material conditions 
of an entire institutional population. 

For psychiatrists 
it is a reminder 
that the work of treating 
severe mental illness 
inside a maximum-security setting 
is already high-stress; 
the additional trauma 
of watching a purpose-built unit evaporate, 
while colleagues 
are demoted or scattered, 
compounds burnout and moral injury. 

For social anthropologists 
the relevant objects 
are the disrupted households, 
the shattered professional community, 
and the cultural meaning of 
“quiet moments” snatched before a 4 a.m. 
shift in a place 
where ordinary collegiality 
has already failed.

The 2014 recollection 
of rising at four in the morning 
for a few quiet minutes by oneself 
is not incidental. 

It is the residual practice 
of someone attempting to maintain 
a personal boundary 
inside an environment 
that had already begun to dissolve 
both professional and institutional boundaries. 

When the larger project collapsed, 
that private interval 
became one of the few 
remaining sites of predictability.

The same threads
—dispersal, 
reliance that is broken, 
the absence of any external agent 
that will intervene 
on behalf of the people 
caught in the middle
—lend themselves to a different register.

Nobody Praying For the Quiet Ones
(in the style of Seether)

I’m the whisper lost upon the wind
of a unit that was never opened wide.
I’m the ember of a contract signed
then the water 
that took the house and the ride.

I’m a star that turned black hole 
when the statute changed,
fruit decaying on the yard 
they said would hold.

I’m the tree that fell 
and made no sound
when the staff were told the beds 
would not be filled.

I make no sound.
’Cause if I stand up,
 I break the lease,
and everybody loves to see 
the fall unfold.

Ain’t nobody giving notice,
’cause nobody gives a fuck.
Stand up, break the bones 
of the plan you sold.
Everybody wants the condemned 
they just can’t hold.
There’s nobody praying for me.

I am fungus in the forest 
of the East Block empty now.
I’m the lizard 
with the poisoned tongue of a chief 
who got demoted.

I’m the child in the manger 
of a social-worker CEO’s decree,
the one who 
sacrificed the resident 
and the courtesy.

Rust is showing 
on the armor of the four a.m. quiet.
I am wheezing like the old man 
done with the court order’s promise.
I’m a product of the anger 
that the legislation left behind.

I’m the bullet in a loaded gun 
that never found the hospital line.
Stand up, I break my bones.
Everybody loves to see a fall unfold.

Ain’t nobody giving up,
’cause nobody gives a fuck.
Stand up and break my bones.
Everybody wants what they just can’t hold.
There’s nobody praying for me.If I stand up, 
I break my bones.

Everybody loves to see a fall unfold.
Ain’t nobody giving up,
’cause nobody gives a fuck.
Stand up, break my bones.
Everybody wants what they just can’t hold.
There’s nobody praying for me.

The quiet moments remain. 
The system reorganized without them.

Narrative Control 101:  Queue up @jayblantonuk “I eat growth for breakfast” opinion in the HL.  Jay makes some excellent points on Kentucky future growth that aligns with state strategies, BUT in self-serving fashion believes only #universityofkentucky through continual growth can provide.

Fact check:

$500M “UK Investment” in housing - this was largely private investment and managed by an out of state management company.

9.35B in capital since 2011 - if accurate that means $4B alone in the last two years as public reports were $5.4 Billion in June of 2024.

15,000 employees since 2011 - difficult to validate as public information has various contradictions in reports by UK leadership.

22,000-unit housing shortage - accurate but it is an affordability gap.

Where his argument breaks down: costs to the city, causation (most of taxes come from healthcare not enrollment), the funding sources (private, debt-financed, and agency funded).  The tell that @ukymonday and @ukyprovost strategy is only growth for growth’s sake is the contradiction between the need for out of state students to fund the tuition gap and needing more enrollment growth to make Kentucky prosperous.  

The bottomline is that the Work Ready Kentucky Study in 2018 found the core problem at the time was that too few Kentuckians were working alongside a “middle-skill problem”.  The fix was to re-engage 165K people and expand technical credentials and apprenticeships.  Education focus was the credentials between a HS diploma and a bachelor's degree.  In other words, the education that UK doesn't offer yet they get the majority of state funding. In 2026, the new KWIB plan does add Professional, Scientific, and Technical services that would require bachelor's degrees and non-bachelor degrees.

It is a disappointment to me and should be to all of Kentucky that our flagship university is more focused on growth and money than they are on employee morale, quality care, academic rankings, health inspections, and fully-cooked chicken.  Fix the performance funding model that favors a "degree mill" over the other public institutions in Kentucky who end up begging for left overs.

text:
Imagine a festival that feels less like a party and more like stepping into a living prayer.
At Ise Jingu, the Kannamesai Festival is one of the most sacred events in Shinto. Every year in mid-October, the first rice of the new harvest is offered to the deities of Ise Jingu. At the heart of the festival is an act of gratitude: people are giving thanks for the year’s harvest and praying for continued protection, harmony, and abundance.
For someone seeing it for the first time, it can be striking because it doesn’t look like a loud modern festival. Instead, it feels solemn, ancient, and deeply symbolic. You may see long processions moving through the streets, enormous wagons carrying offerings, attendants in traditional dress, white ropes, chanting or singing, bags of newly harvested rice, and sacred cypress wood. Everything seems deliberate. Nothing is random.
The rice is the center of the meaning. In Japan, rice is more than food — it has long been tied to life, survival, gratitude, and the relationship between humans, nature, and the divine. During Kannamesai, the season’s first rice is presented as an offering to Amaterasu Omikami, the sun goddess enshrined at Ise Jingu and one of the most important deities in Shinto tradition. This is why the festival is so revered: it connects the land, the harvest, the people, and the sacred heart of Japan.
The procession itself helps make the invisible visible. Instead of just telling people to be grateful, the festival lets them walk that gratitude into the shrine. The white rope can suggest ritual purity and a boundary between ordinary space and sacred action. The cypress wood recalls Ise Jingu’s special association with renewal, purity, and sacred building traditions. The chanting gives the event a pulse — something communal, almost meditative, that carries the group forward together.
What makes Kannamesai powerful is that it is both public and hidden. Visitors can watch the processions and sense the atmosphere, but the innermost rituals are private. That mystery is part of its power. You are allowed close enough to feel its presence, but not to consume it like a performance.
In vivid terms, it feels like autumn gratitude turned into ceremony: the harvest gathered from the earth, placed on great wagons, escorted by people in reverent motion, and carried toward one of Japan’s holiest places. It is old Japan still breathing in the present.

text:
From Harvest to Finance: Building a More Transparent Agricultural Market

SECP Chairman Dr. Kabir Ahmed Sidhu proposed a digital national agricultural spot market at PIDE’s “Mission 100 Billion Dollars” conference, connecting farmers, warehouses, banks and buyers through standardised grading, transparent bidding and electronic warehouse receipts.

The model could help farmers use stored produce to secure bank financing, avoid distress sales and reach better market prices. It also offers a practical route to reduce post-harvest losses, strengthen accountability and improve the quality of produce entering domestic and export markets.

The need is significant: agriculture contributes 23.44% to Pakistan’s GDP, with crops valued at Rs 8.8 trillion. Yet approved storage capacity is about 326,000 metric tonnes, compared with 55.7 million tonnes of dry production. Modern storage and reliable digital records could make a meaningful difference, beginning with crops such as wheat, rice, maize, cotton and sugar.

Dr. Sidhu also highlighted the need to widen participation in Pakistan’s capital market, with a target of 2.5 million PSX investors supported by financial literacy and simpler account opening. He called for an independent legal framework for audit oversight to strengthen financial reporting and market confidence.

text:
The Thursday after the Nineteenth Sunday after Trinity Sunday

October 15, 2026 

Scripture: Hebrews 10:1-10 (NKJV)
 
10:1 For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with these same sacrifices, which they offer continually year by year, make those who approach perfect. 2 For then would they not have ceased to be offered? For the worshipers, once purified, would have had no more consciousness of sins. 3 But in those sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. 4 For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats could take away sins.
 
5 Therefore, when He came into the world, He said:
 
“Sacrifice and offering You did not desire, but a body You have prepared for Me.
 
6 “In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin You had no pleasure.
 
7 “Then I said, ‘Behold, I have come—in the volume of the book it is written of Me—to do Your will, O God.’”
 
8 Previously saying, “Sacrifice and offering, burnt offerings, and offerings for sin You did not desire, nor had pleasure in them” (which are offered according to the law), 9 then He said, “Behold, I have come to do Your will, O God.” He takes away the first that He may establish the second. 10 By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
 
Devotion
 
What we see in today’s reading is not limited to the ceremonial law. Even the moral law, as summarized by the Ten Commandments, cannot make us perfect. Instead, it is a continual reminder of sins, year by year, day by day. We men can not make those sins go away by our sacrifices. But the Son of God became a man to do the will of His Father. He became flesh and blood and offered it upon the cross, once for all. He atoned for the sins of the world. He took away the demands of the ceremonial law and its required sacrifices, and He established the Gospel, founded upon His own self-sacrifice.
 
This is what stands behind His power and authority to forgive sins. He is no mere man. He is God in the flesh, who paid the price for all sin with His own precious blood. He has every right to announce the forgiveness of sins to those who believe in Him and are baptized. And He has every right to raise their bodies on the Last Day, permanently purified from all sin and weakness.
 
Collect: O Almighty and most Merciful God, of Thy bountiful goodness keep us, we beseech Thee, from all things that may hurt us; that we, being ready, both in body and soul, may cheerfully accomplish those things that Thou wouldest have done; through Jesus Christ, Thy Son, our Lord, Who liveth and reigneth with Thee and the Holy Ghost, ever One God, world without end. Amen.

Yes, it is and the church has taught that.

1. Brigham Young — March 15, 1857
Speaking with Orson Hyde, Brigham Young stated:

"I have never been in Jackson County. Now it is a pleasant thing to think of and to know where the Garden of Eden was. Did you ever think of it? I do not think many do, for in Jackson County was the Garden of Eden. Joseph has declared this, and I am as much bound to believe that as to believe that Joseph was a prophet of God."

Source: Journal History of the Church, March 15, 1857, page 1. Reproduced in the Church's July 2001 Ensign. 

2. Brigham Young — Recollection recorded by Wilford Woodruff
"Joseph the Prophet, told me that the Garden of Eden was in Jackson County, Missouri. When Adam was driven out he went to the place we now call Adam-ondi-Ahman, Daviess County, Missouri. There he built an altar and offered sacrifices."

Source: Matthias F. Cowley, Wilford Woodruff: History of His Life and Labors (1909), page 481. Also quoted in the Church's Doctrine and Covenants student manual. 

3. Heber C. Kimball — June 27, 1863
Kimball, another close associate of Joseph Smith, declared:
"The spot chosen for the garden of Eden was Jackson County, in the State of Missouri, where Independence now stands."

Source: Journal of Discourses, volume 10, page 235. 

4. Joseph Smith — What can actually be documented?
BYU's Religious Studies Center acknowledges:

"This understanding does not come from Joseph Smith’s recorded revelations, but rather is based on statements made by him and reported by contemporaries who heard and recorded what the Prophet was reported to have said."

Source: BYU Religious Studies Center — The History and Doctrine of the Adam-ondi-Ahman Revelation⁠.

text:
I'm on the fence about Prop B, which is asking voters in St. Louis City to approve a half-cent sales tax to fund "early childhood education."

Two main questions: We're already funding early childhood education through our property taxes, which go to STL Public Schools and charter schools. Why add a new sales tax on top of that? Are we going to be paying twice?

And while the tax's backers like @wepower_stl talk up "early childhood education," won't a lot of this money just go for subsidized daycare?

(For background: The new tax would generate ≈$22.4 million annually. Needs 60% to pass. STL City already has the highest sales tax rate of any big city in MO. This would push the combined city-state tax to over 10%. It would cost a family of four with total household income of $77,000 an extra $195 each year, the tax's backers estimate.)

WePower and its allies have made attempts in the past to get public money to subsidize "quality" daycare for kids from birth to age 5. A recent proposal to get $100 million of Rams settlement money fizzled. Thus the campaign for Prop B on the November ballot. There's no organized opposition, as far as I've seen.

Here's the thing: STL Public Schools @SLPS_INFO says its early childhood program offers "free preschool for students who are fully toilet trained and have turned 3 or 4" including services for special-needs kids. Is this claim true? Is this program considered "quality"? If so, it would seem to serve a large number of the kids from moderate- and low-income households that Prop B is targeting. Everyone knows the district has huge problems. But the Prop B website is curiously silent about the programs at SLPS and how they fit into the early-childhood landscape. It also ignores the free pre-K programs some charter schools offer. Why? (Funds from Prop B can be used for childhood programs at public schools.) But if our public schools aren't offering "quality" programs, why are we funding them? Do we need to fix this before adding on yet another tax? What does "quality" even mean?

Second, what's the diffference between "early childhood education" and "daycare," especially when it comes to kids who are just one or two years old? "Early childhood education" sounds impressive, for sure. But Missouri has the same core licensing rules for places that serve kids, whether they're called daycare, preschool or early childcare. It looks like a big chunk of Prop B money will simply be used for subsidized daycare, even for households that make over $100K a year.

And maybe this is OK! I realize by raising these questions on X, I'm leaving myself open to attacks from people who will claim "you hate kids" or some such nonsense. But St. Louisans should have this conversation before we decide whether a regressive sales tax that will cost many households over 200 bucks a year is the right answer.

text:
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded this year's Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences on Monday to Robert Hall, 83, of Stanford, and Michael Woodford, 70, of Columbia, for the academic framework behind "forward guidance" — the idea that central banks can move the economy just by signaling where interest rates are headed, not only by actually moving them.

Here's why the timing matters. That's the same framework Fed chair Kevin Warsh has been openly skeptical of since taking the seat — and Woodford's own comments this week hand Warsh the strongest argument for that skepticism. Woodford admitted forward guidance worked when rates were pinned near zero after 2008, but conceded it offers no real answer for an energy-driven inflation shock like the 1970s oil crisis, when a guidance-heavy approach left inflation spiraling for a decade with no real response plan.

Here's why it matters.

That's exactly the environment we're in now: an energy shock tied to the Iran war, layered on top of inflation the Fed already let get away from it during the "transitory" years. Committee chair John Hassler praised the framework for leaving economists "better equipped to deal with shocks" — but being equipped with better theory isn't the same as being equipped with the discipline to act on it. The 1970s didn't fail for lack of academic models. It failed because central bankers trusted signaling and guidance over hard, credible action.

Warsh's skepticism isn't anti-intellectual. It's a corrective, aimed at an academic consensus that's better at explaining inflation after the fact than preventing it in advance.

This isn't just an award for two respected economists. This is a reminder that the framework being celebrated is the same one a new Fed chair is right to distrust, with another oil shock already here.

text:
🌱 Can Europe make green industrial policy work?

Across Europe, governments are deploying subsidies, grants and tax credits to retrofit legacy industries, develop new technologies and rebuild manufacturing bases. Attention has turned to conditionality: contractual clauses that reward firms only when their behaviour serves public goals. But conditions on paper do not guarantee results.

France shows why. Paris is subsidising upgrades at its 50 highest-emitting industrial sites, which account for around 60% of industrial emissions. The contracts set measurable emissions targets, pay out in instalments and allow funds to be clawed back if projects are not completed. Yet officials have significant discretion over enforcement. Sometimes that is sensible flexibility for projects piloting new technologies. But the line can blur: several officials described occasionally overlooking eligibility requirements or extending deadlines.

💡 In a new essay for BIG, Gabriel Kahan argues that green industrial policy is only as strong as the bureaucracies that enforce it. History offers an answer: planning agencies made conditions stick by aligning ministries and building coalitions with industry.

🇪🇺 For Europe, this means building long-term planning institutions that can strike pacts with industry and turn them into widespread compliance. Emerging clean-tech sectors could be part of that coalition, but could such an arrangement endure long enough to bear fruit?

text:
Why Relying Only on Online Distribution Cost Xiaomi Its #1 Spot

A few years ago, Xiaomi seemed unstoppable.

By selling phones directly on the internet through flash sales, cutting out middlemen, and keeping prices low, Xiaomi took over the market.

- At its peak (2018–2020): Xiaomi held over 30% of India’s smartphone market. Almost 1 out of every 3 phones sold was a Xiaomi.
- Where it stands today: That share has dropped to around 12–14%, losing more than half of its dominance to competitors like Vivo and Samsung.

What went wrong?

Xiaomi relied too heavily on online selling. Here is how that hit its business:

1️⃣ Online sales hit a natural ceiling

Selling online worked great for tech-savvy city buyers. But in large markets like India, more than half of all smartphone buyers still prefer going to a physical shop.

When millions of first-time buyers in smaller towns and rural areas wanted a phone, they went to local stores they trusted—not website flash sales. Xiaomi simply wasn't visible where these customers were looking.

2️⃣ Competitors won the local shopkeepers

While Xiaomi stayed focused on screens, rivals like Vivo and Oppo focused on street corners.

They gave local shop owners better profit margins, commissions, and free branded shop signs. Naturally, shopkeepers recommended the brands that made them more money. Xiaomi’s low-margin model left very little profit for local retailers, so shopkeepers had little reason to sell their phones.

3️⃣ People want to touch expensive products

It is easy to buy an ₹8,000 phone online based on specs alone.

But as customer budgets grew and people started looking for phones priced at ₹25,000, ₹40,000, or more, their behavior changed. They wanted to hold the phone, test the camera in person, and see a reliable service center nearby. Without a strong physical showroom network, it was hard to convince people to spend big money on Xiaomi.

The Big Lesson for Any Business

For long-term survival, relying on just one channel is dangerous.

Online channels are great for starting fast, keeping overhead low, and reaching early customers. But physical offline channels build trust, reach non-digital buyers, and offer the hands-on experience customers want before spending bigger money.

A healthy business cannot afford an "either/or" approach:

- If you stay only online, your growth will eventually plateau.
- If you stay only offline, your operations will be too slow and expensive.

For true, long-term sustainability, an omnichannel approach—balancing both online ease and real-world presence—is essential.

text:
Could a cheap deworming pill become part of the fight against drug resistant lung cancer? Scientists are investigating whether medicines originally developed to treat parasitic infections might offer unexpected benefits in cancer research. The concept may sound surprising, but it reflects a serious scientific strategy known as drug repurposing. Instead of developing every potential treatment from scratch, researchers examine existing compounds to see whether they could affect diseases beyond their original purpose.

Lung cancer can become difficult to treat when cancer cells develop resistance to medicines that once controlled their growth. Researchers are searching for ways to target these cells through different biological pathways, including mechanisms that influence cell survival, metabolism, and the tumor's response to treatment. Some existing drugs have attracted attention because laboratory experiments suggest they may affect processes involved in cancer growth. Yet the results depend on the specific drug, cancer type, dose, and experimental conditions. A finding in cells grown in a laboratory does not establish that the same effect will occur in a human body.

That distinction matters because cancer treatment decisions carry serious consequences. A medicine that is inexpensive and familiar may still cause harm if used at an inappropriate dose or in combination with other treatments without medical supervision. Researchers must establish whether it can reach the tumor, whether the potential benefits outweigh the risks, and whether patients experience meaningful improvements in carefully controlled clinical trials. Until then, this remains a research possibility, not a replacement for established lung cancer care. The exciting part is the question scientists are asking: could an existing medicine reveal a new way to tackle treatment resistance? The answer requires evidence, but the investigation itself shows how researchers continue searching for new options. 🔬

text:
🔥 THE CROWD WANTED TO WORSHIP PAUL AND BARNABAS AS GODS!

In the ancient city of Lystra, an extraordinary miracle took place, which left the people astonished.

There was a man who had been unable to walk from birth.
He had never walked.
And he sat listening as Paul preached the Word of God.
Paul looked directly at him and saw that the man had enough faith to be healed.

Then Paul called out with a loud voice, "Stand up on your feet!"
At that, the man immediately jumped up and began to walk.
(Acts 14:10, NKJV)

The crowd could hardly believe what they had witnessed.

Instead of understanding the miracle pointed to the power of the living God,
they began shouting that the gods had come down to them in human form.

They called Barnabas "Zeus" and Paul "Hermes."
The priest of Zeus even brought oxen and garlands, preparing to offer sacrifices to them.

But when Paul and Barnabas heard what was happening,
they were horrified.
They tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, crying out that they were ordinary human beings just like them.

They urged the people to turn away from worthless idols and worship the one true living God,
The Creator of heaven and earth,
the sea and everything in them.

What a powerful lesson!

Even when God works through ordinary people in an extraordinary ways, the glory belongs to God alone.

💫 Paul and Barnabas refused to accept the worship of the people, because they were ordinary servants for the Lord, not gods.

📖 Have you ever wondered why God sometimes works through ordinary people to accomplish extraordinary things?

God frequently uses ordinary, untrained, and unexpected people to perform miracles throughout the entire Bible, while emphasizing the power comes from Him rather than human status or skill.

Below Are Some Examples Of Ordinary People God Used To Perform Extraordinary Things: 👇

🔹️ Peter and John (Acts 3:1–8, Acts 4:13):
Peter and John were "unschooled, ordinary men" - fishermen by trade with no formal religious training,
Yet, through the power of Jesus Christ, they healed a man who had been lame from birth at the temple gate called, "Beautiful."

🔹️Moses (Exodus 3–4, 14):
A stutterer and fugitive shepherd tending sheep in the desert, Moses was used by God to perform dramatic plagues, confront Pharaoh, and hold out a simple wooden staff to part the Red Sea.

🔹️Gideon (Judges 6–7):
Self-described as the least in his father's house and full of fear. Gideon used unconventional, everyday items like horns, jars, and torches to defeat a massive Midianite army with just 300 men.

🔹️Samson (Judges 15:15):
An ordinary man physically empowered by the Holy Spirit of God, Samson used the jawbone of a donkey to strike down 1,000s of Philistines.

🔹️David (1 Samuel 17):
A young, overlooked shepherd boy without armor or royal standing, David used a simple sling and a stone to defeat the giant Goliath.

🔹️The Apostle Paul (Acts 19:11):
Though educated, Paul worked as a tentmaker, and the Bible notes that "God worked unusual miracles through Paul," even using handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him to heal the sick and cast out evil spirits.

When God calls you to do extraordinary things, simply say, "Here I am, Lord, Your servant is willing."

May God Bless You. 🙏

text:
Venerable Antonino Celona was an Italian diocesan priest and founder of a religious congregation. He was born on 13 April 1873 in Ganzirri near Messina. He received his early Christian formation from his parents and a priest uncle. At the age of eleven he entered the diocesan seminary of Messina and was ordained a priest on 12 December 1895. After a short period of pastoral work he was sent to Rome, where he completed studies in theology and obtained a license in canon law.

He later served as spiritual director of the seminary, professor of theology, and canon of the cathedral in Oppido Mamertina. After the devastating earthquake that struck Messina in 1908, he returned to the diocese to assist the poor and disoriented population. Struck by the material and moral poverty of the area, he collaborated with Saint Annibale Maria di Francia. In 1915 he entered the Rogationists, completed the novitiate, and made vows, but soon left that institute in order to found the Congregation of the Handmaids of Reparation of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. The congregation was dedicated to reparation for offenses against God through day and night Eucharistic adoration and to the Christian education of children and youth. Its first house opened in 1918.

In 1928 he oversaw the inauguration of the Temple of Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament in Messina, where he also resided. In the following years he endured divisions within the institute he had founded, misunderstandings with the superior general and the archbishop of Messina, and various accusations. He accepted these trials with humility and in a spirit of reparation, continuing his pastoral ministry as rector of the Sanctuary of Montalto and later as dean of the cathedral of Messina. During the bombardments of the Second World War he withdrew to Ganzirri.

Afflicted by illness and moral sufferings that he offered in reparation, he died in Ganzirri on 15 October 1952. Pope Francis declared him Venerable on 5 June 2015.

text:
Dispensationalism is indeed an American-born theological system that took shape in the 19th and 20th centuries. It originated largely through the teachings of John Nelson Darby in the UK, but found its true cultural and institutional home in the United States through figures like C.I. Scofield, the Scofield Reference Bible, and Bible institutes like Moody Bible Institute and Dallas Theological Seminary.

From a Covenantal perspective, there are several foundational reasons why Dispensationalism is viewed as fundamentally misrepresenting the work and person of Christ:

A Divided Kingdom and Deferred Victory: Dispensationalism postpones the full inauguration of Christ's Kingdom to a future, earthly thousand-year reign. In doing so, it minimizes the present, complete reign of Jesus, who declared after His resurrection that "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me" (Matt 28:18).

Two Distinct Peoples of God: By maintaining a permanent, eternal distinction between earthly ethnic Israel and the heavenly Church, Dispensationalism divides what Christ explicitly united. Paul emphasizes in Ephesians 2 that Christ broke down the dividing wall of hostility to create "one new man" out of the two.

A Rebuilt Temple and Reinstated Sacrifices: Dispensational eschatology anticipates a future physical temple in Jerusalem with reinstated animal sacrifices. From a New Covenant standpoint, this undermines the finality of the cross and the book of Hebrews, which states that Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time (Heb 10:12) and that the Old Covenant system was rendered obsolete and disappeared in the first century (Heb 8:13).

Fixation on Physical Geography: Dispensationalism focuses heavily on physical land, political borders, and a physical city in the Middle East. New Testament theology redirects the believer's focus to the New Creation and the New Jerusalem—the heavenly city that is the mother of all believers (Gal 4:26; Heb 12:22–24), where righteousness reigns in the human heart through the Holy Spirit.

By framing history around physical, future, earthly carnal expectations rather than the spiritual, present, finished reality of Christ's Kingdom, Dispensationalism ultimately shifts focus away from the ultimate victory Jesus accomplished in the first century.

text:
The AI Agent Has Come to the Phone: From a $100 Phone, 23,166 Facebook Posts Became My Fishing Story

The AI agent has come to the phone. Muse is a personal AI assistant from Meta, and it does not live in a research lab or behind an enterprise contract — it runs as an agent on an ordinary phone, in my case a phone worth about a hundred dollars. From that phone, by simply asking in plain words and approving the steps that mattered, I directed work that once would have needed a researcher, an editor, and a video producer. This essay is about what it actually did.

I started fishing in the last week of March 2019, and for seven years Facebook quietly kept the record — every trip, every catch, every photograph. This week I asked Muse to find my most memorable fishing pictures. The first lesson was about scale and honesty. Facebook offers no way to list albums directly, so Muse read my timeline the long way: all 23,166 unique posts, across 1,162 pages, from July 25, 2008 to October 12, 2026. Technically, this was the hardest part. Album photos hide inside the timeline as a special post type, the pagination is ordered by post ID rather than by date — so any shortcut that stops at a date boundary silently loses years — and the only correct way to finish is to page until Facebook itself reports there is no next page. The posts were deduplicated by ID and saved progressively, so when the scan stalled once, around page 1,097, it resumed from its saved state instead of starting over. Out of the archive came 648 album photos and 464 fishing-related posts, classified with word-boundary matching on captions — a technical detail that matters, because plain substring matching counts "pike" hiding inside unrelated words and pollutes the results. And Muse also corrected me. I had assumed my fishing pictures went back to 2015. They do not. My own post from 2023 says I started fishing in March 2019, so before that date there is simply nothing to find. A good agent does not just search — it tells you when your premise is wrong.

Out of that archive, Muse built me a complete fishing timeline, year by year, and ranked the photographs by real engagement — the comments of friends, not an algorithm's guess. That ranking needed a second pass, an individual read of each candidate post, because comment counts are not included in the timeline data itself. The most-reacted fishing photo of my life turned out to be two of the four salmon we caught out of Manistee, Michigan, in August 2022, with 13 comments. Then it wrote the text-based story as a post in my own voice: the first lesson at Rocky River in March 2019; two Lake Erie walleyes and a Fish Ohio qualifier within three months; a 32.5-inch walleye that same year, half an inch under the Ohio state record; the discovery of salmon and a 23-pound fish trolling out of Olcott, New York; the best salmon trip of my life in May 2021, six coho and three king salmon in ninety minutes; a 12-pound, 31-inch king at Manistee; the 64-inch sturgeon from the St. Clair River, still the biggest fish I have ever caught; and the cold steelhead winters on the creeks of Pennsylvania and Ohio.

Then came the video. The post data contains no image files, and the photo links refuse unauthenticated requests, so the nine photographs in the final cut were downloaded at full resolution through a signed-in browser session — and even then, the first photo of two albums was the wrong frame entirely (a guide's truck decal, the back of a boat), so the albums had to be browsed and each chosen frame verified against its caption. Muse adapted the written story into narration, recorded it in a generated voice, and timed every photograph to its own part of the telling: each narration segment was measured to the fraction of a second, and its slide length set to match. The film itself was rendered in FFmpeg at 1920×1080 — each photo set over a blurred copy of itself so portrait and landscape shots both fill the screen, with a slow cinematic zoom, a caption, and the music mixed using sidechain compression, so it automatically softens whenever the narration speaks and returns in the pauses. The first music beds, which Muse composed programmatically, I rejected as artificial; the final version uses a real piano recording — Erik Satie's Gymnopédie No. 1, performed by Kevin MacLeod and used under a Creative Commons license. The finished film runs two minutes and thirty-six seconds. It took four versions to get the pictures and the music right, and I kept every one of them, because an agent that works for you should leave you the drafts as well as the result.

None of this required a desk, a laptop, or any technical skill from me. I asked, I corrected, I approved — and the agent did the reading of twenty-three thousand posts, the writing, the recording, and the editing. That is the real change here. The capability of an AI agent used to belong to companies. Now it sits in the pocket of anyone with a phone, even a hundred-dollar one, waiting to turn the record of an ordinary life into something worth keeping.

text:
The peculiar case of https://t.co/QQUUe3lCte

The site presents itself as a national referral network for people injured by robots and AI systems. Its homepage promises to connect victims of autonomous technology incidents with specialized attorneys. It offers pages organized by city and by industry, a blog, and an application for lawyers who want to join. A visitor scanning it quickly could come away believing a large practice area already exists, with its own case law and specialist bar.

I was immediately struck by it:  it looks like a lot of work to put this together, and perhaps it's a great source of product liability information.  It certain seems like there is a bustling practice of law around these issues, which is a little surprising to me.  

But after reviewing the site, its two sister sites, and the domain registration record, I have questions about whether it is what it appears to be.  And that puts it nicely.  

The site names no attorneys, no operator, and no legal entity. It reports results I could not verify, carries dates earlier than its own domain, and lists itself for sale. Any one of these could have an innocent explanation. With all of them in view, I think its reasonabler to ask whether the site is an anonymous content property assembled in late 2025 for resale.

I go into further depth below. I could not identify the operator, and everything here comes from pages and records anyone can view.

Statistics without sources or attorneys
The homepage claims more than $2.3 billion in total settlements (seriously?), more than 15,000 cases filed (what???? that's a lot!!!), specialized attorneys in 50 major cities (really???), and a 94% success rate for qualified claims (okay sure buddy). 

The attorney recruitment page adds a network of more than 850 attorneys (literally who are these people). 

The New York page reports 1,847 cases filed in the last 12 months, 34 network attorneys, a $680,000 average settlement, and $112 million recovered in 2023 and 2024.

I mean . . . how do you take any of this at face value. 

The site gives no source or methodology for any of these figures. More telling, I could not find a single attorney or law firm named anywhere on it.  If you were the Perry Mason of humanoid litigation I don't think you'd be coy about it.  

The city pages describe local courts, statutes of limitations, and comparative fault rules, and then invite the reader to request a free consultation.

A network of 850 lawyers would presumably name at least one of them. A directory that names no one would have trouble working as a directory.

The site also lacks disclosures a referral service would ordinarily carry. I found no attorney-advertising disclaimer, no responsible attorney or firm, and no registration as a lawyer referral service, which several states regulate. The Terms of Service describe the contract as one with "https://t.co/DurfEQBkCo" and name no legal entity, and a search of a public business-registry aggregator turned up no entity by that name.

Cases with no public record
This is where I think we may be wading into a sea of AI slop.  The homepage features three results presented as real outcomes. Morrison v. AutoServe Robotics is described as a $3.2 million jury verdict in Phoenix in 2024 involving a home cleaning robot.  I can't find an "AutoServe Robotics" as every existing.  Chen Family v. MediBot Inc. is described as an $8.7 million settlement in Houston in 2024 after an AI medication system administered a fatal overdose. Williams v. SafeHome Systems is described as a $1.4 million Chicago settlement in 2023 over a thermostat fire.  The only safehome systems I could find is a battered women's shelter in Covington Virginia.  The New York page adds Goldstein v. Manhattan Medical AI at $5.8 million and Rodriguez v. Brooklyn Hospital Network at $3.2 million.

None of the five listings gives a court, a docket number, a filing date, or the lawyers involved. The defendant names follow a generic pattern (AutoServe, MediBot, SafeHome) that would fit placeholder text. A $3.2 million verdict against a domestic robot manufacturer in 2024 would very likely have drawn trade press coverage, and I found none.

 Dates earlier than the domain
The public registration record shows the domain was registered on November 4, 2025, through GoDaddy, with the owner's identity masked by GoDaddy's privacy service, Domains By Proxy. The site's own pages carry earlier dates. The Terms of Service and the Privacy Policy both list an effective date of January 1, 2025. The About page, the attorney network page, and the for-sale page each carry January 1, 2024 publication dates in their metadata.

Because the domain did not exist before November 2025, someone entered those earlier dates, either deliberately or by leaving template defaults in place. On a static site generator like Hugo, which all three related sites use, an author sets each page's date in a text field. Either way, a visitor sees a site that appears older than it is.

The substantive pages were updated in a burst between December 4 and December 10, 2025, and the Wayback Machine holds no archived snapshots of the domain. Both would be consistent with a site built out in roughly a month and online for a short time.

The site lists itself for sale
A link in the footer leads to a page titled "Domain For Sale," which is tagged so search engines will not index it. The page calls https://t.co/DurfEQBkCo a premium domain with "established authority" in the sector. That claim is hard to square with a registration date only weeks earlier.

The operator offers two packages. The first is the domain alone. The second adds the complete website codebase, all content covering 50 cities and 8 industries, an SEO-optimized structure, a component library, and setup documentation. The page names law firms, legal directories, insurers, technology companies, and investors as ideal buyers and cites its own unsourced market figures. The inquiry form promises a reply within 48 hours and asks for serious offers only.

The site also has a second line of business. An Enterprise page offers risk assessments, compliance program builds, and incident-response planning to companies in healthcare, manufacturing, transportation, and other sectors, including on an annual retainer. A single operator marketing plaintiff referrals and compliance consulting to the same industry would be unusual. The pairing would make more sense on a property pitched to law firms, insurers, and technology companies alike.

With the listing in view, one plausible reading is that the operator added the site's other features to prepare it for sale. Large statistics, featured verdicts, and older publication dates would each make a site look more established to a prospective buyer who spends a few minutes on it. Other explanations are possible. An early-stage venture could be using illustrative figures while it recruits attorneys, or the operator could be testing demand before deciding whether to build the business or sell it. The registration expires on November 4, 2026, so the owner faces a renewal decision within weeks.

Three sites, one template
https://t.co/DurfEQBkCo links in its footer to two related sites, https://t.co/GoefX5QWoD and https://t.co/wCG9MNvF23. All three run on the same version of Hugo (0.147.7), and none names an owner or author. The About page on https://t.co/wCG9MNvF23 describes the three as one network of legal resources.
https://t.co/GoefX5QWoD publishes city-by-city pages on robot injury lawyers, most dated within the first ten days of December 2025. Its About page attributes the content to a team of legal researchers, investigative journalists, and technology analysts who accept no funding from robotics or AI companies. It names no member of that team.

https://t.co/wCG9MNvF23 covers AI in healthcare and professional malpractice and shows articles dated as early as June 2025. A public list of newly registered .com domains includes https://t.co/wCG9MNvF23 on November 23, 2025, the same day the https://t.co/DurfEQBkCo registration record shows an update. Lists of this kind can include re-registered domains, so I treat the overlap as suggestive. If the list is accurate, the June 2025 articles would also predate their domain.

Here is why this is a bit hairy -- some people already treat these sites as authorities. 
Earlier this year, a participant in a Canadian online forum linked to the Tesla Autopilot page on https://t.co/GoefX5QWoD to support an argument. Each citation of this kind adds an inbound link, and inbound links raise the price a search-optimized site can command.

Policymakers, journalists, and insurers looking for evidence of robot injury litigation would find few real cases.  If a site with confident numbers and named verdicts tries to fill the gap, maybe people and their 
AI tools won't be terribly diligent and simplly allow it without much scrutiny.  In particular, AI search tools that summarize the web could repeat the figures without context. Advocates on either side of a regulatory debate could then cite unverified litigation figures without knowing where they came from.
 
A law firm that buys the starter package would inherit content that presents unverified results as real. State rules modeled on ABA Model Rule 7.1 prohibit misleading communications about a lawyer's services, and rules modeled on Model Rule 7.2(b) restrict paying for referrals. A buyer would need to remove or verify most of the site before using it.

Ultimately, it seems like a domain for sale situation.
