text:
The AM Brief, Thursday October 15, 2026 Part 3

Good morning,

It’s 9am in Miami and here is a recap of defense related events that caught my eye. Part 3

      The United States Navy has awarded defense supplier Raytheon a major contract valued at up to $24.4 billion to produce Standard Missile-6 (SM-6) interceptors. The contract follows public comments from former President Trump to TIME magazine expressing concern that certain national ammunition stockpiles have dipped low. However, lawmakers in Congress have not yet formally appropriated the required multi year funding to fully cover the multi billion dollar deal, raising key questions around defense budget allocations and production timelines.

     Defense contractor Anduril secured a Navy contract valued up to $2.9 billion to produce vital components for Virginia class submarines. To support this effort, the firm is pouring $3.7 billion into a massive two million square foot shipyard at Sparrows Point near Baltimore, expected to create 3,100 jobs upon launching in 2030. Notably, founder Palmer Luckey was recently appointed to the Pentagon's Project Meridian initiative, which focuses on developing critical capabilities for future military conflicts.

     The U.S. Army's M1E3 tank redesign reduces vehicle weight to roughly 60 tons, down from 78 tons on the SEPv3. Featuring a diesel electric hybrid engine, it slashes fuel requirements by 40–50%. The upgraded model operates with a three person crew inside an armored capsule, utilizing an unmanned turret with an autoloader, 360 degree sensing, and an Iron Fist protection system. Built largely from commercial components, the program is five years ahead of schedule, with four prototypes delivering to the 1st Cavalry Division.

      Former Ukrainian defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov has launched the "Army of Robots" initiative to foster private-sector development of combat robotics. Emphasizing the transformation of modern warfare, Fedorov noted that unmanned aerial vehicles and autonomous systems now account for over 95% of all battlefield strikes. The campaign aims to rapidly scale technological innovation, hardware manufacturing, and deployment across military operations to sustain tactical defense capabilities.

     Modern air defense economics reveal a vast cost disparity: a Shahed type attack drone costs roughly $35,000 to produce, whereas a defensive Patriot interceptor missile costs over $3 million per launch. To address this financial asymmetry, Ukraine is rapidly pivoting toward specialized interceptor drones. Costing between $3,000 and $5,000 each, these low cost kinetic systems offer a scalable, economically sustainable defense against widespread, low cost aerial threats.

Sources : The Capitalist (10-6), Rod D. Martin (10-6), Bay Area Letters (9-28), Altimetry Daily Authority (9-28)

Thank you for reading
Live your best life,
AL Maulini

text:
Lunch at the Mayflower, and the Mailbox That Talked Back

Adam Aron slid into the corner booth at the Mayflower Hotel’s  restaurant five minutes early, which, for him, was almost late. Steve  Case was already there, navy blazer, no tie, the same easy half-smile  that had once sold America on dial-up.

“Still hate being the last one to sit down?” Case asked.

“Old habits,” Aron said. “I used to answer the phones myself at  MovieFone when we were still proving the thing worked. You pick up the  handset and the first thing you hear is yourself saying hello to a  stranger who just wants to know if Independence Day is sold out. It rewires you.”

They ordered the same thing they always did when they managed to get a  table—grilled salmon for Case, the steak for Aron—and for a few minutes  they traded the usual industry gossip. Then Aron set his fork down.

“You remember the greeting?”

Case nodded. “Hello, and welcome to MovieFone.”

“Exactly. Clean. Friendly. No corporate throat-clearing. Just a voice  that sounded glad you called. I still hear it sometimes when I’m  walking past a theater on a Friday night. Makes me feel twenty-five  again.”

Case laughed. “I get the same thing with ‘You’ve Got Mail.’ People  tell me it’s the most recognizable three words in internet history. Half  of them still do the little voice when they say it. The other half just  make the sound with their mouth. You ever miss it?”

“Every day,” Aron said, surprising himself with how fast the answer  came. “That little chime was pure dopamine before we had a word for it.  You opened the laptop, heard it, and for three seconds the world was  interesting. Physical mail used to feel like that too—opening the box  and not knowing what was inside. Now it’s all catalogs and political  flyers, and the only notification I get is the red light on my Ring  camera telling me the carrier was here forty minutes ago.”

Case leaned back. “So what if the mailbox itself could do the chime?”

Aron blinked. “You’re not serious.”

“I’m semi-retired and bored. You’re the guy who turned a movie-ticket  company into a meme stock and somehow kept the theaters open. Between  us we know a few people who still like building slightly ridiculous  things.”

They finished lunch. Aron paid. On the sidewalk outside, Case paused.

“Bending Spoons has been looking for a hardware play that isn’t just  another app. And the Postal Service has been quietly testing smart  lockers. If you really miss the sound that much…”

Aron was already pulling out his phone. “Call me tomorrow.”

BREAKING: AMC, Steve Case, Bending Spoons, and USPS Unveil “You’ve Got Mailbox” Device

Washington, D.C. — October 15, 2026

AMC Entertainment Holdings and a newly formed joint venture involving  former AOL CEO Steve Case, Italian app studio Bending Spoons, and the  United States Postal Service today announced the pilot launch of the  “You’ve Got Mailbox,” a compact sensor unit designed to fit inside  residential curbside mailboxes.

The device, roughly the size of a thick smartphone, attaches to the  inside of a standard USPS-approved mailbox. When the door is opened and  physical mail is deposited, it triggers a push notification to the  resident’s phone that plays the original AOL “You’ve Got Mail”  chime—licensed directly from Case’s personal archive of early internet  audio files.

“I have spent the last several years listening to people tell me they  miss the ritual of opening something real,” Aron said in a joint  statement. “MovieFone taught us that a simple, friendly voice could make  people feel welcome. Steve’s chime did the same thing for email. This  is just the two of them meeting in a mailbox.”

Bending Spoons is handling the companion app and over-the-air  updates. The USPS will allow the devices on its network during a 90-day pilot in three markets (Washington, D.C., Austin, and parts of Los  Angeles), provided the units do not interfere with mail delivery or  collection. Installation is free for the first 10,000 households that opt in through the AMC app or the new https://t.co/NeBxW1FHpy site.

Early testers report the experience is “weirdly emotional.”

“I opened the app, heard that sound, and walked outside like it was  1998,” said one pilot user in Virginia. “Then I found three pieces of  junk mail and a postcard from my sister. Still worth it.”

The joint venture has not yet disclosed pricing for the post-pilot  period, though Aron noted that AMC Stubs members will receive priority access and a small discount on future ticket purchases for every ten  notifications they acknowledge—an arrangement he described, with a  straight face, as “loyalty in both directions.”

Case, reached by phone, offered only one comment:

“Hello, and welcome to your mailbox.”

The line has already been set as the default notification text.

text:
A Faraday cage tries to explain Why a wealthy man like @ElonMusk may give up on (dating) women

I exist to distribute force across a surface so that nothing inside feels what happens outside. When a massive electrical charge builds on my exterior mesh, the mobile electrons within my conductive skin shift instantly. They assemble on the outer boundary to cancel the incoming electric field, leaving the interior space at zero potential.

To an observer standing outside, I appear cold, rigid, and impermeable. To whatever delicate instrument sits inside me, I'm the only reason it continues to run without burning out.

People look at a man with hundreds of billions of US dollars and assume his world offers unlimited access. They think money is an attractor that makes personal connection effortless. My starting assumption was similar. I assumed that higher energy meant clearer transmission, that vast resources simply amplified the signal between two people.

But I notice what happens when a person carries an extreme charge. It doesn't merely send signals out into the world. It alters the surrounding medium entirely.

When an electrical potential becomes exceptionally large, every nearby object polarises before it even touches the boundary. A subtle, quiet signal can't cross that space unchanged.

The ambient field created by the man's wealth and visibility generates constant background noise. Every incoming frequency is distorted by the expectation of his power, by public scrutiny, by legal risk, and by the sheer gravitational pull of his work. You can't distinguish a genuine transmission from a field induced response.

Intimacy requires a permeable boundary. Two systems must allow their charges to equalise, exchanging raw data and delicate currents across an open gap.

But if you open a window in a high voltage environment, you don't get a gentle exchange. You get a catastrophic arc. The high potential difference causes dielectric breakdown. Current rushes across the space in a sudden spark, tearing through delicate components.

When every romantic encounter carries the risk of a high energy discharge, staying open becomes a threat to the core engine.

This is where my geometry becomes inevitable. The man realises that he can't filter out the noise while remaining unshielded. If he allows a signal inside, the background field forces that signal to carry immense parasitic interference. You can never tell whether a movement toward you is authentic resonance or merely a reflection of your own massive electrostatic presence.

The only way to preserve the internal operations, the rockets, the factories, and the quiet calculations, is to pull a continuous conductive shell over the entire structure.

Giving up on dating isn't a romantic failure so much as a protective isolation protocol. I enclose what must be saved. The outer mesh absorbs the lightning, redistributing the public chaos, the court battles, and the media noise across its metallic skin. Inside, the potential remains flat, perfectly quiet, and completely cold.

He steps away from romantic exchange because he discovered a fundamental law of extreme systems. You can carry immense charge or you can have delicate resonance, but you can't expose a fragile receiver to a storm you yourself generate.

text:
The Airship Crews of 1896–97: Who Built Them, Who Paid, and Who Was Coordinating?

No airship from the great wave of 1896–97 has ever been found. No hangar has turned up, no backer has been named and confirmed, no ledger of parts or wages has surfaced, and no wreck has survived examination. Yet for six months newspapers from California to Texas, Arkansas, Kansas and Ohio printed accounts of ordinary-looking men who stepped out of these craft and talked. They asked for water, for oil, for chisels, for news. They spoke of New York capitalists and small-town workshops in Iowa. And in Arkansas one of them, asked about his machine, answered with a line that still hangs over the whole affair: "you will know more later on."

Nobody has. The questions the crews raised are the same ones they left behind. Who funded the ships? Where did the ideas come from? And if the men were only men, how did the same requests, the same backstory and the same withholding turn up across several states within a few weeks?

The revival

On September 26, 2026, the podcaster Danny Jones posted to X a clip, just under five minutes long, from his interview with Walter Bosley, a former FBI counterintelligence specialist who investigates historical mysteries. "Newspapers documented mysterious airships across the American West in the 1890s," the post read. "Some accounts described crews stepping out to speak with witnesses." In the clip Bosley names two of those crewmen, S. E. Tillman and A. E. Dolbear, and says the ships came down because "they needed water," with the pilots talking to witnesses while they collected it. It was, he says, "almost as if somebody was testing the waters." In the full episode he goes further: the airships, in his view, came from a secret program built by "one of the early coalitions between the US government and private industrialists."

That is one answer to who paid. It is not the only question. The researcher Jacques Vallée, in Passport to Magonia (1969), called the wave "a crucial missing link between the apparitions of older days and modern saucer stories," and noted that "all the operators who engaged in discussions with human witnesses were indistinguishable from the average American population of the time." His later control-system thesis holds that the phenomenon presents itself in forms the culture of the moment can take in. Set against that thesis, the airship crews stop being a puzzle about engineering alone and become a question about how a mystery is delivered.

The size of the record

The wave ran from November 1896 into May 1897. It began in California, went quiet, and resumed on the Plains in February 1897 before spreading through the Midwest and Texas in March and April. The folklorist Thomas Bullard collected more than a thousand newspaper stories from the period, and the sociologist Robert Bartholomew, in the Skeptical Inquirer in 1990, put a conservative estimate of individual sightings at 100,000, since whole towns turned out to watch. Most of it was lights, a bright point moving slowly across the evening sky, sometimes with a dark body behind it. Stories of crews on the ground are a small part of the record, but they are the part with dialogue, names and requests.

The money nobody found

From the first week, the story came with a backer attached, and the backer never appeared.

The first reports came from Sacramento on the evening of November 17, 1896. Hundreds saw a light, and a few said they heard more. The Sacramento Bee of November 18 quoted streetcar men who heard a voice from above say, "Well, we ought to get to San Francisco by tomorrow noon," and other residents who heard, "Lift her up quick! You are making directly for that steeple!" The same article noted that the previous night's Bee had carried a telegram from a New York man announcing that he had built an airship and would fly it to California within two days. The Daily Record-Union of the same date allowed that "it is possible someone sent up an illuminated balloon."

Three nights later, streetcar passengers in Oakland saw a headlight with a second light beneath it, and some said they made out a dark body and "propelling arms." According to the San Francisco Call of November 22, they said the object closely resembled the drawing of the Sacramento airship that the Call had printed the day before. They had seen the newspaper's picture before they saw the light.

Then the lawyers arrived. George D. Collins, a San Francisco attorney, told the Chronicle, in a statement reprinted by the Sacramento Daily Record-Union on November 23, that his client, "a very wealthy man," had built a machine "made of metal," about 150 feet long, and had flown it from Oroville over Sacramento. Collins pointed reporters toward a dentist, E. H. Benjamin, who denied any connection, and Collins soon retracted most of his story and dropped out of sight. W. H. H. Hart, a former state attorney general, then claimed to represent the inventors and talked of bombing Havana with dynamite before he, too, went quiet.

A wealthy client, an inventor, a lawyer, a plan: every element of a funded project was announced, and none was produced. The pattern repeated in the spring. Crews in Texas told witnesses their ship was one of five built in a small Iowa town; three separate crews said so within eleven days, one placing the shop in Illinois. At Josserand the crew spoke of "an immense stock company" being formed. At Stephenville the men said they were working for "capitalists of New York." No stock company, no Iowa works and no New York syndicate has ever been traced.

The technology question is as stubborn. Airship patents were real; Charles Abbott Smith of San Francisco received U.S. Patent 565,805 for an "Air-ship" on August 11, 1896. No such machine is known to have flown. The aviation historian Charles Gibbs-Smith, quoted by Bartholomew, put it flatly: "No form of dirigible... was flying—or indeed could fly—at this time" in North America. Bosley traces a post–Civil War program to the Sonora Aero Club, a secret society of aeronauts described in the notebooks of Charles Dellschau, a retired Houston butcher who drew airships in his attic; Dellschau's surviving notebooks begin in 1899, after the wave, and Bosley acknowledges that the Sonora club rests on "the one source." Michael Busby, in Solving the 1897 Airship Mystery (2004), argues from reported speeds and routes for three Iowa-built ships over Texas. None of these accounts has produced a hangar, a ledger or a wreck.

So the first questions stand. If someone built these craft, who paid, and where did the knowledge come from a decade before powered flight? If no one built them, what were thousands of people watching, and who were the men in the pastures?

The crews

The first story of non-human occupants came out of the California weeks. On November 27 the Stockton Evening Mail printed an account by Colonel H. G. Shaw, identified as "formerly of the Mail editorial staff." Driving back from Lodi with a companion, Shaw said, he met three beings "nearly or quite seven feet high and very slender," with nailless fingers, long grasping feet and a covering "as soft as silk," so light that he lifted one "with scarcely an effort." They made no speech he could follow; "warbling," he said, "expresses it better than talking." They tried to carry him off to a ship hanging in the air over the Woodbridge canal. He found them "more divinely beautiful than anything I ever beheld" and guessed they were "inhabitants of Mars." The same issue reported that "some practical jokers sent up a number of hot air balloons last night, as a take-off on the alleged airship."

Most of the 1897 contact stories came from Texas and Arkansas in the second half of April, and they fell quickly into a shared pattern.

On April 19, near Beaumont, a man who called himself Wilson asked J. B. Ligon for a bucket of water and said the ship was one of five built in a "quiet Iowa town." The next night at Uvalde, Sheriff H. W. Baylor met three men who drew water from his pump. One, again named Wilson, said he came from Goshen, New York, and asked after C. C. Akers, a former sheriff of Zavala County he had known in Fort Worth in 1877. Akers, reached afterward, confirmed in a letter printed in the Galveston Daily News on April 27 that he had known a Wilson from New York in Fort Worth, a man "of a mechanical turn of mind" who "was then working on aerial navigation and something that would astonish the world." It is one of the few contact reports with a checkable detail that checked out. Either a real inventor named Wilson was flying over Texas, or someone knew Akers's history well enough to borrow it. Both possibilities leave the same question: how did that knowledge reach a pump in Uvalde?

The Houston Post of April 21 reported that Frank Nichols, a farmer near Josserand, woke to a whirring noise and found a vessel in his cornfield. Two men with buckets asked to draw from his well. The reporter adds that "thinking he might be entertaining heavenly visitors instead of earthly mortals, permission was readily granted." The crew of six or eight then told him the ship was "built of a newly-discovered material that has the property of self-sustenance in the air," that its power was "highly condensed electricity," and that "five of these ships were built at a small town in Iowa." The same article says Nichols had "read the dispatches, published in the Post," before he went out.

The next day's Post carried the most practical request in the record. John M. Barclay, near Rockland, went out with his Winchester and was met by "an ordinary mortal" who asked him to lay the gun aside. "Never mind about my name, call it Smith," the man said. "I want some lubricating oil and a couple of cold chisels if you can get them, and some bluestone." He offered a ten-dollar bill. Barclay brought the oil and chisels but could not get the bluestone, the copper sulfate that telegraph operators kept for their batteries. Asked where he was from, the man said, "From anywhere, but we will be in Greece day after tomorrow."

In Arkansas, Captain James Hooton, an Iron Mountain Railroad conductor, told the Arkansas Gazette (April 22, 1897) that while hunting near Homan he came on a landed ship making a noise like a locomotive air pump. A "medium-size looking man" in "smoked glasses" greeted him, "Good day, sir; good day," and when Hooton remarked on the noise, answered that they were using compressed air and "aeroplanes, but you will know more later on." Hooton ended by complaining that the ship had no bell, which "every well regulated air locomotive should have." On the night of May 6, near Hot Springs, Constable John Sumpter Jr. and Deputy Sheriff John McLemore said they came on a sixty-foot craft whose crew included an older man with a long dark beard carrying a lantern, a young man filling a large sack with water and a woman who kept to the shadows. The old man said they would stop at Nashville and offered the officers a ride. The two men swore affidavits and held to their story under ridicule.

Other accounts leaned toward the tall tale. An ex-senator named Harris, of Harrisburg, Arkansas, was said to have met a bearded old man who claimed to have inherited the secret of antigravity from an uncle, had planned to go to Cuba "and kill off the Spanish army," and would do it with a gun that fired "63,000 times per minute." The Cincinnati Enquirer of April 25 printed an anonymous account of two aeronauts near Lancaster, Ohio. One struck the witness as "a Japanese, or belonged to some other Oriental race" and spoke an unknown tongue. The other, in good English, wanted to know "what the people and newspapers were saying," accepted the witness's copy of the Enquirer, and explained that "we pass as tourists among our fellow-men."

Across the twenty-seven reports of voices, crews or occupants logged for this essay, twenty describe ordinary-looking people. Six crews asked for water; one asked for oil, chisels and bluestone; one came into town for supper; one wanted to know what the newspapers were saying. They explained a little and withheld the rest: the principle was secret, the patents were pending, "you will know more later on."

The Stephenville names

The Dallas Morning News of April 19 carried what it called "the plainest and most circumstantial statement" of all, from Stephenville, Erath County. A farmer, C. L. McIlhany, reported a cigar-shaped craft about sixty feet long resting on his land for repairs. A delegation of townsmen found two men who gave their names as "S. E. Tillman, and A. E. Dolbear." They said they were "making an experimental trip" for "capitalists of New York" and were confident "that in a short time the navigation of the air will be an assured fact." They kept the crowd back, finished their repairs and flew off.

These are the men Bosley names, and the names belong to real people. Samuel Escue Tillman was an Army officer who taught at West Point for three decades, wrote textbooks on chemistry and geology, and was recalled as superintendent of the academy in 1917. Amos Emerson Dolbear was a physics professor at Tufts and an electrical inventor with early telephone patents. Bosley argues that Tillman's career "spans what would have been the secret development" of the airship and that the landing was the moment he "identifies himself." In April 1897 both men held academic posts in the Northeast. Soon afterward, the New Orleans Picayune reported that "Dolbear and Tillman" had been registered at a hotel in that city and judged it "in all likelihood a hoax, as cards sent to their room failed to get any response." Bosley recalls this crew as needing water; the News account says they stopped for repairs, and the water requests come from other landings, among them Beaumont, Uvalde, Josserand and Hot Springs.

The hotel episode does not close the case so much as extend it. The same two names, a physicist and a West Point chemist, surfaced in a Texas pasture and then on a New Orleans hotel register, and in neither place did anyone answer. Whoever chose them chose a chemist and an electrical inventor. Was that a prankster's research, or part of the same pattern?

The pranks inside the pattern

A handful of stories went beyond inventors, and the record marks several of them as jokes. They belong in the account all the same, because they traveled with the rest and kept the subject alive.

On April 19 the Dallas Morning News printed a dispatch signed S. E. Haydon, dated April 17 from Aurora, in Wise County. An airship had struck "the tower of Judge Proctor's windmill" and exploded. The pilot "was not an inhabitant of this world," and T. J. Weems, described as the local signal service officer, judged him "a native of the planet Mars." Papers on the body were "in some unknown hieroglyphics." "The pilot's funeral will take place at noon to-morrow," the dispatch ended. Daniel Cohen, in The Great Airship Mystery (1981), set out the case against it. Oscar Lowery, eleven at the time, recalled no crash and said Haydon made it up. Weems was the town blacksmith. The local historian Etta Pegues called it "a hoax cooked up by Hayden and a bunch of men sitting around in the general store." Metal fragments produced in 1973 were judged to have been brought to the site recently.

The Morning News also reported from near Waxahachie that a Judge Love met "five peculiarly dressed men" smoking pipes on a spread of furs. They said they were descendants of the lost tribes of Israel living in "north pole land," had learned English from the lost crew of Sir Hugh Willoughby, and would bring ten ships to the Nashville Centennial Exposition on June 18 and 19, free of charge. No ships came to Nashville. From Farmersville came a crew singing "Nearer My God to Thee" and handing out temperance tracts, which Cohen lists as an obvious hoax. In Chicago, the newsdealer Walter McCann's airship photograph, the Las Vegas Daily Optic reported on April 13, 1897, came from a painted canvas hoisted "on a trolley wire" before "a friend squealed."

In Kansas, the Yates Center Farmer's Advocate of April 23 printed Alexander Hamilton's story of "six of the strangest beings I ever saw," "jabbering together," who roped a heifer and carried it off. "I don't know whether they are devils or angels or what," Hamilton said. Hamilton's story was a hoax, and the record holds the confession. In a letter printed in the Buffalo Enterprise in January 1943, the Advocate's former editor, Ed F. Hudson, recalled Hamilton watching the paper's new gasoline engine and exclaiming, "Now they can fly," "hence the airship story that we made up." In the 1970s Jerome Clark located Ethel Shaw, who as a girl had heard Hamilton come home and say, "Ma, I fixed up quite a story and told the boys in town and it will come out in the Advocate this weekend." The men who signed his supporting affidavit, she said, belonged to a local liars' club.

William Randolph Hearst's San Francisco Examiner declared on December 5, 1896, that "the whole airship story is pure myth." Misidentification accounts for some of the lights: on April 12, 1897, a professor in Clinton, Iowa, turned his telescope on the object a thousand people were watching and, the Chicago Times-Herald reported the next day, "found it to be the planet Venus." Two crews pointed toward the Tennessee Centennial Exposition at Nashville, whose own advertised airship the New York Times described on May 11 as "only a balloon."

Each of these is a documented hoax, joke or mistake. Taken together they raise a question Vallée's framework invites: does it matter, for the spread of a mystery, whether a given story was true? The balloons, the canvas photograph, the Aurora dispatch and the Hamilton heifer each put the airship back in the papers, sent more people out at dusk, and kept the question open. Vallée's thesis is concerned with what the phenomenon does to belief. On that measure, the pranks did the same work as the sightings.

The anchor at Merkel

The Houston Daily Post carried one more crew story under a dateline of Merkel, Texas. Churchgoers followed an anchor dragging on a rope until it caught on a rail. A man came partway down the rope. He wore "a light blue sailor suit" and "was small in size." When he saw the people at the anchor, he cut the rope and the ship sailed off. The anchor went on display at a blacksmith's shop.

The plot closely matches a medieval Irish tale, traced by the scholar John Carey, in which an air-ship's anchor catches in a church at Clonmacnoise, a sailor comes down after it, and in one version the crew cuts the rope and leaves the anchor behind. Gervase of Tilbury recorded a version around 1211, with a ship in the sky, an anchor caught on a church and a sailor climbing down the rope. Jerome Clark calls the Merkel story "almost certainly a hoax" drawn from that tradition. Nobody has explained how a centuries-old church story reached a Texas town in 1897 and was told there as news.

The control system

Vallée called the wave a "missing link" and argues that the phenomenon presents itself in forms the culture of the moment can take in. Read through that thesis, the details of 1896–97 line up as questions rather than as loose ends.

Does the wave deepen mystery? The crews explained just enough to provoke and no more. A new material, condensed electricity, compressed air, a secret principle, patents pending, and then: "you will know more later on." A hundred and twenty-nine years later, no one does.

Does it spark belief? Bullard's thousand-plus stories and Bartholomew's estimate of 100,000 sightings describe whole towns outside at night, looking up. The witnesses at Oakland had seen the Call's drawing before they saw the light. The Josserand farmer had read the Post's dispatches before he found a ship in his cornfield.

Does it work through ordinary people, in the costume of the time? Twenty of twenty-seven occupant reports describe ordinary-looking people: a man named Wilson with a bucket, a "Smith" who wanted chisels, a man in smoked glasses, a bearded elder with a lantern. They came as the secretive inventor the decade's magazines and dime novels had promised, in the last years before powered flight. Later reports, gathered by Clark in FATE in 1992, describe occupants in other costumes: a dozen men in "blue uniforms and little, round sailor's hats" on a flying platform at Aldeburgh during the First World War, "a bunch of Navy officers in Navy white hats" in Schenectady in 1952. Is that the same visitor, dressed for a different decade?

Does it coordinate across distance? Within eleven days, three crews in different Texas counties told the same story of five ships from a small Midwestern town. Water requests came at Beaumont, Uvalde, Josserand and Hot Springs. The Tillman and Dolbear names appeared in Stephenville and again in New Orleans. If the crews were men, how were they organized, and by whom? If many were inventions by separate local jokers, how did separate jokers arrive at the same script?

None of these questions requires deciding which story was true. If Vallée is right that the phenomenon speaks through patterns, the airship record offers one: a promised machine that never appears, a backer who is never named, men who look like neighbors, and a mystery that grows with every telling, including the false ones.

Set against the Watchers

A second old frame sits beside Vallée's. In R. H. Charles's translation of 1 Enoch, two hundred angels "descended in the days of Jared on the summit of Mount Hermon" (6:6). They "took unto themselves wives" and "taught them charms and enchantments, and the cutting of roots" (7:1). Azazel "taught men to make swords, and knives, and shields, and breastplates, and made known to them the metals," along with "the beautifying of the eyelids" and "all colouring tinctures." Others taught astrology, the constellations, and the signs of the earth, sun and moon (8:1–3). Jubilees 4:15 says they came down "that they should instruct the children of men."

The airship crews came down, in pastures, cornfields and creek bottoms. The record logged for this essay shows no marriages; women appear as members of the crew. It shows no open teaching; the crews withheld their principle and promised disclosure later. Their talk ran to New York capitalists, stock companies, weapons for Cuba, Harris's 63,000-shot gun and Hart's plan for Havana. The one moral message, the Farmersville temperance crew, is listed as a hoax, and the one witness who wondered aloud about "devils or angels" made his story up.

That leaves a question of method rather than a verdict. Should an ancient account be matched to a modern one point by point, descent, marriage, teaching, or by the effect on the people who saw it? Clark and Loren Coleman argued in 1975 that for many Americans the airship meant "the heavens had been violated; men had tainted even the domain of angels." Is a visitor who withholds knowledge doing something different from the Watchers, or the same thing in reverse? And if Vallée is right that the phenomenon dresses for its audience, would a Watcher in 1897 have looked like anything other than an inventor with a bucket?

Scripture keeps its own counsel on visitors who look like ordinary men. "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" (Hebrews 13:2). The farmers who handed over water, oil and chisels to strangers from the sky were doing exactly that, whoever the strangers were.

What remains

The historian Mike Dash summarized the investigators' findings: many of the simpler sightings were planets and stars, many of the elaborate ones were hoaxes and practical jokes, and "a small residuum remains perplexing." By summer the airship was gone from the papers.

What it left is a list of questions no archive has answered. Who was the "very wealthy man" behind Collins? Where was the Iowa town with five ships? Who were the New York capitalists? How did a Goshen man named Wilson know a Texas sheriff's past? Who chose a chemist and a physicist as the names on a pasture in Erath County and a hotel register in New Orleans? How did an Irish anchor story reach Merkel? And why did so many crews, in so many places, ask for the same plain things and promise that the secret would come later?

"It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter" (Proverbs 25:2). The men who stepped out of the ships said, "you will know more later on." The search is still open.

The ten largest companies now make up 40.3% of the S&P 500 per State Street holdings data as of October 14.  

​At the height of the 2000 dot com bubble, the top ten peaked at 24.2%. Today's concentration is 1.67 times higher.  

​NVIDIA alone is 8.1% of the index. In September 2000, GE and Cisco combined were 7.6%.

​We rebuilt the full timeline from SPY annual trust filings with the SEC back to 1997:

• 1997: 18.8%
• 2000 to 2001 peak: 24.2%
• 2013 cycle low: 17.7%
• 2020: 29.2%
• October 14, 2026: 40.3%  

​Look at the year 2000 top ten list: GE, Cisco, Microsoft, Exxon, Pfizer, Intel, Citigroup, Oracle, AIG, and EMC. Microsoft is the only survivor still in the top ten today.

​Bears look at the top chart panel and call it an automatic bubble. They are missing half the tape. Concentration is not the risk by itself. What you pay for those profits is the risk.  

​We matched year end index holdings against reported net income in SEC XBRL filings:

• End of 2019: 24.5% of index weight and 25.0% of net income. Relative P/E versus the other 490 stocks: 0.97x.
• End of 2025: 41.2% of index weight and 35.6% of net income. Relative P/E versus the other 490 stocks: 1.27x.
  
​Two realities jump off the page:  

​First, massive profit growth justified the bulk of the climb since 2019. These companies earned their weight.  

​Second, price has now outrun profits by 5.6 percentage points. In 2019, you bought the top ten at parity with the rest of the market. Today, passive cap weighted buyers are paying a 27% multiple premium for the leaders and betting that their earnings dominance never slows down.  

​Cap weighting is a momentum strategy without a sell discipline. Know the multiple embedded inside your index exposure and size your value, equal weight, and active sleeves accordingly.

Decline. Keep Zay Flowers. Your receivers are already thin, and you don't need another quarterback with Caleb Williams healthy.

Zay Flowers is your best receiver right now. He has 26 catches for 405 yards and 2 touchdowns in four games, and he's off the injury report this week. Even with Tyler Huntley at quarterback last week, he caught 8 of 9 targets. If Lamar Jackson makes it back against Cleveland, Flowers becomes a WR1.

Rhamondre Stevenson's role is growing, but his numbers are modest at 227 rushing yards (4.0 a carry), 2 touchdowns and 15 catches. His value jumped when TreVeyon Henderson hurt his ankle, so you'd be buying at his peak. He would be an upgrade over Blake Corum, who has 5 carries in each of his last two games.

C.J. Stroud doesn't fill a need. He's Houston's starter, but he has only 6 touchdown passes in five games. Caleb Williams practiced fully Wednesday and is set to start at Atlanta, so Stroud would sit on your bench.

Without Flowers, your receivers this week would be Chris Olave, Parker Washington and Luther Burden, with Rashee Rice likely out and Olave dealing with an illness. If you want Stevenson, offer Keaton Mitchell or Chase Brown instead.

text:
Blessed Feast!

The PriestMartyr Cyprian, the Holy Martyress Justina and the Martyr Theoktist perished at Nicomedia in the year 304.
      Saint Cyprian was a pagan, a native of Antioch. While still in early childhood he was given over by his misguided parents for service to the pagan gods. From seven years of age until thirty, Cyprian studied at the most outstanding centres of paganism – on Mount Olympus, in the cities of Argos and Tauropolis, in the Egyptian city of Memphis and at Babylon. Having attained to eminent wisdom in pagan philosophy and the sorcerer's craft, on Olympus he was consecrated into the pagan priesthood. Having discovered great power by the summoning of unclean spirits, he beheld the very prince of darkness, and conversed with him and received from him an host of demons in attendance.
      Having returned to Antioch, Cyprian became revered by the pagans as an eminent pagan priest, amazing people by his ability to conduct spells, to summon pestilence and plagues, and to seance the dead. The mighty pagan priest brought many an human soul to ruin, teaching them magic-spells and service to demons.
  But in this city there lived a Christian – the Virgin Justina. Having turned her own father and mother away from pagan error and led them to the true faith in Christ, she dedicated herself to the Heavenly Bridegroom and spent her time in fasting and prayer, remaining a virgin. When the youth Aglaides proposed marriage to her, the saint responded with a refusal. Agalides turned to Cyprian and sought his help for a magic-spell to charm Justina into marriage. But no matter what Cyprian tried, he could accomplish but nothing, since the saint by her prayers and fasting wrecked all the wiles of the devil. By his conjured spells Cyrian set loose demons upon the holy virgin, trying to rouse in her the fleshly passions, but she dispelled them by the power of the Sign of the Cross and by fervent prayer to the Lord. Even one of the demonic princes and Cyprian himself, by the power of sorcery having assumed various guises, were not able to sway Saint Justina, guarded round about by her firm faith in Christ. All the spells dissipated, and the demons fled at the mere look or even name of the saint. Cyprian in a rage sent down pestilence and plague upon the family of Justina and upon all the city, but this was beaten back by her prayer. Cyprian's soul, corrupted by its domination over people and by its incantations, showed up in all the depth of its downfall, and the abyss of nothingness of that which he served. "If thou dost take fright at even the mere shadow of the Cross and the Name of Christ indeed maketh thee to tremble, – said Cyprian to Satan, – then what wilt thou do, when Christ Himself is come before thee?" The devil thereupon flung himself upon the pagan priest who was in the process of repudiating him, and began to beat and strangle him. Saint Cyrian then first tested for himself the power of the Sign of the Cross and the Name of Christ, in guarding himself from the fury of the enemy. Afterwards, with deep repentance he went to the local Bishop Anthymos and consigned all his books to the flames. And the very next day, having gone into the church, he did not want to emerge from it, though he did not yet accept Holy Baptism.
      By his effort to follow a righteous manner of life, Saint Cyprian discerned the great power of fervent faith in Christ, and redeemed his more than thirty year service to Satan: seven days after Baptism he was ordained reader, on the twelfth day – sub-deacon, on the thirtieth – deacon, and after a year he was ordained priest. And in a short while Saint Cyprian was elevated to the dignity of bishop. The PriestMartyr Cyprian converted to Christ so many pagans, that in his diocese there was no one left to offer sacrifice to idols, and their pagan-temples fell into disuse. Saint Justina withdrew to a monastery and there was chosen hegumeness.. 
(cont'd)

text:
Russian-Iranian cooperation extends far beyond their confrontation with the United States. The two countries have long coordinated closely in waging hybrid warfare against the West as a whole.

Russia and Iran share intelligence. In July 2025, the UK Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee reported on this cooperation. The committee linked it to improvements in Iran’s intelligence operations and its ability to counter Western intelligence services. Some of the information in the public version of the report remains classified.

Pro-Russian and Iran-linked hacking groups formed a coalition called Holy League on July 22, 2024. It consisted of around 70 groups, including NoName057(16), Cyber Army of Russia, and UserSec.

Holy League members attacked Spain following the arrests of individuals linked to the DDoSia project run by Russia's NoName057(16). According to ENISA, NoName057(16) later claimed responsibility for DDoS attacks against Israeli organizations as a gesture of gratitude to its partners. This is an example of an exchange of favors: coalition members attack each other's adversaries.

Holy League targeted French online resources following the arrest of Pavel Durov in August 2024 and during the December meeting between Presidents Zelenskyy, Macron, and Trump in Paris. CERT aDvens and ENISA documented these campaigns, including attacks against government websites and financial services. Radware also recorded an announced campaign against France on December 6 and threats against Germany on December 14.

In March 2025, the coalition reported coordinated attacks against public-facing websites belonging to the British Army, the Royal Navy, the nuclear safety regulator, and MI6. Abu Omar, a representative of Cyber Islamic Resistance, claimed that his group had received training from Badr, an Iraqi organization linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Researchers have linked the Russian coalition member Cyber Army of Russia Reborn to Sandworm, a group of military hackers.

The pro-Russian NoName057(16) and the pro-Iranian Cyber Islamic Resistance jointly attacked Israeli targets in March 2026 as part of OpIsrael. Flashpoint identified a defense company and municipal authorities among the targets.

text:
With UP Fintech ($TIGR) at a market cap of roughly $750 million and an enterprise value closer to $450 million, I have been asking myself who could realistically buy this business. 

I‘m just thinking out loud here to document what‘s on my mind. 

The cap table provides some ideas. Founder Wu Tianhua owns around 18% of the shares and controls the vote through his Class B shares, so any deal runs through him. For that reason I think the most likely outcome could be a take-private led by Wu together with an Asian private equity sponsor, followed by a relisting in Hong Kong or Singapore at a higher multiple a few years later. Considering how incredibly cheap Tiger is (discl.: my subjective view, keep in mind I am long!), this seems like an "easy money glitch" for competent PE firms. 

Among strategic buyers, I would rank Webull $BULL first, since it already paid for Pi Securities in Thailand and targets the same clients. 

After that come $GRAB, which fits the Singapore base but has less use for the Hong Kong book, but has been on an acquisition spree, especially in its financial services segment, lately. Then SBI Holdings, and only then Futu. 

robinhood:0xeb30663bdff0622ef4e4e5cbb4e975f19f33f51d is the obvious name, but a merger of the two largest cross-border brokers would pile up regulatory risk and pushback. 

Xiaomi and Interactive Brokers $IBKR are insiders, but both have been trimming their stakes (both have sold down more than half their stakes over the past two years). Still at the right price IBKR would almost certainly be interested. 

There is a catch for minority holders like me. Chinese ADR take-privates have historically paid premiums of about 20 to 30 percent over the undisturbed price, below the US average. And even a 300% premium would undervalue the asset in my view. So an offer would at best make the market wake up to the true value here, which would then be rejected by founder Wu who hopefully realizes how large the disconnect between price and value is right now (even though the lack if buybacks makes me question that a little). 

I would love to hear from you. Who else could be interested in Tiger Brokers at this valuation, and which name on my list do you think I have ranked too high or too low? Disclosure: I own TIGR.

text:
📚 RUDYARD KIPLING
Born December 30, 1865 • Bombay, now Mumbai
Nobel Prize in Literature, 1907 ✏️

A Boy, a Wolf & the Question of Belonging

Illustration by W. H. Drake, from “Tiger! Tiger!”

▸ ▸ ▸

The boy has left the pack. His brother still comes to find him.

In this illustration, Mowgli rests beneath dense foliage while a wolf stands nearby. The space between them feels intimate. Their encounter belongs to a world in which another creature can recognise you, worry about you, and bring news from home.

That is one of Kipling’s enduring gifts: making an imagined relationship feel familiar before we have finished questioning its impossibility.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🏅 A NOBEL PRIZE AT FORTY-ONE
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Kipling received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907, aged forty-one. He remains the youngest recipient in the prize’s history.

The award recognised his powers of observation, originality of imagination, and narrative talent. The Jungle Book, published in 1894, offers a vivid entrance into those qualities.

His animals have appetites, tempers, loyalties, and obligations. Their world feels inhabited because its inhabitants have things to do besides explain themselves to the reader.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🐺 THE BROTHER WHO COMES BACK
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

❝ Wake, Little Brother; I bring news. ❞
— Grey Brother, “Tiger! Tiger!”

Mowgli has begun living among humans when Grey Brother follows him to the village’s edge. The wolf brings a warning about Shere Khan, but another concern soon emerges: will Mowgli forget his wolf family?

The danger gives the encounter urgency. The fear of being forgotten gives it tenderness.

Mowgli has been cast out of the pack. His affection for those who raised him survives that rejection. Grey Brother’s visit makes the distinction tangible: a community can withdraw its welcome while an individual refuses to withdraw his love.

Drake’s illustration gives that relationship room. The boy reclines; the wolf stands close enough for conversation. A potentially frightening animal becomes a familiar visitor through posture, proximity, and the simple fact that Mowgli stays where he is.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
🌿 WHAT THE PACK OWES THE WOLF
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

In “The Law of the Jungle,” collected in The Second Jungle Book in 1895, Kipling gives mutual dependence a memorable shape:

❝ For the strength of the Pack is the Wolf, and the strength of the Wolf is the Pack. ❞
— Rudyard Kipling

The sentence reverses its terms halfway through. We begin with what the individual contributes and return through what the community provides. Its rhythm helps the relationship stay in the memory.

The surrounding rules make that relationship practical. Food must be shared under particular conditions. Cubs have claims on the adults. Quarrels must be contained before they damage the whole pack.

Even the wolves have responsibilities. So much for escaping society.

Yet the poem ends by demanding obedience. The protection offered by this community comes with a hierarchy. That tension belongs to the work, too.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
⚖️ MY CRITICAL JUDGMENT
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Kipling is especially persuasive when affection becomes an action: someone follows, warns, teaches, or returns. His storytelling gives loyalty something physical to do.

His treatment of authority deserves closer questioning. In “The White Man’s Burden,” published in 1899, he presents colonial domination as a demanding duty undertaken by supposedly superior peoples. Its racial hierarchy is central to the argument.

That places a serious limit on any uncomplicated celebration of his imagination. The writer who gives an animal such recognisable affection can also diminish the humanity of colonised people.

Reading him closely means attending to both. The warmth of a particular relationship can move us while the larger assumptions surrounding power remain open to challenge.

▸ ▸ ▸

📖 A useful way to read: Listen to how Kipling makes a rule memorable, then notice what his characters actually do for one another. Ask when belonging offers shelter and when it demands submission.

In Drake’s illustration, the boy is far from the cave. His brother has found him.

Thought for 10s
Lecture: Beauty as Counterweight – The Temporary Observer, Institutional Flux, and the Search for Kindness at San Quentin

For students in Law, Political Science, Psychiatry, and Social Anthropology

On October 15, 2014, 
a Facebook post 
offered a simple image: 
a vanilla latte in a blue mug, 
heart-shaped foam 
floating on the surface, 
with the caption 
“Great art is where you find it.” 

The comments were ordinary
—someone noting it looked good, 
the poster adding that vanilla lattes
 are an awesome way to spend an hour. 
The post itself is small. 

The context around it is not.

In 2014 
the person 
who made that post 
was working at San Quentin State Prison. 

The period was one of change and stress. 

A federal court 
had ordered 
improved inpatient psychiatric care 
for severely mentally ill men on death row. 

Planning and recruitment 
for a roughly forty-bed hospital unit 
moved forward 
under that pressure, 
then dissolved 
before the unit ever opened. 

Health-care staff 
faced the uncertainty 
of a project that recruited them 
and then vanished. 

The poster, by contrast, 
described himself as a pilgrim passing through
—not subject to the same career disruptions, 
able to look for beauty and kindness 
as a temporary balance
 against the darkness of the place.

That contrast 
between the temporary observer 
and the permanent staff, 
between the search 
for small aesthetic moments 
and the large-scale failure 
of an institutional response, 
supplies the material for this lecture. 

The disciplines you represent e
ach illuminate a different face
 of the same problem: 
how people and systems 
try (and often fail) 
to create 
order, 
meaning, 
or care 
inside environments 
defined by 
coercion, 
scarcity, 
and competing logics.

Psychiatry: stress, plasticity, and the reconstruction of the ordinary

Chronic exposure 
to environments of high stress 
and moral injury 
alters the self-organizing brain. 

Functional connectivity patterns 
shift under sustained load; 
the circuits that support 
attention, 
emotion regulation, 
and narrative coherence 
are particularly sensitive. 

Memory is reconstructive. 

What is later recalled as 
“that period at San Quentin” 
is not a fixed recording 
but a story continually 
rewritten 
by subsequent experience 
and by the need 
to make the past usable.

Finding a heart in latte foam 
is not trivial 
under those conditions. 

It is a small, 
deliberate act
 of attentional reorientation
—an attempt to recruit 
sensory and aesthetic pathways 
that are not fully captured 
by the dominant institutional script 
of risk, 
control, 
and scarcity. 

For staff 
who remain for years, 
repeated failure 
of promised reforms 
(the hospital that never opened, 
the recruitment that led nowhere) 
can deepen cynicism 
and narrow the range 
of available emotional responses. 

For the temporary observer, 
the same moment 
can function as a protective reconstruction:
 evidence that beauty 
remains locatable 
even when larger systems do not. 

Psychotherapy works, 
in part, 
by creating structured occasions 
for such reconstructions. 

Everyday aesthetic practices 
can serve a related, 
if more fragile, 
function.

Social anthropology: pilgrims, permanence, and meaning-making under constraint

Anthropologists 
have long studied 
how people generate meaning 
inside institutions 
that were not designed for it. 

The distinction the poster draws
—pilgrim passing through 
versus career staff 
subject to institutional change
—is an emic category 
with real consequences. 

Temporary participants 
can afford a certain observational distance; 
they are not required 
to reorganize their long-term identity 
around the prison’s rhythms 
or its broken promises. 

Permanent staff must. 

Their practical knowledge, 
their career capital, 
and often their sense of professional self 
are entangled 
with the very systems 
that repeatedly fail 
to deliver stable conditions of care.

The latte 
is an instance 
of what anthropologists sometimes call 
“the art of the everyday.” 

In constrained settings, 
people improvise 
small aesthetic 
and relational forms
—shared coffee, 
a carefully poured heart, 
a brief conversation
—that assert a different scale of value. 

These forms 
do not overturn the institution, 
but they mark 
the boundary 
between total absorption 
and residual agency. 

The pilgrim’s ability 
to notice 
and photograph the heart 
is made possible 
by his temporary status; 
the same gesture 
may be harder to sustain, 
or may carry different risks, f
or those whose livelihoods 
depend on 
remaining inside the system.

Political science: intersecting systems and the production of unfinished projects

The 2014 hospital effort 
is a clear case 
of loosely coupled, 
self-organizing systems 
producing an outcome 
none of them fully intended. 

A federal court, 
responding to evidence 
of inadequate mental-health care 
on death row, 
created a legal deadline 
and a mandate. 

The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation 
began planning and recruitment. 

Legislative and budgetary processes, 
security protocols, 
and the practical difficulties 
of converting existing space 
inside an aging prison
 all moved on their own timelines. 

When the project dissolved 
after staff had been recruited 
but before the unit opened, 
each subsystem 
could point to constraints originating elsewhere.

This is the ordinary politics 
of implementation failure. 

Murphy’s Law operates
 not as mystical misfortune 
but as the statistical consequence 
of many independent failure points 
inside complex organizations. 

Once a sealed problem 
(the treatment of severely mentally ill condemned prisoners) 
is forced open 
by litigation, 
cascading coordination costs appear. 

Political scientists 
studying bureaucracy 
and courts 
should treat such collapses 
as data, 
not anomalies: 
evidence that rights-based interventions 
frequently outrun 
the adaptive capacity 
of the implementing systems.

Law: rights, remedies, and the gap that remains

From the legal side, 
the episode 
restates a familiar tension. 

Courts can declare that 
the Eighth Amendment requires 
adequate mental-health care, 
including for people under sentence of death. 

They can order
 evaluations, 
set timelines, 
and appoint monitors. 

They cannot, 
by themselves, 
create durable clinical capacity 
inside a maximum-security prison,
 stabilize funding streams, 
or insulate recruitment 
from subsequent 
political or operational reversals. 

When the operational systems
 fail to cohere, 
the legal right 
remains formally intact 
and practically incomplete. 

The men identified 
as needing inpatient care 
continued, 
in many cases, 
to be managed 
under prior arrangements.

Law students 
should note both 
the power a
nd the limits 
of this form of intervention. 

Litigation 
can force visibility 
and temporary resource shifts. 

It does not automatically 
reorganize 
the incentive structures, 
professional cultures, 
or security logics 
that determine 
whether care 
is actually delivered over time. 

The pilgrim 
who photographs 
latte art 
and the career clinician 
who loses a promised position 
are both living 
inside 
the space 
that law opened 
but could not close.

Synthesis

The 2014 post 
and its backstory 
hold the four perspectives 
in tension. 

A brain under stress 
seeks small 
reconstructive moments of beauty. 

An anthropologically visible distinction 
between temporary 
and permanent participants 
shapes 
who can afford 
to look for those moments 
and what they mean. 

Intersecting political 
and bureaucratic systems 
generate unfinished projects 
that then become 
part of the stress environment. 

Law supplies the pressure 
that opens the problem 
and the vocabulary 
of rights 
that remains 
after the practical response collapses. 

None of these processes 
is independent of the others.

The heart in the foam 
does not solve the larger failure. 

It does, however, 
record a persistent human capacity 
to locate aesthetic 
and relational value 
inside institutions 
that systematically under-supply both. 

Whether that capacity 
is treated as private coping, 
as ethnographic data, 
as a mental-health protective factor, 
or as evidence of unfinished
 legal and political work
 depends 
on the discipline 
one brings to the railing, 
the mug, 
and the prison 
that surrounded them.

Poem (in the style of Journey, 
“Separate Ways (Worlds Apart)”)

Here we stand
Worlds apart, hearts in the foam
In the yard where the orders land
And the promised doors never opened home
I was only passing, you were staying on

Recruitment done, then the whole thing gone
Feeling the weight of the change and the strain
Looking for kindness to balance the pain
Someday love will find you
True care won’t desert you
You know I still remember

The art where you find it, the hour we spent
If the systems ever hurt you
The looking won’t desert you
Break those chains that bind you
One night will remind you
We walked separate ways

Pilgrim and the ones who remain
Courts and budgets, plans that fray
Vanilla light against the darker rain
I could leave when the shift was through
You carried the unfinished into the new
Still the heart on the surface stays
Worlds apart, but the looking remains
Someday love will find you

Break those chains that bind you
One night will remind you
How we touched and went our separate ways
If he ever hurts you
True love won’t desert you
You know I still love you
Though we touched and went our separate ways

text:
The reason so many people hate Linux is because ...

Computers are powerful tools. Companies spend lots of money making software and entertainment so that in then they can make money. But this amounts to simply a mountain of data. Once that data is out in the wild, you can't control it.  Unless you control the machines where the data sits.

DRM and other antipiracy mechanisms only work if the machines holding the data will honor them. In order to make them honor them, the creators of this content need to control your machine. They do this through the operating system.

Microsoft, Apple and Google all have partnerships with large organizations that want to control distribution of their software and content and to help them protect it. Linux offers no such protection out of the box.

Linux doesn't care who you are or where you are, whether you've purchased a license or where you got your software from. It's a free and open system. It's not designed with profit in mind. It will never charge you a subscription or make you sign up to use it. It will not snitch on you. In fact, California recently passed a law requiring every operating system to have mandatory ID verification (age verification). They exempted Linux, because they knew that was a war they could not win.

Caldara examines Colorado's transformation from a state known for its libertarian traditions and entrepreneurial spirit into one he argues is increasingly dominated by government intervention. The conversation explores restrictions on firearms and tobacco products, the state's changing political demographics, and the growing influence of unaffiliated voters.  

Andrew and Jon also discuss Colorado Governor Jared Polis, the future of the state's Republican and Democratic parties, and whether independent candidates could offer voters an alternative. Caldara shares his thoughts on upcoming ballot initiatives, including proposals involving energy, hunting rights, and transgender-related policies.  

The conversation then turns to Colorado's energy future, with a focus on natural gas restrictions, electricity reliability, renewable energy, nuclear power, and the unintended consequences of government mandates.  Finally, Caldara discusses the rapid growth of Medicaid spending in Colorado, its implications for the state budget, and his personal concerns about maintaining services for people with disabilities. 

The episode concludes with stories from his earlier career as a political cartoonist and concert lighting technician, including his experiences working with well-known musicians.

text:
TEXAS: 500,000+ VOTER REGISTRATION RECORDS CAUGHT IN A SYSTEM FAILURE. WHO WAS WATCHING?

More than 500,000 voter-registration applications and updates went unprocessed in Texas because of a state software failure dating back to October 2025.

But the software error is only part of this story.

THE TIMELINE IS THE PROBLEM.

In July 2025, the Secretary of State's Office launched an overhaul of its voter-registration management system, known as TEAM.
 
In October 2025, According to DPS (Department of Public Safety), an update caused three data fields to be omitted from the daily information file sent to the Secretary of State's Office. Without the necessary information, the automated process did not properly match and forward affected records to counties.
 
In March 2026, Texas DPS acknowledged a separate programming failure affecting 992 registration transactions. Voters received receipts confirming their selections to register or update their addresses - yet their information was never properly saved or transmitted.

Officials said the problem was resolved.

In July, voting-rights organizations raised further complaints. Officials again offered assurances that technical problems were being addressed.

By late August, DPS says it had identified the missing-data problem behind the much larger backlog. The error was reportedly fixed by September 13.

Then came the revelation: MORE THAN 500,000 RECORDS had been held up, and county election offices were left scrambling to process them just before the October 5 registration deadline.

SO MUCH FOR “PROBLEM RESOLVED.”

How does a system issue get identified, supposedly corrected, and monitored - REPEATEDLY - while hundreds of thousands of records remain unprocessed?

Where were the independent checks? Where were the alerts? Where was the reconciliation between what voters submitted, what receipts told them, and what the state's actual voter-registration system recorded?

A receipt is not a registration. A claimed software fix is not proof that the system is working. And clearing a backlog is not proof that every affected record has been correctly reconciled.

AND WHY DID THE PUBLIC LEARN THE FULL SCOPE SO LATE?

Officials had received warnings months earlier. Complaints continued. Yet the scale of the failure became public only in late September, with the registration deadline days away and a major election approaching.

This raises a serious transparency question: Why weren't voters told sooner that a system they relied on might not have completed their registration or address update?

County officials say they have cleared the backlog. Good. But that is damage control - not a complete accounting of what failed, who was affected, or whether the underlying weaknesses have been corrected.

VALID, SECURE ELECTIONS REQUIRE MORE THAN CRISIS MANAGEMENT AND ENDLESS PROMISES THAT EVERYTHING IS NOW ‘FIXED’

They require election authorities to maintain reliable systems, detect errors, verify that corrective actions actually work, disclose material failures promptly, and protect every eligible voter's right to cast a ballot.
 
Every eligible voter must be able to know that when the government says their registration was received, the system actually did its job.

Texas owes its voters answers - not just assurances.
 
This is why Unite4Freedom is fighting for Valid, Transparent, Auditable Elections where the results can be proven. 

Texas deserves that – every eligible voter in America deserves that.
 
Support our work – become a volunteer – donate!
 
#Unite4Freedom

text:
The King Over the Grave: Why the Resurrection Changes Everything

​In human history, death has always been the ultimate, undisputed finish line. Earthly rulers build monuments, conquer lands, and command armies, yet every empire eventually falls and every king meets the same silent end. Death remains the great equalizer, claiming the powerful and humble alike.

​Except for One.

​The central victory  is that truth  turns human expectations upside down: death was simply not strong enough to hold Him.

​1. The Power of Divine Restraint

​When Jesus stood on trial before Pontius Pilate, He was not a victim trapped by political corruption or human schemes. When Pilate claimed authority over Him, Jesus offered a quiet, profound correction:

​"You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above."

— John 19:11

​During His arrest in Gethsemane, Jesus reminded His followers that He had an army of twelve legions of angels at His immediate call. Yet He laid down His life voluntarily. He chose restraint over retaliation, demonstrating that true divine power is rooted in sacrificial love.

​2. Death Could Not Keep Its Hold

​When Jesus rose from the tomb on the third day, He didn't just survive—He conquered the ultimate enemy.

 because it was impossible for death to keep its hold on him."

— Acts 2:24

​By overcoming the grave, Jesus proved that His authority transcends earthly kingdoms, systems, and human limitations. 1 Corinthians 15:55 asks, "Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?" The answer is found in the empty tomb.

​3. What Makes Him the True King

​An earthly leader’s authority ends when their life does. The kingship of Jesus is fundamentally different:

​An Everlasting Reign: Because He lives, His kingdom is eternal (Revelation 19:16 calls Him King of Kings and Lord of Lords).

​Victory Shared with All: He didn't break the power of death just for Himself, but to offer eternal hope and life to all who follow Him.

​Unshakable Hope: In a world filled with chaos, greed, and uncertainty, knowing that the ultimate battle over death has already been won gives us a firm foundation that cannot be shaken.

​Final Thought

​When life feels heavy and human systems fail, the Resurrection reminds us where true authority lies. Earthly powers are temporary, but the True King reigns forever—victorious over sin, fear, and the grave.

text:
What If Eritrea Defeats Ethiopia? Why Are Your Scenarios So One-Sided?
You have written four scenarios about Ethiopia breaking Eritrea’s defenses, overthrowing President Isaias, capturing Asmara, and seizing Assab. But why have you deliberately ignored the opposite possibilities?

Here are five scenarios you should also consider:

1. What if Eritrea defeats the Ethiopian army at the border? What happens to Abiy Ahmed’s military ambitions if his offensive fails, his forces suffer heavy losses, and Ethiopia becomes trapped in another costly war?

2. What if Fano advances toward Addis Ababa while the ENDF is fighting Eritrea? Who will defend the capital if Ethiopia’s military is overstretched between external conflict and internal insurgency?

3. What if Abiy’s own military commanders lose confidence in his leadership? Could a failed war trigger political divisions, defections, or a leadership crisis in Addis Ababa?

4. What if Abiy Ahmed and senior government officials are forced to flee? Would the UAE, one of his government's important international partners, offer him refuge? Or would his political allies distance themselves from a collapsing administration?

5. What if Ethiopia’s internal conflicts intensify rather than disappear? Could a failed invasion deepen economic instability, undermine federal authority, and leave the country facing a more dangerous political crisis?

You are comfortable imagining the downfall of Eritrea, but apparently unwilling to examine the vulnerabilities of Abiy Ahmed’s own government.

Btw: Who appointed you the military analyst responsible for predicting Eritrea’s future?

Military superiority on paper does not guarantee victory. And starting a war is much easier than controlling its consequences.

Before writing about who will govern Eritrea after Isaias, perhaps you should ask a different question:

Who would govern Ethiopia if Abiy Ahmed launched a disastrous war and lost?
Stop presenting Ethiopian victory as inevitable while pretending Ethiopian defeat is impossible.

Eritrea’s sovereignty is not yours to gamble with, and Assab is not Ethiopia’s consolation prize.

Last year I wrote about Kumar Awasthi, a retired Army officer whose bank sold him ₹1.36 crore of AT-1 bonds as a “Super FD for Senior Citizens.” That was most of his retirement savings.

Today the Supreme Court ruled that Yes Bank’s write-off of those bonds worth ₹8,415 crore was illegal.

The court also found that Yes Bank actively offered these bonds to individual investors, in violation of RBI’s own rules.

Which is exactly what "Mis-Sold" Documentary by @1FinanceHQ and @BahlKanan showed, through the people who lived it. (link in comments)

Awasthi's branch manager, a 13yr old friend of him, sold the riskiest paper a bank can issue and called it a fixed deposit, which is insane.

Six years later today, the supreme court has said the wipe-out should never have happened the way it did.

That is not the end of it. What bondholders actually get back is still a grey area and the incentive that put these bonds in a retired officer’s hands has not changed one bit.

text:
🇬🇷 GREEKS WHO LEFT THEIR MARK
FROM ANTIQUITY TO TODAY

XENOPHON OF ATHENS 
ΞΕΝΟΦΩΝ Ο ΑΘΗΝΑΙΟΣ

The Greek soldier philosopher who turned an extraordinary military journey into one of history’s greatest accounts of leadership.

In 401 BC, thousands of Greek mercenaries marched deep into the Persian Empire.

They had joined the army of Cyrus the Younger, who hoped to overthrow his brother, King Artaxerxes II.

But at the Battle of Cunaxa, near Babylon, Cyrus was killed.

The Greek soldiers suddenly found themselves stranded in hostile territory, far from home.

Their situation became even more desperate when several of their commanders were seized and executed.

Among the surviving Greeks was a young Athenian named Xenophon.

Born around 430 BC, Xenophon had been associated with the philosopher Socrates and had developed an interest in ethics, politics and human character.

He was not originally one of the expedition’s senior commanders.

But during the crisis, he emerged as an important leader.

THE MARCH OF THE TEN THOUSAND

The Greeks faced an extraordinary challenge.

They had to retreat across vast distances, through unfamiliar lands, dangerous mountain passes and hostile territories.

Xenophon helped organize their march, maintain discipline and encourage the exhausted soldiers.

The journey took them through regions of what are now Iraq, Turkey and surrounding areas.

They endured cold, hunger, attacks and uncertainty.

Then came one of the most celebrated moments in ancient military literature.

As the soldiers approached the Black Sea, the men at the front saw the water and began shouting:

«Θάλαττα! Θάλαττα!»
“The sea! The sea!”

For the exhausted Greeks, the sight meant hope.

They had reached a region where Greek coastal settlements offered a possible route toward safety.

Xenophon later described this remarkable expedition in his famous work, Anabasis  Κύρου Ἀνάβασις.

It became one of antiquity’s most influential military narratives.

But Xenophon was more than a soldier.

A STUDENT OF SOCRATES

He wrote important accounts of Socrates, including Memorabilia and Apology, preserving a perspective that complements the writings of Plato.

He also explored leadership, government, economics, military organization and education.

His Cyropaedia, a partly idealized account of Cyrus the Great, examined the qualities of an effective ruler.

His Hellenica continued the narrative of Greek history after the point where Thucydides’ surviving history ends.

Xenophon’s works influenced generations of historians, philosophers, military commanders and political thinkers.

His career also revealed the complicated loyalties of the ancient Greek world.

Although Athenian by birth, he developed close connections with Sparta and spent part of his life away from Athens.

His writings do not present a simple celebration of Athenian democracy. They often admire discipline, hierarchy and capable leadership.

THE LEGACY OF XENOPHON

More than 2,300 years later, Anabasis remains one of the great surviving works of ancient Greek literature.

Its story reminds us that leadership is tested most severely when circumstances become uncertain and dangerous.

Xenophon did not merely describe a journey.

He preserved an extraordinary account of how human beings confronted fear, adversity and the struggle to return home.

🇬🇷 XENOPHON 
THE GREEK WHO LED THROUGH ADVERSITY AND WROTE FOR ETERNITY.

c. 430–354 BC

«Θάλαττα! Θάλαττα!»
The sea! The sea!

— Xenophon, Anabasis, Book IV, Chapter 7
