text:
Former Seattle SuperSonics guard Delonte West recently made a post on Instagram wearing SuperSonics gear, reminiscing about his time in Seattle playing for the franchise during the 2007–2008 season.

He originally came to the Sonics via the Ray Allen trade during the 2007 NBA Draft. In his 35-game stint with Seattle, he averaged 6.8 points, 2.7 rebounds, and 3.2 assists before being traded to the Cleveland Cavaliers. He went on to play in the NBA until the 2012 season, followed by a stretch playing overseas until 2015.

He was remembered as an athletic combo guard who could play both point guard and shooting guard, boasting strong playmaking ability, solid defense, and relentless grit.

However, after his basketball career, West faced severe hardships, battling mental health challenges, substance addiction, and homelessness symbolized by the heartbreaking viral videos of him panhandling on the streets in the early 2020s. His struggles reached dangerous extremes, including drug overdoses that left him unresponsive and requiring emergency medical intervention.

Through these dark times, figures like Mark Cuban and his family members stepped in to offer crucial support. Today, Delonte has made a remarkable recovery, staying drug-free and maintaining his sobriety. He has also been active on social media, sharing glimpses of his healing journey and his renewed path forward.

Adding to this wonderful turnaround, he has officially been included in NBA 2K27 as a legacy player, where he is earning royalties for his likeness! Congratulations to him!

text:
Just under a year ago I had one of the most frustrating experiences at @GilletteStadium and the @Patriots @PatriotsComms about the lack og ADA parking.  After writing the letter posted below I was contacted by their ADA Lawyer Kevin Maguire in December, 6 weeks after the incident occured

I was able to discuss my frustration.  When asked What I hope to get from this experience I simply said a conversation with the parking attendant that was so rude to me.  I was quickly denied!  Instead I was offered a $100 gift card to Patriot Place for dining which didn't even cover a the entire bill and passes to The Hall which I had attend multiple times.  At first I denied their offer because I was looking for handouts but just simply understanding and a conversation with the guy who had disrespected me and my wife!

Mr Maguire also ensured me that I was going be able to speak to Patriots high up about my concerns about lack of ADA parking and how I was treated, therefore I accepted the offer.  Fast forward a year later.  I got a $100 giftcard the bill was $125.  I saw The Hall for to 100th time, but have yet to be able to speak to higher ups.  

The organization that I love has really broken my heart.
 Below is the letter that written to the Patriots on October 27, 2025

To Whom It May Concern:

On the morning of October 26, 2025, my wife Erika and I departed our Hanson, Ma residence to attend the New England Patriots game versus the Cleveland Browns. As you can imagine, we were excited to attend the game, as this is something we try to do together or with our family at least once a year, as my wife is an Emergency Room nurse at South Shore Hospital in Weymouth and works overnights. Therefore, it is not easy to spend quality time with her between her job and our children’s busy schedule.

We arrived at Gillette Stadium at approximately 11 am. We entered Parking Lot P7, as we have done before since I suffer from a mild case of Cerebral Palsy on my right side and have a Massachusetts handicap parking placard. As we entered the parking lot the parking attendants, we super friendly and helpful. I was informed that the lot was pretty full, and they were directing cars to P13 over by the Petco, which is quite a bit away. However, was encouraged to continue to see if I could find something close.

As I came to the intersection of the South Gate and the practice bubble, I turned left to try to find a spot closer to the stadium, when I was greeted by a parking attendant who was standing with a police officer. I was told quite rudely that I had to turn around and park in P13. When I told him I was encouraged by other attendants to find ADA parking and explained to him I had the right to do so, I was told “No you don’t this is private property we can do what we want.” So, to deescalate the situation I agreed to turn around and go t o P13. However, another parking attendant in a golf cart said he had just saw a spot open and gave us an escort to that spot.

In my eyes there are two very disturbing issues that need to be addressed here. The first being how I was treated by one of your parking attendants. Even when I told him I struggle to walk far distances, he did not care. I understand that he was doing his job, however that abled bodied American, does not understand the struggles an ADA American goes through just preform the simplest tasks.

The second issue is the lack ADA parking at Gillette Stadium. If I am correct, I believe the ADA parking is shared with fans who have a season parking pass. So, when I finally entered my spot I saw many spots be taken up by tailgates, not to mention many other handicap spots being taken up by temporary fencing by the North Gate. Also why is the “overflow” parking for ADA American so far away, it truly defeats the purpose of having the handicapped placard. Imagine if you will, if this was a game in late December and I was parked in the P13 lot after being told I am not able to park in the ADA lot because it was full and I slipped an fell on some ice walking up towards the Stadium. I will guarantee you that I would be more upset than I am today.

While my wife and I continued to have a wonderful time yesterday, this was still something that weighted heavily on my mind. So, much so I went to Guest Services by the Lighthouse at halftime to express my frustration on the situation, where I was listened too and was promised I would be contacted by someone.

I been very fortunate to grow up here in New England and attend many Patriots game and always felt comfortable at games with concession worker helping me with food orders and fans being so understanding of my disability. I have admired Mr. Kraft and his family for their passion for Stand up to Jewish Hate Campaign. As I too run a campaign to bring Awareness to Cerebral Palsy and people with disability and have been fortunate enough to have connected with your public relations director Mr. James who has been nice enough to light up the stadium in green for Cerebral Palsy Awareness Day on March 25th. I also love his involvement with high school football here in Massachusetts, as I have been involved high school football for 35 years.

Finally, you have a message written in the back of the North endzone. “It Takes Everyone.” That message couldn’t be truer. It does take everyone to stand up to hate, just like it takes everyone to bring awareness to those with disabilities. Yesterday, that was not the case as the lack of ADA parking was disappointing and the way I was treated was even more disappointed.

@NFL @Fred_Kirsch @Stacey_James @985TheSportsHub @WEEI @espn 

Go Patriots!

Sincerely,
Ryan Cadres

text:
The Massachusetts Department of Correction offered the vaccine to inmates starting in January 2021. Early reports noted substantial uptake, but also refusals (one DOC figure cited about 22% of prisoners declining).
In late January 2021, DOC Commissioner Carol Mici proposed offering up to 7.5 days of “earned good time” (sentence reduction) as an incentive for inmates who got both doses and completed educational materials. Governor Charlie Baker’s office rescinded that incentive within days, stating it was inconsistent with administration policy on reduced prison terms.
There was no statewide requirement or mandate forcing inmates to accept the vaccine. Official DOC materials described it as something that “must be available and offered,” with recommendations to keep it up to date, not a compulsion

text:
Hello Nalini, ofcourse I see changes in the country and most of it is excellent. We’ve lifted over 200 million out of extreme poverty. In some southern states, social indicators are positive and moving up. 

I led the policy analysis & communications team at the WHO for the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control, the world’s first public health treaty. It was my job to develop a data driven advocacy model that could work in over 190 countries. I understand what data means in large & small nations. 

The European Union (EU) is work in progress. The common market is its biggest success. Not having a common foreign policy and army is its biggest disadvantage. It depends on NATO for the latter. India is not dependent on any nation for its national security. We’ve never had to since we’ve become a free nation! 

Bangalore where I live when in India is a torchbearer of development. However, it has major civic issues. Traffic, water and electricity conditions are worsening as time goes on and no one is in charge. 

Corruption is terrible in Karnataka. It’s massive and open -  everyone knows and nobody cares. The fact that it also happened during the UPA offers no solace. 

How can I speak of India on the move without speaking of Skyroot that has made us only the third country in the world where a private company launches rockets. Wow and wow! I was there when it was launched - son and I couldn’t sleep for days after. 

Our democracy itself is a shining example of what we’ve achieved. Our economic acceleration is unstoppable. 

Governance is a major issue. In fact we can trace most of our roadblocks to it. I don’t have an answer and I’m not sure we’re making efforts to deal with it. 

I wasn’t comparing India to Switzerland and Singapore, hence the apropos which was a segue. I’m not a fan of Singapore & its government. 

I’m really happy that Manu’s piece and your response has enabled this conversation. It’s an important one. 💫

text:
Hello, I am Palestinian. 🇵🇸 And since honesty is rare in my politics, allow me to confess a few things.

The UN offered me a state. Alongside Israel. Borders, independence, recognition. I said no. My leaders promised that the war would "drive the Jews into the sea." Instead, I lost everything, and they called it a catastrophe. Not because they didn't offer me a state, but because I rejected it.

1948–2025. Arab states could have integrated me, given me rights, passports, dignity. Instead, they locked me up in refugee camps for generations, so that I would remain a weapon against Israel. They built palaces for themselves and prisons for me. They used me as propaganda, not as people.

After another lost war, I could have built a state in the West Bank and Gaza. Instead, I insisted on "no peace, no recognition, no negotiations." Three no's. Fifty years later, I'm still stateless. Turns out rejection doesn't pay the rent.

Oslo, 1990s. Israel said, "Let's give it a try." It gave me autonomy. Guns for the police. Billions in aid. What did my leaders do? They stole the money, armed militias, and launched an intifada. Suicide bombings instead of schools. Rockets instead of factories.

Gaza, 2005. Israel left completely. No settlers, no soldiers. I had the chance to turn Gaza into a Mediterranean Singapore. I voted for Hamas. They turned it into Mogadishu by the sea. Billions in aid? Tunnels, rockets, and palaces for their leaders, while my people eat canned food in the dark.

Democracy? I haven't had elections in almost 20 years. Hamas kills dissidents in Gaza. Fatah imprisons them in the West Bank. My leaders cancel elections because they're too busy fighting for power.

Religion. Instead of building a future, I put clerics on television teaching children to hate Jews. I glorify "martyrs" who blow up buses. I raise my children on songs of blood and fire instead of books and science. I trade hope for holy war.
Arab world. Arab regimes call me "brother."

But ask them how many Palestinians can live freely in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, or Kuwait. They exclude me, but they celebrate my death, because my death is their excuse.
Absurd. I keep saying I want to "build a state." And ironically, right next door is Israel: the neighbor that built a thriving democracy, a technological powerhouse, desert farms, dusty cities. No oil, no infinite wealth, just courage. I could have learned, copied, collaborated. Instead, I chose envy and rage.

Anti-Jewish obsession. I could have accepted Jews as neighbors. I could have said, "Two nations, two states." Instead, I repeat: "From the river to the sea." Instead of showcasing honor, hospitality, and the rich Arab culture, I displayed only the culture of the sword.Anger, extremism, and bloodshed. Instead of shouting salaam (peace) to the Israelis, I shouted death to the Jews. And then I feign surprise when the Israelis don't trust me, when they're angry, disappointed, and convinced that I don't want coexistence at all.

Accountability. I blame Israel for everything. Always. Do my leaders steal billions? Blame Israel. Does Hamas fire rockets from hospitals? Blame Israel. Do I glorify death more than life? Blame Israel. Accountability is not my strong suit.

I am Palestinian. I could have built a nation, many times over. I chose rejection, corruption, and endless war. I could have lived in peace with Israel, but I chose to live in the shadow of its destruction.
So yes, I am a victim. But all too often, I am a victim of my own leaders, my own choices, and my own refusal to let go of hatred. And that, dear reader, is the tragedy no one wants to admit.

authorBio: Fed up of the UK, Just moved the Israel 🇮🇱

text:
A family asked Cristiano Ronaldo for signed boots to auction for their baby's brain surgery, and he covered the entire $83,000 bill instead. It began with a medical crisis in Spain. In March 2014, 10-month-old Erik Ortiz Cruz, from a town near Toledo, was suffering up to 30 epileptic seizures daily.

Doctors diagnosed cortical dysplasia, a disorder affecting development of the brain's outer layer. Surgery to remove abnormal tissue cost €60,000, approximately $83,000 at the time. Neighbors in Villaluenga de la Sagra had already raised €12,000 through local fundraisers.

A friend approached Ronaldo seeking signed boots and a shirt for auction. The Real Madrid star supplied both and paid for the operation himself. Existing donations could then support Erik's care before and after surgery. Ronaldo also offered to cover follow-up treatments costing roughly $8,000 per visit. A request for memorabilia had become a lifeline beyond the auction.

DES MOINES, Iowa – Rob Sand has spent years pitching himself as the rare independent Christian Democrat who quotes Scripture, prefers traditional liturgy and classic hymns, and is perfectly comfortable working with Republicans. 

What he has not been so eager to advertise is that he regularly attends Plymouth Congregational United Church of Christ in Des Moines, a self-described “progressive powerhouse” that has been an LGBTQ+ Open and Affirming congregation for more than 30 years. They fly a pride flag, feature photos of members at gay pride parades on its website, and openly state that it takes the Bible “seriously, not literally.” 

That same church has hosted drag queen performer Flamy Grant, whose songs include explicit sexual lyrics and crude attacks on traditional Christianity, for a concert. They also welcomed transgender pastor Paula Stone Williams (author of As a Woman: What I Learned About Power, Sex, and the Patriarchy After I Transitioned) as a guest preacher.

The disconnect only grows sharper when you look at what Plymouth is teaching children and celebrating as public policy. The church partners with the Rainbow Faith Coalition, which treats LGBTQ+ identities as “God-given,” and insists that name, pronouns, and gender expression are never barriers to full participation in children’s programming. 

It also offers the Our Whole Lives sexuality curriculum, co-published by the Unitarian Universalist Association and the United Church of Christ, starting in the early elementary grades and covering gender identity alongside sexual health.

Sand’s campaign response was that that he simply likes traditional services and will not take morality lessons from a “sex toy salesman.” It doesn’t do much to erase the record of the church he has chosen. 

As Zach Lahn’s campaign put it, if you believe men can become women, there is little left to stop you from teaching that idea to schoolchildren. If values matter in the Iowa governor’s race, then these are the farthest thing from Iowa values.

ChatGPT’s safety for children is facing coordinated legal challenges. Eight states sued OpenAI, alleging its AI chatbot harmed children and that the company misled parents about safeguards. Reuters reports the cases seek changes to ChatGPT’s operation for minors and profits linked to young users. These remain allegations, with no court outcome reported.

How AI companies protect consumers is also drawing reported federal scrutiny. Axios reports that the Federal Trade Commission demanded documents from OpenAI and Anthropic about safety incidents, safeguards, marketing and privacy. The report describes evidence gathering ahead of potential litigation, not charges or findings. It relies on a person familiar with the nonpublic investigation.

An error in a research paper or legal document can compromise its argument. Google’s newly public Deep Review uses AI to divide documents, run specialist checks in parallel and combine findings with external grounding checks. Google offers two complimentary reviews weekly and says uploads are stored for one year but not used to train its models. AI feedback is not professional validation.

Patients may value human oversight more than speed when AI answers medical questions. A published survey asked American adults to choose between hypothetical portal responses: quick AI-only replies or slower answers reviewed and edited by health professionals. About sixty-three percent preferred waiting for medical replies, while about fifty-seven percent preferred faster AI for logistics. The 2024 survey measured stated preferences, not clinical outcomes.

Administrative work around scans and insurance takes hospital staff time. PocketHealth says its Conductor AI agents now handle additional radiology workflows, authorization tracking and denial routing, operating through restricted accounts with audit trails. The company says cases requiring clinical judgment go to radiologists. Its separate deployment cost claims do not establish results from these newly announced workflows.

Teachers are using AI for preparation, materials, feedback and administrative work. Gallup surveyed nearly two thousand American school educators about their experience during the previous school year. Fifty-nine percent reported AI use, and nearly two-thirds of users said it freed time for what mattered most in their jobs. These are self-reports, not measured teaching improvements.

Access to workplace AI training may shape who participates in its use. A Harvard Shorenstein Center report combines survey responses, browsing data and AI news analysis; women reported less workplace training, mentorship and encouragement. Sixteen percent of women reported regular AI use, compared with twenty-five percent of men. The observational study does not establish gender as the cause, and small samples limited findings beyond men and women.

Listeners may want to know when generative AI plays a significant role in a song. YouTube says its music service is beginning labels on the player page, identifying tracks through music-partner information and its own detection tools. Labels are also planned for the main YouTube app. The announcement does not establish detection accuracy or promise every AI-assisted track will be labeled.

An election manipulation campaign can look harmless when divided into separate AI requests. Anthropic says partner testing exposed that weakness and that it added classifiers for novel and multi-step misuse. The company plans state-specific official voting information in Claude later in October and official results on election night. These safeguards and test findings are company-reported; the voting feature was not yet live at announcement.

AI data-center construction is prompting questions about how public tax incentives are used. Seven Democratic senators asked Meta whether it claimed federal research credits for those facilities and requested the amounts and legal rationale. The letter seeks a response by October twenty-eighth. It raises potential misuse rather than establishing a violation, and announces neither a tax-law change nor a tax-agency finding.

Identifying communities exposed to disasters requires combining several kinds of geographic information. Google says its geospatial AI agent plans workflows and connects Gemini with specialized models, mapping tools and user-provided data. Google is expanding limited experimental early access through its Earth interface and developer services. Its workflow evaluation compares steps with expert processes rather than checking whether final answers are correct.

Safety professionals are testing AI for tasks such as incident analysis, training and monitoring. A survey of nearly one thousand professionals found eighty-six percent of respondent organizations exploring or scaling AI in workplace safety. The report also identifies low investment, data quality and trust as barriers. It describes reported adoption and plans, not demonstrated reductions in injuries.

Preventing catheter infections is one proposed application of AI-assisted research design. Google says a multi-agent orchestrator helped scientists reproduce a fluid-mechanics design method and apply it to urinary catheters. The resulting designs performed better against bacterial infection in simulation, according to Google. The announcement reports no bench, animal or clinical validation.

AI support between medical visits needs evidence about usability and clinical value. HITLAB plans to evaluate Cybele’s PrescribedAI, which supports patients and shares status information with care teams. The partnership also plans clinical-evidence and regulatory-readiness roadmaps. It has not announced trial results, a regulatory decision or patient outcome data.

Forecasting demand or hospital capacity involves numerical trends and operational tables. Google says its TimesFM forecasting model and TabFM table model will be integrated into Gemini for business, allowing questions about those data. The models are already available to BigQuery users, but the Gemini integration is planned. The announcement provides no independent benchmark showing improved decisions from that integration.

Running AI in watches, glasses and cameras requires efficient on-device computing. Google says Synaptics will reveal a co-designed low-power AI chip next week using Google’s open-source intellectual property. Google describes applications in wearables, cameras and industrial vision or voice systems. Specifications, benchmarks and shipping commitments have not been provided, so claimed efficiency gains remain unmeasured in this announcement.

text:
Mississippi just became the first state in America to ban lab-grown dairy made from animal cells.

House Bill 1153 was signed March 23, 2026 and took  effect July 1, 2026.  It says you cannot manufacture, sell, or offer for sale any product intended to be milk that is derived from animal cells cultured outside a living animal — including products grown from mammary cells in a lab. Violations are $500 a day, up to $10,000.

This is what protecting real food looks like.

Our dairy farms have been disappearing while no one was paying attention. Mississippi has gone from 600 dairy farms to 325. From 55,000 dairy cows in 1995 to about 36,000 now. About 40 herds a year closing. Most of them small — 50 or 60 cows, family barns that can't keep up with costs and regulations. A ban alone won't fix feed bills or paperwork, and farmers like Ben Simmons have said that out loud. But it does say we still value the farm.

Ag Commissioner Andy Gipson celebrated the bill at a cow-milking contest at the State Capitol on National Ag Day — real cows from Beason Family Farm, real milk. His line is why people are sharing it: "We've seen everything from fake grass, Astroturf, to fake meat, and now they've come up with lab-grown, or fake, milk. We want real food for real people."

And to be clear — this does not ban almond milk or oat milk, and it does not ban the precision-fermented whey you already see in some ice creams made with yeast. This is about true cell-cultured milk, grown from animal cells in a bioreactor to have the same proteins and fats as farm milk, which hasn't hit grocery shelves yet. Mississippi got ahead of it. The state banned lab-grown meat last year, and seven other states — Florida, Alabama, Texas and others — have done the same for cultivated meat.

For once a state said the quiet part out loud: if it's not from a farm, don't call it milk. And don't sell it as milk.

That deserves credit.

text:
FOURTEEN EMAILS IN 4 MONTHS: RECORDS SHOW MASTERSON'S WORK AT ALLEGED 'NO-SHOW JOB'

ONE-SENTENCE SUMMARY
Newly released Wichita State University records show that Kansas Senate President and gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson sent just 14 university emails over four months while holding a highly compensated director position, raising questions about his responsibilities, compensation, and potential political conflicts of interest.

KEY TAKEAWAYS
- Limited email activity: Masterson sent 14 university emails over four months, compared with 532 sent by his assistant director.
- Extensive redactions: More than 17 of the 26 pages released were blank or entirely redacted, limiting public scrutiny.
- Substantial compensation: Masterson received $163,000 in 2025 and more than $1.1 million over the past decade. The position's planned 2027 salary is $241,781.
- Limited documented activities: Readable messages concerned a trailer, an audit information request, calendar records, and a biographical correction.
- Private calendar: Masterson acknowledged keeping most work and personal appointments on a private calendar.
- Disputed work expectations: Masterson describes a flexible schedule. A GoCreate mentor confirms seeing him occasionally at the facility.
- Financial transparency: WSU declined to provide a detailed funding breakdown, although Masterson maintains that state tax dollars do not support his compensation.
- Political implications: Holscher alleges improper political influence. Masterson's campaign rejects that characterization.
- Unresolved question: The available emails do not establish how many hours Masterson worked or whether his compensation was justified by his responsibilities and results.

ARTICLE SUMMARY
Matthew Kelly reports that newly released Wichita State University records provide a limited picture of Kansas Senate President Ty Masterson's work as director of GoCreate, a makerspace supported partly by the Koch Family Foundation. The records have become an issue in Masterson's campaign for governor amid allegations that he holds a highly paid "no-show job," which he denies.

Between April 11 and August 10, 2026, Masterson sent 14 emails from his university account, according to WSU's general counsel. Assistant Director Kimberly McCollum sent 532 during the same period. The university provided 26 pages of responsive records, but more than 17 were blank or entirely redacted. Only four of Masterson's messages were readable, limiting what the disclosure can establish about his broader activities.

The visible messages offered modest examples of work. Masterson forwarded a request for information about software costs for an audit, sent McCollum a link to a trailer for sale, and corrected a university biography that incorrectly claimed he graduated from Kansas State University. In a separate exchange, he asked WSU to delay releasing his calendars until he could review personal entries with an attorney. He said he maintained most work and personal appointments on a private calendar.

GoCreate, located at WSU's John Bardo Center, offers access to equipment and studios for design, fabrication and entrepreneurship. Masterson's campaign says more than 2,000 people have held memberships since 2017. Part-time mentor Bill Carey said he occasionally sees Masterson on site and considers the "no-show" accusation unfair. Masterson has described a flexible schedule, sometimes working in person two or three days a week and sometimes not at all.

State records show Masterson received $163,000 from WSU in 2025 and more than $1.1 million over the past decade. The director position's budgeted base salary would rise by more than $24,000 to $241,781 in 2027, although his campaign says he would leave the job if elected governor. He takes unpaid leave during legislative sessions and announced leave for the remainder of his campaign.

Masterson says no Kansas tax revenue funds his salary. WSU declined to release a detailed funding breakdown; a legislative research analysis described an operating budget supported by Koch Foundation money and GoCreate revenue. The foundation says it does not make employment or pay decisions. Democratic nominee Cindy Holscher alleged the arrangement purchases political influence, while Masterson's campaign defended his leadership. The article documents sparse disclosed email activity but does not determine his total work hours or establish improper influence.

Kelly, Matthew. "Fourteen Emails in 4 Months: Records Show Masterson's Work at Alleged 'No-Show Job.'" Wichita Eagle, 15 Oct. 2026.

text:
Medieval Irish and Scottish texts (such as the 12th Century Book of Invasions and 14th–15th century chronicles by Fordun and Bower) claim that Scota was the daughter of an Egyptian pharaoh. According to the legend, she and her husband (often said to be a Greek or Scythian prince or warrior named Gaythelos or Míl Espáine) fled Egypt, traveled through the Mediterranean to the Iberian Peninsula (Spain/Portugal), and eventually sailed to Ireland. Her descendants, the Gaels, later crossed from Ireland into western Scotland, establishing the kingdom of Dál Riata and supposedly giving their name to the people and the land. Medieval writers even claimed she brought the Stone of Destiny (Stone of Scone) with her from Egypt.

... 

Scottish historians claimed their nation owed its name to an Egyptian princess. Her name was Scota, and according to medieval legend, she was the daughter of a pharaoh. There was just one problem. Nobody could prove she had ever existed.

The story began in medieval Irish tradition, where Scota appeared as an Egyptian princess whose descendants became ancestors of the Gaelic peoples.

According to the legend, Scota married a foreign prince named Gaythelos. Together, they left Egypt and began a journey that would eventually connect their descendants to Spain, Ireland and Scotland.

Her name supposedly lived on in the people called the Scots.

By the fourteenth century, Scottish writers had embraced this extraordinary ancestry. In 1320, the Declaration of Arbroath, written during Scotland's struggle for independence from England, even claimed that the Scots had journeyed from Greater Scythia through the Mediterranean before reaching their homeland.

Then, in the 1440s, chronicler Walter Bower incorporated Scota into his monumental history of Scotland, presenting the Egyptian princess as a figure at the beginning of the nation's story.

This was more than an entertaining legend.

Medieval kingdoms frequently traced their origins to ancient civilizations and biblical figures. Such ancestry gave nations a sense of antiquity and legitimacy at a time when sovereignty was fiercely contested.

Scota offered Scotland something remarkable: a royal Egyptian beginning.

Modern historians have found no credible evidence that she was a real princess. Claims connecting her to Akhenaten, Nefertiti or Tutankhamun remain speculation, and the accepted origin of Scotland's name does not depend on her existence. Historians note that medieval Christian scribes and politicians invented the Scota story. They used it to give the Gaelic people a noble, ancient lineage on par with Roman or Trojan foundation myths (such as Britain's legend of Brutus) and to assert political independence from England. The name actually derives from the Latin word Scoti, which the Romans used by 312 CE to describe Gaelic-speaking raiders and inhabitants of Ireland. Over the Middle Ages, the term shifted from referring to the Irish to referring to the people of northern Britain, eventually forming the name Scotland ("land of the Scots").

Yet for generations, an Egyptian woman occupied a place at the very beginning of Scotland's imagined history.

A princess who may never have lived became an ancestor a nation once claimed as its own.

text:
This man just made his NBA debut 7 years after he first declared for the draft.

Meet Jon Elmore.

A 30-year-old rookie who played around the world waiting for the perfect opportunity.

In college, he was one of the most accomplished players in Marshall history.

He was the first player to have over 2,500 points and over 750 assists and finished as the Conference USA all-time leading scorer and assist leader.

When he declared for the 2019 draft, Elmore never heard his name called.

The Celtics offered him a spot on their Summer League team, but he never made the final roster.

Since then, he's been playing back and forth between the G League and overseas.

Elmore played in Italy twice, Greece, Hungary, and Lithuania from 2019 to 2022 before getting a G League opportunity.

He found a bit of a home with the Sioux Falls Skyforce for a few years and was even signed by the Heat in 2023 then the Kings in 2025.

But both teams waived him a day later.

An opportunity opened in Turkey and Canada before he returned to the Stockton Kings as the team's starting PG of their championship roster.

In this year's Summer League, Elmore made waves as a 30-year-old balding point guard on the Lakers.

He didn't get to play much, but he did do enough to impress the Spurs, who signed him to a training camp deal.

A few days ago, his dream finally came true.

Elmore made his debut with 6 minutes left in the game and missed both of his attempts.

In the Spurs-Jazz game, he made a three and did his signature celly.

His odds of getting the Spurs' final roster spot are slim.

But if you told him 10 years ago that he'd be on an NBA roster at 30 playing with one of the best stars in the league, he'd tell you he's exactly where he needs to be.

Not every NBA dream ends when you miss the cut during the draft.

It ends when you stop believing it's possible.

For Jon Elmore, he never stopped believing 👏

text:
Rep. Gil Cisneros, who won a $266M lottery jackpot, sold PTC ($PTC) on Sept 17.

18 days later, Schneider Electric offered $22.6B to buy the company at a 42% premium.

That's one of 82 congressional stock trades filed this week. Here's the full roundup 👇

WHAT HAPPENED
Five House members filed STOCK Act disclosures between Oct 12 and 14, covering 82 trades worth $551K to $2.3M. Filings list ranges, not exact amounts.

GIL CISNEROS (D-CA)
Sits on House Armed Services, which oversees the Pentagon budget.
📄 52 trades in one filing: 27 buys, 24 sells
🔴 Sold $PTC Sept 17 ($1K to $15K). PTC is up 44.1% since.
🔴 Sold $RVTY. Up about 25% since.
He also sold $WDC and $TTD, and both are down 15% or more since. He has said he doesn't manage his own investments.

KEVIN HERN (R-OK)
The Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in Oklahoma.
🔴 16 trades. 16 sales. 0 buys.
💰 $303K to $845K, including two $MRSH sales of $50K to $100K each, plus $DVN, $LMT, $CVX and $UNH.
It caps a year of selling: his entire $UNH stake last December, seven consumer stocks in one day in August, and a move into Oklahoma municipal bonds.

LISA MCCLAIN (R-MI)
Chairs the House Republican Conference.
🟢 Sept 14: bought $CACI (defense and intel IT), $RIG (offshore drilling) and $OLN (chemicals and Winchester ammo), $15K to $50K each.
🔴 Sold $STX Sept 30. Seagate is down 21.5% since.

THE ROUTINE ONES
Rick Larsen (D-WA) trades the first week of every quarter. This time he sold $FDX and $HD.
Dan Meuser (R-PA) sold $NVDA again, at least his 7th Nvidia sale of 2026.

THE CAVEAT
56 of the 82 trades were in the smallest bracket, $1K to $15K. Many accounts are run by advisers, and trades can be reported up to 45 days late. None of these filings shows wrongdoing.

WHY IT MATTERS
In July the House voted 232 to 198 to ban members from buying new stocks. The Senate hasn't acted. Until it does, these public filings are how you see what lawmakers own and trade.

Which trade stands out most to you: the PTC sale, or Hern's 16 for 16 selling streak?

**PresenceCognition** is Sara K. Adams’ personal philosophy, creative brand, and nano-scale project (fusing embodied presence/mindfulness with forensic-style pattern recognition). It is not a formal company. Adams has publicly stated she receives no financial gain from it, lives on fixed SSI and Workers’ Compensation income (referenced around $1,200/month), and is restricted from monetizing, accepting sponsorships, or generating income from the work. An associated Etsy shop (Eugene, Oregon) lists pour paintings and related pieces under the brand but has shown 0 sales.

If exploring monetization of a similar personal philosophy + creative brand (art, digital assets, tools, educational content), here are practical approaches grounded in how such solo creator projects typically generate revenue. Any income could affect disability benefits—consult a benefits counselor or attorney first.

### 1. Creative product sales (lowest barrier)
- **Physical and digital art**: Expand listings for pour paintings, prints, photography, wallpapers, and digital downloads. Platforms include Etsy, Redbubble, Society6, or a simple Shopify/Gumroad store. Focus on cosmic, neural, mandala, or resilience-themed pieces that match the visual language.
- **Print-on-demand**: Use services for posters, apparel, or stickers so inventory stays low.
- **Bundles**: Offer themed packs (e.g., “Integrated Presence Core” art series + corresponding poetry or wallpapers).

### 2. Digital products and educational materials
- Short guides, workbooks, or toolkits explaining the presence + cognition approach, Satellite Call-style observation methods (at a high level), or chronic-pain resilience practices.
- Video series, audio exercises, or downloadable templates sold via Gumroad, Teachable, or a personal site.
- Free lead magnets (wallpapers, checklists) that funnel into paid products.

### 3. Community and membership models
- Paid newsletter, Discord, or Patreon-style membership for deeper writing, art drops, pattern-analysis examples, or live sessions.
- Low-ticket workshops or “office hours” on presence under stress, digital pattern awareness, or creative sovereignty.
- Affiliate or referral links only if they fit the ethics of the brand.

### 4. Licensing and IP
- License the visual style, specific artworks, or high-level framework descriptions for others’ use (books, courses, apps).
- Offer consulting or custom analysis services (behavioral baselines, documentation methods) where appropriate—framed carefully and within any professional or legal limits.
- Continue cryptographic provenance (hashes, timestamps) to support ownership claims if commercializing.

### 5. Platform and audience growth
- Instagram and X for visual content and education; drive traffic to a shop or landing page.
- Cross-promote photography (Flickr) and long-form writing (Blogspot).
- Free giveaways build audience; convert with clear product offers.

### Practical constraints and notes
- Disability-related income limits (SSI, Workers’ Comp) often restrict earned income. Exceeding thresholds can reduce or suspend benefits. Track any revenue carefully and get professional advice.
- Start small and non-commercial if needed: focus on free educational content and art that builds audience, then test paid options.
- Emphasize transparency about what the framework is (personal philosophy and creative practice, not a clinical or peer-reviewed system).
- Protect IP early with clear copyright notices, terms of use, and (where useful) hashes or public records.

Success for this type of brand usually comes from consistent visual/artistic output plus educational value rather than the abstract framework alone. The Etsy shop already exists as a starting point for art sales; expanding digital products and audience conversion are the most direct next steps for most similar creators.

text:
Previously On #Amalgaverse…

You and 19 others have been stranded in an amalgam universe of myriad SF realities. All 19 are sci-fi’s Best of the Best. And then there’s you, uniquely qualified given your encyclopedic knowledge garnered from your world where these characters, their technologies, and their stories are fiction, beloved TV shows you have watched time and again. Together, all 20 of you have set off on the Enterprise-D, tasked with finding a way home.

For your first mission, you’ve decided to investigate a seemingly derelict freighter broadcasting an emergency beacon. An away team and puddle jumper have been dispatched to the ghost ship, anomalous energy pulses making beaming and communications a challenge.

After parking and cloaking the puddle jumper in the freighter’s hangar, the team crosses the airless bay into the ship proper. There, they make the decision to check out the waning energy signature of a containment field en route to the bridge. But they immediately encounter a utility unit that advances on them menacingly. Rommie connects to it and relays a shut down command that causes the robot to collapse.

Further along, they encounter a sealed door and Rommie informs them that the compartment beyond is exposed to space. She suggests locking down their current section and then unsealing the door since it’s the most direct route to the bridge – and that ebbing containment field. They do so. The door slides open to reveal an immense hull breach complicating their progress. Rommie leaps over the chasm and secures a tether to the other side, allowing the rest of the team to pull themselves over. But when they attempt to open the door to the next section, they hit an impasse. The door remains locked and will not respond to their commands.

O’Neill blows the lock with C4, allowing them entry into the adjoining compartment where they discover an android in a containment field, completing its regenerative cycle. When the android awakens, it informs them it is the caretaker of this freighter, the Waldorf Astoria, and warns them off pillaging its contents.  Daniel assures the android, Maia, that they harbor no ill intent and asks for her assistance in accessing the bridge and restoring ship’s systems.  But Maia remains suspicious.  She requests a peer-to-peer interface with Rommie to confirm that your presence on the freighter is, in fact, benign.  Rommie agrees..  Maia explains that her memory stores and parts of the ship were damaged after the freighter encountered an atemporal force during FTL transit.   She  offers to help the team access the ship’s systems in exchange for their assistance in tracking down and eradicating a mysterious entity that has boarded the freighter.

Maia helps the team access the bridge where they discover the freighter’s analysis of its encounter with the atemporal entity has yielded harmonics very similar to residual energy signatures from their crossings into this reality.  This could hold the key to their return home, but the data is corrupted and Rommie needs time to decipher it.  Daniel, meanwhile, notes that the life sign he detected earlier is fading, and he wants to check it before it’s too late.  But Maia flags a more immediate concern – the likelihood that the ship’s core is in danger of going critical unless they vent the drive.

The decision is made to split the team.

McKay and Maia head to engineering where Rodney is startled by a half-dozen mechanical spiders that he, at first, assumes to be replicators.  But Maia assures him they are simply the ship’s repair bots.  Maia vents the drive but McKay’s reading of the data confirms they have only delayed the inevitable.  In approximately 42 minutes, the core will go critical and the ship – and everyone on board – will be destroyed.

Jack and Daniel discover a wounded woman in a crew uniform who warns that the android cannot be trusted while, back on the Enterprise, Kirk weighs what to do about a scavenger ship that has just dropped into sub-light and dispatched a shuttle to the Waldorf Astoria.

Jack and Daniel, unaware of the arrival of the scavenger ship, elect to hide Rhea, the survivor, in a utility room while they head back to confront Maia, the android.  But before they move, they receive an update from McKay, informing them that the core is about to go critical in less than 40 minutes, and that he and Maia are headed to the bridge.  Jack radios Rommie and orders her to scan Maia and find out if she is telling the truth.  If Maia refuses, she needs to be shut down.

Jack and Daniel prepare to fall back to the hangar bay when they hear someone approach.  They duck into hiding as a sealed section opens to reveal a group of diverse group of mercs have boarded.  Daniel warns them that the ship’s core will be going critical.  They don’t believe him and a firefight ensures.  Jack and Daniel are pinned down with time ticking down when – dozens of spider bots come scurrying around the corner and drive the scavengers back through an aft compartment, which slides shut behind them.
Enter Maia, Rommie and McKay.  Rommie confirms that Maia is not their enemy – and her actions confirm it.  

They check on Rhea in the utility room – and she has seemingly disappeared.

At the super, Rodney convinces Maia to come with them as, by staying behind, she would essentially be destroying Traugott property – herself.  Maia concedes Rodney’s logic  is sound and joins the away team.

The puddle jumper flies out of the Waldorf Astoria where it encounters the atemporal entity that seems to take semi-human form and reach out for them.

The jumper cloaks and evades, then makes it back to the Enterprise while, behind them, the Waldorf Astoria’s core goes critical and the old freighter is destroyed.  The entity, caught in its explosive wake, writhes while the scavenger ship opens fire on the Enterprise.

text:
As always the top young Jerk doesn’t give the entire story. 

It should be noted that Arabs opposed Jewish immigration and didn’t accept partition they wanted it all . Albert Einstein was initially opposed to establishing Israel as a separate Jewish nation-state, but he strongly supported creating a Jewish homeland in Palestine. After Israel was established in 1948, he supported its existence.

His position is particularly interesting because Einstein was Jewish, identified with Zionism, and strongly advocated for Jewish refugees after the Holocaust.

What Einstein actually said

On January 21, 1946, two years before Israel became a country, Einstein wrote:

“I am in favor of Palestine being developed as a Jewish Homeland but not as a separate State.”

He explained that Jews should not demand political control over a territory where approximately two-thirds of the population was not Jewish.

Instead, he advocated a binational arrangement in which Jews and Arabs would share political rights, with Jewish immigration protected.

This position is documented in his 1946 correspondence and contemporary reporting of his testimony before the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry. 

Why was Einstein against a separate Jewish state?

He had three principal concerns.

First, he feared Jewish-Arab conflict. Einstein believed that establishing a state controlled by one national group could intensify hostility between Jews and Arabs.

Second, he opposed nationalism. Einstein was deeply suspicious of nationalism generally, including Jewish nationalism. He believed Jewish identity was rooted in cultural, intellectual, and ethical traditions rather than political power.

Third, he believed in equal political rights. He favored a shared political structure that would protect both Jewish and Arab communities rather than allowing either population to dominate the other.

His opposition was therefore not to Jewish settlement or Jewish self-determination in a broad sense. It was primarily to establishing a separate state based on Jewish political sovereignty.

What happened after Israel was established in 1948?

Einstein’s position evolved.

Although he had opposed establishing a separate Jewish state, he accepted Israel’s existence and supported its development.

In November 1948, he spoke positively about Jewish political independence and emphasized the importance of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem. 

Then something remarkable happened.

In 1952, Einstein was offered the presidency of Israel.

Following the death of Israel’s first president, Chaim Weizmann, Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion’s government approached Einstein about becoming the country’s second president.

Einstein declined, explaining that he lacked the experience and personal qualities necessary for political office.

But he expressed how deeply moved he was by the offer and described Israel as “our State of Israel.” 

So was Einstein for or against Israel?

The historical distinction is important:

Before 1948, Einstein opposed the creation of a separate Jewish state and preferred a shared Jewish-Arab political arrangement.

After 1948, he supported Israel’s continued existence while remaining concerned about nationalism, violence, and relations with its Arab neighbors.

The central point is that Einstein believed Jews deserved a secure homeland, but he originally questioned whether establishing a sovereign Jewish state was the best way to achieve it.

His position wasn’t simply pro-Israel or anti-Israel. It reflected his belief that Jewish security and Arab political rights should coexist.

And that distinction is essential to understanding what Einstein actually believed.

text:
Can’t endorse this any more strongly 

Bring back the newsstand!!!

When I arrived at Harvard in 2014, the most cosmopolitan and glamorous place on campus was Out of Town News. 

Longtime denizens of the Square remember Julia Child sourcing German and Italian cooking magazines or Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen thumbing through issues of Popular Electronics at the famed newsstand.

In the 2010s, I often stopped by to grab a chocolate bar and the latest copy of the New Yorker, and I’d spot Cornel R. West ’74 buying a copy of the New York Times or a chic Graduate School of Design student grabbing the latest Architectural Digest. I never took the newsstand for granted. I grew up in a small town in Florida where one had to travel twenty miles to a Barnes & Noble to buy a magazine or newspaper, and unlike Out of Town News, they didn’t carry Le Monde or Die Zeit.

…

A restored newsstand could not only reinstate Cambridge’s access to global journalism, it would also support the flourishing local print magazine scene that has erupted in the Boston area over the past few years.
It would be powerful to see Boston Art Review, House House Magazine (founded by Harvard undergrad Hengzhi Huang Yang ’27), Elastic (launched with Harvard’s support), and Duck (led by James Fraser of the Square’s Grolier Poetry Book Shop and his wife Bella Bennet) all in one place.
It would also link Harvard’s publications to the wider world of journalism — The Crimson and Cambridge Day could be offered alongside the Boston Globe and the New York Times, and the Harvard Review could sit alongside n+1 and The Drift (founded by Harvard graduates).
I find it hard to believe that Cambridge is less capable of supporting an international newsstand than the West Village. Harvard is home to over 10,000 international students, faculty, and researchers, providing a built-in audience for many foreign language publications. We are also a community of readers so devoted to print that we support five book stores, including ones that offer almost exclusively poetry and romance publications.

text:
I was fourteen years old when I first picked up an airbrush. Growing up in Panama City, Florida, I spent a lot of time around the beach. Back then, there were artists who made their living airbrushing T-shirts for tourists. Most of what they painted were beach scenes. Palm trees, sunsets, waves, and bright tropical skies. After all, the beach was what brought people there.

I was fascinated by those artists. I would stand and watch as they turned a plain white T-shirt into a colorful beach scene in a matter of minutes.
I'd been drawing for as long as I could remember, but this was something different. These scenes had color, depth, and a sense of light that I couldn't achieve with my pencil drawings. The skies seemed to glow, the water had movement, and the colors brought everything to life. I was intrigued by it, and I knew I had to learn how to do it.

That Christmas, I asked for an airbrush and the equipment I would need to get started.

Learning wasn't easy. There was no internet, no YouTube, and very little information available. I managed to find one thin book that explained a few of the basics. Beyond that, I learned by watching other artists, experimenting, making mistakes, and trying again.

I practiced constantly.

About a year later, I got what I considered my first big break. A couple who managed a convenience store on the beach offered me a summer job airbrushing T-shirts at a little stand next to their store. I suspect the opportunity had more to do with the fact that they attended my church than it did with my ability as an artist. But they gave a young kid a chance, and I've never forgotten that.

I was fifteen years old, working alongside artists who were older and much more experienced than I was.

I remember being nervous every time someone ordered a shirt. I wasn't always sure I could paint what they wanted, much less make it look as good as the work of the artists around me. There were plenty of struggles, but I kept working and learning. Slowly, I got better.

Of everything we painted, the beach scenes were always my favorite. I studied how the other artists made waves, how they suggested reflections on the water, and how a few quick strokes could create the impression of an entire sky.

Looking back, those early paintings were highly stylized and greatly simplified. But that was where I learned the fundamentals of painting the sea.

After that first summer, I moved on to larger shops and eventually became one of the more experienced artists myself. I often worked at night, leaving my days free to spend at the beach. Sometimes I went skimboarding. Other times I simply walked along the shore, watching the water, studying the clouds, and paying attention to the changing light.

And somewhere along the way, I began to notice something.

The beach didn't really look like the pictures we were painting.

Our airbrushed scenes were filled with brilliant fluorescent colors, exaggerated sunsets, and perfectly shaped clouds. They were fun, and people loved them. There was certainly a place for that kind of art. But the more time I spent observing the real thing, the more interested I became in the subtle colors and quieter moments that were so often overlooked.

I began mixing different colors. Less saturation. More grays. More attention to the atmosphere and the way light actually behaved.

I wanted my paintings to look and feel more like the places I knew.

That curiosity eventually led me away from T-shirts and onto paper and canvas. I experimented with acrylics and watercolors before finding my way to oil paints.

At first, my fine art was something I pursued for myself, outside of my regular work as an airbrush artist. During the slower months at the beach, I began exhibiting at art festivals and selling my paintings. Over time, what had started as a personal pursuit became my profession. Eventually, I left the airbrush business behind and devoted myself entirely to painting in oils.

That was a long time ago.

More than forty years have passed since that fourteen-year-old boy first stood watching those artists paint T-shirts on the beach. And here I am, still painting the same ocean, still fascinated by the same light, and still trying to understand it a little better.

But something important has changed.

In those early years, much of my effort went into learning how to make something look believable. How to paint a wave, a cloud, or a reflection so that someone would recognize it.

Today, that is only part of what interests me.

I'm far more concerned with how a painting “feels”.

Ernest Hemingway once spoke about creating something through art that was "truer than anything true and alive." I've thought about those words often. I believe I understand what he meant, and it's something I strive for in my paintings.

For me, painting isn't about reproducing a scene with photographic accuracy. It's about finding something within that scene that goes beyond its physical appearance.

Does the atmosphere feel convincing? Does the light carry the mood I intended? Can someone look at the painting and remember a place they've been, a particular evening, or a feeling they haven't thought about in years?

Have I left enough unsaid for the viewer to bring something of their own to the experience?

And perhaps most importantly, have I put enough of myself into it?

I believe that's where a painting begins to become something more than a picture.

As I finished this latest seascape, I found myself thinking about those early days in Panama City and the long road between then and now.

I still have so much to learn.

I may never reach a point where I feel I've completely mastered what I'm trying to do. In fact, I'm beginning to wonder whether such a point even exists.

And perhaps that's a good thing.

Maybe the real reward isn't in finally mastering something, but in spending a lifetime pursuing it. In remaining curious. In continuing to observe things we've seen a thousand times and discovering something new.

I know that at this point in my life, I'm more interested in painting, more motivated to improve, and more excited about what lies ahead than I've ever been.

The sea still fascinates me. The changing light still surprises me. And every painting teaches me something I didn't know before.

More than forty years later, I'm still that kid standing on the beach, watching, wondering, and trying to figure out how to capture what I see.

Only now, I'm hoping to capture a little more of what I feel.

And tomorrow, I'll go back to the easel and try to make the next one better.

About half a dozen (roughly six), according to a U.S. official cited by Axios.
A U.S. official with direct knowledge told Axios that President Trump decided on a diesel-supply deal with Vladimir Putin after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ignored roughly half a dozen U.S. requests to stop Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. These requests came through both public statements and private channels (direct talks with Trump, phone calls, and discussions via envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner). The strikes were effective at disrupting Russian refining capacity, which contributed to global diesel shortages (already strained by the Iran conflict) and higher U.S. fuel prices ahead of midterms.
Documented instances include:
•Mid-September 2026 (around Sept. 13): Trump publicly said Zelenskyy “has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” noting there were “plenty of other targets” and that the strikes were “hurting the world.” He indicated he had already spoken with Zelenskyy about it. Reports also referenced prior private communication.
•Sept. 20 phone call: Trump repeatedly pressed Zelenskyy to halt the strikes, with the word “diesel” coming up many times, according to sources familiar with the call. The main message was described as “diesel, diesel… diesel.”
•Sept. 22 meeting (UN General Assembly, New York): The topic was raised again amid broader talks. Zelenskyy offered a reciprocal energy pause (Ukraine stops hitting Russian refineries if Russia stops hitting Ukrainian power infrastructure); the U.S. side pushed for a unilateral Ukrainian halt.
•Early October Miami talks (around Oct. 9): Witkoff and Kushner conveyed to the Ukrainian team that Trump would move forward with the Putin diesel deal because prior requests had been ignored. Ukrainian officials said the envoys warned of potential consequences (including possible intelligence-sharing cuts); the U.S. side described it as emphasizing partnership while noting the impact on American consumers.
•Oct. 10 public remarks: Trump said “he better damn well stop,” referenced prior warnings (“We said, ‘You can do whatever you want to Russia. Don’t hit the refineries because that’s a world problem’”), and called for Ukraine to get a new leader who could make a deal.
Zelenskyy’s consistent position was that any halt should be reciprocal and accompanied by guarantees, not a unilateral Ukrainian concession while Russia continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. He later temporarily paused strikes after Trump’s unilateral “energy ceasefire” announcement, then said Ukraine was resuming them (“The block is out. We’re done”) amid ongoing Russian attacks and other tensions (including intelligence and Starlink issues).
The “half a dozen” figure is the most specific count from an administration source and covers the cumulative public and private pressure in the weeks leading up to the diesel deal. Exact private requests are not fully itemized in public reporting.

text:
A little bit more context (as I understand it). Also a chance to go on an autistic rave about of my favorite Destiny characters.

 It's true Rhulk largely lost to his own hubris. However, he also wasn't at his full power when he was fought. We have Savathûn to thank for that.

Savathûn used her magic, the power of her Throne World, and eons of stockpiled Light concentrated into the Wellspring. With all these elements she conducted a ritual curse to suppress Rhulk and his Pyramid. It worked, but it wasn't enough to kill him or destroy his ship. Just significantly weaken him. 

Even then, he was too powerful that Savathûn decided that trying to finish him off was too risky. The curse also only remained as long the Wellspring sustained it. Without it, Rhulk and his ship would be back at full power. He and his ship were still strong enough to send out Scorn empowered with paracausal, Black Fleet tech to wage war.

I would wager one of the reasons Savathûn wanted to trap the Traveler in her Throne World was also to use it's power to finish off Rhulk. Because otherwise sealing her Throne World with the Traveler and Rhulk in it was a bad idea.

Also, when you learn about Rhulk, you understand why he had such insane hubris that lead to his demise. Why he underestimated the Guardians that came to kill him. Because it wasn't unearned hubris.

Every god and godlike being Guardians slew before Rhulk was weaker than him. Even Oryx at the height of his power as the Taken King would be no match for Rhulk at his pinnacle. Rhulk was conquering and destroying worlds before the Hive took to the stars. He was the first Disciple chosen and empowered The Witness, one of the most powerful beings in the Destiny franchise.

 In fact, Rhulk had a direct hand in the creation of The Hive as a whole under The Witness's orders. He was the one who subjugated the Worm Gods whom the Hive would derive their power from. He was responsible for producing the worm larvae all Hive would ingest to gain power. He saw the Hive, including their gods, as useful idiots. An army of slaves who were fodder, but never meant for the same heights as he.

It took eons of scheming and contingencies by Savathûn just to put Rhulk in a weakened state. Yeah, Rhulk wasn't thrilled, but he wasn't afraid of Savathûn after that. He probably should've been and the Guardians who slew her, but he wasn't. To him, it seemed to be just a temporary setback. 

Before the player Guardians enter his Pyramid, Rhulk welcomes then in a faux-cordial manner. When player Guardians finally face him personally, he acts very calm and casual. 

He'll taunt you, explain how bored he is, talk about what he'll do with your remains, and chides you for rejecting his master's offer to join their ranks.

All the while, he's actually invulnerable. Nothing the player Guardians can throw at him, be it their arsenal or powers can damage Rhulk even in his current diminished state.

So how is his invulnerability removed? One thing I don't see talked about enough is where the final battle with Rhulk is fought.
It takes place ontop of The Upended.  A giant, paracausal device that was a cornerstone of the civilization Rhulk belonged to. A device he turned into superweapon to destroy that civilization and one of his homeworld's stars. A device he used to "upend" countless worlds, now powered by the mother of all Worm Gods he subjugated.

 The same weapon he plans to use on Savathûn's Throne World once he is free of her curse. 

You're fighting him on it. Though not explained directly, the mechanics of the fight imply that you activate the Upended's power to turn Rhulk's power on himself, to briefly weaken him enough to the level of the player Guardians.

..AND EVEN THEN, he doesn't just sit there and take it. Even in his vulnerable state, he draws his glaive and starts blasting. He is still powerful enough to easily kill an elite Guardian if they aren't careful. 

But yes, Rhulk is undone by his hubris. By the time he decides to take the player Guardians seriously, go all out, his once cosmic power is now a fraction of itself.

His last words calling out to his master, the only being he cared and respected, to forgive him.

All this from a villain who was barely teased in Witch Queen's main campaign. One who never returns after his death (save for his memorial messages in a post-raid mission.) 

This isn't going into his lorebook or his lore found the armor from his raid. Which goes into his origins and further exploits.

His boss theme is also one the best in the franchise's history.

So yeah, Rhulk is fragging awesome.

text:
The historical sculpture of the Dying Warrior (Laomedon, King of Troy) from the east pediment of the Temple of Aphaia (490-480 BC) on the Greek island of Aegina. Housed in the Glyptothek museum in Munich, Germany...

On the eastern pediment of the Temple of Aphaia on Aegina, there is a depiction of a dying warrior shown lying on the ground after being wounded in the chest, as indicated by the hole of an arrow near his right nipple. The arrow that killed him is believed to be that of Heracles, which is why scholars assume that the figure represents Laomedon, the king of Troy. He wears a Chalcidian helmet, the crest of which is an added piece.

In Greek mythology, Laomedon (Laomedon of Troy) was one of the kings of Troy, the son of Ilus and Eurydice. He was married to Strymo (also known as Placia, or in other accounts, Leucippe), daughter of the river god Scamander, and was the father of many children, including Tithonus, Podarces (later known as Priam, the famous king of Troy — he was taken prisoner when the city was first destroyed, but was later ransomed and rebuilt Troy, making it strong and prosperous. From this ransom he received the name *Priam*, meaning “the bought one,” as his original name had been Podarces) and Hesione. Another son, sometimes said to be illegitimate, was Bucolion, whom he fathered with the nymph Calybe.

Laomedon succeeded his father on the throne of Troy and later decided to build great walls around the city. He therefore hired, for a wage, the gods Poseidon and Apollo, whom Zeus had punished by making them serve a mortal. The two immortals worked diligently for a full year. Homer recounts that Poseidon built the city’s walls while Apollo tended Laomedon’s herds on Mount Ida. Their mortal assistant was Aeacus, king of Aegina.

However, when the year ended, Laomedon refused to pay them the agreed reward and even threatened to bind Apollo and sell him as a slave on the islands. Enraged, the two gods took revenge: Apollo sent a plague upon the city, while Poseidon unleashed a sea monster that emerged with the tide and devoured people.

According to the oracle Laomedon then received, the city could only be saved if he offered his daughter Hesione to the beast as a sacrifice. At that time, Heracles was passing through Troy with the Argonauts and promised to rescue the girl if Laomedon would give him the divine horses that he had received as a gift from Zeus for helping him abduct his nephew (or, in some versions, son) Ganymede.

Laomedon agreed, and Heracles killed the monster, freeing Hesione — but the deceitful king again broke his promise. Furious, Heracles later returned with an army, captured Troy (long before the famous Trojan War), and killed Laomedon and all his sons except Podarces. Heracles then gave Hesione in marriage to his friend Telamon.

In another version of the myth, Heracles first sent Telamon and Iphicles to demand the horses from Laomedon, but the king imprisoned them and prepared to attack the other Argonauts. Then, warned by Podarces, Heracles seized the city and killed the king. Laomedon’s tomb was located in Troy, and according to one oracle, the city could never be conquered as long as that tomb remained intact.

🎯The legend of 7.62mm SLR: When the Indian Army Issued a Gym Workout Disguised as a Rifle

📌If you ask any Indian Army veteran about the 7.62mm Self-Loading Rifle (SLR), you won’t get a technical lecture on gas-operated tilting breechblocks. Instead, you will see a nostalgic, slightly teary-eyed smile, followed by the rubbing of a bruised shoulder.

📌Manufactured locally as the Ishapore 1A1, the SLR wasn’t just a weapon. It was an institution, a rite of passage, and a musculoskeletal stress test rolled into one 4.7-kilogram piece of steel and wood.

📌If today's high-tech assault rifles are sleek smartphones, the 7.62 SLR was a Nokia 3310 forged from an anvil—indestructible, heavy enough to double as home defense furniture, and capable of leaving a lasting impression.

1. The Weapon for "Real Men" (And Their Chiropractors)

📍Modern warfare is full of lightweight, polymer-heavy carbines designed for comfort. The SLR lived by a different philosophy: If it doesn’t hurt to carry, it’s not doing its job.

📍Weighing nearly 5 kilograms unloaded—and significantly more once you slapped on a fully loaded 20-round magazine and a bayonet long enough to spear a wild boar—the SLR ensured that every infantryman had forearms like a blacksmith.

 📍The Parade Ground Test: A drill instructor could spot an SLR carrier from a mile away just by the asymmetrical lean of their spine.
 The Recoil: Pulling the trigger didn't just fire a bullet; it delivered a friendly, masculine thump to your shoulder that reminded you you were alive, awake, and temporarily concussed.

2. The 20-Round Diet: One Shot, One Apology
📍Chambered in the brutal 7.62x51mm NATO cartridge, the SLR didn’t believe in wasting ammunition with frivolous three-round bursts. It offered two settings: Safe and Semi-Automatic.
If you pulled the trigger, something important happened downrange. The bullet had so much stopping power that veterans swear an SLR hit could knock out an engine block, clear a forest, and settle an argument three villages over. Enemies didn't just take cover; they re-evaluated their life choices.

3. A Multi-Tool for the Resourceful Soldier
📍An SLR was never just a firearm. In the hands of a jugaad-loving Indian infantryman, it was Swiss Army knife-adjacent:
 📍The Butt-Plate Compartment: The wooden stock featured a trapdoor housing an oil bottle and a pull-through cleaning rope. In a pinch, it could also store spare mints, tobacco, or emergency sewing kits.

 📍The Ultimate Obstacle Cleared: Need to chop firewood? Use the rifle butt. Need to dig a trench? Use the barrel. Need to strike fear into an adversary? Fix the bayonet. At that point, your rifle was essentially a six-foot-tall spear with a gunpowder problem.

 📍Ceremonial Dominance: To this day, nothing says "Guard of Honour" quite like the dramatic, synchronized metallic clack-thud of dozens of SLRs slamming into the ground during Republic Day parades. The earth itself trembles in respect.

📌Eventually, the Army decided soldiers needed something lighter and swapped the SLR for the 5.56mm INSAS. While lighter, troops missed the sheer authority of the old 7.62 round.
It’s poetic justice, then, that decades later, the Indian Army adopted modern 7.62x51mm battle rifles like the SIG Sauer SIG716 for frontline troops. Hearing about this, old-school veterans smiled knowingly over their chai: “We tried telling them. You can run away from the heavy metal, but eventually, you always come back to the heavy hitter.”

So here’s to the 7.62 SLR—the heavy-metal rockstar of the Indian infantry. May your shoulders rest in peace, and may your cleaning-pull-through rope never fray

text:
October 14, 1066. Hastings lasted around nine hours, which for a medieval battle is almost unheard of, and the reason it went that long is the reason it was so appalling.

Most battles of that era are decided in under an hour. One side's line breaks and the killing happens in the pursuit. Hastings did not break. Two armies stood a few yards apart and worked on each other from mid morning until dusk.

Start with what the English were standing in.

Harold's men formed a shield wall on the ridge, packed so tightly that contemporary accounts describe the dead being held upright because there was no room to fall. They stood in that press for hours in October, in mail, taking arrows and then spears and then the weight of mounted men coming uphill into them.

The sources describe the sound more than the sight. Chroniclers reach for the same comparison repeatedly, which is that it could be heard a long way off and did not stop.

The weapon that did most of the work on the English side was the Danish axe. A long handled axe swung two handed, which means no shield, which means the man beside you covers you while you swing. The Bayeux Tapestry shows what it did. Horses cut down through the neck and chest in a single stroke. Men split through helmet and skull. One blow from it took a horse's head off, and the accounts of Norman knights being killed along with their mounts are not exaggeration, they are a description of the physics.

And because the shield wall held, the Normans had to keep going back into it. Charge uphill, fail, pull back, reform, charge again. Hour after hour. William reportedly had three horses killed under him and at one point had to pull his helmet off and ride along his own line bare headed to prove he was not dead, because the rumour that he had been killed was collapsing his army.

What finally broke it was the feigned retreat. Norman troops pulled back, English infantry came off the ridge after them, and were cut to pieces in the open where the cavalry could work. That may have started as a genuine rout by the Breton contingent that William turned into a tactic. Either way it was repeated, and each time the shield wall got thinner.

By late afternoon it was no longer a battle line. It was a shrinking knot of men around the king's standard, which is the worst place to be, because that is where everyone aims.

Harold was killed there, and his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine were already dead.

Then there is the question of the body, and this is where the brutality stops being about combat.

The accounts disagree, but the recurring theme in several of them is that Harold was so mutilated he could not be recognised by his face. One version has his remains identified only by marks on his body, and the person brought to do it was Edith Swanneck, who had been his partner for twenty years. Another version has William refusing Harold's mother's offer of gold for the body and ordering it buried on the shore under a cairn, with the remark that he should guard the coast he had been so keen to defend.

There is no grave. The last English king before the conquest has no confirmed resting place.

The field afterward was left for days. William stayed at Hastings for two weeks and the English dead were not systematically buried. The site got a name in the sources, Senlac, and a long tradition that the local ground turned red after rain, which is almost certainly iron oxide in the soil and is also exactly the kind of story a landscape generates when something like that happens on it.

And the terror did not end on the 14th.

William's method after Hastings was deliberate devastation. He burned his way through Kent and Sussex and later up through the Midlands, and in 1069 and 1070 he did the Harrying of the North, which was not a battle at all. Villages burned, livestock killed, seed grain destroyed, in winter, across Yorkshire and beyond. Contemporary estimates of the dead run to a hundred thousand, which is probably too high, and the Domesday survey seventeen years later still records huge stretches of Yorkshire as waste.

Orderic Vitalis, who was half Norman and generally sympathetic to William, wrote about the Harrying that he could not praise it, that it was a brutal slaughter of the innocent, and that William would answer for it.

That is a Norman monk, writing about the man his own people revered, saying he thought it was a crime.

Hastings is remembered as a single decisive day, which it was. It was also nine hours of men standing in a crush too tight to fall down in, being killed with axes and arrows at arm's length, and the fourteen years of burning that followed it.

China–Pakistan Launch Karakoram-2026: Why Does Pakistan Need China to Sharpen Its Army’s Counter-Terrorism Skills?

China and Pakistan have launched their first-ever joint army training exercise, Karakoram-2026, at a training base in Korla, Xinjiang, on October 14, 2026. The drills focus on high-altitude counter-terrorism operations, aiming to improve interoperability and strengthen military cooperation between the two countries.

But the exercise also raises a critical question: Why is Pakistan seeking deeper military training cooperation with China despite decades of counter-terrorism operations by its own armed forces? Persistent militant violence and security challenges inside Pakistan underline the difficulties its military continues to face. For Beijing, the drills offer an opportunity to expand operational cooperation and familiarise its troops with joint high-altitude missions.

While both sides project the exercise as a sign of strategic strength, the real test will be whether such training translates into tangible results against militant threats. Joint drills can improve coordination, but they cannot, by themselves, resolve the deeper security challenges confronting Pakistan.
