text:
🎙️Diesel, big war and SVO in the humanitarian sphere (Escalation)🎙️

Alexander Dugin

Interviewer: Let’s talk about the “energy truce” between Russia and Ukraine that Trump has announced — though, so far, he has declared it alone. Journalists from Axios have already asked Trump himself what he means, and it seems that Ukraine now cannot strike Russian refineries, but also Russia to strike Ukrainian oil refineries. But in Ukraine there is a nuance: they have a refinery as such already and not, there is hardly one left, and he does not really work.

How do we look at this situation and what is really happening after this “diesel deal” of Trump, as well as after his harsh statements that elections should be held in Ukraine, since Zelensky is non-negotiable and does not want to stop the confrontation, although he could have done it for a long time or at least agree with our demands? How will we describe this whole design?

Alexander Dugin: It is necessary to clearly understand why Trump right now decided to touch, promote and highlight this topic. The fact is that on the nose the midterm elections to Congress, where Republicans are highly likely to lose a majority in the House of Representatives, and perhaps even in the Senate. In such a case, Trump in the full sense of the word turns into a “lame duck” – a leader who is critically dependent on the opposition democratic majority. And the Democrats are committed to his course uncompromisingly: they will seek not only to strain him and impose obligations, but also to try to criminalize both his past steps and himself.

The situation for Trump is extremely unfavorable. In the electoral agenda, a sharp jump in diesel prices played a huge role - it has risen in price very significantly. The Americans are purely practical, and the war with Iran is absolutely not interesting, they oppose it. There is a paradox: Trump is trying to claim what he is good that he helped Israel and fights Iran, but the American layman is alien. And here also the increase in the price of diesel, which became the main trump card in the hands of his opponents – including internal critics in the ranks of the Republicans themselves. They say openly: “We warned that we should not get involved in the conflict with Iran. You went on about Israel, the diesel took off, and now you're losing the election.'

And now Trump, thinking purely as a pragmatic businessman, sees that the debit with the loan does not converge: instead of the plus, it turns out a fat minus that threatens political bankruptcy. He is convulsively looking for a way to lower the price of diesel. In other ways, it does not come out: the Iranian factor is blocked, Iran controls the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis are Bab el-Mandeb, which means that prices alone will not fall. Diesel in the market is sorely lacking. And then he offers a purely situational solution: if Russia has diesel, let's take a step towards it, and we will deal with the rest later, after the elections. It's a situation manager's reactive behavior without a long-term strategy. If he manages to bring down the price of fuel, he will write it in an asset; if Kiev obeys him, he will say that he has arranged an “energy truce”. Although no one seriously believes in its peacekeeping potential. He's playing short.

At the same time, it is obvious that the main catch for any truce is in Kiev. After the Anchorage summit, Trump never bothered Zelensky and did not force him to accept the conditions, because all of the collective Europe and American Democrats stood behind the Kiev regime. The part of the West, which is aimed at war with us and Russia's strategic defeat, simply blocked the Trump initiatives. They directly conveyed to Zelensky: “Don’t worry, Trump is left for a short time, after the midterm elections we will tie him on his hands and feet, so keep and do not go to him on the occasion.” Kaba Trump really showed hard will, he could insist on his and then. But for him it was never a priority, although internally he was certainly inclined to freeze this conflict.

For Trump, Russia is not the main enemy – unlike the European Union, the European leadership of NATO and American globalist democrats. His primary opponent is Iran, as Trump has unreservedly fit into the Israeli foreign policy line and China’s main strategic opponent. In addition to this, the establishment of total control over the Western Hemisphere, over Latin America, which, unfortunately for Latin Americans, is quite good.

Since Trump seriously does not consider Russia an enemy number one, he does not care. But at the same time to fight for our interests or for peace it too is not going and under external pressure easily surrenders its positions. In this sense, Trump is an extremely unreliable ally for us: ideologically, politically, and even tactically.

However, when he offered a deal on diesel, it was perfectly correct for us to say, "Please, diesel is so diesel, no problem." To support this conflict between Trump and the rest of the West, as well as between Trump and Kiev, is an absolutely logical and winning step for us on a short circuit. We sell fuel anyway, and sell it to Trump or Europe is the right pragmatic move.

The only thing we need to understand clearly is:

It's not for long. Trump himself, even if he works, instantly forgets everything and refuses to agree on the first change of the market.
Trump does not control Kiev. Zelensky simply sends him, saying through the press: "You don't understand anything, you are a temporary, your time is gone. We will hold you back a little, and after the election, everything will return to normal – as under Biden and how the European Union wants.

Zelensky is pulling time and is not going to any negotiations exactly because he sees a deep split in the West. He understands that Trump is far from all-powerful and represents only a temporary factor. We rightly punish Zelensky in our rhetoric, calling him a scumbag and an illegitimate dictator. But he is not an independent figure, he is only a function and a part of the Western system. And we are fighting not with him personally, but with the collective West, in which Trump is only one of the elements.

Trump's line is very slightly different from that of other globalists. I want to emphasize: it is small. Trump is not at all for multipolarity or peace. He also declared war on the BRICS and tries to undermine any independent centers of power. Just his main blow is directed against China, and in the Middle East policy he completely blindly follows Israel.

In its system of priorities Russia is somewhere in the sixth or seventh place. Probably, he would like Russia not to be at all, but now it is not his first task. And on a very narrow time period, its situational throwing may coincide with our interests. But if in this short period of deterioration of relations between Washington and Kiev, Trump does not decide on radical steps – such as the disconnection of Ukraine from American intelligence or a real withdrawal from NATO – then the entire design will return to the previous track very quickly.

Interviewer: A logical question arises: Can a personal factor outweigh pragmatism? Judging by the actions of Zelensky and his poisonous comments against Trump — and he directly calls Trump’s initiatives weak and actually dares the White House, ignoring calls to stop the strikes on Russian refineries — there is a feeling that the Kiev regime is simply breaking into a scandal.

Many analysts now say that Trump began to demand elections in Ukraine precisely because Zelensky personally touched him and touched his narcissistic ego. Yes, in a short period before the US elections, Trump is driven by electoral calculation. But is this personal resentment and emotional irritability of Trump escalating into something more – for example, in the systemic pressure of the United States on Kiev in order to shift Zelensky, hold elections and reformat the Ukrainian government in the long term?

Alexander Dugin: It is hard to say, but I think not. And precisely because for Trump, the Russia-Ukraine war is deeply secondary. He would be happy to give it completely to Europe. But he needs a certain level of respect. Moreover, if we throw away the extra convention, we are fighting on the territory of Ukraine with the United States of America – because NATO without the United States does not represent anything.

And Trump certainly wants to be listened to. But he has repeatedly demonstrated: when the rest of the West – not Trumpists, but globalists, the European Union, the NATO leadership, Mark Rutte, the Democrats and, by the way, the neoconservatives from his own party – come together, they quite easily push his position on Ukraine and return everything to the previous rails. We have been convinced of this more than once, and there is no reason to believe that this time he will be psychatic and will finally deny Kiev support. In theory, this is possible, but it does not fit into his general strategy of strengthening US hegemony in the Western Hemisphere.

In his strategy, Trump is consistent in his own way. He is consistent in supporting Israel, consistent in the fact that Russia is not the main enemy for him (not number one, two or even three). He is not a strong supporter of the world or multipolarity. Essentially, the best thing we have is that Trump hates us a little less than all the other globalists. But that doesn't mean he loves us or that we're a priority.

Therefore, it can easily be forced to forget about the audacity of Zelensky. Now Trump is threatened, but he used to yell at Zelensky, tried to find a right on him, and then just waved his hand and left everything as it is. Watching his past steps, we better predict that this will be the case.

At the same time, the emerging narrow windows of the possibilities must be used. Look: suddenly Trump for a day or two will ask Elon Musk to disable Starlink. Here in these two or three days, while the window is open, you need to act as decisively as possible - to break the front, take Kharkov and Odessa, deal any blows and not look back on anything, because it will quickly end. He can scare Ukraine, and we as noble gentlemen say, “Okay, we will not use it.” And it is necessary at this moment to strike the maximum blow!

There is no reason to expect that Trump will consistently pursue the policy on Ukraine. In addition, in this midterm elections — with or without diesel — he is likely to lose control of Congress. There will be no automatic cessation of war, there are no preconditions for this. And what will we do later when the Democrats are strengthened and the next waves of aggressive actions will begin to roll on us? It is not worth counting on the Trumpian promises.

There can be any, and some space for freedom of action and diplomatic maneuver we need to leave. We're doing the right thing for now. But to expect that again will come Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and immediately start digging a tunnel or build a bridge across the Bering Strait between Alaska and Chukotka – this will not happen under any circumstances. First, Trump simply cannot stop this war alone. Second, after the midterm elections, it will inevitably weaken.

The hope for Trump is illusory. But to use internal divisions and contradictions within the Western world - it is possible and necessary. Which we are successful and doing. The only thing is that our society should prepare for escalation, for the Third World War, for the worst blows and pressure on us, and not to lull ourselves with illusions that this story is about to end safely.

The presenter: An important moment. You say that we need to support this division. And to what stage? What exactly do we want to achieve ideally? What should this final look like – a direct military or economic clash between Europe and the United States, a full-fledged collapse of NATO with the denunciation of documents or something else?

Alexander Dugin: It would be excellent both. The civil war in the West, the tough conflict between Republicans and Democrats in the United States, the direct confrontation between Trump and Europe – because the American Democrats just support the European globalists and, in fact, brought these leaders to power in the EU. We benefit from the conflict between the United States and Israel, the conflict between the United States and Europe, the conflict between the UK and the European Union.

We need absolutely all the fault lines of the West. In the West today, as we have said many times in our program, there are five key centers: the United States, globalists, the British, continental Europe and Israel. Ultimately, they all act in order to preserve and strengthen a unipolar world, but in different ways and with different hierarchies of priorities. And if they all quarreled among themselves, quarreled, and even better – they got into a real confrontation, for example, Trump for Greenland with Denmark and the European Union or Canada with the United States, it would be perfect.

Of course, our opportunities to influence this are not so grandiose. But if we have at least the slightest chance and a small diplomatic gap to facilitate these processes, we must use it. Our fundamental task is to achieve the weakening of the West, its fragmentation, dismemberment and, ultimately, its strategic defeat.

The direct conflict with the West is dangerous because it will immediately escalate into a nuclear war with all the attendant consequences. This will finally bring down the last deterrent mechanisms left over from the Yalta world. Now everything is based solely on the fear of nuclear weapons, which prevents global destruction.

Therefore, everything that is before a direct nuclear confrontation, we must use to the maximum. It is time for us to completely forget the illusion that they are our “partners” or that one of them is “good” and that someone is “bad.” All these poles are our opponents, but the degree of their aggressiveness varies. For example, Israel is not directly aggressive against Russia. So, we must build our hierarchy. Our most direct, sworn and frantic enemies today are the European Union, the British and the American globalists. Trump and Israel are less: they are also opponents, but not priorities.

Here between them we need to filigreely navigate, and to do it as proactively and offensively as possible.

The moderator: Here it turns out an interesting picture. It turns out that even in the current situation, the conclusion by us of any — even the most local — agreement with the United States in itself drives a wedge between Europe and the United States. Does this mean that we need to continue to make every effort to make new deals with Washington in order to pull it away from Europe? Should we consciously take such steps?

Alexander Dugin: Absolutely right. Exactly like that. The only thing you understand, we should be masking not in relation to our own society, but outwardly in relation to external players.

We're doing the opposite. Look: it is only necessary to talk about the conclusion of a contract on diesel, as the patriotic camp immediately raises a wave of indignation. How can we supply the enemy with energy and fuel? As if in 1942 the Soviet Union would supply oil to Hitler simply because it is hard to fight with us. For them, it looks unthinkable, although historical and geopolitical contexts are completely incomparable.

On the other hand, the liberals are connected, who are gleefully caught: “Well, finally! Let us freeze, let us go under Trump's conditions, make concessions on the line of contact and territorial issues. This is the window of opportunity!”

Both are deeply wrong. I am inclined to think that many nuances of foreign policy on the internal audience are simply not necessary. The president is working, and fine. Why would he interfere? And he is hindered by: both patriots who do not understand the full depth of the strategic maneuver, and liberals, who inflate any factor of negotiations to readiness for surrender, which is absolutely detrimental to the country.

As a result, we, trying to support the President as his convinced supporters and geopolitically responsible people, are forced to speak publicly about things that may not be worth to broadcast to the general public at all. Let Vladimir Vladimirovich quietly engage in this external strategy, and the people would at this time watch the ballet "Swan Lake" or cartoons - and it would be only for the benefit.

In internal problems - yes, it is necessary to involve society. Questions of how to equip the economy, education, social sphere - here civil participation is necessary. But as for foreign policy, let’s finally free people from these constant psychological stresses. From the experiences of Anchorage, the trips of Kirill Dmitrieva, visits of Uitkoff and Kushner, etc.

Let them come, let Dmitriev fly to Miami, let the diesel trade go - but it is not necessary to cry about it on every corner and make a media show out of it. Foreign policy is not a matter for the everyman. An ordinary citizen, due to the absence of the full picture, will still make an erroneous conclusion. Let us trust this to professionals, patriots and personally to the President. He needs to untie his hands. And at us and patriots, and liberals from different sides try to emphatically and informationally blackmail.

Let's give up this vicious practice. The president understands everything perfectly, he is at the top of the awareness, and we delegated to him the full power. Let him deal with it. But save the society, Comrade President, from this constant swing on psychological-emotional swing. Do what is necessary for the country – you will do everything right and lead the country to Victory. And we will not disturb, but we will only help.

Interrogator: Alexander Gelevich, here came a new statement by Zelensky: he absolutely seriously wonders why the United States does not conclude an agreement on the supply of diesel fuel with Ukraine, because “it is Kiev that decides whether Russian refineries will work and whether the Russian tanker fleet is running.” Is the man okay? What do such statements show?

Alexander Dugin: Everything is fine with him. It is not necessary to overestimate his addiction to illicit drugs in the Russian Federation. In fact, Zelensky is simply consistently betting on the enormous power in the West, which is not just equal to Trump, but objectively stronger. This is the deepest state. Trump in due time declared war on him, but could not win.

The Western political system is radically different than ours. There, not everything depends on the personality of the leader, and often nothing. Western presidents are, in fact, actors on stage. We have real power in the hands of the ruler, the president. They don't have that.

Therefore, Zelensky behaves quite logically and consistently: he actually sends Trump. He says to him, "Who are you, Grandpa? You've got a month or two, we'll roll over somehow. And if you try to disable us a switch or cut off the connection, you will immediately come to you dozens of generals, admirals, your own sponsors and representatives of the largest corporations and say: "Well, put the switch on the place and go to build a ballroom in the White House - this is your level."

And we have repeatedly seen in recent years that in critical matters Trump first loudly noise, writes audacious posts in social networks about what will rename the whole world to America, and then quietly does what is required of him.

Therefore, Zelensky is firmly betting on the continuation and escalation of the conflict. We, as we said above, are betting on the division of the West and on the use of any internal contradictions - and we do it absolutely right. But at the same time it is not necessary to nourish illusions, as if any long-term truce is possible. There is an inevitable escalation, and in the near future it will only increase.

Moreover, in the West, more and more often declare the need for a full-fledged hot war of high intensity between the West and Russia.

Let's understand the gradation:

The low-intensity war is what happened in the Donbass until 2022 (local skirmishes and shelling).
The medium-intensity war is what is going on right now in Ukraine.
A high-intensity war is a direct clash with the West with the partial use of nuclear weapons.

And in the West, experts and military strategists are already openly counting on how to inflict strategic defeat on Russia in the context of a high-intensity war. That's where we are, not in the illusions that Trump will shout, and Zelensky will take under the visor! The diesel deal is the right tactical move, but hoping it will lead to a global turnaround is unrealistic.

It is necessary to prepare to defend the country and to inflict strategic defeat on the enemy. The military knows that any conflict consists of two phases: wars of attrition and wars of crushing. Now between us and the West there is a war of attrition. Yes, the West is partially depleted, but we are exhausted. And they believe that while everything is going according to their plan, and at some point the war of attrition should escalate into a war of crushing – when the West considers that we are sufficiently weakened. How and what they measure it is a question for their strategists. But the transition to high-intensity war just means the transition from exhaustion to collapse.

If the prospect of war on the crushing — on the part of our enemies against us — is quite real (and today NATO leaders openly talk about it, and there is nothing to be surprised at), then we also need to think about in this paradigm. Why would we not allow the appearance of our own window of opportunity to strike a crushing blow against the enemy? This cannot be discounted.

This means that we are entering into a spiral of mutual, escalation, which we manage. We need to constantly remind the West: you can play the escalation together. This is not chess, where someone imagines that you can make a move for yourself, then “turn the board” and make a move for the enemy, again returning the move to yourself. This is how the West is used to playing with us, imagining that a non-serious subject is sitting opposite them.

But opposite them sits the great grandmaster – our President Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin. By the way, taking this opportunity, although I have already congratulated him in my channel, as well as the whole country, I would like to congratulate him once again on his birthday. Our grandmaster is well aware of all this. He understands that at some critical moment we may indeed need to carry out a large-scale operation to crush our enemy. And we must be absolutely ready for what will come in response not what is coming now, but something immeasurably more serious.

It is in this consciousness—consciousness, fully immersed in the process of profound escalation of our relations with the West—that we must live. This is the only right approach. When we truly realize the seriousness of the current moment, we will begin to behave much more discreetly and responsibly.

Sometimes there are some characters who say, “We want to lead the patriotic opposition to the president’s course.” Look, during the war, statements like this are not just stupid, it's a military rebellion! There should be no opposition. Our entire country, our entire people — both right and left, however much we diverge in detail — must now be monolitically united for the unconditional support of the president and the warring country.

And the country, I will repeat, on the threshold of transition. We are moving from a medium-intensity war to a high-intensity war. Ahead is a possible operation to crush. The military is well aware of what it means. This is how we need to soberly assess our situation, this is how we plan the future and clearly understand: we do not have to count on relaxation, rest and “vacation” in the near future.

text:
📕The world egg and the twilight of modern man📕

Mauro Cardone
From the Dissolution of the Individual to the Return of Civilisations: Guénon, Dugin, and the Metaphysical Dimension of the Emerging World Order.

The West is discovering that it may lose the world at the very moment it claims the power to remake man. It raised the individual to the status of the universal measure of existence, progressively emancipating him from belonging, spiritual hierarchies, community and transcendence, only to find itself facing a creature that modernity itself now considers inadequate. Man, having been proclaimed sovereign over himself, is today disassembled into data, behaviours, preferences and functions, while technology promises to overcome his biological limits and artificial intelligence begins to contest prerogatives that once seemed inseparable from his nature. At the same time, an international order founded upon the universalisation of the Western model encounters the resistance of civilisations that claim their own understandings of man, power, time and the sacred.

These processes are generally studied in isolation. Economists speak of technological transformation, analysts of geopolitical competition, political scientists of the crisis of liberal democracy, and philosophers of posthumanism. Yet, examined in depth, they seem to belong to a single fracture: the progressive dissolution of the anthropology upon which Western modernity constructed its claim to universality.

Long before the advent of digital society, René Guénon had identified the paradoxical character of this process. In The Reign of Quantity and the Signs of the Times, published in 1945, he describes two successive moments of the modern cycle: solidification and dissolution. The first corresponds to the progressive dominion of quantity, measurement, matter and uniformity. Everything is reduced to what can be calculated, classified and reproduced. Qualitative differences lose their meaning; human beings become statistical units, labour is separated from the work it produces, money from its symbolic function, and knowledge from the apprehension of principles. Yet just when this construction appears to have reached its greatest solidity, it begins to lose coherence. Solidification gives way to dissolution: what appeared stable disintegrates, while the barriers erected by a materialistic conception of the world reveal their fragility.

Guénon employs the image of the “fissures in the Great Wall.” A world that believed it had definitively enclosed itself within the boundaries of material reality becomes permeable once more, but the opening does not necessarily lead upwards. It may open towards the lower regions of existence, amid growing confusion between the psychic and the spiritual, manifestation and principle, simulation and authenticity. This distinction is decisive: not every crossing of a boundary is an elevation.

It is here that the symbolism of the World Egg acquires an extraordinary significance. In “The Heart and the World Egg” and “The Cave and the World Egg,” collected in Symbols of Sacred Science, Guénon explains that the Egg does not represent the cosmos in its fully manifested state, but rather the central, germinal condition from which manifestation unfolds. It contains, still enfolded and undifferentiated, the possibilities that are to be deployed. The symbol refers to the centre, the heart and the spiritual embryo; in the Hindu tradition, to Hiranyagarbha, the Golden Germ. The cave offers a corresponding image: it shelters the possibility of birth, but initiatic fulfilment ultimately requires an exit from the cave itself, a passage beyond the limits of cosmic manifestation.

It would be philologically incorrect to identify the World Egg with a historical order breaking apart. Rather, it expresses the centrality of principle and the potentiality of manifestation. Precisely for that reason, it offers a key with which to question the present: is what is losing its form merely one historical configuration of existence, or is humanity forgetting the centre from which forms receive their meaning? And do the possibilities now opening up belong to genuine regeneration, or to a further stage of dissolution?

Contemporary geopolitics rarely dares to ask such questions, having progressively abandoned inquiry into the nature of the subjects whose relations it studies. It speaks of states, economies, populations and markets as though these categories were universal givens. Yet a state is not necessarily a civilisation; a nation does not always coincide with a people; and a people is not simply the sum of individuals. Above all, the individual of liberal modernity does not exhaust the possible understandings of the human being.

Alexander Dugin has brought this question back into the centre of political philosophy. In his recent “Dividualism and the Ontological Turn,” published on 3 October 2026, he returns to the anthropological debate over the so-called ontological turn and challenges the persistence, even in seemingly pluralist theories, of a Western, linear conception of history. Modern humanity continues to be presented as the completed form of universal development, while different anthropological forms are relegated to the past, to the archaic or to the primitive. Dugin therefore introduces the category of “alter-humans”: people belonging to different civilisations who are not remnants of an unfinished humanity but expressions of other configurations of existence.

The reference to the dividual is particularly fertile. McKim Marriott had used the concept in his studies of India before Marilyn Strathern made it central to Melanesian anthropology. From these perspectives, a person is not necessarily a self-sufficient entity that enters into relationships with others only afterwards. Personhood can be conceived as constituted by the relations, exchanges, forms of belonging and continuities that make it what it is. The anthropological distinction should not be hardened into an absolute opposition between an individualist West and a communal rest of the world; specialists themselves debate its limits. Dugin nevertheless takes a further, properly philosophical and political step: if there is no single ontology of the person, why should there be only one universal model for organising society?

This question touches the very core of the Fourth Political Theory and Noomakhia. The plurality of civilisations is no longer conceived as a mere variety of customs within a single historical trajectory. It refers to different Logoi, different ways of understanding being, time, the sacred and the relationship between man and cosmos. Multipolarity thus becomes something far more demanding than the redistribution of influence among great powers. It requires recognition of a plurality of historical and spiritual worlds, each possessing its own legitimacy to exist.

We can therefore understand why Dugin traces the crisis of the West, in part, to the medieval dispute over universals. In his thought, nominalism, by denying ontological reality to universals, prepares a long transformation leading to social atomism, individualism and the rise of liberalism. As an exclusive historiographical explanation of modernity this genealogy is contested; nevertheless, its internal coherence cannot be dismissed as mere medieval nostalgia. It suggests that the West gradually replaced a qualitative and hierarchical conception of being with a universe of separate, measurable units available for use. The world of quantity described by Guénon thus encounters the abstract individual criticised by Dugin.

The contemporary paradox is that this same individual, having dissolved traditional forms of belonging, is now himself dissolved by the technical apparatuses of advanced modernity. The subject who claimed to depend on nothing becomes entirely dependent upon systems he does not control. His identity is reconstructed through streams of information, his behaviour anticipated by predictive models, his attention turned into a commodity, his decisions steered by algorithmic architectures. Even knowledge increasingly tends to be reduced to processing capacity, as though the power of computation could take the place of discernment.

We must not confuse this digitally fragmented individual with the anthropological dividual of Marriott and Strathern. The latter arises from a relational conception of personhood; the former may be the outcome of reducing a person to manipulable elements. The terminological resemblance therefore conceals a potential reversal of meaning. Where traditional relationships may constitute identity, algorithmic relationships may disarticulate it. Where the former situate the human being in a web of reciprocity and obligations, the latter risk converting him into a collection of information usable by external actors.

Modern man thus appears caught between two opposing movements. He is dismantled from below, through the quantitative fragmentation of his existence; yet he may be surpassed from above, through the recognition of principles that transcend individuality. But in the traditional sense, this second form of overcoming does not mean absorbing the person into a mass, a state or a collective machine. No political organisation, however powerful, thereby becomes a spiritual principle. This vertical overcoming concerns a different hierarchy of being, not the mere subordination of the individual to an earthly authority.

Daria Dugina’s reflections introduce an additional dimension here. In her presentation “The Sublime and the Aesthetics of the Great God Pan,” originally delivered at a seminar on Platonic aesthetics in 2020, Daria engages with Arthur Machen’s tale and the experience of the sublime. Beauty remains within a threshold that man can contemplate; the sublime crosses it, confronting him with something radically beyond the possibilities of ordinary perception. Drawing upon Rudolf Otto’s numinous, Daria shows that contact with the sacred can involve fascination and terror simultaneously, attraction and the collapse of familiar certainties.

In Machen’s story, a scientist uses a surgical procedure to artificially expand a young woman’s perception, giving her access to a reality she cannot master. Daria is not proposing a theory of contemporary transhumanism, but the connection is philosophically striking. Technology may open a threshold; it cannot guarantee that the human being possesses the spiritual capacity to cross it. An increase in faculties does not necessarily amount to an elevation of being. Power may be increased immeasurably without wisdom increasing by a single degree.

The technological singularity promises a way of surpassing the human through the intensification of operational capacities. Transhumanism presents itself as liberation from limitation, disease, frailty and, in its most radical versions, mortality itself. But what conception of man survives within that promise? If intelligence becomes merely the processing of information and consciousness a reproducible function, what is announced as a surpassing of the human might instead definitively erase the very dimension that makes man irreducible to a machine.

Guénon would have recognised in this claim an essentially qualitative problem. His distinction between the psychic and spiritual domains prevents us from identifying every expansion of possibilities with genuine transcendence. In his conception, counter-tradition does not merely deny the sacred outright: it may imitate it, invert its symbols and promise a false spiritual restoration. The “great parody” does not necessarily destroy the forms of tradition; it may preserve their appearance while emptying them of principle. The hypothesis that contemporary technology might produce such an imitation belongs to our interpretation of the present, not to a literal prediction made by Guénon. But the philosophical problem remains: will a civilisation increasingly capable of simulating thought, presence and even personality still know how to distinguish the reproduction of a function from the reality of being?

The answer concerns more than laboratories developing artificial intelligence. It reaches into the material structure of world power. Those who possess the most advanced semiconductors, computing capacity, cloud infrastructure, communication networks, information platforms and payment systems exercise an influence that goes beyond the ownership of economic assets. They establish the conditions under which other actors can know, produce, communicate and decide. Monetary, technological and informational sovereignty thus become a single strategic question: those who control the infrastructures indispensable to the exercise of autonomy can also constrain the formal freedom of those who depend on them.

It is no coincidence that on 3 June 2026 the European Commission presented a package dedicated to technological sovereignty, addressing semiconductors, artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure and open-source software. The Union’s own institutions now recognise that political autonomy depends upon the capacity to control strategic technologies, data and infrastructures. Yet the decisive question remains unanswered: technological sovereignty for which subject? For an integrated market, a regulatory apparatus, a federation of states, or a civilisation capable of recognising itself as such?

On 6 October, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the Union’s enlargement as a “geopolitical imperative.” On the same day, the NATO Military Committee, including representatives of all thirty-two Allied countries, travelled to Kyiv to discuss Ukraine’s military priorities and the transformations of contemporary warfare. These are distinct events, and they do not justify conflating legal membership of the Alliance, military cooperation and direct participation in a conflict. They do, however, demonstrate how deeply strategic competition has penetrated the definition of Europe’s future arrangements. The Union discusses enlargement, resilience, security and autonomy while its geopolitical position remains intertwined with the Atlantic architecture.

The war in Ukraine brings this contradiction into sharp relief. Dugin now explicitly interprets it as a civilizational war, a confrontation in which, he argues, not merely a territorial configuration but Russia’s very existence as an autonomous historical subject in relation to the Western order is at stake. This is his interpretation, not a universally accepted legal characterisation of the conflict. Nor does a civilisational dimension, even if recognised, erase the sovereignty of states, responsibility for military decisions or the rights of the populations involved. Rather, it reveals how inadequate it would be to confront a crisis of such depth through exclusively technical and diplomatic categories while ignoring the worldviews that guide its protagonists.

The crisis of unipolarity, moreover, is not confined to the Russian-Western confrontation. At the BRICS summit in New Delhi in September 2026, the participating states reaffirmed the demand for a more representative international order, grounded in sovereign equality, the reform of multilateral institutions and economic and financial cooperation. This is a real process, though not one without contradictions: participating countries frequently have divergent interests, strategic orientations and understandings of sovereignty. Membership in BRICS does not imply adherence to traditionalist philosophy. Yet the emergence of platforms alternative to Western centrality indicates growing limits to any monopoly over the political representation of the world.

Here a distinction is required, without which multipolarity risks becoming another version of the old politics of power. A world made up of several centres of force is not necessarily a world capable of recognising the plurality of civilisations. Geopolitical multipolarity can coexist with anthropological homogenisation, technological uniformity and the same subordination of all human activity to economic calculation. Rival states may struggle for control of infrastructures while sharing the same quantitative conception of man. In such a case, a change in the balance of power would by no means coincide with the overcoming of modernity.

Dugin’s thought invites reflection precisely upon this difference between a plurality of powers and a plurality of Logoi. Leonid Savin, in his reflections on ethnoi, peoples, nations and civilisations, offers further tools to prevent historically distinct categories from being reduced to a single abstract political subject. A civilization-state is not born of the mere addition of territory, population and military capacity. It presupposes historical and cultural continuity, a shared memory and a conception of existence capable of reaching beyond the horizon of administrations and economic cycles.

One question, however, cannot be avoided: what prevents a civilisation from transforming its own particularity into a new imperial universalism? To acknowledge a plurality of worlds is to accept that civilisations other than one’s own are subjects, rather than mere objects, of history. No power can consistently demand the right to its own singularity while denying that right in principle to others. Moreover, a civilisation cannot be identified without remainder with the state that claims to represent it, nor does the depth of a tradition automatically certify the legitimacy of every political decision.

For Europe, this reflection takes on particularly grave significance. European civilisation predates the institutions of the European Union by many centuries and cannot be identified with them. Its history includes Greece and Rome, Latin and Byzantine Christianity, scholastic philosophy and mysticism, national traditions, universities, empires, monarchies and free cities. It also includes the great religious ruptures, rationalism, the Enlightenment and the modernity that Dugin subjects to criticism. To reduce this complexity to a body of procedures, regulations and economic indicators is to confuse the present-day administration of a space with the civilisation that brought it into being.

At the same time, Europe cannot simply proclaim a return to Tradition as though the intervening centuries could be reversed. Historical continuity cannot be reconstructed by decree, nor can spiritual rebirth be achieved by outwardly replicating institutions of the past. Guénon sharply distinguished authentic Tradition from traditionalism understood as an ideological attitude. Nostalgia for forms, once the understanding of principles has been lost, can itself become another manifestation of the decline it claims to oppose.

Likewise, the idea of a Third Rome, so important in Russian historical and religious imagination, cannot be mechanically transposed onto the European question. Russia possesses its own Byzantine and Orthodox genealogy; Western Europe developed different relations among spiritual authority, temporal power and political community. The two histories have influenced and fought one another, and they share part of an inheritance, but they are not interchangeable. The possibility of a different relationship between Europe and Russia, beyond subordination and permanent hostility, would also depend upon recognising this distinction.

A genuinely sovereign Europe would therefore have to undertake a task more complex than acquiring industrial or military autonomy. It would have to ask anew about its identity, relations among its nations, its position between the Atlantic West and Eurasia, the meaning of freedom and the limits it intends to place upon technology and the market. A Europe understood as a civilisation could not emerge from the erasure of European peoples: it would lose precisely the historical plurality that is among the grounds of its existence. Nor could it be authentically independent merely by replacing one geopolitical dependency with another.

The horizon opened by the contemporary crisis thus calls for a distinction among at least three levels of sovereignty. The first is material: energy, currency, industry, technology, knowledge and defensive capability. The second is political: the ability to decide according to one’s own interests, without necessarily being carried along by the strategies of external powers. The third is civilisational: the ability to preserve and develop one’s own conception of man, community and historical destiny. Without the first, autonomy risks remaining rhetorical; without the second, it becomes the administration of decisions made by others; without the third, even a formally independent state may do no more than reproduce the anthropological model of the dominant civilisation.

This intertwining of material power and spiritual order brings us back to Guénon and the question of counter-initiation. In an essay written in 1997 and republished in 2026, Dugin acknowledges the metaphysical coherence of Guénon’s doctrine but emphasises the difficulties that arise when one tries to identify concrete historical agents of dissolution. The passage from symbol to organisation, from principle to person, from metaphysical structure to network of power demands rigorous discipline. It is an essential lesson for contemporary geopolitical inquiry as well. The existence of financial concentrations, technological dependencies, networks of influence and coordinated interests can and should be examined through verifiable documents, flows, institutions and decisions. There is no need to turn every convergence into a single hidden command centre, or to pretend that a metaphysical explanation alone constitutes historical proof.

Esotericism, taken seriously, is not a shortcut that excuses us from verification. It is an inquiry into levels of meaning that purely material observation cannot exhaust. Geopolitics, in turn, does not become more profound by attributing an invisible cause to every war; it becomes more profound when it understands that material interests, collective representations, symbols and conceptions of being all participate in shaping historical decisions. The philosophy of Tradition can illuminate this complexity, provided it is not reduced to a mythological apparatus designed to justify any political conclusion whatever.

Our age thus seems to present a dual possibility. On the one hand, the universalisation of the techno-economic model may continue even within a formally multipolar geopolitical order. We could witness the emergence of more empires, more monetary areas and more artificial-intelligence systems without any genuine anthropological diversity. It would be the multiplication of centres of power within a single civilisation of quantity. On the other hand, the crisis of hegemony could restore space to different conceptions of existence, to traditions capable of questioning anew the relationship between man and transcendence, and to political communities that do not regard the indefinite expansion of production and consumption as the ultimate purpose of history.

Neither possibility is guaranteed. The advent of multipolarity does not automatically entail spiritual rebirth; nor does the development of artificial intelligence, in itself, demonstrate the approach of an eschatological catastrophe. Traditional philosophy offers categories through which to interpret the meaning of a transformation, not an infallible calendar of events. Perhaps the greatest danger is to mistake for liberation what merely changes the form of dependency.

The image of the World Egg returns, then, to question us. In its germinal centrality it contains possibilities that must not be confused with the contingent forms of history. Authentic verticality does not consist in indefinitely enlarging modern man, in making him biologically longer-lived or technically omnipotent, but in recognising that his individuality does not exhaust being. Nor can the political task consist simply in building ever larger apparatuses unless we first clarify what conception of man they are meant to serve.

Perhaps the true frontier of the coming world will not pass only between West and East, Atlantic and Eurasian powers, established states and emerging poles. It will also run through every civilisation, every political order, every human being. On one side lies the reduction of existence to function, information and quantity; on the other, the possibility of recognising a qualitative order of being, a plurality of forms of belonging and a spiritual dimension that no machine can produce through the mere accumulation of power.

text:
Mr. Chairman of the DEM Party, Tuncer Bakirhan, with respect.
The psychological dimension is central: learned helplessness means that resistance, over generations, gets internalized as deadly  the power of the state starts to feel like a law of nature. 
The decision feels rational, but it’s rationalization. From the outside you see the trap; from the inside, only a considered choice. 
The Kurds know both. Still, they stay true to their conscience  that’s not weakness, it’s the most radical form of political dignity.
The Kurdish question is not a PKK question. It’s the question of the rights of millions: language, education, political participation, self-governance. 
Turkey is obligated under international law to guarantee these rights institutionally, not just rhetorically. 
A century of silence is not an accident  it’s the record of a state policy that defined Kurdish identity as a security problem instead of a political reality.
A peace process where only one side gives up its position is not a negotiation. It’s unilateral disarmament. 
The structural trap: language is the only thing Ankara can concede without losing power  a dictionary, a radio station, an elective course. 
Everything beyond that political participation, self governance, the question of who decides in Diyarbakır gets criminalized as separatism immediately. 

Whoever lays down weapons for a promise that turns out to be only cultural disarms permanently, without being emancipated.
What Ankara offers is not a solution but a surrender dressed up as peace: 
the Kurds should end the armed struggle, give up their weapons, and then exist under the Turkish umbrella  as a managed minority, not as an equal political subject. 
That’s not a peace offer. 

It’s a submission offer with a deadline.
And the method behind it is coercion. Many Kurds feel forced to submit to this arrangement because the alternative fate is annihilation. 
Either this path  or the end. Coercion only works as long as the affected side believes it has no alternative. 
The Kurds do have one. Not war. Endurance. And that, the Turkish state has never been able to break in forty years.

Turkey is obligated under international law to guarantee these rights institutionally, not just rhetorically. 
A century of silence is not an accident  it’s the record of a state policy that defined Kurdish identity as a security problem instead of a political reality.
A peace process where only one side gives up its position is not a negotiation. It’s unilateral disarmament. 
The structural trap: language is the only thing Ankara can concede without losing power  a dictionary, a radio station, an elective course. 
Everything beyond that political participation, self governance, the question of who decides in Diyarbakır gets criminalized as separatism immediately. 

Whoever lays down weapons for a promise that turns out to be only cultural disarms permanently, without being emancipated.
What Ankara offers is not a solution but a surrender dressed up as peace: 
the Kurds should end the armed struggle, give up their weapons, and then exist under the Turkish umbrella  as a managed minority, not as an equal political subject. 
That’s not a peace offer. 

It’s a submission offer with a deadline.
And the method behind it is coercion. Many Kurds feel forced to submit to this arrangement because the alternative fate is annihilation. 
Either this path  or the end. Coercion only works as long as the affected side believes it has no alternative. 
The Kurds do have one. Not war. Endurance. 
And that, the Turkish state has never been able to break in forty years.

Old story: Bruce King was 3 time governor of New Mexico. Rancher, conservative Dem, in the top 3 going all the way back to the 1500s. This guy knew Santa Fe like no one else ever did.

My dad was publisher of our town paper when Bruce was finishing his last term. Bruce agreed to be interviewed and my dad sat in. Bruce started off with his boilerplate stuff. My dad cut in with, "Bruce, why don't you tell us how to be a good governor."

Bruce blinked, and proceeded to tell about how in Dec. 1970, as he was about to start his first term, he went to see Dave Cargo, the departing (Rep) governor. He asked, "Who should I keep?"

Cargo told him about this guy who handled all the personnel matters. If some committee chair comes in and says he wants his nephew to have a job, this guy handles it, and handles getting rid of folks who are a problem.

Then Cargo mentioned a numbers guy. He knows every detail of the budget. If you need to save some money to put into something else, this guy knows where to get the money and how so it doesn't poison your relationship with this chairman.

Bruce said, when Jerry Apodaca was coming in in 1974, he offered to tell him what Cargo had told Bruce. But Jerry said he had his own guys for those jobs. And, Bruce said, Jerry was an ineffective governor despite having solid majorities in both houses.

Thing is, Bruce said, if you don't have effective people working for you, you spend all your time on little stuff, and you don't have time for the big things you want to make happen.

In Timbo's case, he had no St Paul experience, so he became wholly dependent on his top staffers, who were all lefties. And that's how the budget blew up, and Covid and the riots were handled so badly. Tim didn't know how and his aides had their own agenda.

text:
What actually changes when an AI agent evolves its own harness?

We’re sharing Harness RSI, the interactive research companion to our survey, From Harness Optimization to Recursive Self-Improvement: A Survey of Language Model Agents.

Our work connects three questions: How does harness improvement work? What actually evolves? When does the improvement process itself become recursive?
Our contributions:

🔍 Traceable evidence of what evolved. We assemble 95 category–source records from 62 research papers and one benchmark resource, covering 20 task subcategories across four domains. Each record connects starting capabilities, concrete modifications, reported outcomes and evidence limits.

🛠️ Concrete lessons for building better harnesses. We compare changes such as preserving multiline edit payloads, bounding tool outputs, repairing action–object mappings and adding failure-specific recovery. We examine when these changes help—and when more tools or context fail to improve results.

🔄 A clearer distinction between harness optimization and recursive improvement. We examine whether revised agents, improvement skills or search policies participate in producing subsequent revisions.
The public website offers interactive cross-domain comparisons, benchmark-level evidence and publication trends for our broader collection of 235 papers and manuscripts. We’ll continue adding verified studies and corrections through dated updates.
With Chengyuan Liu, Wenxin Long, Haochen Zhang and Lingzhou Xue at Penn State.

text:
In De Soto, Kansas—a small city with a population of fewer than 10,000—the developer Digital Realty is offering a $10,000 tax credit per household to secure local support for the construction of a massive data center. Some residents, however, remain skeptical.

According to a report by CBS, Andy Power, President and CEO of Digital Realty, stated on the 14th that the company is advancing critical infrastructure essential to the modern economy, adding, "We believe we have a responsibility to support the communities that make such economic growth possible."

Digital Realty plans to invest $20 million in De Soto to construct roads for a 280-acre data center site. The project is expected to eventually expand to 1,400 acres, generating tax revenue and creating jobs for the local area. Construction is slated to begin in 2027.

To garner community backing, Digital Realty is working with the De Soto city government to offer each household a $1,000 annual credit—applied toward utility costs and property taxes—for a period of 10 years.

Headquartered in Austin, Texas, Digital Realty is a publicly traded company with a market capitalization exceeding $67 billion. Its client roster includes major firms such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft, and Nvidia. The De Soto data center project is projected to create 250 full-time positions for local vendors and contractors, with thousands of additional construction jobs expected over time.

However, a recent CBS poll indicates that more De Soto residents oppose the data center project than support it. Concerns among opponents include potential environmental damage, the depletion of local resources, and the possibility of rising utility costs.

Resident Sara VanDeCreek noted that the $1,000 annual tax credit could be quite helpful for many households in De Soto. However, resident Christina Hileman remarked, "My first thought is that this amount of money isn't enough to entice anyone to move here." She noted that property taxes in De Soto are quite high; while the tax credits might help, their impact would be minimal.

Another resident, Doug Geist, suggested that the city should hold a public referendum on the data center project, using the outcome to guide the final decision.

We sourced the gas, sized the generators, picked the miners and ran the sites day to day.

President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14296 on May 9, 2025, directing federal agencies to redirect funds that may have been spent on housing or services for undocumented immigrants toward the construction of a new National Center for Warrior Independence for homeless veterans in Los Angeles.

The order designates the Department of Veterans Affairs’ West Los Angeles campus, a 388-acre site originally donated more than a century ago by Senator John Percival Jones and Arcadia Bandini de Stearns Baker on the condition it house disabled veterans, as the location for the new center. Trump directed VA Secretary Doug Collins to produce an action plan within 120 days to restore capacity to house up to 6,000 homeless veterans at the site by January 1, 2028. The order also instructed the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development to work with Collins on a voucher program to support homeless veterans both in Los Angeles and nationwide.

The order itself states that “too many veterans are homeless in America,” adding that “each veteran deserves our gratitude” but that “the Federal Government has not always treated veterans like the heroes they are.” As of 2024, Los Angeles had approximately 3,000 homeless veterans, more than any other city in the country and about 10 percent of the national total. Collins said in a statement that the order “builds on the progress we’ve made so far and puts us on a path to fixing some of the department’s most vexing problems,” and described the goal as creating a place for veterans nationwide to “find housing and support and start their journey back to self-sufficiency.”

The move lands amid an ongoing legal fight over the same campus. A federal judge, David O. Carter, had already ruled the VA failed in its duty to house veterans there and invalidated leases held by private tenants including UCLA, a decision the VA has appealed. The Veterans Collective, which holds a contract to build roughly 1,200 housing units on the campus, said it “enthusiastically applauds President Trump’s plan for a national center for homeless veterans,” according to the Los Angeles Times. The order does not identify a specific funding pool or dollar figure tied to immigrant housing, and the VA has not detailed how the new center’s programs would differ from services already offered.

text:
Me: Law firms that handle these kinds of incidents

Ai: Several U.S. law firms specialize in the types of incidents discussed earlier—online defamation, cyberstalking/harassment, social media disputes, intentional infliction of emotional distress claims, content removal, and related digital reputation or privacy matters. These are typically plaintiff-side (for people targeted by the conduct), though some also handle defense work involving First Amendment or anti-SLAPP issues.

Frequently mentioned specialists (U.S.)
•  Minc Law (based in Cleveland, Ohio; national practice): One of the most focused firms in the country, with an exclusive emphasis on internet defamation, online harassment, cyberbullying, content removal, and digital reputation protection. It is Chambers-ranked in First Amendment Litigation (mainly plaintiff) and reports handling hundreds of cases across many states, along with extensive content-removal work. The firm offers free case evaluations.
•  C.A. Goldberg, PLLC (Brooklyn, New York): A victims’-rights firm focused on technology-facilitated abuse, including online stalking/harassment, image-based sexual abuse (“revenge porn”), sextortion, doxxing, and related claims. It also litigates against platforms in some cases and handles orders of protection. Founder Carrie Goldberg is known for this work.
•  Cyber Law Firm (national practice with attorneys licensed in multiple states): Handles online harassment, cyberstalking, doxxing, internet defamation, digital extortion, and related technology-facilitated harms. Client reviews describe experience with these matters; verify current licensing and fit for your jurisdiction.
Other firms that regularly appear in discussions of internet/social-media defamation or reputation work include Kronenberger Rosenfeld, RM Warner Law, Clare Locke LLP (high-stakes defamation, more traditional media-oriented), and various boutique or mid-size practices with internet-law groups. Larger media or First Amendment practices (sometimes ranked by Chambers) more often handle defense-side or high-profile media cases.

Outside the U.S. (examples)
In the UK, firms such as Brett Wilson and Cohen Davis (often associated with harassmentlawyer. co. uk or similar) specialize in online harassment, defamation, and related claims under UK law (including the Protection from Harassment Act). Other countries have their own media, privacy, or digital-rights specialists.

Practical notes
•  Jurisdiction and licensing matter. Many of these firms practice nationally (or internationally with local counsel) but must be properly admitted or work with local counsel. Confirm the firm’s experience with cases in your state or country and the applicable statutes of limitations.
•  What they typically do. Demand letters, content-removal efforts, identifying anonymous posters (via John Doe suits and subpoenas), civil lawsuits for damages, requests for injunctions or protective orders, and coordination with law enforcement when criminal elements are present.
•  How to find and evaluate more options. Use state bar lawyer-referral services, directories such as Super Lawyers, Best Lawyers, Martindale-Hubbell, or Avvo, and search for “internet defamation attorney,” “online harassment lawyer,” or “cyberstalking attorney” plus your location. Look for firms that list these as core practice areas rather than occasional work, check peer rankings, and review recent client feedback where available.
•  Many offer free or low-cost initial consultations. Have your evidence package (archives, screenshots with URLs/timestamps, chronological log, etc.) ready.

- Thursday's volume: about 14.5M shares, roughly 1.6 times its two-week average.

The quoted post ended on Copart's balance sheet: no debt, about $4.5B of cash and investments, and a business that "can afford to wait." The deadline it named has passed. Copart's cash offer to buy ACV Auctions shares directly from their owners expired at 5pm ET Thursday. When the deal closes, about $1.9B of that $4.5B goes out the door, leaving roughly $2.6B (arithmetic).

The verdict: Thursday's jump said nothing new about the business. Copart can still afford to wait, but on a cushion about two-fifths smaller than the one the quoted post counted, and the past year shows where the rest went. From here the case rests on the business, starting with the November count of cars insurers send it.

No outlet of record named a cause for Thursday's gain, and Copart announced nothing. The antitrust news came out Wednesday morning; Copart set its one-year low hours later. Two comparisons:

- Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP) at $215.00, +$2.91 / +1.37% on Thursday.
- RB Global (RBA) at $87.13, -$0.69 / -0.79% on Thursday.

The fund is a basket of 500 large US stocks, so no Len5 applies. RB Global owns IAA, Copart's main rival in auctioning insurers' wrecked cars, and it fell. Part of Copart's day was a good day for ordinary stocks; the rest was its own, not its industry's. That is a reading of the prices, not a reported cause. RB Global sits on none of the six Len5 watchlists: at about 38 times its past year's profit, the value-minded Len5es see no discount.

Where the ACV deal stands, by Copart's own statements:

- October 7: 52.84% of ACV's shares handed in, past the more-than-half the offer needs, from 47.78% on September 30.
- October 13, 11:59pm ET: the federal antitrust review window, when regulators can challenge a deal, ended.
- October 15, 5pm ET: the offer expired. No final count by this evening.

ACV Auctions (ACVA) at $10.50, +$0.00 / +0.00% on Thursday, a one-year high and exactly the offer price. Buyers see little chance the deal falls apart. The dealer-to-dealer used-car marketplace sits on no Len5 watchlist; its price tracks the offer.

Now where the cash went. In the year to July 31 (arithmetic):

- Cash and investments: about $4.79B at the start, $4.49B at the end.
- Free cash flow, the cash left after running the yards and buying land and equipment: $1.27B.
- Buybacks, Copart purchasing its own stock: 43.4M shares at an average $37.63, $1.63B in all.

About $1.41B of that came in February through April. None came in May through July, as the price kept falling (arithmetic). Thursday's close is 26% under the average Copart paid, so those shares are worth about $429M less than it spent (arithmetic). Companies negotiating a deal often pause buybacks, so the pause alone is no verdict on the price.

The second check: ACV, about $1.9B, 45% above its price on August 10, a month before the deal was announced. That is about 1.5 times Copart's yearly free cash flow and about 7% of its own stock market value (arithmetic). What it buys, in the April-June quarter: $213.9M of revenue and an $8.2M loss. ACV also owed $205M on a credit line at June 30, against $242M of cash, so "no debt" becomes a little debt unless Copart repays it. Copart's case: ACV opens a path into dealer-to-dealer sales, should leave profit per share flat in the first full year, then add to it from fiscal 2028.

That is the fair argument about Copart now. Not whether the cushion exists, but whether $3.5B in about a year, its own shares at $37.63 and ACV at a 45% premium, was the best use of it.

Copart is now first of 199 on the Deep-Value & Special-Situations Len5, up from second at the quoted post. That Len5 hunts a sound business priced below a cautious value. The sound half holds: $1.27B of free cash flow and no debt of its own. The price half thinned a little Thursday: about 18 times its fiscal 2026 profit of $1.55 a share, from about 17 at the quoted post (arithmetic). The soft spot is that profit, down from $1.59 the year before, with ACV adding nothing to it for a year. It also sits 10th of 76 on the Quality-Value Len5, which wants a durable business at a fair price: 250-plus yards in 11 countries are the durable half, and its price is mid-pack among those names. And it fits the Quality Len5: after the direct costs of its yards and the cars it sells for itself, it kept about 45 cents of each revenue dollar, earned about 16% on its owners' $9.1B stake, and carries no debt (arithmetic); debt climbing past that stake would knock it off the Quality Len5, and ACV's credit line is nowhere near it. What would knock Copart off the Deep-Value & Special-Situations and Quality-Value Len5es: U.S. insurers sending fewer cars again in the November report even with the lost customer set aside, with no ACV profit to cover the gap. Last quarter, without that customer, they sent 2.3% more.

What comes next:

- Any day: Copart's announcement of the final ACV count and the closing.
- Thursday, November 19, after the close, tentatively, not yet confirmed by Copart: results for August through October, with only a sliver of ACV in them.

The key risk: insurers keep sending fewer cars while part of the cushion sits in a business still losing money.

Copart has turned $3.5B of its cushion into two bets in about a year. November 19 is the first report where the insurers, not the cash, have to carry the case.

He was a Mankato West High School student and football player (RB/SS) who had just finished his junior year and was looking forward to his senior year. He worked at a Papa Murphy’s and was described by his mother, Carissa Weber, as a fitness-focused, driven teen who loved football, planned to graduate, and had talked about becoming an electrician or leaving town to be independent. He had younger siblings.

The problem was that he was selling THC vapes and weed, and that made him the target of a robbery. 

Abdikhadar Fakhi Mohidin , Ahmed Fuad Mohamud , and Ahmed Mohamed Mohamud conspired to set up a fake buy from Goodsell so they could rob him. It went wrong and Goodsell wound up shot.

- Abdikhadar Fakhi Mohidin (20, St. Peter) - Charged with second-degree murder (later amended in connection with intentional murder while committing a felony), attempted first-degree aggravated robbery, conspiracy, illegal firearm/ammunition possession, and assault charges. He was on conditional release related to a December 31, 2024, incident in which he was accused of shooting a woman sleeping in her car. High bail was reported. He was the one who shot Goodsell.

-  Ahmed Fuad Mohamud , and Ahmed Mohamed Mohamud participated in the attempted robbery.

- Ryan Robert Wolner (18, rural Mankato) is alleged to have orchestrated the plan. He asked people for “plugs” (slang for drug dealers) to rob, specifically targeted Goodsell, and sought a rifle. - Jaxon Richard Sageng (18, Mankato) allegedly contacted Goodsell, arranged the cannabis purchase, and lent Wolner his silver 2010 Chevrolet Impala and cellphone so the meeting would appear legitimate.

- Devon Bruce Bakke (18, St. Peter) allegedly stored Wolner’s AR-style rifle, magazines, and ammunition in a duffle bag at his home for about two months. Wolner retrieved it that night, saying he needed it for the robbery.

- Christa Marie Wolner (53, Ryan’s mother): Charged with aiding an offender by obstructing the investigation and harboring/concealing (picking up her son, searching for discarded phones, paying for a hotel for codefendants, moving evidence including a gold-colored auto-sear switch described in coded language as a “Pokémon card,” deleting business security footage, allowing use of her phone, and lying to police).

Clearly Abdikhadar Fakhi Mohidin is a threat to society and should face the harshest punishment possible, but what about the rest.

THE PEACE GAMBIT THAT FAILED: IZADI TELLS NAWFAL THE REAL REASON WHY IRAN KEPT OIL FLOWING  

Professor Foad Izadi from Teheran, speaking with host Mario Nawfal, confirms the real reason Iran allowed ships to keep moving through the Strait of Hormuz. The decision was never a loss of capability. It was a deliberate calculation aimed at one outcome.  

THE PEACE CHANCE  
➡️ Iran was trying to give peace a chance.  
By not striking too many ships and letting oil keep flowing, Tehran hoped Trump would see oil prices stay manageable and finally reach an agreement.  
“They were hoping that by not hitting too many ships, by letting oil down, they would help Trump to maintain oil prices at a level that it could basically reach an agreement with Iran.”  
The strategy was simple: keep the market from exploding so a deal became possible before the midterms.  

THE MIXED CARGO REALITY  
➡️ Some of the oil that left was Iranian oil.  
It traveled mixed with UAE, Kuwaiti, and Iraqi barrels under a UAE-led operation backed by American military support.  
Smaller tankers carried Iranian crude through the strait, then transferred it ship-to-ship onto larger vessels.  
“In the middle of UAE oil, Kuwaiti oil, Iraqi oil, you had some Iranian oil. That’s why Iran was letting it drop.”  
Americans correctly claimed oil was getting out. They simply left out that part of it belonged to Iran.  

THE FAILED CALCULATION  
➡️ Iranian leaders ran a clear cost-benefit analysis.  
They judged that forcing the United States to end its reckless policy and declare victory, or return to a real agreement, would be a better outcome than waiting indefinitely.  
“That strategy failed. Trump was not interested in an agreement.”  
The window stayed open. The other side never walked through it.  

THE BOTTOM LINE  
Iran deliberately kept ships moving through Hormuz, including some of its own oil, to give diplomacy one last chance and push Trump toward a deal he could claim as a win. The calculation collapsed because Washington had no interest in any agreement that required restraint. The quiet oil flow was never weakness. It was the last peaceful offer on the table.

Rep. Ilhan Omar could face prison time and lose her U.S. citizenship and House seat if federal investigators uncover criminal wrongdoing, legal experts warn, Washington Times reports. Federal agents on Monday raided her home in the District of Columbia, seizing her cellphone, laptop computer, notebooks and passport. No criminal charges have been filed.

The probe reportedly centers on how Omar obtained citizenship, including her date of birth listed on her father’s 2000 naturalization paperwork, as well as allegations of a sham marriage and falsified congressional financial disclosures. Omar has denied wrongdoing, saying she is the victim of “baseless lies and smear campaigns” by President Trump, who said he was not involved in ordering the raid.

Federal agents have issued over a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including relatives, a source said. Matt O’Brien, a former immigration judge, said the case appears to be both a criminal investigation and a civil denaturalization inquiry. Prosecutor Jeanine Pirro said several probes are underway.

text:
Montana doesn’t need another candidate selling a resume instead of answering hard questions.

Seth Bodnar says he will answer only to Montanans. Fine. Then explain what happens when residents oppose a data center and developers still want to build it.

His “Protect Montana” pledge says communities should have the final say, ratepayers shouldn’t absorb the costs, and Montana workers should handle construction. Meanwhile, residents around Broadview and Butte have organized against proposed projects. A promise of local control needs an answer: Who gets to say no, through what process, and what makes that decision binding?

Bodnar is proposing to manage development, not halt it. His pledge also calls for companies to support workers displaced by AI. Before politicians negotiate assistance for people losing their livelihoods, they should explain what they will do to protect those livelihoods in the first place.

His immigration platform leaves another gap. Asked to identify specific policies, Bodnar offered strong borders, due process, and comprehensive reform that works for Montana’s farms, ranches, and hospitals. His published answer did not address H-1B visas or Gianforte’s India recruitment push. Does he support expanding employer-sponsored recruitment overseas? What protections would he demand for Montana workers? Voters should not have to guess.

Then there is the independent branding. Shannon O’Brien resigned as Montana Democratic Party chair to endorse him. Bodnar welcomed her support while promising to answer only to voters. An endorsement does not prove control, but establishment backing deserves scrutiny regardless of the letter beside a candidate’s name.

An independent label isn’t a record of independence. A pledge isn’t an enforceable protection. Bodnar needs to explain what he would prohibit, whose interests he would confront, and whether a community’s no actually means no.

Sources
Jonathon Ambarian, KTVH. “Montana U.S. Senate Candidates Discuss How to Manage Data Centers, AI.” September 1, 2026. Documents the pledge, displaced-worker provision, and opposition in Broadview and Butte.

Zeke Lloyd, Montana Free Press. “Montana Candidates on the Issues: Immigration.” October 14, 2026. Publishes Bodnar’s immigration answer in full.

Montana Public Radio. “Montana Democratic Party Chair Resigns to Back Independent in the U.S. Senate Race.” October 14, 2026. Documents O’Brien’s resignation and reasons for supporting Bodnar.

Washington Examiner. “Montana Democratic Party Chairwoman Quits, Backs Independent in Senate Race.” October 12, 2026. Quotes Bodnar welcoming the endorsement and promising to answer only to Montanans.

text:
#PrinceOnThisDay
 
The Arms of Orion (edit) b/w I Love U In Me by Prince with Sheena Easton (Warner Bros. 7-22757, US release 16 October 1989) is a classic late-’80s Prince single that pairs a lush, cinematic ballad with a more intimate, sexually direct B-side. It was the third single from the Batman soundtrack, following the dance-oriented “Batdance” and “Partyman,” and it continued the commercial tie-in with Tim Burton’s film. 

The A-side is a slow, romantic orchestral-pop ballad credited to Prince with Sheena Easton (lyrics by Easton, music and production by Prince). Recorded on 25 January 1989 at Paisley Park, it is built around piano, synthesizer strings, a subdued LinnDrum groove, and atmospheric rain/thunder samples. The lyrics use the constellation Orion as a metaphor for lovers separated by distance yet held together by celestial scale: “Orion’s arms are wide enough to hold us both together / Although we’re worlds apart.” On the album it is framed as a song for Bruce Wayne and Vicki Vale. The 7-inch edit runs about 3:52 (album version 5:03). 

Contemporary reviews were mixed-to-skeptical. Music Week called it a “decidedly MOR ballad” that sounded like Lionel Richie and Whitney Houston—commercially viable but “sub-standard floss.” Smash Hits dismissed the “corniest words ever about love and the stars.” Music & Media noted it was probably the most commercial track on the Batman album. In hindsight it divides fans: some hear a tender, beautifully arranged duet with genuine emotional weight and Easton’s complementary vocals; others find it overly saccharine or out of step with Prince’s funkier material. It peaked at No. 36 on the Billboard Hot 100 (and No. 33 Cash Box), No. 21 Adult Contemporary, and No. 27 in the UK—solid but not a smash. 

The B-side, “I Love U In Me,” is a previously unreleased Prince solo track (basic tracking summer/autumn 1989 at Paisley Park, ~4:12). A quiet-storm ballad with frank, sexually explicit lyrics rather than the usual metaphors, it opens with a stormy intimate scene (“She took off her dress, and I took a peek / While thunder storm played hide and seek”) and reaches the memorable (and debated) line “When she makin’ love, it’s like surgery.” It celebrates a confident, unapologetic lover and the narrator’s vulnerability. Prince liked it enough to reuse it as the B-side of 1991’s “Insatiable”; it later appeared on The Hits / The B-Sides and received an acoustic revisiting with Andy Allo. Fans often prefer it to the A-side for its directness and sensual atmosphere. 

The US 7-inch (catalog 7-22757) features the A-side edit and the non-album B-side; cover art follows the Batman single series with a variation on the yellow-and-black bat logo. Packaging and promotion kept the movie connection alive months after the June album release. Note that some Discogs/45cat listings give slight runtime variations (e.g., 3:40 for the edit), but standard references list 3:52 / 4:12. 

Overall, this is an enjoyable, characteristically Prince single: the A-side offers polished, starry-eyed romance that fits the Batman mood (if not every fan’s idea of peak Prince), while the B-side delivers the more personal, body-focused intimacy that was his specialty. It is not among his most essential releases, but it is a well-crafted 1989 artifact with lasting appeal for collectors and anyone who likes his ballad side. The commercial performance and dual-track approach (glossy duet + exclusive B-side) made it a typical late-decade Warner single from the artist.
